t2087_text: 王城西北二百餘里至大雪山。山頂有池，請雨祈晴，隨求果願。聞諸先志曰：昔健馱邏國有阿羅漢，常受此池龍王供養。每至中食，以神通力，并坐繩床，凌虛而往。侍者沙彌密於繩床之下，攀援潛隱，而阿羅漢時至便往，至龍宮乃見沙彌，龍王因請留食。龍王以天甘露飯阿羅漢，以人間味而饌沙彌。阿羅漢飯食已訖，便為龍王說諸法要。沙彌如常為師滌器，器有餘粒，駭其香味，即起惡願，恨師忿龍：「願諸福力，於今悉現，斷此龍命，我自為王。」沙彌發是願時，龍王已覺頭痛矣。羅漢說法誨喻，龍王謝咎責躬；沙彌懷忿，未從誨謝。既還伽藍，至誠發願，福力所致，是夜命終，為大龍王，威猛奮發，遂來入池，殺龍王，居龍宮，有其部屬，總其統命。以宿願故，興暴風雨，摧拔樹木，欲壞伽藍。時迦膩色迦王怪而發問，其阿羅漢具以白王。王即為龍於雪山下立僧伽藍，建窣堵波，高百餘尺。龍懷宿忿，遂發風雨。王以弘濟為心，龍乘瞋毒作暴，僧伽藍、窣堵波六壞七成。迦膩色迦王恥功不成，欲填龍池，毀其居室，即興兵眾，至雪山下。時彼龍王深懷震懼，變作老婆羅門，叩王象而諫曰：「大王宿殖善本，多種勝因，得為人王，無思不服。今日何故與龍交爭？夫龍者，畜也，卑下惡類，然有大威，不可力競。乘雲馭風，蹈虛履水，非人力所制，豈王心所怒哉？王今舉國興兵，與一龍鬪，勝則王無伏遠之威，敗則王有非敵之恥。為王計者，宜可歸兵。」迦膩色迦王未之從也。龍即還池，聲震雷動，暴風拔木，沙石如雨，雲霧晦冥，軍馬驚駭。王乃歸命三寶，請求加護，曰：「宿殖多福，得為人王，威懾強敵，統贍部洲，今為龍畜所屈，誠乃我之薄福也。願諸福力，於今現前。」即於兩肩起大煙焰，龍退風靜，霧卷雲開。王令軍眾人擔一石，用填龍池。龍王還作婆羅門，重請王曰：「我是彼池龍王，懼威歸命，唯王悲愍，赦其前過。王以含育，覆燾生靈，如何於我獨加惡害？王若殺我，我之與王，俱墮惡道，王有斷命之罪，我懷怨讎之心，業報皎然，善惡明矣。」王遂與龍明設要契，後更有犯，必不相赦。龍曰：「我以惡業，受身為龍，龍性猛惡，不能自持，瞋心或起，當忘所制。王今更立伽藍，不敢摧毀。每遣一人候望山嶺，黑雲若起，急擊揵槌，我聞其聲，惡心當息。」其王於是更修伽藍，建窣堵波，候望雲氣，於今不絕。聞諸先志曰：窣堵波中有如來骨肉舍利，可一升餘，神變之事，難以詳述。一時中窣堵波內忽有煙起，少間便出猛焰，時人謂窣堵波已從火燼，瞻仰良久，火滅煙消，乃見舍利如白珠幡，循環表柱，宛轉而上，升高雲際，縈旋而下。
translation: Two hundred and more *li* northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Great Snowy Mountain (Mahāhimavat). On the summit of the mountain is a pool; those who pray for rain or for clear weather have their wishes fulfilled according to their requests. According to ancient records, there was formerly an arhat in the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) who regularly received offerings from the nāga king of this pool. Every day at the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to sit upon his rope bed and travel through the void. His attendant, a novice (śrāmaṇera), secretly clung to the underside of the rope bed and hid himself. When the time for the meal arrived, the arhat departed; upon reaching the nāga palace, he discovered the novice. The nāga king then invited them both to stay for the meal. The nāga king served the arhat with heavenly nectar, while he served the novice with human food. Once the arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the nāga king. The novice, as was his custom, washed the bowls for his master. Finding leftover grains in the bowl and being astonished by their fragrance, he immediately gave rise to an evil vow, resenting his master and feeling anger toward the nāga: "May all the power of my merit manifest now, that I may cut off this nāga’s life and become the king myself." At the moment the novice made this vow, the nāga king already felt a headache. The arhat spoke words of instruction and exhortation, and the nāga king apologized for his faults and blamed himself; however, the novice remained resentful and did not follow the instruction to forgive. Once they had returned to the monastery (saṃghārāma), the novice made a vow with utmost sincerity. Due to the power of his merit, he died that very night and was reborn as a great nāga king. Fierce and impetuous, he came to enter the pool, killed the former nāga king, occupied the nāga palace, took possession of his retinue, and assumed command over them. Because of his former vow, he stirred up violent storms and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery. At that time, King Kaniṣka, feeling puzzled, inquired about the matter, and the arhat explained everything to the king. The king then established a monastery (saṃghārāma) for the nāga at the foot of the Snow Mountains and erected a stupa (stūpa) over one hundred feet high. The nāga, harboring his former resentment, proceeded to stir up wind and rain. The king was intent on universal salvation, while the nāga, fueled by the poison of his anger, committed acts of violence, causing the monastery and the stupa to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times. King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his work was not being completed, wished to fill in the nāga’s pool and destroy his dwelling; he immediately mobilized his troops and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains. At that time, the nāga king, feeling deep fear, transformed himself into an old brahmin, knocked on the king’s elephant, and remonstrated, saying: "Great King, you have cultivated good roots in the past and planted many superior causes, which has enabled you to become a human king to whom all submit. Why, then, do you contend with a nāga today? A nāga is merely an animal, a base and vile species, yet he possesses great power and cannot be contested by force. Riding the clouds and driving the wind, treading on the void and walking on water—these are things not controlled by human power; how could they be objects of the king’s wrath? If the king now mobilizes the entire nation to fight against a single nāga, then if you win, the king will gain no prestige for subduing a distant foe, and if you lose, the king will suffer the shame of being defeated by an unworthy opponent. For the sake of the king’s own interests, it would be best to withdraw the troops." King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice. The nāga then returned to the pool, and with a sound like rolling thunder, violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, clouds and fog obscured the light, and the army’s horses were terrified. The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and prayed for protection, saying, "By virtue of the many blessings I cultivated in past lives, I became a king of men, deterring powerful enemies and ruling over Jambudvīpa; that I am now humiliated by this dragon beast is truly due to my meager merit. May all the power of my merit manifest at this moment." Immediately, great smoke and flames arose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind grew still, and the clouds and fog rolled away. The king ordered his army to each carry one stone to fill the dragon pool. The dragon king transformed back into a Brahmin and entreated the king again, saying, "I am the dragon king of that pool; fearing your majesty, I submit to you. May the king have compassion and forgive my past offenses. The king nurtures and protects all living beings; why would you inflict harm upon me alone? If you kill me, both you and I will fall into the evil realms; you will be guilty of taking a life, and I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity—karmic retribution is clear, and good and evil are manifest." The king then made a clear covenant with the dragon, stating that if there were any further offenses, he would certainly not forgive them. The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received a body as a dragon. The nature of a dragon is fierce and evil, and I cannot control myself; if a heart of anger arises, I may forget what has been stipulated. Now that the king is establishing a monastery (saṃghārāma), I dare not destroy it. I will send one person to keep watch on the mountain ridge; if black clouds arise, they must strike the ghaṇṭā (gong) urgently. When I hear that sound, my evil heart will cease." The king thereupon renovated the monastery and built a stūpa, and the practice of watching for clouds continues to this day without interruption. According to the records of predecessors, there is more than one *sheng* of the Tathāgata’s bone and flesh relics inside the stūpa, and the miraculous events associated with them are difficult to describe in detail. Once, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, followed shortly by fierce flames. The people of the time thought the stūpa had been reduced to ashes, but after gazing at it for a long while, the fire died down and the smoke vanished. Then, the relics were seen like a banner of white pearls, circling the central pillar and winding upwards to the edge of the clouds before whirling back down.

t2087_text: 王城西北大河南岸舊王伽藍內，有釋迦菩薩弱齡齠齓，長餘一寸。其伽藍東南有一伽藍，亦名舊王，有如來頂骨一片，面廣寸餘，其色黃白，髮孔分明。又有如來髮，髮色青紺，螺旋右縈，引長尺餘，卷可半寸。凡此三事，每至六齋，王及大臣散花供養。頂骨伽藍西南有舊王妃伽藍，中有金銅窣堵波，高百餘尺。聞諸土俗曰：其窣堵波中有佛舍利升餘，每月十五日，其夜便放圓光，燭燿露盤，聯暉達曙，其光漸斂，入窣堵波。
translation: Inside the Old Royal Monastery (Jiuwang Jialan) on the south bank of the great river to the northwest of the royal city, there is a tooth of the Bodhisattva Śākya from his childhood, over an inch long. To the southeast of this monastery is another monastery, also named Old Royal, which possesses a piece of the Tathāgata’s skull bone over an inch wide; its color is yellowish-white, and the hair pores are distinct. There is also hair of the Tathāgata, the color of which is dark blue, spiraling to the right, drawn out to over a foot in length, and curled to about half an inch. Regarding these three items, whenever the six fast days arrive, the king and his ministers scatter flowers in offering. To the southwest of the Skull Bone Monastery is the Old Queen’s Monastery (Jiuwangfei Jialan), in which there is a gold and copper stūpa over a hundred feet high. According to local tradition, there is more than a *sheng* of the Buddha’s relics inside this stūpa. On the night of the fifteenth day of every month, it emits a circular light that illuminates the dew basin, shining continuously until dawn, at which point the light gradually withdraws into the stūpa.

t2087_text: 城西南有比羅娑洛山（唐言象堅）。山神作象形，故曰象堅也。昔如來在世，象堅神奉請世尊及千二百大阿羅漢，山巔有大盤石，如來即之，受神供養。其後無憂王即盤石上起窣堵波，高百餘尺，今人謂之象堅窣堵波也。亦云中有如來舍利，可一升餘。象堅窣堵波北山巖下有一龍泉，是如來受神飯已，及阿羅漢於中漱口嚼楊枝，因即種根，今為茂林。後人於此建立伽藍，名鞞鐸佉（唐言嚼楊枝）。自此東行六百餘里，山谷接連，峯巖峭峻，越黑嶺，入北印度境，至濫波國（北印度境）。
translation: To the southwest of the city is the mountain of Pīlusāra (比羅娑洛山; Tang language: "Elephant-Strong" [象堅]). The mountain deity takes the form of an elephant, hence it is called "Elephant-Strong." Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, the Elephant-Strong deity invited the World-Honored One and twelve hundred great arhats. On the mountain peak there is a large flat rock; the Tathāgata sat upon it and accepted the deity's offerings. Afterward, King Aśoka (無憂王) built a stūpa on the flat rock, over one hundred feet high, which people today call the Elephant-Strong Stūpa. It is also said that it contains more than a sheng of the Tathāgata's relics. Below the mountain cliff to the north of the Elephant-Strong Stūpa is a nāga spring; this is where the Tathāgata, after receiving the deity's meal, and the arhats rinsed their mouths and chewed willow twigs, which then took root and became the dense grove that exists today. Later people established a saṃghārāma here, named Biduoqie (鞞鐸佉; Tang language: "Chewing Willow Twigs"). Traveling east from here for over six hundred li, through continuous mountains and valleys with steep peaks and precipitous cliffs, one crosses the Black Range (黑嶺), enters the territory of North India, and reaches the country of Lampā (濫波國) (territory of North India).

t2087_text: 若其封疆之域，可得而言。五印度之境，周九萬餘里。三垂大海，北背雪山。北廣南狹，形如半月，畫野區分，七十餘國。時特暑熱，地多泉濕。北乃山阜隱軫，丘陵舃鹵；東則川野沃潤，疇壠膏腴；南方草木榮茂；西方土地磽确。斯大概也，可略言焉。
translation: As for the boundaries of its territory, they may be described. The realm of the Five Indias (五印度) measures more than 90,000 li in circumference. On three sides it borders the great sea, and in the north it rests against the Snow Mountains (Himālaya). It is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon, with the land divided into more than seventy countries. The climate is exceptionally hot, and the ground is often damp with springs. To the north, mountains and ridges rise in succession, and the hills are of saline-alkaline soil; to the east, the plains are fertile and moist, and the cultivated fields are rich and productive; in the south, the vegetation is lush and flourishing; and in the west, the land is stony and barren. This is the general situation, which can be briefly stated.

t2087_text: 濫波國，周千餘里，北背雪山，三垂黑嶺。國大都城周十餘里。自數百年，王族絕嗣，豪傑力競，無大君長，近始附屬迦畢試國。宜粳稻，多甘蔗，林樹雖眾，果實乃少。氣序漸溫，微霜無雪。國俗豐樂，人尚歌詠，志性怯弱，情懷詭詐，更相欺誚，未有推先。體貌卑小，動止輕躁。多衣白㲲，所服鮮飾。伽藍十餘所，僧徒寡少，並多習學大乘法教。天祠數十，異道甚多。
translation: The country of Lampāka (濫波國) is over a thousand *li* in circuit. To the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on the other three sides, it borders the Black Range (黑嶺). The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circuit. For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct, and powerful men have contended for strength, leaving the country without a great sovereign; only recently has it become a dependency of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much sugarcane; although trees are numerous, they yield little fruit. The climate is gradually becoming warmer, with light frost but no snow. The customs of the country are prosperous and joyful, and the people are fond of singing and chanting; however, their dispositions are timid and weak, their hearts are deceitful, and they engage in mutual deception and mockery, lacking any sense of deference. Their physical stature is small, and their movements are restless. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and their attire is bright and decorative. There are more than ten monasteries with few monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahayana. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.

t2087_text: 從此東南行百餘里，踰大嶺，濟大河，至那揭羅曷國（北印度境）。那揭羅曷國，東西六百餘里，南北二百五六十里。山周四境，懸隔危險。國大都城周二十餘里。無大君長，主令役屬迦畢試國。豐糓稼，多花果，氣序溫暑，風俗淳質，猛銳驍雄，輕財好學。崇敬佛法，少信異道。伽藍雖多，僧徒寡少，諸窣堵波荒蕪圮壞。天祠五所，異道百餘人。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for over a hundred li, crossing a great mountain range, and fording a large river, one arrives at the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Nagarahāra is over six hundred li from east to west and two hundred and fifty or sixty li from south to north. Mountains surround its four borders, which are precipitous and dangerous. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. There is no great monarch; the ruler is subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is rich in grain and crops, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is warm and hot. The customs of the people are simple and honest; they are fierce, brave, and valiant, valuing wealth lightly and loving learning. They revere and respect the Buddha-Dharma and have little faith in heterodox paths. Although there are many saṃghārāmas, the number of monks is small, and the various stūpas are desolate and ruined. There are five Deva temples and over a hundred followers of heterodox paths.

t2087_text: 城東二里有窣堵波，高三百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。編石特起，刻雕奇製，釋迦菩薩值然燈佛，敷鹿皮衣，布髮掩泥，得受記處。時經劫壞，斯迹無泯。或有齋日，天雨眾花，群黎心競，式修供養。其西伽藍，少有僧徒。次南小窣堵波，是昔掩埿之地，無憂王避大路，遂僻建焉。城內有大窣堵波故基。聞諸先志曰：昔有佛齒，高廣嚴麗。今既無齒，唯餘故基。其側有窣堵波，高三十餘尺。彼俗相傳，不知源起，云從空下，峙基於此。既非人工，寔多靈瑞。城西南十餘里有窣堵波，是如來自中印度凌虛遊化，降迹於此，國人感慕，建此靈基。其東不遠有窣堵波，是釋迦菩薩昔值然燈佛，於此買華。
translation: Two li to the east of the city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is constructed of piled stone rising prominently, with exquisite carvings and a unique design; it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦菩薩) encountered the Buddha Dīpankara (然燈佛), spread out his deerskin garment, and laid down his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction. Although aeons have passed and the world has been destroyed, this trace has not vanished. On certain fast days, the heavens rain down various flowers, and the populace, vying in their devotion, perform offerings. To its west is a saṃghārāma with few monks. Further to the south is a small stūpa; this is the site where the mud was once covered, which King Aśoka built in this secluded spot to avoid the main road. Inside the city are the old foundations of a great stūpa. I have heard from the records of the ancients that it formerly held a Buddha tooth and was tall, broad, and magnificent. Now that the tooth is gone, only the old foundations remain. Beside it is a stūpa over thirty feet high. Local tradition says, without knowing its origin, that it descended from the sky and established its base here. Since it was not made by human hands, it possesses many spiritual marvels. More than ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa marking the spot where the Tathāgata, traveling through the air from Central India to convert beings, descended; the people of the country, moved by admiration, built this spiritual foundation. Not far to its east is a stūpa where the Bodhisattva Śākya once encountered the Buddha Dīpankara and purchased flowers.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: there was once a Buddha tooth here, which was tall, broad, and magnificent → 昔有佛齒，高廣嚴麗: the stūpa formerly held a Buddha tooth and was tall, broad and magnificent (Mizutani: 仏の歯が収納されていて高くもあり広くもありりっぱな)

t2087_text: 城西南二十餘里至小石嶺，有伽藍，高堂重閣，積石所成。庭宇寂寥，絕無僧侶。中有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。伽藍西南，深㵎陗絕，瀑布飛流，懸崖壁立。東崖石壁有大洞穴，瞿波羅龍之所居也。門徑狹小，窟穴冥闇，崖石津滴，磎徑餘流。昔有佛影，煥若真容，相好具足，儼然如在。近代已來，人不遍覩，縱有所見，髣髴而已。至誠祈請，有冥感者，乃暫明視，尚不能久。昔如來在世之時，此龍為牧牛之士，供王乳酪，進奉失宜；既獲譴責，心懷恚恨，即以金錢買華，供養受記窣堵波，願為惡龍，破國害王。即趣石壁，投身而死；遂居此窟，為大龍王，便欲出穴，成本惡願。適起此心，如來已鑒，愍此國人為龍所害，運神通力，自中印度至。龍見如來，毒心遂止，受不殺戒，願護正法。因請如來：「常居此窟，諸聖弟子，恒受我供。」如來告曰：「吾將寂滅，為汝留影，遣五羅漢常受汝供。正法隱沒，其事無替。汝若毒心奮怒，當觀吾留影，以慈善故，毒心當止。此賢劫中，當來世尊，亦悲愍汝，皆留影像。」影窟門外有二方石，其一石上有如來足蹈之迹，輪相微現，光明時燭。影窟左右多諸石室，皆是如來諸聖弟子入定之處。影窟西北隅有窣堵波，是如來經行之處。其側窣堵波有如來髮、爪。隣此不遠有窣堵波，是如來顯暢真宗，說蘊界處之所也。影窟西有大盤石，如來甞於其上濯浣袈裟，文影微現。
translation: Traveling over twenty *li* southwest of the city to a small rocky ridge, there is a monastery with lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, constructed from piled stones. The courtyards and buildings are desolate, and there are absolutely no monks. In the center is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Southwest of the monastery is a deep, precipitous ravine with a waterfall flowing down and cliffs standing like walls. On the stone wall of the eastern cliff is a large cave, which is the dwelling place of the dragon Gopāla (瞿波羅龍). The entrance path is narrow, the cave is dark and gloomy, the cliff rocks drip with moisture, and the path is wet with the remaining flow. In the past, there was a shadow of the Buddha, shining as if it were his true form, with all the marks and characteristics complete, appearing just as if he were present. Since recent times, people have not been able to see it fully; even if they do see it, it is only indistinctly. Those who pray with utmost sincerity and have a spiritual response may see it clearly for a moment, but it cannot last long. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who supplied milk and curds to the king, but he failed to present them properly. Having been reprimanded, he harbored resentment in his heart; he then used gold coins to buy flowers to offer to the Stūpa of the Prediction (受記窣堵波), wishing to become a wicked dragon to destroy the country and harm the king. He then rushed to the stone wall and threw himself to his death. Consequently, he resided in this cave and became a great dragon king, intending to emerge from the cave to fulfill his evil vow. Just as this thought arose, the Tathāgata perceived it. Compassionate toward the people of this country who were about to be harmed by the dragon, he exercised his supernatural powers and arrived from Central India. When the dragon saw the Tathāgata, his poisonous intent ceased; he accepted the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma. The dragon then requested the Tathāgata, "May you always reside in this cave, and may your holy disciples constantly receive my offerings." The Tathāgata replied, "I am about to enter nirvana, but I shall leave my shadow for you and send five arhats to constantly receive your offerings. Even when the True Dharma has faded away, this practice shall not cease. If your poisonous heart should flare up in anger, you should look upon the shadow I have left behind; because of my compassion and goodness, your poisonous heart will cease. In this Bhadrakalpa, the World-Honored Ones who are yet to come will also have compassion for you and will all leave their images behind." Outside the entrance of the Shadow Cave (佛影窟), there are two square stones. On one of the stones is the footprint of the Tathāgata, where the wheel mark is faintly visible and light occasionally shines forth. To the left and right of the Shadow Cave are many stone chambers, all of which are places where the various holy disciples of the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration. In the northwest corner of the Shadow Cave is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata used to walk. Beside it is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata manifested and expounded the True Doctrine, and where he spoke of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (蘊界處). To the west of the Shadow Cave is a large flat rock where the Tathāgata once washed his kaṣāya robe, and the faint traces of its pattern are still visible.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: a *stūpa* of prediction → 受記窣堵波: the Prediction Stūpa just described (Mizutani: 受記翠堵波) | because of its compassionate nature → 以慈善故: because of [my] compassion and goodness (Mizutani: 我が慈善の心により) | spoke of the aggregates and realms → 說蘊界處: aggregates, elements and sense-bases

t2087_text: 城東南三十餘里至醯羅城。周四五里，竪峻險固，花林池沼，光鮮澄鏡。城中居人，淳質正信。復有重閣，畫棟丹楹。第二閣中有七寶小窣堵波，置如來頂骨。骨周一尺二寸，髮孔分明，其色黃白，盛以寶函，置窣堵波中。欲知善惡相者，香末和埿，以印頂骨，隨其福感，其文煥然。又有七寶小窣堵波，以貯如來髑髏骨，狀若荷葉，色同頂骨，亦以寶函緘絡而置。又有七寶小窣堵波，有如來眼睛，睛大如㮈，光明清徹，曒映中外，又以寶函緘封而置。如來僧伽胝袈裟，細㲲所作，其色黃赤，置寶函中，歲月既遠，微有損壞。如來錫杖，白鐵作鐶，栴檀為笴，寶筒盛之。近有國王聞此諸物竝是如來昔親服用，恃其威力，迫脇而歸；既至本國，置所居宮，曾未浹辰，求之已失，爰更尋訪，已還本處。斯五聖迹，多有靈異，迦畢試王令五淨行給侍香花。觀禮之徒，相繼不絕。諸淨行等欲從虛寂，以為財用人之所重，權立科條，以止諠雜。其大略曰：諸欲見如來頂骨者，稅一金錢；若取印者，稅五金錢；自餘節級，以次科條。科條雖重，觀禮彌眾。重閣西北有窣堵波，亦甚高大，而多靈異，人以指觸，便即搖震，連基傾動，鈴鐸和鳴。
translation: Thirty-some *li* southeast of the city, one arrives at the city of Haḍḍa (醯羅城). It is four or five *li* in circumference, with steep and rugged defenses, and flower groves and ponds that are bright, fresh, and clear as mirrors. The people living in the city are honest, simple, and possess upright faith. There is a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars. In the second story of the pavilion is a small stupa made of the seven precious substances, in which the crown bone of the Tathāgata is placed. The bone is one foot and two inches in circumference, with distinct hair pores, and its color is yellowish-white; it is contained in a precious casket and placed inside the stupa. Those who wish to know the signs of their good or evil karma mix incense powder with clay and press it onto the crown bone; according to the response of their merit, the patterns appear clearly. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances to store the Tathāgata’s skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf and is the same color as the crown bone; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eyeball, which is as large as a *nai* (㮈, crab-apple) fruit, brilliant and transparent, shining through from inside to out; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. The Tathāgata’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) is made of fine cotton cloth (㲲), its color is yellowish-red, and it is kept in a precious casket; as the years have been long, it is slightly damaged. The Tathāgata’s *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) has rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood; it is kept in a precious tube. Recently, a king heard that all these objects were things the Tathāgata had personally used in the past, and relying on his power, he forcibly took them away. Once they arrived in his own country, he placed them in the palace where he resided, but before even twelve days had passed, when he sought them, they were already lost; upon further searching, they had already returned to their original place. These five sacred sites possess many spiritual wonders, and the king of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) has appointed five pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) to provide incense and flowers in service to them. Pilgrims coming to pay their respects arrive in an unbroken succession. The pure-practitioners, desiring to pursue emptiness and tranquility, and considering that wealth is something people value, have provisionally established a schedule of fees to put an end to the clamor and confusion. The general outline is as follows: those who wish to see the Tathāgata’s crown bone must pay a tax of one gold coin; if they wish to take an impression, they must pay a tax of five gold coins; for the remaining items, there is a graded schedule of fees. Although the fees are heavy, the number of those coming to pay their respects only increases. To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is also very tall and displays many spiritual wonders; if a person touches it with a finger, it immediately begins to shake, its very foundations tilt and move, and its bells ring in harmony.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: *nā* (crabapple) → 㮈 nai, crab-apple | fine *nü* (a type of fine cotton or wool fabric) → 細㲲: fine cotton cloth | see the Tathāgata’s skull bone (fee clause) → 頂骨: crown bone, as earlier in the passage (skull = 髑髏骨)

t2087_text: 從此東南山谷中行五百餘里，至健馱邏國（舊曰乾陀衛，訛也。北印度境）。健馱邏國，東西千餘里，南北八百餘里。東臨信度河。國大都城號布路沙布邏，周四十餘里。王族絕嗣，役屬迦畢試國。邑里空荒，居人稀少，宮城一隅有千餘戶。穀稼殷盛，花果繁茂，多甘蔗，出石蜜。氣序溫暑，略無霜雪。人性恇怯，好習典藝，多敬異道，少信正法。自古已來，印度之境作論諸師，則有那羅延天、無著菩薩、世親菩薩、法救、如意、脇尊者等本生處也。僧伽藍千餘所，摧殘荒廢，蕪漫蕭條，諸窣堵波頗多頹圮。天祠百數，異道雜居。
translation: From here, traveling southeast through mountain valleys for over five hundred li, one reaches the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) (formerly called Qiantuowei [乾陀衛], which is incorrect; it is in the region of North India). The country of Gandhāra is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. To the east, it borders the Sindhu (信度河) River. The great capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura (布路沙布邏), which is over forty li in circumference. The royal lineage has died out, and it is subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The towns and villages are desolate, and the inhabitants are few; in one corner of the palace city, there are over a thousand households. The crops are abundant, flowers and fruits are lush, there is much sugarcane, and it produces rock sugar. The climate is warm and hot, with almost no frost or snow. The people are timid and cowardly; they are fond of studying the arts and classics, and they mostly revere heterodox paths, having little faith in the True Dharma. Since ancient times, this has been the birthplace of various masters in the Indian region who composed treatises, such as Nārāyaṇa-deva, Asanga Bodhisattva, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, Dharmatrāta, Manoratha, and the Venerable Pārśva. There are over one thousand saṃghārāmas, which are ruined, desolate, and overgrown with weeds; many of the stūpas are dilapidated. There are about a hundred deva temples, where heterodox practitioners live together.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: “eight hundred li” → 南北八百餘里 over eight hundred | “formerly called Gandhavatī” → 乾陀衛 is an old Chinese transcription (Qiantuowei), not a Sanskrit form | “rock honey” → 石蜜 rock sugar | “one hundred deva temples” → 天祠百數 deva temples numbering about a hundred / some hundreds

t2087_text: 王城內東北有一故基，昔佛鉢之寶臺也。如來涅槃之後，鉢流此國，經數百年，式遵供養，流轉諸國，在波剌斯。城外東南八九里有卑鉢羅樹，高百餘尺，枝葉扶疎，蔭影蒙密。過去四佛已坐其下，今猶現有四佛坐像。賢劫之中，九百九十六佛皆當坐焉。冥祇警衛，靈鑒潛被。釋迦如來於此樹下南面而坐，告阿難曰：「我去世後，當四百年，有王命世，號迦膩色迦，此南不遠起窣堵波，吾身所有骨、肉舍利，多集此中。」
translation: Inside the royal city, to the northeast, there is an old foundation; it was formerly the precious pedestal of the Buddha’s alms bowl. After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the bowl drifted to this country, where it was formally worshipped for several hundred years; it then circulated through various countries and is now in Persia (波剌斯, Pārasa). Eight or nine li to the southeast of the city, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high, with wide-spreading branches and leaves that provide a dense shade. The four Buddhas of the past have already sat beneath it, and images of these four Buddhas still exist there today. During the Bhadrakalpa, the nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas will all sit there as well. Deities guard and protect it, and its spiritual influence is secretly bestowed. The Śākya Tathāgata once sat under this tree facing south and told Ānanda: "Four hundred years after I pass away, a king will appear in the world named Kaniṣka; not far to the south of this spot, he will erect a stūpa, and a great portion of the relics of my bones and flesh will be gathered within it."

t2087_text: 卑鉢羅樹南有窣堵波，迦膩色迦王之所建也。迦膩色迦王以如來涅槃之後第四百年，君臨膺運，統贍部洲，不信罪福，輕毀佛法。畋遊草澤，遇見白兔，王親奔逐，至此忽滅。見有牧牛小豎，於林樹間作小窣堵波，其高三尺。王曰：「汝何所為？」牧豎對曰：「昔釋迦佛聖智懸記：『當有國王於此勝地建窣堵波，吾身舍利多聚其內。』大王聖德宿殖，名符昔記，神功勝福，允屬斯辰，故我今者先相警發。」說此語已，忽然不現。王聞是說，嘉慶增懷，自負其名，大聖先記，因發正信，深敬佛法。周小窣堵波，更建石窣堵波，欲以功力彌覆其上。隨其數量，恒出三尺，若是增高，踰四百尺，基趾所峙，周一里半，層基五級，高一百五十尺，方乃得覆小窣堵波。王因嘉慶，復於其上更起二十五層金銅相輪，即以如來舍利一斛而置其中，式修供養。營建纔訖，見小窣堵波在大基東南隅下傍出其半。王心不平，便即擲棄，遂住窣堵波第二級下石基中半現，復於本處更出小窣堵波。王乃退而歎曰：「嗟夫，人事易迷，神功難掩，靈聖所扶，憤怒何及！」慚懼既已，謝咎而歸。其二窣堵波今猶現在，有嬰疾病欲祈康愈者，塗香散華，至誠歸命，多蒙瘳差。大窣堵波東面石陛南鏤作二窣堵波，一高三尺，一高五尺，規摹形狀如大窣堵波。又作兩軀佛像，一高四尺，一高六尺，擬菩提樹下加趺坐像，日光照燭，金色晃曜，陰影漸移，石文青紺。聞諸耆舊曰：數百年前，石基之隙有金色蟻，大者如指，小者如麥，同類相從，齧其石壁，文若雕鏤，廁以金沙，作為此像，今猶現在。大窣堵波石陛南面有畫佛像，高一丈六尺，自胸已上，分現兩身，從胸已下，合為一體。聞諸先志曰：初，有貧士傭力自濟，得一金錢，願造佛像。至窣堵波所，謂畫工曰：「我今欲圖如來妙相，有一金錢，酬功尚少，宿心憂負，迫於貧乏。」時彼畫工鑒其至誠，無云價直，許為成功。復有一人，事同前迹，持一金錢，求畫佛像。畫工是時受二人錢，求妙丹青，共畫一像。二人同日俱來禮敬，畫工乃同指一像，示彼二人，而謂之曰：「此是汝所作之佛像也。」二人相視，若有所懷。畫工心知其疑也，謂二人曰：「何思慮之久乎？凡所受物，毫釐不虧。斯言不謬，像必神變。」言聲未靜，像現靈異，分身交影，光相照著。二人悅服，心信歡喜。大窣堵波西南百餘步，有白石佛像，高一丈八尺，北面而立，多有靈相，數放光明。時有人見像出夜行，旋繞大窣堵波。近有群賊欲入行盜，像出迎賊，賊黨怖退，像歸本處，住立如故。群盜因此改過自新，遊行邑里，具告遠近。大窣堵波左右，小窣堵波魚鱗百數。佛像莊嚴，務窮工思，殊香異音，時有聞聽，靈仙聖賢，或見旋繞。此窣堵波者，如來懸記，七燒七立，佛法方盡。先賢記曰：成壞已三。初至此國，適遭大火，當見營搆，尚未成功。
translation: To the south of the Pippala tree is a stupa built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa. He did not believe in merit or demerit and slighted the Buddha’s Dharma. While hunting in the marshes, he encountered a white rabbit; the king personally gave chase, but it suddenly vanished at this spot. He saw a young cowherd among the trees making a small stupa three feet in height. The king asked, "What are you doing?" The cowherd replied, "Long ago, the holy wisdom of Śākya Buddha prophesied: 'A king will appear who shall build a stupa on this excellent site, and many of my bodily relics will be gathered within it.' Your Majesty’s holy virtues were cultivated in the past, your name matches the ancient prophecy, and your divine merit and superior fortune are destined for this very moment; therefore, I have come ahead to alert and inspire you." Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and reverence. Reflecting on his name and the Great Sage’s prior prophecy, he developed true faith and deeply respected the Buddha’s Dharma. Around the small stupa, he built a stone stupa, wishing to use his power to cover it completely. Yet, as he increased the height, the small stupa always emerged three feet above it. Only when the height exceeded four hundred feet—with the base standing one and a half li in circumference and a five-tiered foundation one hundred and fifty feet high—was he finally able to cover the small stupa. The king, rejoicing at this auspicious event, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper rings above it, and placing one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics within them, he performed offerings in this manner. No sooner was the construction finished than he saw the small stupa protruding halfway out from beneath the southeast corner of the great foundation. The king was displeased and cast it away; it then lodged halfway within the stone base under the second tier of the stupa, while another small stupa emerged once more at its original location. The king then withdrew and sighed, saying: "Alas, human efforts are easily misguided, but divine merit is difficult to conceal. When supported by the holy and spiritual, what can anger achieve?" Having felt shame and fear, he confessed his fault and returned. Those two stupas are still present today; those who are afflicted with illness and wish to pray for recovery apply incense and scatter flowers, and with sincere devotion take refuge, most of them obtaining a cure. To the south of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stupa, two stupas are carved, one three feet high and the other five feet high, their design and shape modeled after the great stupa. Two Buddha images are also fashioned, one four feet high and the other six feet high, imitating the seated image with crossed legs under the Mahā-bodhi tree; when the sunlight shines upon them, the golden color glitters brilliantly, and as the shadows gradually shift, the stone patterns appear dark blue. I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone base, the large ones like fingers and the small ones like grains of wheat, which followed one another to gnaw at the stone wall, the patterns appearing as if carved and inlaid with gold sand, forming these images, which are still present today. On the southern side of the stone steps of the great stūpa (大窣堵波) there is a painted Buddha image sixteen feet high; from the chest upward it appears as two bodies, but from the chest downward it is joined into one. I have heard from the records of the ancients that in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor and, having obtained one gold coin, wished to have a Buddha image made. He went to the place of the stūpa and said to a painter, "I now wish to depict the exquisite features of the Tathāgata (如來), but I have only one gold coin, which is insufficient to reward your labor; I have long cherished this desire but am burdened by worry, being constrained by my poverty." At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not speak of the price but promised to complete the work. Later, there was another man whose circumstances were the same as the former; he brought a gold coin and requested that an image of the Buddha be painted. The painter then accepted the money from both men, sought out excellent pigments, and painted a single image for them both. When the two men came on the same day to pay their respects, the painter pointed to the one image, showed it to them, and said, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned." The two men looked at each other, as if they had some misgivings. The painter, knowing their doubts in his heart, said to the two men, "Why are you so long in thought? Whatever I have received, I have not diminished by even a hair's breadth. If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest a divine transformation." Before his voice had ceased, the image manifested a miracle: the bodies separated and their shadows intertwined, and the light of the image shone brilliantly. The two men were convinced and filled with faith and joy. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa (mahāstūpa), there is a white stone Buddha image eighteen feet high, standing and facing north; it possesses many divine signs and frequently emits light. At times, people have seen the image go out at night to walk, circumambulating the great stupa. Recently, a group of thieves intended to enter and commit theft, but the image went out to meet them; the band of thieves was terrified and retreated, and the image returned to its original place, standing as before. Because of this, the group of thieves reformed and renewed themselves, traveling through the towns and villages to tell everyone, far and near. To the left and right of the great stupa, there are hundreds of small stupas arranged like fish scales. The Buddha images are adorned with the utmost craftsmanship, and extraordinary fragrances and strange sounds are sometimes heard; divine immortals and sages are occasionally seen circumambulating them. Regarding this stupa, the Tathāgata prophesied that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, at which point the Buddhadharma would come to an end. The records of the ancients state that it has already been built and destroyed three times. When I first arrived in this country, I happened to encounter a great fire, and I saw it being constructed, though it was not yet completed.

t2087_text: 大窣堵波西有故伽藍，迦膩色迦王之所建也。重閣累榭，層臺洞戶，旌召高僧，式昭景福。雖則圮毀，尚曰奇工。僧徒減少，並學小乘。自建伽藍，異人間出。諸作論師及證聖果，清風尚扇，至德無泯。第三重閣有波栗濕縛（唐言脇）尊者室，久已傾頓，尚立旌表。初，尊者之為梵志師也，年垂八十，捨家染衣。城中少年更誚之曰：「愚夫朽老，一何淺智！夫出家者，有二業焉，一則習定，二乃誦經。而今衰耄，無所進取，濫迹清流，徒知飽食。」時脇尊者聞諸譏議，因謝時人而自誓曰：「我若不通三藏理，不斷三界欲，得六神通，具八解脫，終不以脇而至於席！」自爾之後，唯日不足，經行宴坐，住立思惟，晝則研習理教，夜乃靜慮凝神，綿歷三歲，學通三藏，斷三界欲，得三明智，時人敬仰，因號脇尊者焉。脇尊者室東有故房，世親菩薩於此製《阿毘達磨俱舍論》，人而敬之，封以記焉。世親室南五十餘步，第二重閣，末笯曷剌他（唐言如意）論師於此製《毘婆沙論》。論師以佛涅槃之後一千年中利見也。少好學，有才辯，聲問遐被，法俗歸心。時室羅伐悉底國毘訖羅摩阿迭多王（唐言超日），威風遠洽，臣諸印度，日以五億金錢周給貧窶孤獨。主藏臣懼國用乏匱也，乃諷諫曰：「大王威被殊俗，澤及昆蟲，請增五億金錢，以賑四方匱乏。府庫既空，更稅有土，重斂不已，怨聲載揚，則君上有周給之恩，臣下被不恭之責。」王曰：「聚有餘，給不足，非苟為身侈靡國用。」遂加五億，惠諸貧乏。其後畋遊，逐豕失蹤，有尋知迹者，賞一億金錢。如意論師一使人剃髮，輒賜一億金錢，其國史臣依即書記。王恥見高，心常怏怏，欲眾辱如意論師。乃招集異學德業高深者百人，而下令曰：「欲收視聽，遊諸真境，異道紛雜，歸心靡措，今考優劣，專精遵奉。」洎乎集論，重下令曰：「外道論師並英俊也，沙門法眾宜善宗義，勝則崇敬佛法，負則誅戮僧徒。」於是如意詰諸外道，九十九人已退飛矣。下席一人，視之蔑如也，因而劇談，論及火煙。王與外道咸諠言曰：「如意論師辭義有失！夫先煙而後及火，此事理之常也。」如意雖欲釋難，無聽覽者。恥見眾辱，齰斷其舌，乃書誡告門人世親曰：「黨援之眾，無競大義；群迷之中，無辯正論。」言畢而死。居未久，超日王失國，興王膺運，表式英賢。世親菩薩欲雪前恥，來白王曰：「大王以聖德君臨，為含識主命。先師如意學窮玄奧，前王宿憾，眾挫高名，我承導誘，欲復先怨。」其王知如意哲人也，美世親雅操焉，乃召諸外道與如意論者。世親重述先旨，外道謝屈而退。
translation: To the west of the great stūpa is an old monastery, which was built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). With its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, its layered platforms and open windows, it was designed to summon high-ranking monks and to manifest auspicious blessings. Although it has fallen into ruin, it is still considered a work of marvelous craftsmanship. The number of monks has dwindled, and they all study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Since the monastery was built, extraordinary people have appeared there from time to time. The pure influence of the various masters who composed treatises and attained the holy fruits still lingers, and their supreme virtues have not been extinguished. On the third story of the pavilion is the room of the Venerable Pārśva (波栗濕縛; in Tang language, "Ribs" [脇]), which has long since collapsed, though a commemorative marker still stands. Originally, when the Venerable was a teacher of the Brahmins, he was nearly eighty years old when he left his home and donned the dyed robes. The youths in the city mocked him, saying: "What a foolish, decrepit old man, how shallow his wisdom! Those who leave home have two tasks: first, to practice meditation; second, to recite the scriptures. Now, in your senility, you have made no progress; you merely clutter the ranks of the pure, knowing only how to fill your belly." When the Venerable Pārśva heard these reproaches, he took leave of the people of the time and made a vow, saying: "If I do not master the principles of the Tripiṭaka, sever the desires of the three realms, attain the six supernatural powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never let my ribs touch a mat!" From then on, he felt only that the days were insufficient; whether walking, sitting, or standing in contemplation, he studied the doctrines by day and practiced quiet meditation with a concentrated mind by night. After three years, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, severed the desires of the three realms, and attained the three types of clear wisdom. The people of the time respected him and thus called him the Venerable Pārśva (the Venerable Ribs). To the east of the room of the Venerable Pārśva is an old chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論); out of respect, people have sealed it and marked it with a memorial. About fifty paces south of Vasubandhu’s room is a second-story pavilion where the Master Manoratha (末笯曷剌他; translated into Chinese as Ruyi, "As-Desired") composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). This master appeared one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed talent and eloquence; his reputation spread far and wide, and both the clergy and the laity turned their hearts toward him. At that time, King Vikramāditya (毘訖羅摩阿迭多; translated into Chinese as Chaori, "Surpassing the Sun") of the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) extended his majestic influence to distant lands and brought all of India under his rule; every day he distributed five hundred million gold coins to provide for the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the solitary. The treasurer, fearing that the national resources would be exhausted, offered a remonstrance, saying: "Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring power reaches foreign peoples and your benevolence extends even to insects; I pray you increase the distribution by another five hundred million gold coins to relieve the needy of the four quarters. Once the treasury is empty, we shall have to levy further taxes on the landholders; when heavy taxation continues without end and the cries of resentment spread everywhere, then the sovereign above will enjoy the reputation of being a generous provider, while the ministers below will bear the blame for being disrespectful." The King replied, "To gather the surplus and provide for the insufficient is not for the sake of my own luxury or the waste of national resources." He then added five hundred million coins to benefit the poor and needy. Later, while hunting, he pursued a boar and lost its track; someone found the trail, and he rewarded him with one hundred million gold coins. Master Manoratha once had someone shave his head, and he immediately bestowed one hundred million gold coins upon him; the state historian of that country recorded this accordingly. The king was ashamed to be surpassed and felt constant resentment, desiring to publicly humiliate the Master of Shastras, Manoratha (如意論師). He summoned one hundred practitioners of heterodox schools who were of high virtue and profound learning, and issued an order, saying: "Wishing to focus my attention and wander through the various true realms, I find the heterodox paths to be chaotic and my mind at a loss as to where to turn. Now, I shall examine their relative merits so that I may focus my devotion." When they gathered for the debate, he issued a further order, saying: "The heterodox masters are all outstanding men. The assembly of Śramaṇa (沙門) practitioners should be well-versed in their own doctrines; if they win, I shall honor the Buddha-Dharma, but if they lose, I shall execute the monks." Thereupon, Manoratha questioned the various heterodox teachers, and ninety-nine of them had already retreated in defeat. Only one remained in the lower seat, whom he regarded with contempt. They then engaged in a vigorous debate, which touched upon the subject of smoke and fire. The king and the heterodox teacher both shouted out: "Master Manoratha’s words and reasoning are flawed! It is a common principle of reality that smoke comes first and fire follows." Although Manoratha wished to explain the difficulty, no one would listen. Ashamed at being publicly humiliated, he bit off his tongue and wrote a warning to his disciple, Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Do not contend for the great truth among a crowd of partisans; do not debate correct doctrine among the deluded masses." Having finished speaking, he died. Not long after, the king, Vikramāditya (超日王), lost his kingdom, and a rising king took up the mandate, showing respect for the wise and virtuous. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to wipe away the previous shame, came and said to the king: "Great King, you rule with holy virtue and are the master and life-force of all sentient beings." "My late teacher Manoratha (如意) had exhausted the study of the most profound mysteries, yet the former king, harboring an old grudge, allowed the masses to humiliate his great reputation; having received his guidance and instruction, I wish to redress the grievance done to my predecessor." The king, knowing that Manoratha was a man of wisdom and admiring the noble character of Vasubandhu (世親), summoned the various non-Buddhists who had debated with Manoratha. Vasubandhu restated the principles of his predecessor, and the non-Buddhists admitted defeat and withdrew.

t2087_text: 迦膩色迦王伽藍東北行五十餘里，渡大河，至布色羯邏伐底城。周十四五里。居人殷盛，閭閻洞連。城西門外有一天祠，天像威嚴，靈異相繼。城東有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，即過去四佛說法之處。先古聖賢自中印度降神導物，斯地寔多。即伐蘇蜜呾羅（唐言世友。舊曰和須蜜多，訛也）論師於此製《眾事分阿毘達磨論》。城北四五里有故伽藍，庭宇荒涼，僧徒寡少，然皆遵習小乘法教。即達磨呾邏多（唐言法救。舊曰達磨多羅，訛也）論師於此製《雜阿毘達磨論》。伽藍側有窣堵波，高數百尺，無憂王之所建也。雕木文石，頗異人工。是釋迦佛昔為國王，修菩薩行，從眾生欲，惠施不倦，喪身若遺，於此國土千生為王，即斯勝地千生捨眼。捨眼東不遠有二石窣堵波，各高百餘尺。右則梵王所立，左乃天帝所建，以妙珍寶而瑩飾之。如來寂滅，寶變為石；基雖傾陷，尚曰崇高。
translation: Traveling northeast from the monastery of King Kaniṣka for more than fifty *li*, one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkalāvatī (布色羯邏伐底城). It is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circumference. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the houses are connected throughout. Outside the west gate of the city is a temple to a deva; the image of the deva is majestic, and miraculous manifestations occur there in succession. To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. In ancient times, many sages and worthies from Central India descended here to guide living beings. It was here that the śāstra-master Vasumitra (in the Tang language, Shiyou [世友], “World-Friend”; the old name, Hexumiduo [和須蜜多], is incorrect) composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分阿毘達磨論). Four or five *li* to the north of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is small, yet they all follow and study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It was here that the śāstra-master Dharmatrāta (in the Tang language, Fajiu [法救], “Dharma-Saviour”; the old name, Damoduoluo [達磨多羅], is incorrect) composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (雜阿毘達磨論). Beside the monastery is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Its carved wood and patterned stones are quite unlike the work of human hands. This is where the Buddha Śākyamuni, in a former life when he was a king practicing the bodhisattva path, followed the desires of living beings and gave alms without fatigue, regarding the loss of his own body as if it were nothing; in this land, he was king for a thousand lives, and in this very place, he gave up his eyes for a thousand lives. Not far to the east of the place where he gave up his eyes are two stone stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. The one on the right was erected by the Brahmā King (梵王), and the one on the left was built by the Lord of Devas (天帝); they were adorned with exquisite and precious jewels. After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the jewels transformed into stone; although the foundations have collapsed and sunk, they are still considered lofty.

translation: Traveling over fifty li to the northwest of the stūpas of Brahmā and Indra, there is a stūpa where the Śākya Tathāgata converted the Mother of Demon Children (Hārītī) and caused her to cease harming people; therefore, it is the custom of this country to offer sacrifices to her when praying for offspring.

translation: Traveling more than fifty li to the north of the place where the Mother of Demons (Hārītī) was converted, there is a stūpa. This is the place where the Bodhisattva Śyāmaka (formerly called Śāma, which is incorrect) was dutifully providing for his blind parents and gathering fruit, when he encountered a king out hunting and was accidentally struck by a poisoned arrow. His utmost sincerity moved the spirits, and the Lord of Heaven (Śakra) applied medicine; his virtue stirred the enlightened sages, and he was immediately restored to life.

t2087_text: 跋虜沙城東北二十餘里，至彈多落迦山。嶺上有窣堵波，無憂王所建，蘇達拏太子於此棲隱。其側不遠有窣堵波，太子於此以男女施婆羅門，婆羅門捶其男女，流血染地，今諸草木猶帶絳色。巖間石室，太子及妃習定之處。谷中林樹垂條若帷，竝是太子昔所遊止。其側不遠有一石廬，即古仙人之所居也。
translation: More than twenty *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at the mountain of Daṇḍaloka (彈多落迦山). On the ridge there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏) once lived in seclusion. Not far to its side is a stūpa where the prince gave his son and daughter as a gift to a brahmin; the brahmin beat the children, and their blood stained the ground, so that even now the plants and trees there still bear a crimson hue. In the crags is a stone chamber, the place where the prince and his consort practiced meditation. In the valley, the branches of the forest trees hang down like curtains; these are all places where the prince used to roam and rest in the past. Not far to its side is a stone hut, which is the dwelling place of an ancient *ṛṣi*.

translation: Traveling over a hundred *li* to the northwest from the rishi’s hut and crossing a small mountain, one reaches a great mountain. On the southern side of the mountain is a monastery with few monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the One-Horned Rishi (Ekashṛṅga-ṛṣi) formerly resided. The rishi was seduced and led astray by a courtesan, causing him to lose his supernatural powers, and the courtesan then rode upon his shoulders to return to the city.

t2087_text: 跋虜沙城東北五十餘里，至崇山。山有青石大自在天婦像，毘摩天女也。聞諸土俗曰：此天像者，自然有也。靈異既多，祈禱亦眾，印度諸國，求福請願，貴賤畢萃，遠近咸會。其有願見天神形者，至誠無貳，絕食七日，或有得見，求願多遂。山下有大自在天祠，塗灰外道式修祠祀。
translation: Fifty-some *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at a lofty mountain (崇山). On the mountain, there is a blue stone image of the wife of Maheśvara (大自在天), who is the goddess Bhīmā (毘摩天女). According to local tradition, this celestial image appeared there naturally. Because it is highly miraculous, there are many who come to pray; people from all the countries of India, whether noble or humble, gather here from far and near to seek blessings and make vows. For those who wish to see the form of the celestial deity, if they are sincere and single-minded and fast for seven days, some may obtain a vision, and most of their prayers are fulfilled. At the foot of the mountain, there is a temple of Maheśvara where ash-smearing heretics (塗灰外道) perform their ritual worship.

t2087_text: 烏鐸迦漢荼城西北行二十餘里，至婆羅覩邏邑，是製《聲明論》波爾尼仙本生處也。遂古之初，文字繁廣，時經劫壞，世界空虛，長壽諸天，降靈道俗，由是之故，文籍生焉。自時厥後，其源泛濫。梵王、天帝作則隨時，異道諸仙各製文字，人相祖述，競習所傳，學者虛功，難用詳究。人壽百歲之時，有波爾尼仙，生知博物，愍時澆薄，欲削浮偽，刪定繁猥，遊方問道，遇自在天，遂申述作之志。自在天曰：「盛矣哉！吾當祐汝。」仙人受教而退，於是研精覃思，採摭群言，作為字書，備有千頌，頌三十二言矣。究極今古，總括文言。封以進上，王甚珍異，下令國中，普使傳習，有誦通利，賞千金錢。所以師資傳授，盛行當世。故此邑中諸婆羅門，碩學高才，博物強識。婆羅覩邏邑中有窣堵波，羅漢化波爾尼仙後進之處。如來去世，垂五百年，有大阿羅漢自迦濕彌羅國遊化至此，乃見梵志捶訓稚童。時阿羅漢謂梵志曰：「何苦此兒？」梵志曰：「令學《聲明論》，業不時進。」阿羅漢逌爾而笑。老梵志曰：「夫沙門者，慈悲為情，愍傷物類。仁今所笑，願聞其說。」阿羅漢曰：「談不容易，恐致深疑。汝頗甞聞波爾尼仙製《聲明論》，垂訓於世乎？」婆羅門曰：「此邑之子，後進仰德，像設猶在。」阿羅漢曰：「今汝此子，即是彼仙。猶以強識，翫習世典，唯談異論，不究真理。神智唐捐，流轉未息，尚乘餘善，為汝愛子。然則世典文辭，徒疲功績；豈若如來聖教，福智冥滋？曩者南海之濱有一枯樹，五百蝙蝠於中穴居。有諸商侶止此樹下，時屬風寒，人皆飢凍，聚積樵蘇，蘊火其下，煙焰漸熾，枯樹遂燃。時商侶中有一賈客，夜分已後，誦《阿毘達磨藏》。彼諸蝙蝠雖為火困，愛好法音，忍而不去，於此命終。隨業受生，俱得人身，捨家修學，乘聞法聲，聰明利智，並證聖果，為世福田。近迦膩色迦王與脇尊者招集五百賢聖，於迦濕彌羅國作《毘婆沙論》，斯並枯樹之中五百蝙蝠也。余雖不肖，是其一數。斯則優劣良異，飛伏懸殊。仁今愛子，可許出家；出家功德，言不能述。」時阿羅漢說此語已，示神通事，因忽不現。婆羅門深生敬異，歎善久之，具告隣里，遂放其子出家修學，因即迴信，崇重三寶，鄉人從化，於今彌篤。從烏鐸迦漢荼城北踰山涉川，行六百餘里，至烏仗那國（唐言苑，昔輪王之苑囿也。舊云烏場，或曰烏茶，皆訛。北印度境）。
translation: Traveling over twenty li northwest from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), one reaches the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑), which is the birthplace of the ṛṣi Pāṇini (波爾尼仙), the author of the Śabdavidyā-śāstra (聲明論). At the beginning of remote antiquity, written characters were numerous and extensive, but as time passed through the kalpa of destruction, the world became a void, until the long-lived deities descended to inspire both the sacred and the secular, and from this, literary records were born. Since that time, their sources have proliferated. King Brahmā and Lord Indra created models according to the needs of the times, and the various immortals of heterodox paths each devised their own scripts; people followed their predecessors and vied to practice what was handed down, but students' efforts were in vain, as it was difficult to investigate the systems in detail. When the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was the ṛṣi Pāṇini, who was born with great wisdom and broad learning. Pitying the decadence of the age, he wished to prune away the superficial and false, and to edit and refine the cumbersome and redundant. He traveled to various regions to inquire after the Way, and upon meeting Maheśvara (自在天), he expressed his intention to compose a work. Maheśvara said, "Excellent! I shall assist you." Having received these instructions, the ṛṣi withdrew and applied his mind to deep reflection, collecting a vast array of words to compose a lexicon consisting of one thousand stanzas, each containing thirty-two syllables. It exhausted the depths of both the present and the past, and summarized the entirety of literary language. He sealed it and presented it to the king, who found it most extraordinary and issued a decree throughout the kingdom to make it universally studied, rewarding anyone who could recite it with mastery with one thousand gold coins. This is why the tradition of teacher and student has been passed down and flourished in the present age. Consequently, the Brahmins in this town are men of great learning and high talent, possessing broad knowledge and excellent memories. In the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑) there is a stūpa, which is the place where an Arhat converted a later follower of the sage Pāṇini. Nearly five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed away, a great Arhat traveling from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) arrived here and saw a Brahmin beating and scolding a young boy. The Arhat asked the Brahmin, "Why are you tormenting this child?" The Brahmin replied, "I am making him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論), but his progress is not timely." The Arhat smiled gently. The old Brahmin said, "The nature of a Śramaṇa is compassion and pity for all living beings. I wish to hear the reason for your laughter." The Arhat said, "It is not easy to speak of this, for I fear it will cause deep doubt. Have you ever heard that the sage Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* and left it as a teaching for the world?" The Brahmin replied, "He was a son of this town; later generations look up to his virtue, and his image is still here." The Arhat said, "This child of yours is that very sage. Because he possessed a powerful memory, he indulged in the study of worldly texts, discussing only heterodox doctrines without investigating the true principles. His spiritual wisdom was wasted in vain, and his transmigration has not yet ceased; it is only by riding on the merit of his remaining good deeds that he has become your beloved son. However, the literary expressions of worldly texts merely exhaust one's efforts; how can they compare to the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, which nourish merit and wisdom in the dark? Formerly, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree where five hundred bats lived in holes. Some merchants stopped under this tree. At that time, it was windy and cold, and everyone was hungry and freezing. They gathered firewood and brush, and kindled a fire beneath it. The smoke and flames gradually intensified, and the withered tree caught fire. Among the merchants, there was one trader who, after the middle of the night, was reciting the Abhidharma-piṭaka (阿毘達磨藏). Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma and endured it without leaving, and thus they met their end there. Following their karma, they were reborn, all obtaining human bodies. They left their homes to study and practice, and by virtue of having heard the sound of the Dharma, they were intelligent and wise, all attaining the holy fruit and becoming fields of merit for the world. Recently, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) summoned five hundred sages in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) to compose the Vibhāṣā-śāstra (毘婆沙論); these are the very same five hundred bats from the withered tree. Although I am unworthy, I am one of that number. This shows that the superior and the inferior are truly different, and the flying and the crawling are vastly distinct. You should now allow your beloved son to leave home; the merit of leaving home is beyond description." When the Arhat had spoken these words, he displayed his supernatural powers and suddenly vanished. The brahmin was deeply filled with reverence and wonder, and after praising the goodness of this for a long time, he told his neighbors everything. He then allowed his son to leave home to study and practice, and consequently turned to the faith, honoring the Triple Gem. The villagers followed his transformation, and their devotion remains intense to this day. Traveling north from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), crossing mountains and wading through rivers for more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) (In the language of the Tang, this means "garden," as it was formerly the pleasure garden of a Cakravartin king. It was formerly called Wuchang (烏場) or sometimes Wucha (烏茶), but both are incorrect. It is within the territory of North India).

t2087_text: 烏仗那國，周五千餘里，山谷相屬，川澤連原。穀稼雖播，地利不滋。多蒲萄，少甘蔗，土產金、鐵，宜欝金香，林樹蓊欝，花果茂盛。寒暑和暢，風雨順序。人性怯懦，俗情譎詭。好學而不功，禁呪為藝業。多衣白㲲，少有餘服。語言雖異，大同印度。文字禮儀，頗相參預。崇重佛法，敬信大乘。夾蘇婆伐窣堵河，舊有一千四百伽藍，多已荒蕪。昔僧徒一萬八千，今漸減少。並學大乘，寂定為業，善誦其文，未究深義，戒行清潔，特閑禁呪。律儀傳訓，有五部焉：一法密部，二化地部，三飲光部，四說一切有部，五大眾部。天祠十有餘所，異道雜居。堅城四五，其王多治瞢揭釐城。城周十六七里，居人殷盛。
translation: The country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) is over five thousand li in circuit. Mountains and valleys are contiguous, and rivers and marshes connect with the plains. Although grain is sown, the land is not very fertile. There are many grapes but little sugarcane; the land produces gold and iron and is suitable for saffron; the forests are lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The cold and heat are temperate, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are timid and cowardly, and their customs are deceitful. They are fond of learning but do not apply themselves, and they make incantations their professional skill. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and have few other types of clothing. Although their language differs, it is largely the same as that of India. Their writing and etiquette are quite similar. They highly esteem the Buddhadharma and revere and believe in the Mahāyāna. Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate. Formerly there were eighteen thousand monks, but now they have gradually decreased. They all study the Mahāyāna and make silent meditation their occupation; they are skilled at reciting the texts but have not yet fathomed their profound meanings. Their moral conduct is pure, and they are especially skilled in incantations. Regarding the traditions of the Vinaya rules, there are five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are four or five fortified cities, and their king usually governs from the city of Mangala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit and is densely populated.

t2087_text: 瞢揭釐城東北行二百五六十里，入大山，至阿波邏羅龍泉，即蘇婆伐窣堵河之源也。派流西南，春夏含凍，昏夕飛雪，雪霏五彩，光流四照。此龍者，迦葉波佛時生在人趣，名曰殑祇，深閑呪術，禁禦惡龍，不令暴雨，國人賴之，以稸餘糧。居人眾庶感恩懷德，家稅斗穀以饋遺焉。既積歲時，或有逋課。殑祇含怒，願為毒龍，暴行風雨，損傷苗稼。命終之後，為此池龍。泉流白水，損傷地利。釋迦如來大悲御世，愍此國人獨遭斯難，降神至此，欲化暴龍。執金剛神杵擊山崖，龍王震懼，乃出歸依，聞佛說法，心淨信悟，如來遂制勿損農稼。龍曰：「凡有所食，賴收人田，今蒙聖教，恐難濟給，願十二歲一收糧儲。」如來含覆，愍而許焉。故今十二年一遭白水之災。
translation: Traveling two hundred and fifty or sixty *li* northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one enters a great mountain and reaches the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, which is the source of the Śubhavastu (蘇婆伐窣堵) River. The stream flows to the southwest; it contains ice during the spring and summer, and in the evening snow flies, the snowflakes shimmering in five colors and radiating light in all directions. As for this dragon, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was born in the human realm with the name Gangi (殑祇); he was deeply skilled in sorcery and restrained evil dragons from causing torrential rains, so the people of the country relied on him to store surplus grain. The inhabitants and the masses, feeling gratitude and cherishing his virtue, taxed each household one *dou* of grain to present to him. After many years had passed, there were some who defaulted on their payments. Gangi became angry and vowed to become a poisonous dragon, violently unleashing wind and rain to damage the crops. After his life ended, he became the dragon of this pool. The spring flows with white water, damaging the land's productivity. The Śākya Tathāgata, governing the world with great compassion, took pity on the people of this country for suffering this unique disaster and descended to this place, desiring to convert the violent dragon. He had the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神) strike the mountain cliff with his vajra; the Dragon King was terrified and emerged to take refuge. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became pure and he attained faith and enlightenment. The Tathāgata then commanded him not to damage the crops. The dragon said, "Everything I eat depends on the harvest from the people's fields. Now, having received the holy teaching, I fear it will be difficult to sustain myself; I request to collect grain stores once every twelve years." The Tathāgata, in his encompassing compassion, took pity and granted this. Thus, even now, the country suffers the calamity of white water once every twelve years.

t2087_text: 瞢揭釐城南四百餘里，至醯羅山，谷水西派，逆流東上，雜華異果，被㵎緣崖，峯巖危險，谿谷盤紆，或聞諠語之聲，或聞音樂之響。方石如塔，宛若工成，連延相屬，接布崖谷。是如來在昔為聞半頌（舊曰伽，梵文略也。或曰偈他，梵音訛也。今從正音，宜云伽他。伽他者，唐言頌，頌三十二言也）之法，於此捨身命焉。
translation: More than four hundred *li* to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches Mount Hiḍḍa (醯羅山). The valley stream branches to the west and flows back up eastward against its course; various flowers and strange fruits cover the gullies and line the cliffs. The peaks and crags are perilous, and the streams and valleys wind and meander; sometimes one hears the sound of loud talking, and sometimes one hears the strains of music. Square stones resemble pagodas, appearing as if fashioned by craftsmen, stretching out in succession and spreading through the cliffs and valleys. This is where the Tathāgata in a former life sacrificed his body and life to hear half a stanza (Formerly it was called *jie* (伽), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Some call it *jieta* (偈他), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. Following the correct pronunciation now, it should be called *gāthā* (伽他). *Gāthā* means *song* (頌) in the language of Tang, a *song* being thirty-two syllables) of the Dharma.

t2087_text: 瞢揭釐城南二百餘里，大山側，至摩訶伐那（唐言大林）伽藍。是如來昔修菩薩行，號薩縛達之王（唐言一切施），避敵棄國，潛行至此，遇貧婆羅門，方來乞匃。既失國位，無以為施，遂令羈縛，擒往敵王，冀以賞財，迴為惠施。
translation: More than two hundred li south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), by the side of a great mountain, one reaches the Mahāvana (摩訶伐那; in the language of Tang, "Great Forest" [大林]) Monastery. This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king named Sarvadatta (薩縛達; in the language of Tang, "All-Bestowing" [一切施]), having fled his enemies and abandoned his kingdom, traveled in secret to this place and encountered a poor brahmin who had come to beg for alms. Having already lost his royal position and having nothing to give, he ordered the brahmin to bind him and take him captive to the enemy king, hoping that the reward money could be used as a gift of charity in return.

translation: Thirty or forty li to the northwest of the Mahāvana (Great Forest) Monastery, descending the mountain, one reaches the Mayū (摩愉; in the Tang language, "Bean") Monastery. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high. On a large square stone at its side are the footprints of the Tathāgata, left when the Buddha formerly stepped upon this stone and emitted a koṭi of rays of light to illuminate the Mahāvana Monastery, while preaching Jātaka stories for the sake of all humans and devas. Below the base of this stūpa is a stone, yellowish-white in color, which is always moist and oily. It is here that the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, split his bones to write down the scriptures in order to hear the true Dharma.

Seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, he here cut his own flesh to ransom a dove from a hawk.

t2087_text: 代鴿西北二百餘里，入珊尼羅闍川，至薩裒殺地（唐言蛇藥）僧伽藍。有窣堵波，高八十餘尺。是如來昔為帝釋，時遭饑歲，疾疫流行，醫療無功道，死相屬。帝釋悲愍，思所救濟，乃變其形為大蟒身，僵屍川谷，空中遍告；聞者感慶，相率奔赴，隨割隨生，療飢療疾。其側不遠，有蘇摩大窣堵波。是如來昔為帝釋，時世疾疫，愍諸含識，自變其身為蘇摩蛇，凡有噉食，莫不康豫。珊尼羅闍川北石崖邊，有窣堵波。病者至求，多蒙除差。如來在昔為孔雀王，與其群而至此，熱渴所逼，求水不獲，孔雀王以𭪿啄崖，涌泉流注。今遂為池，飲沐愈疾。石上猶有孔雀蹤迹。
translation: Traveling more than two hundred *li* northwest from the place where the dove was ransomed, one enters the Sanirāja River valley and reaches the Sarpauṣadhi (which means "Snake Medicine" in the language of Tang) Monastery. There is a *stūpa* here, more than eighty feet high. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, a time of famine and pestilence occurred; medical treatments were ineffective, and the dead lay one after another on the roads. Indra, moved by compassion and wishing to provide relief, transformed his body into that of a giant python, lying dead in the valley, and proclaimed it to all from the air. Those who heard were moved and rejoiced, rushing to the site; as they cut pieces from the body, it would immediately regenerate, curing their hunger and their illnesses. Not far to the side is a large *stūpa* of Soma. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, during a time of pestilence, he took pity on all sentient beings and transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who consumed it were restored to health and comfort. Beside the stone cliff to the north of the Sanirāja River, there is a *stūpa*. Sick people who come here to pray are often cured of their ailments. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a peacock king, he came to this place with his flock; driven by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any, so the peacock king pecked the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth. This has now become a pool, and drinking from or bathing in it cures illnesses. The tracks of the peacock are still visible on the stone.

translation: Traveling sixty or seventy li southwest of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), on the east bank of a great river, there is a stūpa over sixty feet high, which was built by King Uttarasena (上軍王). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the great assembly: "After my nirvāṇa, King Uttarasena of the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) should be given a share of the relics." When the various kings were about to measure out the shares, King Uttarasena arrived late, and consequently, there was talk of slighting him. At that time, the assembly of devas and men reiterated the words of the Tathāgata’s final charge, so he was allowed to participate in the distribution; he carried them back to his own country and reverently constructed this to honor them.

t2087_text: 觀自在菩薩像西北百五十里，至藍勃盧山。山嶺有龍池，周三十餘里，淥波浩汗，清流皎鏡。昔毘盧釋迦王前伐諸釋，四人拒軍者，宗親擯逐，各事分飛。其一釋種，既出國都，跋涉疲弊，中路而止。時有一雁，飛趣其前，既以馴狎，因即乘焉。其雁飛翔，下此池側。釋種虛遊，遠適異國，迷不知路，假寐樹陰。池龍少女，遊覽水濱，忽見釋種，恐不得當也，變為人形，即而摩拊。釋種驚寤，因即謝曰：「羈旅羸人，何見親拊？」遂欵殷勤，凌逼野合。女曰：「父母有訓，祗奉無違。雖蒙惠顧，未承高命。」釋種曰：「山谷杳冥，爾家安在？」曰：「我此池之龍女也。敬聞聖族流離逃難，幸因遊覽，敢慰勞弊。命有讌私，未聞來旨。況乎積禍，受此龍身，人畜殊途，非所聞也。」釋種曰：「一言見允，宿心斯畢。」龍女曰：「敬聞命矣，唯所去就。」釋種乃誓心曰：「凡我所有福德之力，令此龍女舉體成人。」福力所感，龍遂改形，既得人身，深自慶悅。乃謝釋種曰：「我積殃運，流轉惡趣。幸蒙垂顧，福力所加，曠劫弊身，一旦改變。欲報此德，糜軀未謝。心願陪遊，事拘物議。願白父母，然後備禮。」龍女還池，白父母曰：「今者遊覽，忽逢釋種，福力所感，變我為人，情存好合，敢陳事實。」龍王心欣人趣，情重聖族，遂從女請。乃出池而謝釋種曰：「不遺非類，降尊就卑，願臨我室，敢供灑掃。」釋種受龍王之請，遂即其居。於是龍宮之中，親迎備禮，燕爾樂會，肆極歡娛。釋種覩龍之形，心常畏惡，乃欲辭出。龍王止曰：「幸無遠舍，隣此宅居，當令據疆土，稱大號，總有臣庶，祚延長世。」釋種謝曰：「此言非冀。」龍王以寶劍置篋中，妙好白㲲，而覆其上。謂釋種曰：「幸持此㲲以獻國王，王必親受遠人之貢，可於此時害其王也。因據其國，不亦善乎？」釋種受龍指誨，便往行獻；烏仗那王躬舉其㲲，釋種執其袂而刺之。侍臣、衛兵諠亂階陛，釋種麾劍告曰：「我所杖劍，神龍見授，以誅後伏，以斬不臣。」咸懼神武，推尊大位。於是沿弊立政，表賢恤患。已而動大眾，備法駕，即龍宮而報命，迎龍女以還都。龍女宿業未盡，餘報猶在、每至讌私，首出九龍之頭。釋種畏惡，莫知圖計，伺其寐也，利刃斷之。龍女驚寐曰：「斯非後嗣之利，非徒我命有少損傷，而汝子孫當苦頭痛。」故此國族常有斯患，雖不連綿，時一發動。釋種既沒，其子嗣位，是嗢呾羅犀那王（唐言上軍）。上軍王嗣位之後，其母喪明。如來伏阿波邏羅龍還也，從空下其宮中。上軍王適從遊獵，如來因為其母略說法要。遇聖聞法，遂得復明。如來問曰：「汝子，我之族也，今何所在？」母曰：「旦出畋遊，今將返駕。」如來與諸大眾尋欲發引。王母曰：「我惟福遇，生育聖族，如來悲愍，又親降臨，我子方還，願少留待。」世尊曰：「斯人者，我之族也。可聞教而信悟，非親誨以發心。我其行矣。還，語之曰：『如來從此往拘尸城娑羅樹間入涅槃，宜取舍利，自為供養。』」如來與諸大眾凌虛而去。上軍王方遊獵，遠見宮中光明赫奕，疑有火災，罷獵而返。乃見其母復明，慶而問曰：「我去幾何，有斯祥感，能令慈母復明如昔？」母曰：「汝出之後，如來至此，聞佛說法，遂得復明。如來從此至拘尸城娑羅樹間，當取涅槃，召汝速來分取舍利。」時王聞已，悲號頓躄，久而醒悟，命駕馳赴。至雙樹間，佛已涅槃。時諸國王輕其邊鄙，寶重舍利，不欲分與。是時天、人大眾重宣佛意，諸王聞已，遂先均授。
translation: One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, having traveled through the air far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, forcing himself upon her in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. Though fate has brought us to intimacy, I have not yet heard my parents’ will. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites." The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to visit my dwelling, where I dare to offer you my service." The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, bear a great title, command subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a chest and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon’s instructions and went to present it. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendants and guards were in an uproar on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who are slow to submit and to behead those who are not loyal." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and elevated him to the high throne. Thereupon, he reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and bring the dragon girl back to the capital. Because the dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted and residual retribution remained, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but when he caught her sleeping, he cut them off with a sharp blade. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants; not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the royal clan of this country often suffers from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那; Tang dynasty translation: "Superior Army"). After King Uttarasena succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. The Tathāgata, having subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), was returning and descended through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena happened to be out hunting, so the Tathāgata briefly explained the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Having encountered the Holy One and heard the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out hunting this morning and is now on his way back." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King’s mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown great compassion by personally visiting us. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This man is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to arouse his resolve. I shall depart. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvāṇa among the śāla trees; you should obtain the relics and make offerings to them yourself.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then rose into the void and departed. King Uttarasena was out hunting and saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and he asked joyfully, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" The mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight." "The Tathāgata has gone from here to the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he summons you to come quickly to receive a portion of his relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained his senses and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived between the twin trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon his borderland status and, treasuring the relics, did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and humans restated the Buddha’s intention; having heard this, the kings divided the relics equally, giving him his share first.

t2087_text: 瞢揭釐城東北踰山越谷，逆上信度河，途路危險，山谷杳冥，或履縆索，或牽鐵鎖，棧道虛臨，飛梁危構，椓杙躡蹬，行千餘里，至達麗羅川，即烏仗那國舊都也。多出黃金及欝金香。達麗川中大伽藍側，有刻木慈氏菩薩像，金色晃昱，靈鑒潛通，高百餘尺，末田底迦（舊曰末田地，訛略也）阿羅漢之所造也。羅漢以神通力，携引匠人升覩史多天（舊曰兜率他也，又曰兜術他，訛也）親觀妙相，三返之後，功乃畢焉。自有此像，法流東派。
translation: Going northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing mountains and traversing valleys, and heading upstream along the Indus River (信度河), the path is perilous and the valleys are dark and gloomy. One must tread on rope bridges or cling to iron chains; plank paths are suspended over voids, bridges are built precariously high, and one must step on wooden pegs driven into the rock. After traveling over a thousand *li*, one reaches the valley of Darada (達麗羅川), which is the old capital of the kingdom of Udyāna (烏仗那國). It produces much gold and saffron. Beside a great monastery in the Darada valley, there is a carved wooden statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩). Its golden color shines brightly, and its spiritual efficacy is subtly pervasive. It is over a hundred feet tall and was created by the Arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦) (formerly called Madhyandina, which is an incorrect abbreviation). The Arhat used his supernatural powers to transport a craftsman up to the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天) (formerly called Doushuaita [兜率他], and also Doushuta [兜術他], which are incorrect) to personally observe the Bodhisattva's exquisite features. After three such visits, the work was finally completed. Ever since this statue came into existence, the Dharma has flowed toward the eastern regions.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: “formerly called Duoshita, and also Doushuta” → 兜率他 Doushuaita, 兜術他 Doushuta

t2087_text: 從此東行，踰嶺越谷，逆上信度河，飛梁棧道，履危涉險，經五百餘里，至鉢露羅國（北印度境）。鉢露羅國，周四千餘里，在大雪山間，東西長，南北狹。多麥、豆，出金、銀，資金之利，國用富饒。時唯寒烈，人性獷暴，薄於仁義，無聞禮節。形貌麁弊，衣服毛褐。文字大同印度。言語異於諸國，伽藍數百所，僧徒數千人，學無專習，戒行多濫。
translation: Traveling east from here, crossing ridges and traversing valleys, going upstream along the Sindhu (信度) River, and passing over flying bridges and plank paths, one treads through danger and peril for over five hundred li to reach the country of Balūra (鉢露羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Balūra is over four thousand li in circuit, situated amidst the Great Snow Mountains; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. It produces much wheat and beans, and yields gold and silver; due to the profit from this gold, the state is wealthy and prosperous. The climate is consistently cold and harsh. The people are fierce and violent by nature, lacking in benevolence and righteousness, and have no knowledge of etiquette or propriety. Their appearance is coarse and unrefined, and they wear garments of wool and hair. Their writing is largely the same as that of India, but their language differs from that of other countries. There are several hundred sanghārāmas (伽藍) and several thousand monks; they have no specialized studies, and their observance of the precepts is largely lax.
