t2087_text: 從此復還烏鐸迦漢荼城，南渡信度河，河廣三四里，南流，澄清皎鏡，汩淴漂流。毒龍、惡獸窟穴其中，若持貴寶、奇花果種及佛舍利渡者，船多飄沒。渡河至呾叉始羅國（北印度境）。呾叉始羅國，周二千餘里。國大都城周十餘里。酋豪力競，王族絕嗣，往者役屬迦畢試國，近又附庸迦濕彌羅國。地稱沃壤，稼穡殷盛，泉流多，花草茂。氣序和暢，風俗輕勇，崇敬三寶。伽藍雖多，荒蕪已甚，僧徒寡少，並學大乘。
translation: From here I returned to the city of Udakhanda (烏鐸迦漢荼城) and crossed the Indus River (信度河) to the south. The river is three or four li wide and flows southward; it is clear and bright as a mirror, yet its currents are surging and rapid. Venomous dragons and evil beasts dwell within it, and if those who carry precious gems, rare flowers, fruit seeds, or Buddha relics attempt to cross, their boats are often overturned and lost. After crossing the river, I arrived at the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Takṣaśilā is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. The local chieftains contend for power, and the royal lineage has died out; in the past, it was subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and recently it has become a vassal to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The land is known for its fertile soil; agriculture is flourishing, springs are numerous, and flowers and plants grow luxuriantly. The climate is mild and pleasant, the customs of the people are light and courageous, and they revere the Three Jewels. Although there are many monasteries, they are mostly in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they all study the Great Vehicle.

t2087_text: 大城西北七十餘里有醫羅鉢呾羅龍王池，周百餘步。其水澄清，雜色蓮華同榮異彩。此龍者，即昔迦葉波佛時壞醫羅鉢羅樹苾芻者也。故今彼土請雨祈晴，必與沙門共至池所，彈指慰問隨願必果。
translation: More than seventy li to the northwest of the great city is the pond of the Dragon King Elāpattra (醫羅鉢呾羅), which is over a hundred paces in circumference. Its water is clear and pure, and multicolored lotus flowers bloom there together in diverse hues. This dragon is the one who, in the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, was a bhikṣu that damaged an elāpattra tree. Therefore, when the people of that land now pray for rain or clear weather, they must go to the pond together with a śramaṇa; when he snaps his fingers and offers words of comfort, their wishes are invariably fulfilled.

t2087_text: 龍池東南行三十餘里，入兩山間，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高百餘尺。是釋迦如來懸記，當來慈氏世尊出興之時，自然有四大寶藏，即斯勝地，當其一所。聞諸先志曰：或時地震，諸山皆動，周藏百步，無所傾搖。諸有愚夫，妄加發掘，地為震動，人皆蹎仆。傍有伽藍，圮損已甚，久絕僧徒。
translation: Traveling over thirty li southeast from the Dragon Pond and entering between two mountains, there is a stupa (stūpa) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over a hundred feet in height. It is the prediction of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni that when the future World-Honored One Maitreya (慈氏世尊) appears in the world, there will naturally be four great treasure troves, and this sacred site is one of them. According to ancient records, whenever an earthquake occurs and all the mountains shake, the area for a hundred paces around the treasure remains perfectly still without any quivering. Some foolish men once attempted to dig it up recklessly, but the earth shook and they all fell prostrate. Nearby is a monastery (saṃghārāma), which is severely dilapidated and has long been devoid of monks.

t2087_text: 城北十二三里有窣堵波，無憂王之建也。或至齋日，時放光明，神花天樂，頗有見聞。聞諸先志曰：近有婦人，身嬰惡癩，竊至窣堵波，責躬禮懺，見其庭宇有諸糞穢，掬除灑掃，塗香散華，採青蓮。重布其地。惡疾除愈，形貌增妍，身出名香，青蓮同馥。斯勝地也，是如來在昔修菩薩行，為大國王，號戰達羅鉢剌婆（唐言月光），志求菩提，斷頭惠施。若此之捨，凡歷千生。捨頭窣堵波側有僧伽藍，庭宇荒涼，僧徒減少。昔經部拘摩羅邏多（唐言童受）論師於此製述諸論。
translation: Twelve or thirteen li to the north of the city is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a divine light, and there are many accounts of people seeing and hearing divine flowers and celestial music. I have heard from the records of former sages that recently a woman suffering from malignant leprosy came secretly to the stupa to reproach herself and perform repentance. Seeing that the courtyard was covered in filth, she cleared it away, swept and sprinkled the ground, smeared it with incense, scattered flowers, and gathered blue lotuses to spread over the ground again. Her malignant disease was cured, her appearance became more beautiful, and her body emitted a famous fragrance, as fragrant as the blue lotus. This is a sacred site where the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king named Candraprabha (戰達羅鉢剌婆; in Tang language, "Moonlight"). With a determined quest for bodhi, he severed his head as an act of charity. He underwent such sacrifices for a thousand lifetimes. Beside the Śīrṣa-stūpa (捨頭窣堵波; "Stupa of the Severed Head") is a monastery with a desolate courtyard and few monks. In the past, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (拘摩羅邏多; in Tang language, "Child-Received") composed various treatises here.

t2087_text: 城外東南，南山之陰有窣堵波，高百餘尺，是無憂王太子拘浪拏為繼母所誣抉目之處，無憂王所建也。盲人祈請，多有復明。此太子正后生也，儀貌妍雅，慈仁夙著。正后終沒，繼室憍婬，縱其惛愚，私逼太子。太子瀝泣引責，退身謝罪。繼母見違，彌增忿怒，候王閑隙，從容言曰：「夫呾叉始羅，國之要領，非親子弟，其可寄乎？今者，太子仁孝著聞，親賢之故，物議斯在。」王或聞說，雅悅姦謀，即命太子，而誡之曰：「吾承餘緒，垂統繼業，唯恐失墜，忝負先王。呾叉始羅國之襟帶，吾今命爾作鎮彼國。國事殷重，人情詭雜，無妄去就，有虧基緒。凡有召命，驗吾齒印。印在吾口，其有謬乎？」於是太子銜命來鎮。歲月雖淹，繼室彌怒，詐發制書，紫泥封記，候王眠睡，竊齒為印，馳使而往，賜以責書。輔臣跪讀，相顧失圖。太子問曰：「何所悲乎？」曰：「大王有命，書責太子，抉去兩目，逐棄山谷，任其夫妻，隨時生死。雖有此命，尚未可依。今宜重請，面縛待罪。」太子曰：「父而賜死，其可辭乎？齒印為封，誠無謬矣。」命旃荼羅抉去其眼。眼既失明，乞貸自濟，流離展轉，至父都城。其妻告曰：「此是王城。嗟乎，飢寒良苦！昔為王子，今作乞人！願得聞知，重申先責。」於是謀計，入王內廐，於夜後分，泣對清風，長嘯悲吟，箜篌鼓和。王在高樓，聞其雅唱，辭甚怨悲，怪而問曰：「箜篌歌聲，似是吾子，今以何故而來此乎？」即問內廐：「誰為歌嘯？」遂將盲人，而來對旨。王見太子，銜悲問曰：「誰害汝身，遭此禍釁？愛子喪明，猶自不覺，凡百黎元，如何究察？天乎，天乎，何德之衰！」太子悲泣，謝而對曰：「誠以不孝，負責於天，某年日月，忽奉慈旨，無由致辭，不敢逃責。」其王心知繼室為不軌也，無所究察，便加刑辟。時菩提樹伽藍有瞿沙（唐言妙音）大阿羅漢者，四辯無礙，三明具足。王將盲子，陳告其事，唯願慈悲，令得復明。時彼羅漢受王請已，即於是日宣令國人：「吾於後日，欲說妙理，人持一器，來此聽法，以盛泣淚也。」於是遠近相趨，士女雲集。是時阿羅漢說十二因緣，凡厥聞法，莫不悲耿，以所持器，盛其瀝泣。說法既已，總收眾淚，置之金盤，而自誓曰：「凡吾所說，諸佛至理。理若不真，說有紕繆，斯則已矣；如其不爾，願以眾淚，洗彼盲眼，眼得復明，明視如昔。」發是語訖，持淚洗眼，眼遂復明。王乃責彼輔臣，詰諸僚佐，或黜或放，或遷或死。諸豪世俗移居雪山東北沙磧之中。
translation: To the southeast of the city, on the northern side of the South Hill, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the place where his son, Prince Kuṇāla (拘浪拏), had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother. Blind people who pray here often have their sight restored. This prince was the son of the first queen; he was elegant in appearance and had long been renowned for his kindness and benevolence. After the first queen passed away, the stepmother, who was arrogant and lewd, gave free rein to her muddled stupidity and privately attempted to seduce the prince. The prince wept, took the blame upon himself, and withdrew to apologize for his perceived offense. Seeing her advances rejected, the stepmother’s fury intensified. Waiting for a moment when the king was at leisure, she said composedly, "Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅) is a strategic key to the kingdom; can it be entrusted to anyone other than a close royal scion? Now, the prince is known for his benevolence and filial piety, and because he is both a relative and a man of virtue, public opinion favors him." The king, deluded, heard her and was pleased by the treacherous scheme; he immediately summoned the prince and admonished him, saying, "I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors to continue their rule, and I live in constant fear of losing it and thereby bringing shame upon the late kings. Takṣaśilā is the throat and belt of the kingdom, and I now appoint you to govern that country. The affairs of the state are heavy and complex, and the sentiments of the people are devious and mixed; do not act rashly or carelessly, lest you damage the foundation of our inheritance. Whenever there is a summons, verify it with my tooth-seal. The seal is in my mouth; how could there be any error?" Thereupon, the prince accepted the command and came to govern. As time passed, the stepmother’s anger grew; she forged a royal decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while the king was sleeping, she stole his teeth to make the impression, then dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of condemnation. The assisting ministers knelt to read it, looking at one another in dismay. The prince asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?" They replied, "The Great King has issued a command, a written decree reprimanding the prince, ordering that your two eyes be gouged out and that you be exiled and abandoned in the mountain valleys, leaving you and your wife to live or die as fate decides. Although this command exists, it should not yet be obeyed. We should now request a confirmation, and you should present yourself bound to await your punishment." The prince said, "If a father grants death to his son, how can it be refused? The tooth-seal serves as the signet; truly, there can be no error." He ordered a Caṇḍāla to gouge out his eyes. Once his eyes were blinded, he begged for alms to sustain himself, wandering from place to place until he reached his father’s capital city. His wife said to him, "This is the royal city. Alas, the suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter! Once a prince, now a beggar! I wish for us to make this known and have the previous charge re-examined." Thereupon, they devised a plan to enter the king’s inner stables. In the final watch of the night, weeping as he faced the clear breeze, he sang out in a long, mournful wail, accompanying himself on the konghou (harp). From his high pavilion, the king heard the elegant singing, the lyrics of which were deeply resentful and sorrowful; wondering at it, he asked, "The sound of the singing to the konghou seems to be that of my son; for what reason has he come here?" He immediately asked the inner stables, "Who is singing and wailing?" They then brought the blind man before the king. Seeing the prince, the king asked with suppressed grief, "Who has harmed your body and brought this calamity upon you? My beloved son has lost his sight, yet I remained unaware; how then can I investigate the affairs of all the common people? O Heaven, O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!" The prince wept piteously and replied in apology, "It is truly because of my lack of filial piety that I have incurred the blame of Heaven. On a certain day of a certain month, I suddenly received your compassionate edict; having no way to voice my plea, I did not dare to evade my responsibility." The king, in his heart, knew that his new queen had acted wickedly, but without further investigation, he immediately imposed a severe punishment. At that time, in the Bodhi-tree (菩提樹) monastery, there was a great Arhat named Ghoṣa (瞿沙; Tang language: "Sublime Sound"), who possessed unobstructed mastery of the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three insights. The king brought his blind son to him, explained the situation, and prayed only for his compassion to restore the prince's sight. Having accepted the king's request, the Arhat immediately announced to the people of the country on that very day, "On a coming day, I wish to preach the sublime truth. Let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the Dharma, so as to collect your tears." Thereupon, people from near and far hastened to the site, and men and women gathered like clouds. At that time, the Arhat preached on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Among all those who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, and they used the vessels they carried to collect their falling tears. When the preaching was finished, he collected all the tears and placed them in a golden basin, then made a vow, saying, "All that I have spoken is the ultimate truth of the Buddhas. If this truth is not genuine and my teaching contains errors, then so be it; but if it is not so, I wish to wash these blind eyes with the tears of the multitude, so that his sight may be restored and he may see as clearly as before." Having spoken these words, he took the tears and washed the eyes, and the eyes were immediately restored to sight. The king then rebuked his ministers and interrogated his officials; some were dismissed, some were banished, some were demoted, and some were put to death. The powerful and wealthy families were moved to the sandy desert to the northeast of the Snow Mountains.

t2087_text: 從此東南越諸山谷，行七百餘里，至僧訶補羅國（北印度境）。僧訶補羅國，周三千五六百里，西臨信度河。國大都城周十四五里，依山據嶺，堅峻險固。農務少功，地利多獲。氣序寒，人性猛，俗尚驍勇，又多譎詐。國無君長主位，役屬迦濕彌羅國。
translation: From here, traveling southeast across various mountains and valleys for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Siṃhapura (僧訶補羅國) (in the territory of Northern India). The country of Siṃhapura is three thousand five or six hundred li in circuit and borders the Indus River (信度河) to the west. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it relies on the mountains and occupies the ridges, making it firm, steep, and impregnable. Agriculture requires little labor, yet the land yields abundant harvests. The climate is cold, the people are fierce by nature, their customs prize bravery, and they are also often deceitful. The country has no sovereign ruler and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國).

t2087_text: 城東南四五十里至石窣堵波，無憂王建也，高二百餘尺。池沼十數，映帶左右，雕石為岸，殊形異類。激水清流，汩淴漂注，龍魚水族，窟穴潛泳，四色蓮華，彌漫清潭。百果具繁，同榮異色，林沼交映，誠可遊玩。傍有伽藍，久絕僧侶。窣堵波側不遠，有白衣外道本師悟所求理初說法處，今有封記，傍建天祠。其徒苦行，晝夜精勤，不遑寧息。本師所說之法，多竊佛經之義，隨類設法，擬則軌儀。大者謂苾芻，小者稱沙彌。威儀律行，頗同僧法。唯留少髮，加之露形，或有所服，白色為異，據斯流別，稍用區分。其天師像，竊類如來，衣服為差，相好無異。
translation: Forty or fifty li to the southeast of the city, one reaches a stone stupa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high. There are more than ten ponds surrounding it on the left and right, with banks carved from stone in various shapes and kinds. The clear water surges and flows, gurgling and splashing; dragons, fish, and other aquatic creatures swim deep within their underwater grottoes, while lotus flowers of four colors cover the clear pools. A hundred kinds of fruit trees grow in abundance, flourishing together in different colors; the woods and ponds reflect one another, truly a place for recreation. Beside it is a monastery, long since devoid of monks. Not far from the side of the stupa is the place where the original teacher of the white-robed heretics realized the principles he sought and first preached his doctrine; there is now a memorial mark there, and a deva temple has been built beside it. His followers practice austerities, diligent day and night, without a moment of rest. The doctrine preached by their original teacher largely steals the meaning of the Buddhist sutras, establishing methods according to their own kind and imitating the rules and rituals. The elders are called bhikṣu (苾芻), and the juniors are called śrāmaṇera (沙彌). Their deportment and monastic discipline are quite similar to the Buddhist laws. They differ only in that they retain a small amount of hair, go naked, or, if they do wear clothing, it is white, which serves to distinguish them from other sects. Their image of the heavenly teacher is surreptitiously modeled after the Tathāgata; the clothing is different, but the auspicious marks are no different.

t2087_text: 從此復還呾叉始羅國北界，渡信度河，南東行二百餘里，度大石門，昔摩訶薩埵王子，於此投身飤餓烏擇（音徒）。其南百四五十步有石窣堵波，摩訶薩埵愍餓獸之無力也，行至此地，乾竹自刺，以血啗之，於是乎獸乃噉焉。其中地土，洎諸草木，微帶絳色，猶血染也。人履其地，若負芒刺，無云疑信，莫不悲愴。
translation: From here, I returned to the northern border of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), crossed the Indus River (信度河), and traveled southeast for more than two hundred li, passing through a great stone gate. This is the place where, in the past, Prince Mahāsattva sacrificed his body to feed a starving tigress (The sound is *tú*). About one hundred and forty or fifty paces to the south is a stone stūpa. Pitying the starving beast for its lack of strength, the Mahāsattva had come to this spot, pierced himself with a dry bamboo splinter, and fed it his blood, whereupon the beast devoured him. The soil of this place, as well as the plants and trees, is slightly reddish in color, as if stained with blood. When people tread upon this ground, they feel as if they are carrying thorns on their backs; regardless of whether they are skeptical or faithful, none can help but feel a sense of profound grief.

translation: To the north of the site of the body-sacrifice, there is a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is carved with extraordinary craftsmanship and often illuminates with divine light. Small stūpas and various stone niches, numbering in the hundreds, surround this sacred precinct; those who suffer from illnesses are often cured after circumambulating it. To the east of the stone stūpa is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.

translation: From here, traveling east for more than fifty li, one reaches a solitary hill (孤山). There is a monastery (saṃghārāma) there with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and the springs and ponds are as clear as mirrors. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which marks the spot where the Tathāgata in the past converted an evil yakṣa, commanding him to cease eating meat.

t2087_text: 從此東南行五百餘里，至烏剌尸國（北印度境）。烏剌尸國，周二千餘里，山阜連接，田疇隘狹。國大都城周七八里，無大君長，役屬迦隰彌羅國。宜稼穡，少華果。氣序溫和，微有霜雪。俗無禮義，人性剛猛，多行詭詐，不信佛法。大城西南四五里有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王所建也。傍有伽藍，僧徒寡少，並皆學大乘法教。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Uraśā (烏剌尸國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Uraśā is more than two thousand li in circuit; the mountains and hills are connected, and the fields are narrow. The capital city of the country is seven or eight li in circuit; it has no great sovereign ruler and is a dependency of the country of Kaśmīra (迦隰彌羅國). It is suitable for agriculture, but there are few flowers or fruits. The climate is mild, with slight frost and snow. The customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people’s nature is fierce and violent, they often practice deceit, and they do not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma. Four or five li to the southwest of the great city is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Beside it is a saṃghārāma (伽藍) with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

從此東南，登山履險，度鐵橋，行千餘里，至迦濕彌羅國（舊曰罽賓，訛也。北印度境）。迦濕彌羅國，周七千餘里。四境負山，山極陗峻，雖有門徑，而復隘狹，自古隣敵無能攻伐。國大都城西臨大河，南北十二三里，東西四五里。宜稼穡，多花果，出龍種馬及欝金香、火珠、藥草。氣序寒勁，多雪少風。服毛褐，衣白㲲。土俗輕僄，人多怯懦。國為龍護，遂雄隣境。容貌妍美，情性詭詐。好學多聞，邪正兼信。伽藍百餘所，僧徒五千餘人。有四窣堵波，並無憂王建也，各有如來舍利升餘。《國志》曰：國地本龍池也。昔佛世尊自烏仗那國降惡神已，欲還中國，乘空當此國上，告阿難曰：「我涅槃之後，有末田底迦阿羅漢，當於此地建國安人，弘揚佛法。」如來寂滅之後第五十年，阿難弟子末田底迦羅漢者，得六神通，具八解脫，聞佛懸記，心自慶悅，便來至此，於大山嶺，宴坐林中，現大神變。龍見深信，請資所欲。阿羅漢曰：「願於池內，惠以容膝。」龍王於是縮水奉施。羅漢神通廣身，龍王縱力縮水，池空水盡，龍飜請地。阿羅漢於此西北為留一池，周百餘里；自餘枝屬，別居小池。龍王曰：「池地總施，願恒受供。」末田底迦曰：「我今不久無餘涅槃，雖欲受請，其可得乎？」龍王重請：「五百羅漢常受我供，乃至法盡，法盡之後，還取此國以為居池。」末田底迦從其所請。時阿羅漢既得其地，運大神通力，立五百伽藍。於諸異國買鬻賤人，以充役使，以供僧眾。末田底迦入寂滅後，彼諸賤人自立君長，隣境諸國鄙其賤種，莫與交親，謂之訖利多（唐言買得）。今時泉水已多流濫。摩揭陀國無憂王以如來涅槃之後第一百年，命世君臨，威被殊俗。深信三寶，愛育四生。時有五百羅漢僧、五百凡夫僧，王所敬仰，供養無差。有凡夫僧摩訶提婆（唐言大天），闊達多智，幽求名實，潭思作論，理違聖教，凡有聞知，群從異議。無憂王不識凡、聖，同情所好，黨援所親，召集僧徒赴殑伽河，欲沈深流，總從誅戮。時諸羅漢既逼命難，咸運神通，凌虛履空，來至此國，山棲谷隱。時無憂王聞而懼，躬來謝過，請還本國。彼諸羅漢確不從命。無憂王為羅漢建五百僧伽藍，總以此國持施眾僧。健馱邏國迦膩色迦王，以如來涅槃之後第四百年，應期撫運，王風遠被，殊俗內附。機務餘暇，每習佛經，日請一僧入宮說法，而諸異議部執不同。王用深疑，無以去惑。時脇尊者曰：「如來去世，歲月逾邈，弟子部執，師資異論，各據聞見，共為矛楯。」時王聞已，甚用感傷，悲歎良久，謂尊者曰：「猥以餘福，聿遵前緒，去聖雖遠，猶為有幸，敢忘庸鄙，紹隆法教，隨其部執，具釋三藏。」脇尊者曰：「大王宿殖善本，多資福祐，留情佛法，是所願也。」王乃宣令遠近，召集聖哲。於是四方輻湊，萬里星馳，英賢畢萃，叡聖咸集。七日之中，四事供養。既欲法議，恐其諠雜。王乃具懷白諸僧曰：「證聖果者住，具結縛者還。」如此尚眾。又重宣令：「無學人住，有學人還。」猶復繁多。又更下令：「具三明、備六通者住，自餘各還。」然尚繁多。又更下令：「其有內窮三藏、外達五明者住，自餘各還。」於是得四百九十九人。王欲於本國，苦其暑濕，又欲就王舍城大迦葉波結集石室。脇尊者等議曰：「不可。彼多外道，異論糺紛，酬對不暇，何功作論？眾會之心，屬意此國。此國四周山固，藥叉守衛，土地膏腴，物產豐盛，賢聖之所集往，靈僊之所遊止。」眾議斯在，僉曰：「允諧。」其王是時與諸羅漢自彼而至，建立伽藍，結集三藏，欲作《毘婆沙論》。是時尊者世友，戶外納衣。諸阿羅漢謂世友曰：「結使未除，淨議乖謬，爾宜遠迹，勿居此也。」世友曰：「諸賢於法無疑，代佛施化，方集大義，欲製正論。我雖不敏，粗達微言，三藏玄文、五明至理，頗亦沈研，得其趣矣。」諸羅漢曰：「言不可以若是。汝宜屏居，疾證無學，已而會此，時未晚也。」世友曰：「我顧無學，其猶涕唾，志求佛果，不趨小徑。擲此縷丸，未墜于地，必當證得無學聖果。」時諸羅漢重訶之曰：「增上慢人，斯之謂也。無學果者，諸佛所讚，宜可速證，以決眾疑。」於是世友即擲縷丸，空中諸天接縷丸而請曰：「方證佛果，次補慈氏，三界特尊，四生攸賴，如何於此欲證小果？」時諸羅漢見是事已，謝咎推德，請為上座，凡有疑議，咸取決焉。是五百賢聖，先造十萬頌《鄔波第鑠論》（舊曰《優波提舍論》，訛也）。釋《素呾纜藏》（舊曰《修多羅藏》，訛也）。次造十萬頌《毘柰耶毘婆沙論》，釋《毘奈耶藏》（舊曰《毘那耶藏》，訛也）。後造十萬頌《阿毘達磨毘婆沙論》，釋《阿毘達磨藏》（或曰《阿毘曇藏》，略也）。凡三十萬頌，九百六十萬言，備釋三藏，懸諸千古，莫不窮其枝葉，究其淺深，大義重明，微言再顯，廣宣流布，後進賴焉。迦膩色迦王遂以赤銅為鍱，鏤寫論文，石函緘封，建窣堵波，藏於其中。命藥叉神周衛其國，不令異學持此論出，欲求習學，就中受業。於是功既成畢，還軍本都。出此國西門之外，東面而跪，復以此國總施僧徒。迦膩色迦王既死之後，訖利多種復自稱王，斥逐僧徒，毀壞佛法。覩貨邏國呬摩呾羅王（唐言雪山下），其先釋種也。以如來涅槃之後第六百年，光有疆土，嗣膺王業，樹心佛地，流情法海。聞訖利多毀滅佛法，招集國中敢勇之士，得三千人，詐為商旅，多齎寶貨，挾隱軍器，來入此國。此國之君，特加賓禮。商旅之中，又更選募，得五百人，猛烈多謀，各袖利刃，俱持重寶，躬齎所奉，持以獻上。時雪山下王去其帽，即其座，訖利多王驚懾無措，遂斬其首，令群下曰：「我是覩邏國雪山下王也。怒此賤種公行虐政，故於今者誅其有罪。凡百眾庶，非爾之辜。」然其國輔宰臣，遷於異域。既平此國，召集僧徒，式建伽藍，安堵如故。復於此國西門之外，東面而跪，持施眾僧。其訖利多種屢以僧徒覆宗滅祀，世積其怨，嫉惡佛法。歲月既遠，復自稱王。故今此國不甚崇信，外道天祠，特留意焉。
translation: From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) (formerly called Jibin [罽賓], which is a corruption; it is in the territory of Northern India). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to attack or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west, measuring twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, abounds in flowers and fruits, and produces dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (白㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it has become powerful among its neighbors. The people are beautiful in appearance but deceitful in nature. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas, all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air and, upon reaching the space above this country, said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a kingdom in this land, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda, having attained the six supernatural powers and possessing the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of the great mountain range (大山), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, having developed deep faith, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within this lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king thereupon caused the water to recede and offered the land to him. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; when the lake was empty and the water exhausted, the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him in the northwest of this place, measuring one hundred and more li in circumference; the rest of his kin and dependents were to dwell in smaller pools separately. The dragon king said, "I have bestowed the entire lake and land upon you; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling pool." Madhyāntika acceded to his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased people of low status from various other countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-status people established their own leader. The neighboring countries despised their lowly caste and would not intermarry with them, calling them Kṛta (translated into Chinese as "bought"). At the present time, the spring water has already overflowed in many places. In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne and ruled the world; his majesty extended to distant lands. He had deep faith in the Three Jewels and cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. There was an ordinary monk named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆; translated into Chinese as "Great Heaven" [大天]), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent. He sought deeply into name and reality and composed a treatise through profound reflection that contradicted the holy teachings; those who heard of it followed his heterodox views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he liked and sided with those close to him; he summoned the monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all. When the arhats were faced with this mortal danger, they all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, coming to this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. The arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (伽藍) for the arhats and bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. In the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) ascended the throne in accordance with the prophesied time; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs came to submit to his rule. In his leisure time from state affairs, he would study the Buddhist scriptures, daily inviting a monk to the palace to expound the Dharma. However, the various schools held divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, finding no way to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. Venturing to forget my own unworthiness, I wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire." The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they gathered from the four directions, traveling like stars across ten thousand miles; the brilliant and the wise all assembled. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a doctrinal discussion, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his thoughts to the monks, saying: "Those who have attained the fruits of sainthood may stay; those who are still bound by worldly fetters shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." Still, they were numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights and are equipped with the six supernatural powers may stay; all others shall return." Yet, they were still numerous. He issued another order: "Those who have internally mastered the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) and externally attained the Five Sciences (pañcavidyā) may stay; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine people were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, but he was troubled by its heat and humidity; he also wished to go to the stone cave in Rājagṛha where Mahākāśyapa had conducted the council. The Venerable Pārśva and the others deliberated, saying: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose the treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by yakṣas, its land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals roam and dwell." The assembly deliberated on this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the arhats arrived from there, established a monastery, and compiled the Tripiṭaka, intending to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra was outside the door mending his robes. The arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) are not yet removed, and your pure deliberations are erroneous; you should go far away and not stay here." Vasumitra replied: "You worthies have no doubts regarding the Dharma; you act on behalf of the Buddha to transform others, and are now gathering the great meaning, wishing to compose a correct treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the Five Sciences, and have grasped their essence." The arhats said: "Words cannot be like this. You should withdraw and dwell apart, quickly attain the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said, "I regard the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa) as I would spit or mucus; my aspiration is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, not to pursue the lesser path. I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly attain the holy fruit of 'no-learning'." At that time, the arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride. The fruit of 'no-learning' is praised by all Buddhas; you should attain it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra threw the ball of thread. The devas in the air caught the ball of thread and pleaded, "You are about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will next succeed Maitreya (慈氏); as the most honored one in the three realms and the one upon whom all beings of the four births depend, why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairperson; whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final. These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) (The old name, *Upadeśa-śāstra* (優波提舍論), is a corruption) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏) (The old name, *Sūtra-piṭaka* (修多羅藏), is a corruption). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏) (The old name, *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘那耶藏), is a corruption). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏) (Or it is called *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘曇藏), which is an abbreviation). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa to store them inside. He commanded Yakṣa deities to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out; those who wished to study them were to receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned his army to his capital. He went outside the western gate of this country, knelt facing east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka passed away, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again claimed the kingship, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅王) (In the language of the Tang, "under the snow mountains") in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess vast territories and inherited the royal enterprise; he planted his heart in the soil of the Buddha and poured his sentiments into the sea of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta had destroyed the Buddha-dharma, he gathered three thousand brave warriors from his country, disguised them as merchants, and, carrying many precious goods while concealing weapons, entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and carried heavy treasures, personally bearing their offerings to present them to the king. At that moment, the King of Himatala (雪山下王) removed his cap and took the throne. The King of the Kṛta (訖利多王) was paralyzed with terror, whereupon the king beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra (覩邏國). I am enraged by this base race’s public practice of tyrannical government, and therefore I have executed the guilty one today. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign territory. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monks, established monasteries, and restored peace and order as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and offered alms to the assembly of monks. Because the Kṛta tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of sacrifices on account of the monks, they had accumulated resentment for generations and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, this country does not hold the faith in high esteem today, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist gods.

t2087_text: 新城東南十餘里，故城北，大山陽，有僧伽藍，僧徒三百餘人。其窣堵波中有佛牙，長可寸半，其色黃白，或至齋日時放光明。昔訖利多種之滅佛法也，僧徒解散，各隨利居。有一沙門，遊諸印度，觀禮聖迹，申其至誠。後聞本國平定，即事歸途，遇諸群象，橫行草澤，奔馳震吼。沙門見已，昇樹以避。是時群象相趨奔赴，競吸池水，浸漬樹根，互共排掘，樹遂蹎仆。既得沙門，負載而行，至大林中，有病象瘡痛而臥，引此僧手，至所苦處，乃枯竹所刺也。沙門於是拔竹傅藥，裂其裳，裹其足。別有大象，持金函授與病象，象既得已，轉授沙門，沙門開函，乃佛牙也。諸象圍繞，僧出無由。明日齋時，各持異果，以為中饌。食已，載僧出林，數百里外，方乃下之，各跪拜而去。沙門至國西界，渡一駛河，濟乎中流，船將覆沒。同舟之人互相謂曰：「今此船覆，禍是沙門；必有如來舍利，諸龍利之。」船主檢驗，果得佛牙。時沙門舉佛牙俯謂龍曰：「吾今寄汝，不久來取。」遂不渡河，迴船而去，顧河歎曰：「吾無禁術，龍畜所欺！」重往印度，學禁龍法。三歲之後，復還本國，至河之濱，方設壇場，其龍於是捧佛牙函以授沙門。沙門持歸，於此伽藍，而修供養。
translation: More than ten *li* southeast of the new city, north of the old city, and on the sunny side of the great mountain, there is a monastery with over three hundred monks. In its stupa is a Buddha’s tooth, about an inch and a half long and yellowish-white in color, which sometimes emits light on fast days. In the past, when the Kṛtīya (訖利多) race destroyed the Buddha’s Dharma, the monks dispersed, each living where they found it convenient. There was one śramaṇa who traveled through the various regions of India to observe and pay homage to the sacred sites, expressing his utmost sincerity. Later, hearing that his home country had been pacified, he set out on his return journey. He encountered a herd of elephants moving across the marshes, rushing about and roaring thunderously. Seeing this, the śramaṇa climbed a tree to avoid them. At that time, the elephants rushed together, vied with each other to suck up pond water to soak the roots of the tree, and then collectively pushed and dug at it until the tree finally toppled over. Having captured the śramaṇa, they carried him on their backs into a great forest, where a sick elephant lay suffering from a sore; it led the monk's hand to the afflicted spot, which had been pierced by a piece of withered bamboo. The śramaṇa then pulled out the bamboo, applied medicine, tore his robe, and wrapped the elephant's foot. Another large elephant brought a golden casket and gave it to the sick elephant, who, upon receiving it, passed it to the śramaṇa; when the śramaṇa opened the casket, he found it contained a Buddha’s tooth. The elephants surrounded him, and the monk had no way to leave. The next day at the time of the midday meal, they each brought exotic fruits to serve as his meal. After he had eaten, they carried the monk out of the forest, and only after traveling several hundred *li* did they set him down, whereupon each knelt in worship and departed. The śramaṇa reached the western border of the country and crossed a rapid river; when he reached midstream, the boat was on the verge of capsizing. Those sharing the boat said to one another, "The cause of this boat's impending disaster is this śramaṇa; he must possess a relic of the Tathāgata, and the dragons covet it." The boatman searched and indeed found a Buddha’s tooth. Then the śramaṇa held up the Buddha’s tooth and, looking down, said to the dragon, "I now entrust this to you, and shall return before long to take it back." He did not cross the river, but turned the boat back and departed; looking at the river, he sighed and said, "Because I lack the arts of subdual, I have been deceived by a dragon beast!" He went again to India to learn the methods for subduing dragons. After three years, he returned to his own country; when he reached the riverbank and set up an altar, the dragon then held up the casket of the Buddha’s tooth and presented it to the śramaṇa. The śramaṇa took it back and, at this saṃghārāma (伽藍), performed offerings.

t2087_text: 小伽藍東南三十餘里，至大山，有故伽藍，形製宏壯，蕪漫良甚，今唯一隅起小重閣。僧徒三十餘人，並學大乘法教。昔僧伽跋陀羅（唐言眾賢）論師於此製《順正理論》。伽藍左右諸窣堵波，大阿羅漢舍利並在。野獸、山猨採華供養，歲時無替，如承指命。然此山中多諸靈迹，或石壁橫分，峯留馬迹。凡厥此類，其狀譎詭，皆是羅漢、沙彌，群從遊戲，手指麾畫，乘馬往來。遺迹若斯，難以詳述。
translation: Traveling over thirty li southeast from the small monastery, one reaches a great mountain, where there is an old monastery. Its design was once magnificent, but it is now largely overgrown and in ruins, with only a small multi-storied pavilion remaining in one corner. There are over thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings. Formerly, the śāstra-master Saṃghabhadra (in the language of Tang, "Zhongxian" [Mass of the Virtuous]) composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論) here. In the various stūpas around the monastery, the relics of great arhats are preserved. Wild beasts and mountain apes gather flowers to offer them, never failing throughout the seasons, as if following a command. There are many miraculous traces in these mountains; for instance, stone walls are split horizontally, and horse tracks remain upon the peaks. All such phenomena, with their strange and unusual forms, are said to be the result of arhats and novices playing in groups, pointing and gesturing, or riding horses to and fro. Such remaining traces are too numerous to describe in detail.

t2087_text: 佛牙伽藍東十餘里，北山崖間，有小伽藍，是昔索建地羅大論師於此作《眾事分毘婆沙論》。小伽藍中有石窣堵波，高五十餘尺，是阿羅漢遺身舍利也。先有羅漢，形量偉大，凡所飲食，與象同等。時人譏曰：「徒知飽食，安識是非？」羅漢將入寂滅也，告諸人曰：「吾今不久當取無餘，欲說自身所證妙法。」眾人聞之，相更譏笑，咸來集會，共觀得失。時阿羅漢告諸人曰：「吾今為汝說本因緣。此身之前，報受象身，在東印度，居王內廐。是時此國有一沙門，遠遊印度，尋訪聖教諸經典論。時王持我，施與沙門，載負佛經，而至於此。是後不久，尋即命終。乘其載經福力所致，遂得為人，復鍾餘慶，早服染衣，勤求出離，不遑寧居，得六神通，斷三界欲。然其所食，餘習尚然，每自節身，三分食一。」雖有此說，人猶未信。即昇虛空，入火光定，身出煙焰，而入寂滅，餘骸墜下，起窣堵波。
translation: More than ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, among the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of shastras Skandhila (索建地羅) once composed the *Prakaraṇapāda-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論). In the small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, which contains the bodily relics of an arhat. Previously, there was an arhat whose physical form was immense, and all that he ate was equal to that of an elephant. The people of the time ridiculed him, saying, "You only know how to eat your fill; how could you understand right from wrong?" When the arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the people, "I shall soon attain the state of no-remainder; I wish to speak of the wonderful Dharma that I have personally realized." When the people heard this, they mocked one another, yet they all gathered together to observe his success or failure. Then the arhat said to the people, "I will now tell you the original cause and condition. Prior to this life, I received the retribution of an elephant's body in East India, where I lived in the king's inner stable. At that time, there was a śramaṇa of this country who traveled far to India to search for the scriptures and treatises of the holy teachings. The king took me and gave me to the śramaṇa to carry the Buddhist scriptures, and in this way, I arrived here. Not long after, I died. By virtue of the merit accumulated through carrying the scriptures, I was born as a human. Furthermore, blessed with remaining fortune, I donned the dyed robes early and diligently sought liberation, never resting, until I attained the six supernatural powers and severed the desires of the three realms. However, regarding what I eat, the residual habit remains; I always restrain myself, eating only one-third of what I once did." Although there was this account, people still did not believe it. He then ascended into the void, entered the fire-light samādhi (火光定), and smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered parinirvāṇa; his remaining bones fell to the ground, and a stūpa (窣堵波) was erected over them.

t2087_text: 從此西南，踰山涉險，行七百餘里，至半笯（奴故反）嗟國（北印度境）。半笯嗟國，周二千餘里。山川多，疇壠狹，穀稼時播，花菓繁茂，多甘蔗，無蒲萄，菴沒羅菓、烏淡跋羅、茂遮等菓，家植成林，珍其味也。氣序溫暑，風俗勇烈。裳服所製，多衣㲲布。人性質直，淳信三寶。伽藍五所，並多荒圮。無大君長，役屬迦濕彌羅國。城北伽藍少有僧徒。伽藍北有石窣堵波，寔多靈異。
translation: From here, traveling southwest for over seven hundred li across mountains and through dangerous terrain, one arrives at the kingdom of Parṇotsa (半笯嗟國) (within the borders of North India). The kingdom of Parṇotsa is over two thousand li in circuit. There are many mountains and rivers, and the arable land is narrow; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits grow in abundance. There is much sugarcane but no grapes; fruit trees such as the āmra (mango), udumbara (cluster fig), and moca (plantain) are planted in groves by every household, as their flavors are highly prized. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and valiant. Regarding their clothing, they mostly wear cotton cloth. The people are honest and straightforward by nature, and they have pure faith in the Three Jewels. There are five monasteries, all of which are mostly ruined and desolate. There is no great sovereign, and the country is subject to the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). In the monastery to the north of the city, there are few monks. To the north of the monastery is a stone stūpa, which manifests many spiritual miracles.

t2087_text: 從此東南行四百餘里，至曷邏闍補羅國（北印度境）。曷邏闍補羅國，周四千餘里。國大都城周十餘里。極險固，多山阜，川原隘狹，地利不豐。土宜氣序，同半笯嗟國。風俗猛烈，人性驍勇。國無君長，役屬迦濕彌羅國。伽藍十所，僧徒寡少。天祠一所，外道甚多。自濫波國至於此土，形貌麁弊，情性猥暴，語言庸鄙，禮義輕薄，非印度之正境，乃邊裔之曲俗。從此東南，下山，渡水，行七百餘里，至磔迦國（北印度境）。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for over four hundred li, one reaches the country of Rājapura (within the borders of North India). The country of Rājapura is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. It is extremely steep and secure, with many mountains and hills; the rivers and plains are narrow and confined, and the land is not fertile. The soil, crops, and climate are the same as in the country of Parṇotsa. The customs are fierce, and the people are brave and valiant. The country has no sovereign and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra. There are ten saṃghārāmas, with few monks. There is one Deva temple, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. From the country of Lampā to this land, the people’s appearance is coarse and ugly, their nature is vulgar and violent, their language is crude and base, and their sense of courtesy and righteousness is slight; this is not the proper territory of India, but a remote frontier with rustic customs. From here, traveling southeast, descending mountains and crossing rivers for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ṭakka (within the borders of North India).

t2087_text: 磔迦國，周萬餘里，東據毘播奢河，西臨信度河。國大都城周二十餘里。宜粳稻，多宿麥，出金、銀、鍮石、銅、鐵。時候暑熱，土多風飆。風俗暴惡，言辭鄙褻。衣服鮮白，所謂憍奢耶衣、朝霞衣等。少信佛法，多事天神。伽藍十所，天祠數百。此國已往，多有福舍，以贍貧匱，或施藥，或施食，口腹之資，行旅無累。
translation: The country of Ṭakka (磔迦國) is over ten thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Vipāśā River to the east and faces the Sindhu River to the west. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much winter wheat; it yields gold, silver, brass, copper, and iron. The climate is hot, and the land is subject to many windstorms. The customs of the people are violent and wicked, and their speech is vulgar and obscene. Their clothing is bright white, consisting of so-called *kauśeya* (silk) garments, *chaoxia* (morning glow) robes, and the like. They have little faith in the Buddhadharma and mostly serve the heavenly deities. There are ten *saṃghārāma*s and several hundred *deva* temples. From this country onward, there are many charitable houses (福舍) to provide for the poor and needy, where medicine or food is distributed; with such provisions for their sustenance, travelers are never in want.

t2087_text: 大城西南十四五里，至奢羯羅故城。垣堵雖壞，基趾尚固。周二十餘里。其中更築小城，周六七里，居人富饒；即此國之故都也。數百年前，有王號摩醯邏矩羅（唐言大族），都治此城，王諸印度。有才智，性勇烈，隣境諸國，莫不臣伏。機務餘閑，欲習佛法，令於僧中推一俊德。時諸僧徒莫敢應命，少欲無為，不求聞達；博學高明，有懼威嚴。是時王家舊僮，染衣已久，辭論清雅，言談贍敏，眾共推舉，而以應命。王曰：「我敬佛法，遠訪名僧，眾推此隸，與我談論。常謂僧中，賢明肩比，以今知之，夫何敬哉？」於是宣令五印度國，繼是佛法並皆毀滅，僧徒斥逐無復孑遺。摩揭陀國婆羅阿迭多王（唐曰幼日），崇敬佛法，愛育黎元，以大族王淫刑虐政，自守疆埸，不恭職貢。時大族王治兵將討。幼日王知其聲問，告諸臣曰：「今聞寇至，不忍鬪其兵也。幸諸僚庶赦而不罪，賜此微軀潛行草澤。」言畢出宮，依緣山野。國中感恩慕從者數萬餘人，棲竄海島。大族王以兵付弟，浮海往伐。幼日王守其阨險，輕騎誘戰，金鼓一震，奇兵四起，生擒大族，反接引現。大族王自愧失道，以衣蒙面。幼日王踞師子床，群官周衛，乃命侍臣告大族曰：「汝露其面，吾欲有辭。」大族對曰：「臣主易位，怨敵相視，既非交好，何用面談？」再三告示，終不從命。於是宣令數其罪曰：「三寶福田，四生攸賴。苟任豺狼，傾毀勝業。福不祐汝，見擒於我。罪無可赦，宜從刑辟。」時幼日王母博聞強識，善達占相。聞殺大族也，疾告幼日王曰：「我甞聞大族奇姿多智，欲一見之。」幼日王命引大族至母宮中。幼日母曰：「嗚呼，大族幸勿恥也！世間無常，榮辱更事，吾猶汝母，汝若吾子，宜去蒙衣，一言面對。」大族曰：「昔為敵國之君，今為俘囚之虜，隳廢王業，亡滅宗祀，上愧先靈，下慚黎庶，誠恥面目。俯仰天地，不勝自喪，故此蒙衣。」王母曰：「興廢隨時，存亡有運。以心齊物，則得喪俱忘；以物齊心，則毀譽更起。宜信業報，與時推移，去蒙對語，或存軀命。」大族謝曰：「苟以不才，嗣膺王業，刑政失道，國祚亡滅，雖在縲紲之中，尚貪旦夕之命。敢承大造，面謝厚恩。」於是去蒙衣，出其面。王母曰：「子其自愛，當終爾壽。」已而告幼日王曰：「先典有訓，宥過好生。今大族王積惡雖久，餘福未盡，若殺此人，十二年中，菜色相視。然有中興之氣，終非大國之王，當據北方，有小國土。」幼日王承慈母之命，愍失國之君，娉以稚女，待以殊禮，總其遺兵，更加衛從，未出海島。大族王弟還國自立，大族失位，藏竄山野，北投迦濕彌羅國。迦濕彌羅王深加禮命，愍以失國，封以土邑。歲月既淹，率其邑人，矯殺迦濕彌羅王而自尊立。乘其戰勝之威，西討健馱邏國，潛兵伏甲，遂殺其王，國族大臣，誅鋤殄滅。毀窣堵波，廢僧伽藍，凡一千六百所。兵殺之外，餘有九億人，皆欲誅戮，無遺噍類。時諸輔佐咸進諫曰：「大王威懾強敵，兵不交鋒，誅其首惡。黎庶何咎？願以微躬，代所應死。」王曰：「汝信佛法，崇重冥福，擬成佛果，廣說本生，欲傳我惡於未來世乎？汝宜復位，勿有再辭。」於是以三億上族，臨信度河流殺之；三億中族，下沈信度河流殺之；三億下族，分賜兵士，於是持其亡國之貨，振旅而歸。曾未改歲，尋即徂落。于時，雲霧冥晦，大地震動，暴風奮發。時證果人愍而歎曰：「枉殺無辜，毀滅佛法，墮無間獄，流轉未已。」奢羯羅故城中有一伽藍，僧徒百餘人，並學小乘法。世親菩薩昔於此中製《勝義諦論》。其側窣堵波，高二百餘尺，過去四佛於此說法。又有四佛經行遺迹之所。伽藍西北五六里，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也，是過去四佛說法之處。新都城東北十餘里，至石窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也，是如來往北方行化中路止處。《印度記》曰：「窣堵波中有多舍利，或有齋日，時放光明。」
translation: Fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southwest of the great city, one reaches the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is over twenty *li* in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven *li* in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅) (translated as "Great Clan" in Chinese), who made this city his capital and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the monks dared not respond to the order, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, there was a former servant of the royal household who had long worn the dyed robes (i.e., was a monk), whose rhetoric was refined and elegant, and whose speech was eloquent and quick; the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the order. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet the assembly recommends this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that among the monks, the wise and brilliant were comparable; now that I know this, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and all monks were to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) (translated as "Young Sun" in Chinese) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved his people; because of King Mihirakula’s excessive punishments and tyrannical rule, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula mobilized his troops, intending to punish him. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, and I shall take this humble body and hide in the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and forests. Several tens of thousands of people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and sailed across the sea to attack him. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face, for I have words for you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies; since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You have acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unpardonable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, and she was highly skilled in physiognomy. Hearing that he was about to execute Mihirakula, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mihirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mihirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I cover my face."  The king's mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; existence and extinction have their destiny. If you use the mind to equalize things, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you use things to equalize the mind, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times. Remove your covering and speak; perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mihirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal throne, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will uncover my face to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The king's mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Soon after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mihirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and suffering. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not ultimately be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother's command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king's remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mihirakula returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mihirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After some time had passed, he led his townspeople, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed one thousand six hundred stūpas and sanghārāmas. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprits. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas; do you wish to transmit my evil deeds to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the bank of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, to transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasaptati* (勝義諦論) here. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site with traces of the four Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to spread his teachings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says, "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."

t2087_text: 從此東行五百餘里，至那僕底國（北印度境）。至那僕底國，周二千餘里。國大都城周十四五里。稼穡滋茂，菓木稀疎。編戶安業，國用豐贍。氣序溫暑，風俗怯弱，學綜真俗，信兼邪正。伽藍十所，天祠八所。昔迦膩色迦王之御宇也，聲振隣國，威被殊俗，河西蕃維，畏威送質。迦膩色迦王既得質子，賞遇隆厚，三時易館，四兵警衛。此國則冬所居也，故曰至那僕底（唐言漢封）。質子所居，因為國號。此境已往，洎諸印度，土無梨、桃，質子所植，因謂桃曰至那爾（唐言漢持來），梨曰至那羅闍弗呾邏（唐言漢王子）。故此國人深敬東土，更相指語：「是我先王本國人也。」
translation: Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are timid and weak. Their studies encompass both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten saṃghārāmas and eight deva temples.  In the past, during the reign of King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王), his reputation shook neighboring countries and his might extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had obtained the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was his winter residence, and therefore it is called Cīnabhukti (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Fief"). Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  From this region onward, as far as the various parts of India, the land had no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) (which in the language of the Tang means "brought from Han"), and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏) (which in the language of the Tang means "Han Prince"). Therefore, the people of this country deeply revere the eastern lands, and they point to one another and say, "These are the people from the original country of our former king."

t2087_text: 大城東南行五百餘里，至答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍（唐言闍林）。僧徒三百餘人，學說一切有部，眾儀肅穆，德行清高，小乘之學特為博究，賢劫千佛皆於此地集天、人眾，說深妙法。釋迦如來涅槃之後第三百年中，有迦多衍那（舊曰迦旃延，訛也）論師者，於此製《發智論》焉。闍林伽藍中有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之處。小窣堵波、諸大石室，鱗次相望，不詳其數，並是劫初已來諸果聖人，於此寂滅，羌難備舉，齒骨猶在。繞山伽藍周二十里，佛舍利窣堵波數百千所，連隅接影。
translation: Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍) (in the Tang language, "Dark Forest"). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their moral conduct is lofty, and they are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gathered assemblies of gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. In the three-hundredth year after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana (formerly called Jiazhanyan [迦旃延], which is erroneous) composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Small stūpas and various large stone chambers stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail; these are all places where the various sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction, and it is difficult to enumerate them all, though their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of stūpas containing the Buddha’s relics, with their corners connected and their shadows touching.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 從此東北行百四五十里，至闍爛達羅國（北印度境）。闍爛達邏國，東西千餘里，南北八百餘里。國大都城周十二三里。宜穀稼，多粳稻，林樹扶疎，華菓茂盛。氣序溫暑，風俗剛烈，容貌鄙陋，家室富饒。伽藍五十餘所，僧徒二千餘人，大小二乘，專門習學。天祠三所，外道五百餘人，並塗灰之侶也。此國先王崇敬外道，其後遇羅漢，聞法信悟。故中印度王體其淳信，五印度國三寶之事，一以總監。混彼此，忘愛惡，督察僧徒，妙窮淑慝。故道德著聞者，竭誠敬仰；戒行虧犯者，深加責罰。聖迹之所，並皆旌建，或窣堵波，或僧伽藍，印度境內，無不周遍。
translation: From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國) (in the territory of North India). The country of Jālaṃdhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is twelve or thirteen li in circumference. It is suitable for grain crops, with an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests and trees are lush and spreading, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are fierce and unyielding, their appearance is coarse and ugly, and their households are wealthy and prosperous. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are three Deva temples, and more than five hundred followers of non-Buddhist paths, all of whom are of the sect that smears themselves with ash.  A former king of this country revered non-Buddhist paths, but later he met an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and enlightenment. Therefore, the king of Mid-India, recognizing his pure faith, entrusted to him the sole supervision of the affairs of the Three Jewels throughout the five Indias. He made no distinction between this and that, forgot preferences and aversions, supervised the monks, and thoroughly discerned the virtuous and the wicked. Thus, those whose moral character was renowned were honored with utmost sincerity, while those who violated the precepts were severely punished. At all sites of sacred traces, he erected memorials, whether stūpas or saṃghārāmas, and there is no place within the territory of India where these are not found.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: the king of Mid-India, emulating his pure faith, took overall charge of the affairs of the Three Jewels → 中印度王體其淳信，五印度國三寶之事，一以總監 'the king of Central India, recognizing his pure faith, entrusted to him (the king of Jālaṃdhara) sole supervision of the affairs of the Three Jewels in the five Indias' – wrong subject (Beal: the king of Mid-India… gave him sole control)

t2087_text: 從此東北，踰峻嶺越，洞谷，經危途，涉險路，行七百餘里，至屈（居勿反）露多國（北印度境）。屈露多國，周三千餘里，山周四境。國大都城周十四五里。土地沃壤，穀稼時播，華果茂盛，卉木滋榮。既隣雪山，遂多珍藥，出金、銀、赤銅及火珠、雨石。氣序逾寒，霜雪微降。人貌麁弊，既癭且尰，性剛猛，尚氣勇。伽藍二十餘所，僧徒千餘人，多學大乘，少習諸部。天祠十五，異道雜居。依巖據嶺，石室相距，或羅漢所居，或仙人所止。國中有窣堵波，無憂王之建也。在昔如來曾至此國。說法度人，遺迹斯記。
translation: From here, traveling northeast, crossing steep ridges, traversing deep valleys, passing over perilous routes, and wading through dangerous paths for more than seven hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) (屈 is read 居勿反) (within the borders of North India). The country of Kulūta is more than three thousand *li* in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The land is fertile, grain is sown in its season, flowers and fruits are abundant, and plants and trees flourish. As it borders the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), it is rich in precious medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-pearls and rain-stones. The climate is extremely cold, and frost and snow fall lightly. The people are coarse and ugly in appearance, and are prone to goiters and swollen feet; their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they value spirit and courage. There are more than twenty *saṃghārāmas* (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), while few practice the various schools (Hīnayāna). There are fifteen *deva* temples, where followers of different paths live together. Relying on cliffs and occupying ridges, stone chambers are situated at intervals, some being dwellings of *arhats* and others being places where *ṛṣis* (仙人) have stayed. In the country there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata came to this country, preached the Dharma to save people, and this record remains of his traces.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

translation: Traveling south from the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) for over seven hundred li, crossing a great mountain and fording a large river, one arrives at the country of Śatadru (設多圖盧國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Śatadru is over two thousand li in circuit and borders a large river to the west. The capital city of the country is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The grain crops are abundant, fruits and produce are plentiful, and there is much gold, silver, and precious pearls. The people’s clothing is fresh and plain, though their garments are elegant and fine. The climate is hot, the customs are honest and harmonious, the people are naturally kind and compliant, and there is order between those of high and low status. They are devoted to the Buddha-Dharma and are sincere and respectful in their faith. Inside and outside the royal city, there are ten saṃghārāmas, but the courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is small. Three or four li to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

t2087_text: 復從此西南行八百餘里，至波理夜呾羅國（中印度境）。波理夜呾羅國，周三千餘里。國大都城周十四五里。宜穀稼，豐宿麥，有異稻種六十日而收穫焉。多牛羊，少華菓。氣序暑熱，風俗剛猛。不尚學藝，信奉外道。王，吠奢種也，性勇烈，多武略。伽藍八所，傾毀已甚，僧徒寡少，習學小乘。天祠十餘所，異道千餘人。
translation: From here, traveling southwest for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Pāriyātra (波理夜呾羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Pāriyātra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; there is a unique variety of rice that is harvested in sixty days. There are many cattle and sheep, but few flowers or fruits. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They do not value learning or the arts, and they believe in and practice non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Vaiśya (吠奢) caste; his nature is brave and fierce, and he possesses much martial strategy. There are eight sanghārāmas, which are in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they study the Hīnayāna. There are more than ten deva temples, and over one thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths.

t2087_text: 從此東行五百餘里，至秣菟羅國（中印度境）。秣菟羅國，周五千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里，土地膏腴，稼穡是務。菴沒羅菓家植成林，雖同一名，而有兩種：小者生青熟黃，大者始終青色。出細班㲲及黃金。氣序暑熱，風俗善順，好修冥福，崇德尚學。伽藍二十餘所，僧徒二千餘人，大小二乘，兼功習學。天祠五所，異道雜居。有三窣堵波，並無憂王所建也。過去四佛遺迹甚多。釋迦如來諸聖弟子遺身窣堵波，謂舍利子（舊曰舍利子，又曰舍利弗，訛略也）、沒特伽羅子（舊曰目乾連，訛也）、布剌拏梅呾麗衍尼弗呾羅、（唐言滿慈子。舊曰彌多羅尼子，訛略也）、鄔波釐、阿難陀、羅怙羅（舊曰羅睺，又曰羅云，皆訛略也），曼殊室利（唐言妙吉祥。舊曰濡首，又曰文殊師利，或言曼殊尸利，譯曰妙德，訛也）諸菩薩窣堵波等。每歲三長及月六齋，僧徒相競，率其同好，齎持供具，多營奇玩，隨其所宗，而致像設。阿毘達磨眾供養舍利子；習定之徒供養沒特伽羅子；誦持經者供養滿慈子；學毘柰耶眾供養鄔波釐；諸苾芻尼供養阿難；未受具戒者供養羅怙羅；其學大乘者供養諸菩薩。是日也，諸窣堵波競修供養，珠幡布列，寶蓋駢羅，香煙若雲，華散如雨，蔽虧日月，震蕩谿谷。國王大臣，修善為務。
translation: From here, traveling east more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Mathurā is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the people are devoted to agriculture. Every household plants mango trees to form groves; although they share the same name, there are two varieties: the small ones are green when raw and yellow when ripe, while the large ones remain green from beginning to end. The country produces fine striped cotton cloth and gold. The climate is hot, and the customs are honest and compliant; the people delight in cultivating merit for the afterlife, and they revere virtue and value learning. There are more than twenty monasteries and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are five *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. There are three *stūpas* that were all built by King Aśoka. There are many traces of the four past Buddhas. There are *stūpas* containing the relics of the holy disciples of the Śākya Tathāgata, namely: Śāriputra (formerly called Shelizi or Shelifu, which are erroneous abbreviations), Maudgalyāyana (formerly called Mujianlian, which is erroneous), Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (called Manci Zi in the Tang language; formerly called Miduoluonizi, which is an erroneous abbreviation), Upāli, Ānanda, Rāhula (formerly called Luohou or Luoyun, both of which are erroneous abbreviations), and Mañjuśrī (called Miaojixiang [妙吉祥] in the Tang language; formerly called Rushou [濡首], also Wenshushili [文殊師利], or sometimes Manshushili [曼殊尸利], translated as 'Wonderful Virtue' [妙德], which is erroneous), and the stūpas of the various Bodhisattvas. During the three long fast months of every year and the six fast days of every month, the members of the Saṅgha compete with one another, leading those of like mind to bring offerings and prepare many rare curiosities, presenting them before the images of their respective patrons. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the Sūtras make offerings to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the various bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various Bodhisattvas. On these days, the various stūpas compete in performing offerings; pearl-adorned banners are arrayed in rows, precious canopies are lined up, smoke from incense is like clouds, and flowers are scattered like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the valleys. The king and his ministers make the cultivation of merit their primary duty.

t2087_text: 城東行五六里，至一山伽藍，疎崖為室，因谷為門，尊者鄔波毱多（唐言近護）之所建也。其中則有如來指爪窣堵波。伽藍北巖間，有石室，高二十餘尺，廣三十餘尺，四寸細籌填積其內。尊者近護說法化導，夫妻俱證羅漢果者，乃下一籌，異室別族，雖證不記。石室東南二十四五里，至大涸池，傍有窣堵波。在昔如來行經此處，時有彌猴，持蜜奉佛，佛令水和，普遍大眾。獼猴喜躍，墮坑而死，乘茲福力，得生人中。池北不遠，大林中有過去四佛經行遺迹。其側有舍利子、沒特伽羅子等千二百五十大阿羅漢習定之處，並建窣堵波，以記遺迹。如來在世，屢遊此國，說法之所，並有封樹。
translation: Traveling five or six *li* to the east of the city, one arrives at a mountain monastery where the cliffs were hollowed out to form chambers and the valleys were utilized as gateways; it was built by the Venerable Upagupta (in the language of the Tang, "Close Protector" [Jinhu]). Within it is a *stūpa* containing the finger-nails of the Tathāgata. In the cliffs to the north of the monastery, there is a stone chamber over twenty *chi* high and thirty *chi* wide, filled with fine bamboo tallies four *cun* in length. When the Venerable Close Protector preached the Dharma and provided guidance, whenever a husband and wife both attained the fruit of an Arhat, he would place one tally inside; those from different households or different clans, even if they attained the fruit, were not recorded. Twenty-four or twenty-five *li* to the southeast of the stone chamber, one reaches a large dried-up pond, beside which stands a *stūpa*. In the past, when the Tathāgata was traveling through this place, there was a monkey who brought honey to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha instructed him to mix it with water and distribute it to the great assembly. The monkey, leaping with joy, fell into a pit and died; by the power of this merit, he was reborn among humans. Not far to the north of the pond, in a large forest, are the remains of the places where the four Buddhas of the past walked in meditation. Beside them is the place where Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and one thousand two hundred and fifty great Arhats practiced meditation; *stūpas* have been built at all these sites to mark the remains. While the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled through this country, and at the places where he preached the Dharma, mounds and trees have been established.

t2087_text: 從此東北行五百餘里，至薩他泥濕伐羅國（中印度境）。薩他泥濕伐羅國，周七千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。土地沃壤，稼穡滋盛。氣序溫暑，風俗澆薄，家室富饒，競為奢侈。深閑幻術，高尚異能。多逐利，少務農，諸方奇貨多聚其國。伽藍三所，僧徒七百餘人，並皆習學小乘法教。天祠百餘所，異道甚多。
translation: From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Sthāneśvara is more than seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot. The customs are degenerate; the households are wealthy and prosperous, and they compete in being extravagant. They are deeply skilled in magical arts and highly esteem extraordinary abilities. They mostly pursue profit and pay little attention to farming; rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are three saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than one hundred deva temples (天祠), and there are many heterodox sects.

t2087_text: 大城四周二百里內，彼土之人謂為福地。聞諸先志曰：昔五印度國二王分治，境壤相侵，干戈不息。兩主合謀，欲決兵戰，以定雌雄，以寧氓俗。黎庶胥怨，莫從君命。王以為眾庶者，難與慮始也，神可動物，權可立功。時有梵志，素知高才，密齎束帛，命入後庭，造作法書，藏諸巖穴。歲月既久，樹皆合拱。王於朝坐，告諸臣曰：「吾以不德，忝居大位，天帝垂照，夢賜靈書，今在某山，藏於某嶺。」於是下令營求，得書山林之下。群官稱慶，眾庶悅豫，宣示遠近，咸使聞知。其大略曰：「夫生死無崖，流轉無極，含靈淪溺，莫由自濟。我以奇謀，令離諸苦。今此王城周二百里，古先帝世福利之地。歲月極遠，銘記堙滅，生靈不悟，遂沈苦海。溺而不救，夫何謂歟？汝諸含識，臨敵兵死，得生人中，多殺無辜，受天福樂，順孫孝子，扶侍親老，經遊此地，獲福無窮。功少福多，如何失利？一喪人身，三途冥漠。是故含生，各務修業！」於是人皆兵戰，視死如歸。王遂下令，招募勇烈，兩國合戰，積屍如莽。迄于今時，遺骸遍野，時既古昔，人骸偉大。國俗相傳，謂之福地。城西北四五里，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。甎皆黃赤色，甚光淨，中有如來舍利一斗，光明時照，神迹多端。
translation: Within a radius of two hundred li around the great city, the people of that land call it the Land of Blessedness (Kurukṣetra). According to the records of former times, the Five Indias were once ruled by two kings; their territories bordered each other and were subject to mutual invasions, with wars never ceasing. The two rulers conspired together, wishing to decide the matter through a decisive battle to determine the victor and bring peace to the populace. The common people were all resentful and would not follow the kings' commands. The kings thought that it is difficult to plan the beginning of an undertaking with the masses, but that the divine can move living beings and authority can establish merit. At that time, there was a Brahman known for his great talent; the king secretly presented him with a gift of silk and ordered him into the rear palace to compose a sacred text, which was then hidden in a mountain cave. As time passed, the trees grew to the size of a man’s embrace. The king sat in court and told his ministers: "Because of my lack of virtue, I unworthily occupy this high position; yet the Emperor of Heaven has looked down upon me and granted me a spiritual book in a dream, which is now located on a certain mountain, hidden on a certain ridge." Thereupon, he issued an order to search for it, and the book was found beneath the mountain forest. The officials offered congratulations, and the masses were joyful; it was proclaimed far and near, so that all might hear and know of it. Its general purport was: "Life and death are without bounds, and the cycle of transmigration is endless; sentient beings are submerged and drowning, with no way to save themselves. I, through a marvelous stratagem, shall cause them to depart from all suffering. Now, this royal city and its surroundings of two hundred li were a land of blessings and merit in the ages of former emperors. As the years and months have been extremely long, the inscriptions and records have been obliterated; living beings do not realize this and have consequently sunk into the sea of suffering. If they are drowning and not saved, what is to be said of it?" "All you sentient beings, if you die facing the enemy in battle, you will be reborn among humans; if you slaughter many of the innocent, you will receive the blessings and joys of heaven; and if obedient grandsons and filial sons who serve their elderly parents travel through this land, they shall obtain infinite blessings. With so little effort yielding such great merit, how could you let this advantage slip away? Once you lose this human body, the three paths (the three lower realms of existence) are dark and obscure. Therefore, let all living beings each apply themselves to their practice!" Thereupon, the people all engaged in battle, viewing death as a return home. The king then issued an order to recruit the brave and fierce; the two kingdoms joined in battle, and the piled-up corpses were like dense grass. Down to the present day, skeletal remains are scattered across the fields; as the events took place in ancient times, the human bones are of a massive size. Local custom passes down the name of this place as the Land of Blessings (Kurukṣetra). Four or five li to the northwest of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). The bricks are all a yellowish-red color and are very bright and clean. Inside is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which emit light from time to time and manifest many divine wonders.
