t2087_text: 從此東北行四百餘里，至窣祿勤那國（中印度境）。窣祿勤那國，周六千餘里，東臨殑伽河，北背大山，閻牟那河中境而流。國大都城周二十餘里，東臨閻牟那河，荒蕪雖甚，基趾尚固。土地所產，風氣所宜，同薩他泥濕伐羅國。人性淳質，宗信外道。貴藝學，尚福慧。伽藍五所，僧徒千餘人，多學小乘，少習餘部。商搉微言，清論玄奧，異方俊彥，尋論稽疑。天祠百所，異道甚多。大城東南閻牟那河西，大伽藍東門外，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔，曾於此處說法度人。其側又一窣堵波，中有如來髮、爪也。舍利子、沒特伽羅諸阿羅漢髮、爪窣堵波，周其左右，數十餘所。如來寂滅之後，此國為諸外道所詿誤焉，信受邪法，捐廢正見。今有五伽藍者，乃異國論師與諸外道及婆羅門論議勝處，因此建焉。
translation: From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Srughna is over six thousand li in circuit; it borders the Ganges (gaṅgā) river to the east, rests against great mountains to the north, and the Yamunā river flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit; it borders the Yamunā river to the east. Although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem both merit and wisdom. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions come here to investigate doctrines and resolve doubts. There are one hundred Deva temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā river and outside the eastern gate of a large monastery, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another stūpa, which contains the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen stūpas containing the hair and nails of the arhats Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅). After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted and followed erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five monasteries that exist today were built at the sites where masters from other countries held debates and emerged victorious over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.

t2087_text: 閻牟那河東行八百餘里，至殑伽河河源，廣三四里，東南流入海處廣十餘里。水色滄浪，波流浩汗，靈怪雖多，不為物害，其味甘美，細沙隨流。彼俗書記，謂之福水，罪咎雖積，沐浴便除；輕命自沈，生天受福；死而投骸，不墮惡趣；揚波激流，亡魂獲濟。時執師子國提婆菩薩深達實相，得諸法性，愍諸愚夫，來此導誘。當是時也，士女咸會，少長畢萃，於河之濱，揚波激流。提婆菩薩和光汲引，俯首反激，狀異眾人。有外道曰：「吾子何其異乎？」提婆菩薩曰：「吾父母親宗在執師子國，恐苦飢渴，冀斯遠濟。」諸外道曰：「吾子謬矣！曾不再思，妄行此事。家國綿邈，山川遼敻，激揚此水，給濟彼飢，其猶却行以求前及，非所聞也。」提婆菩薩曰：「幽途罪累，尚蒙此水；山川雖阻，如何不濟？」時諸外道知難謝屈，捨邪見，受正法，改過自新，願奉教誨。
translation: Traveling over eight hundred *li* east from the Yamunā River, one reaches the source of the Ganges River (Gaṅgā), which is three or four *li* wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten *li* wide. The color of the water is a deep blue, and the waves flow vast and wide. Although there are many spiritual anomalies, they do not harm living beings. Its taste is sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows along with the current. According to the records of the local customs, it is called the "water of merit." Even if one has accumulated sins and transgressions, bathing in it removes them. Those who hold life lightly and drown themselves are reborn in heaven and receive blessings; those who cast their remains into it after death do not fall into the evil paths; and by splashing the waves and agitating the current, the souls of the departed obtain salvation.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) had deeply penetrated the true reality and attained the nature of all phenomena. Pitying these foolish people, he came here to guide and instruct them. At that time, men and women had all gathered, young and old alike, and were splashing the waves and agitating the current on the riverbank. The Bodhisattva Deva, mingling with them to draw the water, lowered his head and pushed the water in the opposite direction, his behavior differing from that of the crowd. A non-Buddhist asked, "Why are you acting so strangely, sir?" The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "My parents and relatives are in the country of Siṃhala. I fear they are suffering from hunger and thirst, and I hope to provide them with relief from afar." The non-Buddhists said, "You are mistaken, sir! You have not thought this through and are performing this act in vain. Your home and country are far away, separated by vast mountains and rivers; to splash this water here to relieve their hunger there is like walking backward to try and reach a destination in front—it is unheard of." The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "If those burdened by sins in the dark paths of the afterlife can still receive the benefit of this water, why should it not reach those separated by mountains and rivers?" At that time, the various non-Buddhists (外道), realizing that they were defeated by his logic, abandoned their false views, accepted the true Dharma, reformed themselves, and wished to follow his teachings.

t2087_text: 渡河東岸至秣底補羅國（中印度境）。秣底補羅國，周六千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。宜穀、麥，多華果。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。崇尚學藝，深閑呪術。信邪正者，其徒相半。王，戍達羅種也，不信佛法，敬事天神。伽藍十餘所，僧徒八百餘人，多學小乘教說一切有部。天祠五十餘所，異道雜居。大城南四五里，至小伽藍，僧徒五十餘人。昔瞿拏鉢剌婆（唐言德光）論師於此作《辯真》等論，凡百餘部。論師少而英傑，長而弘敏，博物強識，碩學多聞。本習大乘，未窮玄奧，因覽《毘婆沙論》，退業而學小乘，作數十部論，破大乘綱紀，成小乘執著。又製俗書數十餘部，非斥先進所作典論。覃思佛經，十數不決，研精雖久，疑情未除。時有提婆犀那（唐言天軍）羅漢，往來覩史多天。德光願見慈氏，決疑請益。天軍以神通力，接上天宮。既見慈氏，長揖不禮。天軍謂曰：「慈氏菩薩次紹佛位，何乃自高，敢不致敬？方欲受業，如何不屈？」德光對曰：「尊者此言，誠為指誨。然我具戒苾芻，出家弟子，慈氏菩薩受天福樂，非出家之侶，而欲作禮，恐非所宜。」菩薩知其我慢心固，非聞法器，往來三返，不得決疑。更請天軍，重欲覲禮。天軍惡其我慢，蔑而不對。德光既不遂心，便起恚恨，即趣山林，修發通定，我慢未除，不證道果。德光伽藍北三四里，有大伽藍，僧徒二百餘人，並學小乘法教，是眾賢論師壽終之處。論師，迦濕彌羅國人也，聰敏博達，幼傳雅譽，特深研究《說一切有部毘婆沙論》。時有世親菩薩，一心玄道，求解言外，破毘婆沙師所執，作《阿毘達磨俱舍論》，辭義善巧，理致清高。眾賢循覽，遂有心焉。於是沈研鑽極，十有二歲，作《俱舍雹論》二萬五千頌，凡八十萬言矣。所謂言深致遠，窮幽洞微。告門人曰：「以我逸才，持我正論，逐斥世親，挫其鋒銳，無令老叟獨擅先名。」於是學徒四三俊彥，持所作論，推訪世親。世親是時在磔迦國奢羯羅城，遠傳聲問，眾賢當至。世親聞已，即治行裝。門人懷疑，前進諫曰：「大師德高先哲，名擅當時，遠近學徒莫不推謝。今聞眾賢，一何惶遽？必有所下，我曹厚顏。」世親曰：「吾今遠遊，非避此子。顧此國中，無復監達。眾賢後進也，詭辯若流，我衰耄矣，莫能持論。欲以一言頹其異執，引至中印度，對諸髦彥，察乎真偽，詳乎得失。」尋即命侶，負笈遠遊。眾賢論師當後一日至此伽藍，忽覺氣衰，於是裁書謝世親曰：「如來寂滅，弟子部執，傳其宗學，各擅專門，黨同道，疾異部。愚以寡昧，猥承傳習，覽所製《阿毘達磨俱舍論》，破毘婆沙師大義，輒不量力，沈究彌年，作為此論，扶正宗學。智小謀大，死其將至。菩薩宣暢微言，抑揚至理，不毀所執，得存遺文，斯為幸矣，死何悔哉？」於是歷選門人有辭辯者而告之曰：「吾誠後學，輕凌先達，命也如何？當從斯沒！汝持是書及所製論，謝彼菩薩，代我悔過。」授辭適畢，奄爾云亡。門人奉書至世親所而致辭曰：「我師眾賢已捨壽命。遺言致書，責躬謝咎。不墜其名，非所敢望。」世親菩薩覽書閱論，沈吟久之，謂門人曰：「眾賢論師聰敏後進，理雖不足，辭乃有餘。我今欲破眾賢之論，若指諸掌。顧以垂終之託，重其知難之辭，苟緣大義，存其宿志，況乎此論，發明我宗？」遂為改題為《順正理論》。門人諫曰：「眾賢未沒，大師遠迹，既得其論，又為改題，凡厥學徒，何顏受愧？」世親菩薩欲除眾疑，而說頌曰：「如師子王，避豕遠逝，二力勝負，智者應知。」眾賢死已，焚屍收骨，於伽藍西北二百餘步菴沒羅林中，起窣堵波，今猶現在。菴沒羅林側有窣堵波，毘末羅蜜多羅（唐言無垢友）論師之遺身。論師，迦濕彌羅國人也，於說一切有部而出家焉。博綜眾經，研究異論，遊五印度國，學三藏玄文，名立業成，將歸本國。途次眾賢論師窣堵波也，拊而歎曰：「惟論師雅量清高，抑揚大義，方欲挫異部，立本宗業也，如何降年不永！我無垢友猥承末學，異時慕義，曠代懷德。世親雖沒，宗學尚傳，我盡所知，當製諸論，令贍部洲諸學人等絕大乘稱，滅世親名，斯為不朽，用盡宿心。」說是語已，心發狂亂，五舌重出，熱血流涌。知命必終，裁書悔曰：「夫大乘教者，佛法之中究竟說也。名味泯絕，理致幽玄。輕以愚昧，駁斥先進，業報皎然，滅身宜矣。敢告學人，厥鑒斯在，各慎爾志，無得懷疑。」大地為震，命遂終焉。當其死處，地陷為坑。同旅焚屍，收骸旌建。時有羅漢見而歎曰：「惜哉！苦哉！今此論師，任情執見，毀惡大乘，墮無間獄。」
translation: Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people esteem learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-Dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities. There are more than ten monasteries with over eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Lesser Vehicle teachings. There are more than fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of different paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the master of treatises Guṇaprabha (in the Tang language, "Virtue-Light") composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The master of treatises was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory, being a scholar of great erudition. Originally, he studied the Mahayana, but not having exhausted its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* and subsequently abandoned his former studies to learn the Lesser Vehicle. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahayana and establishing the attachments of the Lesser Vehicle. He also produced several dozen secular books, criticizing and rejecting the canonical treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (in the Tang language, "Heavenly Army") who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. Devasena, using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏 - *Maitreya*), he merely made a long bow and did not prostrate. Devasena said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? You are seeking to receive instruction, so how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光 - *Guṇaprabha*) replied, "Venerable one, your words are indeed a guide. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys the bliss of heavenly rewards and is not a member of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel fit to hear the Dharma, allowed him to travel back and forth three times without resolving his doubts. Guṇaprabha asked Devasena again, wishing to pay homage once more, but Devasena, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not reply. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and went into the mountain forests to practice meditation for the attainment of supernatural powers; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four *li* to the north of the Guṇaprabha monastery, there is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master of treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢 - *Saṃghabhadra*) passed away. The master of treatises was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國 - *Kaśmīra*); he was intelligent and erudite, and from his youth he was renowned for his elegance, having studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親 - *Vasubandhu*), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), in which the language and meaning were skillful and the principles were lofty and refined. Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) read it and was moved to action. Thereupon, he delved deeply into study and research for twelve years, composing the *Hailstone on the Kośa* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and his reach far, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and upholding my correct arguments, I shall drive back Vasubandhu (世親) and blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word was sent from afar that Saṃghabhadra was arriving. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must yield to him, we will be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning scholars. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river; I am old and frail and cannot engage in debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately ordered his companions to pack their book-satchels and set out on the long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, when he suddenly felt his vitality failing. He then composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Thus-Come One passed into extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, each transmitting their own school's learning, each specializing in their own field, favoring those who share their path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) that you composed, which refutes the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters, I—without measuring my own strength—spent years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox school. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?" He then selected from among his disciples those who were eloquent and told them: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate, what can be done? I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." No sooner had he finished dictating these words than he suddenly passed away. The disciples took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "Our master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for." Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise, and after pondering for a long time, he said to the disciples: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior; although his reasoning was insufficient, his rhetoric was more than enough. I now wish to refute Saṃghabhadra’s treatise, and it will be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; furthermore, this treatise clarifies my own school." He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise Following the Correct Principles). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "While Saṃghabhadra was still alive, the Master withdrew far away; now that you have obtained his treatise, you even change its title for him—how can all the students face the shame of this?" Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to remove their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a boar and going far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, they cremated his body and collected his bones. In the Āmra (mango) grove, two hundred paces northwest of the monastery, they erected a stūpa, which still exists today. Beside the Āmra grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (in Tang language, "Stainless Friend"). The master was a man of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and had renounced the household life in the Sarvāstivāda school. He extensively studied the various scriptures and researched heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his years were not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, humbly follow in his footsteps; I have long admired his righteousness and have cherished his virtue across the ages." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted these advanced teachings; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a lesson, guard your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat (羅漢) saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, following his own emotions and holding to his views, slandered and disparaged the Mahāyāna, and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."

t2087_text: 國西北境殑伽河東岸有摩裕羅城，周二十餘里。居人殷盛，清流交帶，出鍮石、水精、寶器。去城不遠，臨殑伽河，有大天祠，甚多靈異。其中有池，編石為岸，引殑伽水為補，五印度人謂之殑伽河門，生福滅罪之所。常有遠方數百千人，集此澡濯。樂善諸王建立福舍，備珍羞，儲醫藥，惠施鰥寡，周給孤獨。
translation: In the northwest territory of the kingdom, on the east bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, lies the city of Mayūra (摩裕羅城), which is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the city is encircled by clear streams; it produces brass, rock crystal, and precious vessels. Not far from the city, bordering the Ganges River, there is a great deva temple with many miraculous manifestations. Within it is a pond with stone-lined banks, replenished by water diverted from the Ganges; the people of the five Indias call it the Gate of the Ganges (Gaṅgādvāra), a place for generating merit and expiating sins. Constantly, hundreds of thousands of people from distant regions gather here to bathe. Benevolent kings have established charitable hostels here, stocked with fine food and stored with medicines, to bestow gifts upon the widowed and solitary, and to provide for the orphaned and destitute.

t2087_text: 從此北行三百餘里，至婆羅吸摩補羅國（北印度境）。婆羅吸摩補羅國，周四千餘里，山周四境。國大都城周二十餘里。居人殷盛，家室富饒。土地沃壤，稼穡時播，出鍮石、水精。氣序微寒，風俗剛猛。少學藝，多逐利。人性獷烈，邪正雜信。伽藍五所，僧徒寡少。天祠十餘所，異道雜居。
translation: From here, traveling north for over three hundred li, one reaches the country of Brahmapura (婆羅吸摩補羅國) (within the borders of North India). The country of Brahmapura is over four thousand li in circuit, and mountains surround its four borders. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The soil is fertile, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and it produces brass and rock crystal. The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are fierce and unyielding. The people have little interest in the arts and are mostly driven by profit. Their nature is wild and violent, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are five sanghārāmas, with few monks. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

translation: In the Great Snow Mountains to the north of this country lies the kingdom of Suvarṇagotra (translated into Chinese as the "Gold Clan"). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women's Kingdom. For generations, the country has been named after women. The husband is also called king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men's only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo, to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan, and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha.

t2087_text: 從末底補羅東南行四百餘里，至瞿毘霜那國（中印度境）。瞿毘霜那國，周二千餘里。國大都城周十四五里，崇峻險固，居人殷盛，華林池沼，往往相間。氣序土宜同末底補羅國。風俗淳質，勤學好福。多信外道，求現在樂。伽藍二所，僧眾百餘人，並皆習學小乘法教。天祠三十餘所，異道雜居。大城側故伽藍中，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺。如來在昔，於此一月說諸法要，傍有過去四佛座及經行遺迹處。其側有如來髮、爪二窣堵波，各高一丈餘。
translation: Traveling southeast from Matipura (末底補羅國) for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Goviṣāṇa (瞿毘霜那國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Goviṣāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it is high, precipitous, and strategically secure, with a dense and prosperous population, and flowery groves and ponds are interspersed throughout. The climate and soil are the same as in the country of Matipura. The customs are simple and honest, and the people are diligent in learning and fond of merit. Many believe in non-Buddhist paths and seek present-day happiness. There are two saṃghārāmas with over one hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than thirty Deva temples, where followers of various paths live together. Beside the old saṃghārāma near the great city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王) that is over two hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for one month to preach the essential Dharma; nearby are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside these are two stūpas containing the hair and nail clippings of the Tathāgata, each over one zhang high.

t2087_text: 自此東南行四百餘里，至堊醯掣呾邏國（中印度境）。堊醯掣呾邏國，周三千餘里。大都城周十七八里，依據險固，宜穀、麥，多林泉。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。翫道篤學，多才博識。伽藍十餘所，僧徒千餘人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠九所，異道三百餘人，事自在天，塗灰之侶也。城外龍池側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。是如來在昔為龍王，七日於此說法。其側有四小窣堵波，是過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Ahicchattra (堊醯掣呾邏國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Ahicchattra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit; it is situated in a secure and rugged position, is suitable for grain and wheat, and has many forests and springs. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs of the people are honest and simple. They delight in the Way and are diligent in their studies, being talented and widely learned. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine deva temples, and more than three hundred sectarians who serve Īśvara (自在天) and are followers of the ash-smearing ascetics. Outside the city, beside a dragon pool, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life when he was a dragon king, preached the Dharma for seven days. Beside it are four small stūpas, which are the sites of the remains of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

t2087_text: 自此東行二百六七十里，渡殑伽河，南至毘羅那拏國（中印度境）。毘羅那拏國，周二千餘里。國大都城周十餘里。氣序土宜，同堊醯掣呾邏國。風俗猛暴，人知學藝。崇信外道，少敬佛法。伽藍二所，僧徒三百人，並皆習學大乘法教。天祠五所，異道雜居。大城中故伽藍內，有窣堵波基，雖傾圮，尚百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔於此七日說《蘊界處經》之所。其側則有過去四佛座及經行遺迹斯在。
translation: From here, traveling east for two hundred sixty or seventy li and crossing the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives south at the country of Vilaśāṇa (毘羅那拏國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Vilaśāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ahicchatrā (堊醯掣呾邏國). The customs of the people are fierce and violent, yet they are knowledgeable in the arts. They revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddha-Dharma. There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Great Vehicle. There are five Deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. Inside an old monastery in the great city, there is the base of a stūpa which, although dilapidated, is still over one hundred feet high; it was built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the Tathāgata in the past spent seven days preaching the *Skandhadhātvāyatana-sūtra* (蘊界處經). Beside it are the seats and traces of the walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

t2087_text: 從此東南行二百餘里，至劫比他國（舊謂僧迦舍國。中印度境）。劫比他國，周二千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。氣序土宜，同毘羅那拏國。風俗淳和，人多學藝。伽藍四所，僧徒千餘人，並學小乘正量部法。天祠十所，異道雜居，同共遵事大自在天。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Kapitha (劫比他國) (the old name is the country of Saṃkāśya; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kapitha is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Viraṇāṇa (毘羅那拏國). The customs are honest and harmonious, and the people are mostly devoted to learning and the arts. There are four saṃghārāmas with more than one thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are ten deva temples where followers of different paths live together, all of whom jointly worship Maheśvara.

t2087_text: 城西二十餘里有大伽藍，經製輪奐，工窮剞劂，聖形尊像，務極莊嚴。僧徒數百人，學正量部法。數萬淨人，宅居其側。伽藍大垣內有三寶階，南北列，東面下，是如來自三十三天降還也。昔如來起自勝林，上昇天宮，居善法堂，為母說法，過三月已，將欲下降。天帝釋乃縱神力，建立寶階，中階黃金，左水精，右白銀。如來起善法堂，從諸天眾，履中階而下；大梵王執白拂，履銀階而右侍；天帝釋持寶蓋，蹈水精階而左侍；天眾凌虛，散華讚德。數百年前，猶有階級，逮至今時，陷沒已盡。諸國君王悲慨不遇，疊以塼石，飾以珍寶，於其故基，擬昔寶階，其高七十餘尺，上起精舍。中有石佛像，而左右之階有釋、梵之像，形擬厥初，猶為下勢。傍有石柱，高七十餘尺，無憂王所建。色紺光潤，質堅密理，上作師子，蹲踞向階，雕鏤奇形，周其方面，隨人罪福，影現柱中。寶階側不遠有窣堵波，是過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。其側窣堵波，如來在昔於此澡浴。其側精舍，是如來入定之處。精舍側有大石，基長五十步，高七尺，是如來經行之處。足所履迹皆有蓮華之文。基左右各有小窣堵波，帝釋、梵王之所建也。釋、梵窣堵波前，是蓮華色苾芻尼欲先見佛，化作轉輪王處。如來自天宮還贍部洲也，時蘇部底（唐言善現。舊曰須扶提，或曰須菩提，譯曰善吉，皆訛也）宴坐石室，竊自思曰：「今佛還降，人、天導從，如我今者，何所宜行？甞聞佛說，知諸法空，體諸法性，是則以慧眼觀法身也。」時蓮華色苾芻尼欲初見佛，化為轉輪王，七寶導從，四兵警衛，至世尊所，復苾芻尼。如來告曰：「汝非初見。夫善現者，觀諸法空，是見法身。」聖迹垣內，靈異相繼。其大窣堵波東南有一池龍，恒護聖迹。既有冥衛，難以輕犯，歲久自壞，人莫能毀。從此東南行，減二百里，至羯若鞠闍國（唐言曲女城國。中印度境）。
translation: More than twenty *li* west of the city is a large monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship exquisite; the sacred forms and venerable images are adorned with the utmost solemnity. There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school, and tens of thousands of monastery servants (淨人) reside in its vicinity. Within the great wall of the monastery are the three precious stairways (三寶階), arranged from north to south and facing east, where the Tathāgata returned from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Jetavana (勝林) and ascended to the heavenly palace, where he resided in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā-sabhā) to preach the Dharma for his mother. After three months had passed, he intended to descend. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, then exercised his divine power to establish a precious stairway: the middle step was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of silver. The Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and, followed by a host of deities, stepped down the middle stairway; the Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, walked on the silver stairway to attend on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped on the crystal stairway to attend on the left; the heavenly host hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues. Several hundred years ago, the stairs still existed, but by the present time, they have completely sunk into the earth. The kings of various countries, lamenting that they could not see them, stacked bricks and stones and decorated them with precious gems upon the original foundation to imitate the ancient precious stairway. It is over seventy feet high, and a *vihāra* (精舍) is built upon it. Inside is a stone Buddha image, and on the stairs to the left and right are images of Śakra and Brahmā, modeled after the original appearance, still in a descending posture. Beside it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its color is dark blue and lustrous, its substance hard and fine-grained. At the top is a lion, crouching and facing the stairway, with strange forms carved and engraved around its four sides; according to the merit or demerit of the person, shadows appear within the pillar. Not far from the precious stairway is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata formerly bathed. Beside that is a *vihāra* (精舍), which is the place where the Tathāgata entered into meditation. Beside the *vihāra* is a large stone, fifty paces long and seven feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata performed walking meditation. The footprints he trod upon all have lotus patterns. To the left and right of the base are small stūpas, built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王). In front of the stūpas of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā (蓮華色), wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace to Jambudvīpa, at that time Subhūti (蘇部底) (in the Tang language, Shanxian, 'Good Manifestation'; formerly called Xufuti [須扶提] or Xuputi [須菩提], translated as Shanji [善吉], 'Good Auspicious', all of which are erroneous) was sitting in meditation in a stone chamber and thought to himself: "Now the Buddha is descending, guided and followed by humans and devas. As for someone like me, what is appropriate to do? I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king, guided by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata replied, "You are not the first to see me. Shanxian (Subhūti), contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena — it is he who has seen the Dharma-body." Within the enclosure of the sacred traces, miraculous signs occurred one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond, and the dragon constantly protects the sacred traces. Because there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; though they have decayed naturally over the long years, no person has been able to destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) (in the language of Tang, the Kingdom of the Hunchbacked Maiden City; it is within the borders of Central India).

羯若鞠闍國，周四千餘里。國大都城西臨殑伽河，其長二十餘里，廣四五里。城隍堅峻，臺閣相望，花林池沼，光鮮澄鏡。異方奇貨，多聚於此。居人豐樂，家室富饒。華菓具繁，稼穡時播。氣序和洽，風俗淳質。容貌妍雅，服飾鮮綺。篤學遊藝，談論清遠。邪正二道，信者相半。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，大小二乘，兼功習學。天祠二百餘所，異道數千餘人。羯若鞠闍國人長壽時，其舊王城號拘蘇磨補羅（唐言花宮）。王號梵授，福智宿資，文武允備，威懾贍部，聲震隣國。具足千子，智勇弘毅，復有百女，儀貌妍雅。時有仙人居殑伽河側，棲神入定，經數萬歲，形如枯木，遊禽棲集，遺尼拘律果於仙人肩上，暑往寒來，垂蔭合拱。多歷年所，從定而起，欲去其樹，恐覆鳥巢，時人美其德，號大樹仙人。仙人寓目河濱，遊觀林薄，見王諸女相從嬉戲，欲界愛起，染著心生，便詣華宮，欲事禮請。王聞仙至，躬迎慰曰：「大仙棲情物外，何能輕舉？」仙人曰：「我棲林藪，彌積歲時，出定遊覽，見王諸女，染愛心生，自遠來請。」王聞其辭，計無所出，謂仙人曰：「今還所止，請俟嘉辰。」仙人聞命，遂還林藪。王乃歷問諸女，無肯應娉。王懼仙威，憂愁毀悴。其幼稚女候王事隙，從容問曰：「父王千子具足，萬國慕化，何故憂愁，如有所懼？」王曰：「大樹仙人幸顧求婚，而汝曹輩莫肯從命。仙有威力，能作災祥，儻不遂心，必起瞋怒，毀國滅祀，辱及先王。深惟此禍，誠有所懼。」稚女謝曰：「遺此深憂，我曹罪也。願以微軀，得延國祚。」王聞喜悅，命駕送歸。既至仙廬，謝仙人曰：「大仙俯方外之情，垂世間之顧，敢奉稚女，以供灑掃。」仙人見而不悅，乃謂王曰：「輕吾老叟，配此不妍。」王曰：「歷問諸女，無肯從命。唯此幼稚，願充給使。」仙人懷怒，便惡呪曰：「九十九女，一時腰曲，形既毀弊，畢世無婚。」王使往驗，果已背傴。從是之後，便名曲女城焉。今王，本吠奢種也，字曷利沙伐彈那（唐言喜增）。君臨有土，二世三王。父字波羅羯羅伐彈那（唐言作光增），兄字曷邏闍伐彈那（唐言王增）。王增以長嗣位，以德治政。時東印度羯羅拏蘇伐剌那（唐言金耳）國設賞迦王（唐言月），每謂臣曰：「隣有賢主，國之禍也。」於是誘請，會而害之。人既失君，國亦荒亂。時大臣婆尼（唐言辯了），職望隆重，謂僚庶曰：「國之大計，定於今日。先王之子，亡君之弟，仁慈天性，孝敬因心，親賢允屬，欲以襲位。於事何如？各言爾志。」眾咸仰德，嘗無異謀。於是輔臣執事咸勸進曰：「王子垂聽，先王積功累德，光有國祚。嗣及王增，謂終壽考；輔佐無良，棄身讎手，為國大恥，下臣罪也。物議時謠，允歸明德。光臨土宇，克復親讎，雪國之恥，光父之業，功孰大焉？幸無辭矣！」王子曰：「國嗣之重，今古為難，君人之位，興立宜審。我誠寡德，父兄遐棄，推襲大位，其能濟乎？物議為宜，敢忘虛薄？今者殑伽河岸，有觀自在菩薩像，既多靈鑒，願往請辭。」即至菩薩像前，斷食祈請。菩薩感其誠心，現形問曰：「爾何所求，若此勤懇？」王子曰：「我惟積禍，慈父云亡；重茲酷罰，仁兄見害。自顧寡德，國人推尊，令襲大位，光父之業。愚昧無知，敢希聖旨！」菩薩告曰：「汝於先身，在此林中為練若苾芻，而精勤不懈。承茲福力，為此王子。金耳國王既毀佛法，爾紹王位，宜重興隆，慈悲為志，傷愍居懷，不久當王五印度境。欲延國祚，當從我誨，冥加景福，隣無強敵。勿昇師子之座，勿稱大王之號。」於是受教而退，即襲王位，自稱曰王子，號尸羅阿迭多（唐言戒日）。於是謂臣曰：「兄讎未報，隣國不賓，終無右手進食之期。凡爾庶僚，同心勠力。」遂總率國兵，講習戰士。象軍五千，馬軍二萬，步軍五萬，自西徂東，征伐不臣。象不解鞍，人不釋甲，於六年中，臣五印度。既廣其地，更增甲兵。象軍六萬，馬軍十萬。垂三十年，兵戈不起，政教和平，務修節儉，營福樹善，忘寢與食。令五印度不得噉肉，若斷生命，有誅無赦。於殑伽河側建立數千窣堵波，各高百餘尺。於五印度城邑、鄉聚、達巷、交衢，建立精廬，儲飲食，止醫藥，施諸羈貧，周給不殆。聖迹之所，並建伽藍。五歲一設無遮大會，傾竭府庫，惠施群有，唯留兵器，不充檀捨。歲一集會諸國沙門，於三七日中，以四事供養，莊嚴法座，廣飾義筵，令相摧論，校其優劣，褒貶淑慝，黜陟幽明。若戒行貞固，道德淳邃，推昇師子之座，王親受法；戒雖清淨，學無稽古，但加敬禮，示有尊崇；律儀無紀，穢德已彰，驅出國境，不願聞見。隣國小王、輔佐大臣，殖福無殆，求善忘勞，即携手同座，謂之善友；其異於此，面不對辭，事有聞議，通使往復。而巡方省俗，不常其居，隨所至止，結廬而舍。唯雨三月，多雨不行。每於行宮日修珍饌，飯諸異學，僧眾一千，婆羅門五百。每以一日分作三時，一時理務治政，二時營福修善，孜孜不倦，竭日不足矣。初，受拘摩羅王請曰，自摩揭陀國往迦摩縷波國。時戒日王巡方在羯朱嗢祇羅國，命拘摩羅王曰：「宜與那爛陀遠客沙門速來赴會。」於是遂與拘摩羅王往會見焉。戒日王勞苦已曰：「自何國來，將何所欲？」對曰：「從大唐國來，請求佛法。」王曰：「大唐國在何方？經途所亘，去斯遠近？」對曰：「當此東北數萬餘里，印度所謂摩訶至那國是也。」王曰：「嘗聞摩訶至那國有秦王天子，少而靈鑒，長而神武。昔先代喪亂，率土分崩，兵戈競起，群生荼毒，而秦王天子早懷遠略，興大慈悲，拯濟含識，平定海內，風教遐被，德澤遠洽，殊方異域，慕化稱臣。民庶荷其亭育，咸歌《秦王破陣樂》。聞其雅頌，于茲久矣。盛德之譽，誠有之乎？大唐國者，豈此是耶？」對曰：「然。至那者，前王之國號；大唐者，我君之國稱。昔未襲位，謂之秦王；今已承統，稱曰天子。前代運終，群生無主，兵戈亂起，殘害生靈。秦王天縱含弘，心發慈愍，威風鼓扇，群凶殄滅，八方靜謐，萬國朝貢。愛育四生，敬崇三寶，薄賦斂，省刑罰，而國用有餘，氓俗無穴，風猷大化，難以備舉。」戒日王曰：「盛哉！彼土群生，福感聖主。」時戒日王將還曲女城設法會也，從數十萬眾，在殑伽河南岸。拘摩羅王從數萬之眾，居北岸。分河中流，水陸並進。二王導引，四兵嚴衛，或泛舟，或乘象，擊鼓鳴螺，拊弦奏管。經九十日，至曲女城，在殑伽河西大花林中。是時諸國二十餘王，先奉告命，各與其國髦俊沙門及婆羅門、群官、兵士，來集大會。王先於河西建大伽藍；伽藍東起寶臺，高百餘尺，中有金佛像，量等王身；臺南起寶壇，為浴佛像之處；從此東北十四五里，別築行宮。是時，仲春月也。從初一日，以珍味饌諸沙門、婆羅門，至二十一日。自行宮屬伽藍，夾道為閣，窮諸瑩飾，樂人不移，雅聲遞奏。王於行宮出一金像，虛中隱起，高餘三尺，載以大象，張以寶幰。戒日王為帝釋之服，執寶蓋以左侍，拘摩羅王作梵王之儀，執白拂而右侍。各五百象軍，被鎧周衛，佛像前後各百大象，樂人以乘，鼓奏音樂。戒日王以真珠雜寶及金銀諸花，隨步四散，供養三寶。先就寶壇，香水浴像，王躬負荷，送上西臺，以諸珍寶、憍奢耶衣數十百千，而為供養。是時唯有沙門二十餘人預從，諸國王為侍衛。饌食已訖，集諸異學，商確微言，抑揚至理。日將曛暮，迴駕行宮。如是日送金像，導從如初，以至散日。其大臺忽然火起，伽藍門樓煙焰方熾。王曰：「罄捨國珍，奉為先王，建此伽藍，式昭勝業，寡德無祐，有斯災異，咎徵若此，何用生為！」乃焚香禮請而自誓曰：「幸以宿善，王諸印度，願我福力，禳滅火災，若無所感，從此喪命！」尋即奮身，跳履門閫，若有撲滅，火盡煙消。諸王覩異，重增祇懼。已而顏色不動，辭語如故，問諸王曰：「忽此災變，焚燼成功，心之所懷，意將何謂？」諸王俯伏悲泣，對曰：「成功勝迹，冀傳來葉，一旦灰燼，何可為懷？況諸外道，快心相賀！」王曰：「以此觀之，如來所說誠也。外道異學守執常見，唯我大師無常是誨。然我檀捨已周，心願諧遂，屬斯變滅，重知如來誠諦之說，斯為大善，無可深悲。」於是從諸王東上大窣堵波，登臨觀覽。方下階陛，忽有異人持刃逆王，王時窘迫，却行進級，俯執此人，以付群官。是時群官惶遽，不知進救。諸王咸請誅戮此人，戒日王殊無忿色，止令不殺。王親問曰：「我何負汝，為此暴惡？」對曰：「大王德澤無私，中外荷負。然我狂愚，不謀大計，受諸外道一言之感，輒為刺客，首圖逆害。」王曰：「外道何故興此惡心？」對曰：「大王集諸國，傾府庫，供養沙門，鎔鑄佛像，而諸外道自遠召集，不蒙省問，心誠愧恥。乃令狂愚，敢行凶詐。」於是究問外道徒屬。有五百婆羅門，並諸高才，應命召集，嫉諸沙門蒙王禮重，乃射火箭，焚燒寶臺，冀因救火，眾人潰亂，欲以此時殺害大王，既無緣隙，遂雇此人，趨隘行刺。是時諸王、大臣請誅外道，王乃罰其首惡，餘黨不罪，遷五百婆羅門出印度之境。於是乃還都也。城西北窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔，於此七日說諸妙法。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪小窣堵波。說法窣堵波南，臨殑伽河，有三伽藍，同垣異門，佛像嚴麗，僧徒肅穆，役使淨人數千餘戶。精舍寶函中有佛牙，長餘寸半，殊光異色，朝變夕改。遠近相趨，士庶咸集，式修瞻仰，日百千眾。監守者繁其諠雜，權立重稅，宣告遠近：欲見佛牙，輸大金錢。然而瞻禮之徒，寔繁其侶，金錢之稅，悅以心競。每於齋日，出置高座，數百千眾，燒香散華，華雖盈積，牙函不沒。伽藍前左、右各有精舍，高百餘尺，石基塼室，其中佛像，眾寶莊飾，或鑄金、銀，或鎔鍮石。二精舍前各有小伽藍。伽藍東南不遠，有大精舍，石基塼室，高二百餘尺，中作如來立像，高三十餘尺，鑄以鍮石，飾諸妙寶。精舍四周石壁之上，雕畫如來修菩薩行所經事迹，備盡鐫鏤。石精舍南不遠，有日天祠。祠南不遠，有大自在天祠。並瑩青石，俱窮雕刻，規摹度量，同佛精舍。各有千戶充其灑掃，鼓樂絃歌晝夜無徙。大城東南六七里，殑伽河南，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。在昔如來於此六月說身無常、苦、空、不淨。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。又有如來髮、爪小窣堵波，人有染疾，至誠旋繞，必得痊愈，蒙其福利。
translation: The country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city moats and ramparts are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions facing one another, and flower groves and ponds that are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy and abundant. Flowers and fruits are plentiful, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is harmonious and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discourse is clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred saṅghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the age when the people of the country of Kanyākubja enjoyed long lives, the old capital city was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅) (In the language of the Tang, this means "Flowery Palace"). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits of wisdom and virtue, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Gaṅgā who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it cast a shade and grew to the size of an arch. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the "Rishi of the Big Tree." The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the world of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi said, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make a request." Hearing these words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your transformation; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (Mahāvṛkṣa-ṛṣi) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed; he ordered a carriage to be prepared and sent her to him. Upon arriving at the hermit’s hut, the king thanked the hermit, saying, "The great hermit has condescended from his transcendent state to show concern for worldly affairs; I dare to offer my young daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The hermit saw her and was displeased, saying to the king, "You slight this old man by matching me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this young one is willing to serve as a maid." The hermit, harboring anger, uttered a wicked curse: "May the ninety-nine daughters all have their waists bent at once; their forms being thus ruined and spoiled, they shall have no marriage for their entire lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Happiness"). He rules over the land, the third king of two generations. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of the Kingdom"). Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (translated into Chinese as "Moon") of the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as "Golden Ear") in East India often said to his ministers, "To have a virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a misfortune for one's own country." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and at the meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (translated into Chinese as "Eloquent and Wise"), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided this day." "The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, speak your mind." The assembly all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession reached Rājyavardhana, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he abandoned his life at the hands of an enemy—this is a great shame for the country and the fault of us, your humble servants. Public opinion and the rumors of the time truly point to your brilliant virtue. If you were to grace the land and the territory, avenge your kin upon the enemy, wash away the shame of the country, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said, "The matter of national succession has been a difficult one from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have been taken from me, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."   He immediately went before the Bodhisattva's image and fasted to make his request. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince said, "I have only accumulated disasters; my benevolent father has passed away, and to add to this cruel punishment, my virtuous elder brother has been murdered. Reflecting on myself, I am lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the great throne to glorify my father's legacy." "I am foolish and ignorant; how dare I hope for the holy decree!" The Bodhisattva replied, "In your former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting. By the power of that merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it; let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the prosperity of the state, you must follow my instructions; then, through hidden blessings, you will have no powerful enemies in the neighboring lands. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King."  Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and assumed the throne, calling himself "The Prince" and taking the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多) (in the language of Tang, this means "Sun of Precepts"). He then said to his ministers, "The vengeance for my brother has not been requited, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a moment to eat with my right hand. Let all you officials be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had 5,000 elephant troops, 20,000 cavalry, and 50,000 infantry, and from the west to the east, he campaigned against those who would not submit. Without the elephants being unsaddled or the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India into submission within six years. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching 60,000 elephant troops and 100,000 cavalry. For nearly thirty years, the weapons of war were not raised, and the government and teachings were peaceful. He devoted himself to frugality, cultivated merit and goodness, and forgot both sleep and food. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges (gaṅgā), he erected several thousand stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hospices (精廬) stocked with food, drink, and medicine to be distributed to travelers and the poor, providing for them without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a monastery (saṅghārāma). Every five years, he held a great pan-charity assembly (pañcavārṣika), emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the classics were merely treated with respect to show his veneration. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to see or hear of them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were otherwise, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to discuss, he would communicate only through the exchange of envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs of the people and did not have a fixed residence, building temporary huts wherever he stopped. Only during the three months of the rainy season did he cease traveling due to the heavy rains. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine meals to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brahmins of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I had accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had offered greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what is it that you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐國) to seek the Buddha-Dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of *li* to the northeast of here; it is what you in India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王天子), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons of war arose on all sides, and the masses were poisoned by suffering. The Prince of Qin, however, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued all sentient beings, and pacified the world. His civilizing influence reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The people, having received his protection and nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Ranks' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard these elegant hymns for a long time now. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said? Is the Great Tang this country?" I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of my sovereign's realm. Before he ascended the throne, he was called the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is titled the Son of Heaven. When the fortune of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master, weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with vast magnanimity, felt compassion in his heart; his majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were pacified, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He loves and nurtures the four forms of birth, reveres and honors the Three Jewels, lightens taxes and levies, and reduces punishments; yet the state’s resources are abundant, and the common people have no need for hidden shelters. His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully describe.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'Magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both land and water. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Wood to the west of the Ganges. At that time, more than twenty kings of various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a large monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he constructed a separate temporary palace. It was then the month of the middle of spring. From the first day of the month until the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brahmans. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, decorated with every ornament, where musicians remained stationed, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a large elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, while a hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and gold and silver flowers at every step as an offering to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; then the King personally carried the image and escorted it to the western terrace, offering tens of hundreds of thousands of jewels and kauśeya garments as offerings. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. In this manner, he escorted the golden image daily, with the procession following as before, until the day of the dispersal. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a respectful petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if by some force extinguishing it, the fire died out and the smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and reverence increased. Afterward, the King’s expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, burning and destroying the finished work; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping in sorrow, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how can we not be grieved? Furthermore, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it from this perspective, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata; this is a great good, and there is no reason for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east to ascend the great stūpa to view the surroundings. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the King. The King, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to advance to rescue him. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and merely ordered that he not be killed. The King personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the grander scheme, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The King asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor such evil intentions?" He replied, "Your Majesty has assembled the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and to cast Buddha images, yet the heretics, who were summoned from afar, have not been granted an audience; they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this violent deception." Thereupon, the King investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, all of them men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the King's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and carry out the assassination. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested that the heretics be executed, but the King only punished the ringleaders, left the remaining partisans unpunished, and banished the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates; the Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ several thousand households of monastery servants (淨人). In the precious casket of the *vihāra* (精舍) is a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary luster and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and the gentry and commoners gather in great numbers, daily numbering a hundred thousand, to perform acts of veneration. Because the overseers were troubled by the noise and confusion, they provisionally established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha's tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of those coming to pay homage remained vast, and they were happy to compete in their hearts to pay the gold tax. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers, and although the flowers pile up, the tooth casket is never submerged.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there is a *vihāra*, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two *vihāra*s is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the *vihāra*, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone *vihāra*, there is a temple to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that temple, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are polished with blue stone and are equally exhaustive in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s *vihāra*. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without cessation. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here speaking on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity of the body. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; when people are afflicted with illness, if they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be cured and receive their blessings.

t2087_text: 大城東南行百餘里，至納縛提婆矩羅城，據殑伽河東岸，周二十餘里。華林清池，互相影照。納縛提婆矩羅城西北，殑伽河東，有一天祠，重閣層臺，奇工異製。城東五里有三伽藍，同垣異門，僧徒五百餘人，並學小乘說一切有部。伽藍前二百餘步，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。基雖傾陷，尚高百餘尺，是如來昔於此處七日說法。中有舍利，時放光明。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。伽藍北三四里，臨殑伽河岸，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。昔如來在此七日說法，時有五百餓鬼來至佛所，聞法解悟，捨鬼生天。說法窣堵波側有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。其側復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。
translation: Traveling southeast from the great city for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Navadevakula (納縛提婆矩羅城). It is situated on the eastern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河) and measures more than twenty *li* in circumference. Flowery groves and clear ponds reflect one another. To the northwest of the city of Navadevakula, on the east side of the Ganges, there is a temple to a deva, with multi-storied pavilions and terraced platforms, featuring extraordinary workmanship and unique construction. Five *li* to the east of the city, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having different gates, with over five hundred monks who all study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school. Two hundred paces in front of the monasteries, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still over one hundred feet high; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Three or four *li* to the north of the monasteries, bordering the bank of the Ganges, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Formerly, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for seven days, at which time five hundred hungry ghosts (preta) came to the Buddha’s presence, heard the Dharma, attained understanding, and, abandoning their ghost bodies, were reborn in heaven. Beside the stūpa of the preaching of the Dharma are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside that, there is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.

t2087_text: 自此東南行六百餘里，渡殑伽河，南至阿踰陀國（中印度境）。阿踰陀國，周五千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。糓稼豐盛，華菓繁茂。氣序和暢，風俗善順，好營福，勤學藝。伽藍百有餘所，僧徒三千餘人，大乘、小乘，兼功習學。天祠十所，異道寡少。大城中有故伽藍，是伐蘇畔度菩薩（唐言世親。舊曰婆藪盤豆，譯曰天親。訛謬也）數十年中於此製作大小乘諸異論。其側故基，是世親菩薩為諸國王、四方俊彥、沙門、婆羅門等講義說法堂也。城北四五里，臨殑伽河岸，大伽藍中，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。是如來為天、人眾，於此三月說諸妙法。其側窣堵波，過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。伽藍西四五里，有如來髮、爪窣堵波。髮、爪窣堵波北，伽藍餘趾，昔經部室利邏多（唐言勝受）論師於此製造經部《毘婆沙論》。城西南五六里大菴沒羅林中，有故伽藍，是阿僧伽（唐言無著）菩薩請益導凡之處。無著菩薩夜昇天宮，於慈氏菩薩所受《瑜伽師地論》、《莊嚴大乘經論》、《中邊分別論》等，晝為大眾講宣妙理。菴沒羅林西北百餘步，有如來髮、爪窣堵波。其側故基，是世親菩薩從覩史多天下見無著菩薩處。無著菩薩，健馱邏國人也，佛去世後一千年中，誕靈利見，承風悟道，從彌沙塞部出家修學，頃之迴信大乘。其弟世親菩薩於說一切有部出家受業，博聞強識，達學研機。無著弟子佛陀僧訶（唐言師子覺）者，密行莫測，高才有聞。二三賢哲每相謂曰：「凡修行業，願覲慈氏，若先捨壽，得遂宿心，當相報語，以知所至。」其後師子覺先捨壽命，三年不報。世親菩薩尋亦捨壽，時經六月，亦無報命。時諸異學咸皆譏誚，以為世親菩薩及師子覺，流轉惡趣，遂無靈鑒。其後無著菩薩於夜初分，方為門人教授定法，燈光忽翳，空中大明，有一天仙乘虛下降，即進階庭敬禮無著。無著曰：「爾來何暮？今名何謂？」對曰：「從此捨壽命，往覩史多天慈氏內眾蓮華中生，蓮華纔開，慈氏讚曰：『善來廣慧，善來廣慧。』旋繞纔周，即來報命。」無著菩薩曰：「師子覺者，今何所在？」曰：「我旋繞時，見師子覺在外眾中，耽著欲樂，無暇相顧，詎能來報？」無著菩薩曰：「斯事已矣。慈氏何相？演說何法？」曰：「慈氏相好，言莫能宣。演說妙法，義不異此。然菩薩妙音，清暢和雅，聞者忘倦，受者無厭。」無著講堂故基西北四十餘里，至故伽藍，北臨殑伽河，中有塼窣堵波，高百餘尺，世親菩薩初發大乘心處。世親菩薩自北印度至於此也，時無著菩薩命其門人，令往迎候。至此伽藍，遇而會見。無著弟子止戶牖外，夜分之後，誦《十地經》。世親聞已，感悟追悔：「甚深妙法，昔所未聞，誹謗之愆，源發於舌，舌為罪本，今宜除斷。」即執銛刀，欲自斷舌。乃見無著住立告曰：「夫大乘教者，至真之理也，諸佛所讚，眾聖攸宗。吾欲誨爾，爾今自悟。悟其時矣，何善如之？諸佛聖教，斷舌非悔。昔以舌毀大乘，今以舌讚大乘，補過自新，猶為善矣，杜口絕言，其利安在？」作是語已，忽不復見。世親承命，遂不斷舌。旦詣無著，諮受大乘。於是研精覃思，製大乘論，凡百餘部，並盛宣行。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li and crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one arrives south at the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Ayodhyā is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are lush. The climate is temperate and pleasant, the customs are virtuous and compliant, and the people are fond of performing meritorious deeds and are diligent in studying the arts. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings with equal effort. There are ten Deva temples, and there are few followers of heterodox paths. Within the great city is an old monastery; this is where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (伐蘇畔度) (in the language of Tang, *Shiqin* [世親]; formerly called *Posoupandou* [婆藪盤豆], translated as *Tianqin* [天親]; this is erroneous) spent several decades composing various treatises on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Beside it are the old foundations of the hall where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu lectured on the meaning of the teachings and expounded the Dharma for kings, talented scholars from the four quarters, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. Four or five li to the north of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, within a large monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. It was here that the Tathāgata preached the various wonderful teachings for three months to an assembly of gods and men. Beside it is a stūpa marking the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Four or five li to the west of the monastery, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. To the north of the hair and nail stūpa are the remains of a monastery where the Sautrāntika master Śrīlabdha (translated into Chinese as Shengshou, "Victorious Reception") formerly composed the Sautrāntika *Vibhāṣā Śāstra*. In a large mango grove five or six li to the southwest of the city, there is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (translated into Chinese as Wuzhuo, "Unattached") sought instruction and guided the common people. At night, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga would ascend to the heavenly palace and receive the *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra Śāstra*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga Śāstra*, and others from the Bodhisattva Maitreya, while by day he would lecture and proclaim these profound principles to the great assembly. More than one hundred paces to the northwest of the mango grove, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The old foundation beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to see the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.  The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a man from the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). One thousand years after the Buddha passed away, he was born with spiritual insight and keen faculties; following the tradition, he awakened to the Way. He left the household life to study in the Mahīśāsaka school, but after a short time, he turned his faith to the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, left the household life and received his training in the Sarvāstivāda school; he was widely learned and possessed a strong memory, having mastered the teachings and investigated their underlying mechanisms. Asaṅga’s disciple Buddhasimha (translated into Chinese as Shizijue, "Lion-Awakened") had a hidden practice that was unfathomable, and he was renowned for his high talent. These two or three sages would often say to one another: "In all our cultivation of practice, we vow to behold Maitreya. If one of us should pass away first, he must return to report and let the other know where he has gone." Afterward, Buddhasimha (Shizijue) passed away first, but for three years he sent no report. Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (Shiqin) also passed away shortly thereafter, and six months went by without any report. At that time, various heterodox practitioners all mocked them, believing that Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Buddhasimha had been reborn in the evil realms and thus possessed no spiritual insight.  Later, in the first watch of the night, as Bodhisattva Asaṅga (Wuzhuo) was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditation, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and the air became brilliantly illuminated. A celestial being descended through the void, approached the courtyard, and paid homage to Asaṅga. Asaṅga asked, "Why have you come so late? What is your name now?"  He replied, "Upon departing this life, I was reborn in the inner assembly of Maitreya (Cishi) in the Tuṣita (Dushiduo) heaven, within a lotus flower. The moment the lotus opened, Maitreya praised me, saying, 'Welcome, Vast-Wisdom (Guanghui), welcome, Vast-Wisdom.' I had only just finished circling him once when I came to report."  Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked, "Where is Buddhasimha now?"  He replied, "When I was circling, I saw Buddhasimha in the outer assembly, indulging in sensual pleasures. He had no time to look at me, so how could he have come to report?"  Bodhisattva Asaṅga said, "That matter is finished. What is Maitreya’s appearance like, and what Dharma does he expound?"  He replied, "Maitreya’s physical marks and excellence are beyond the power of words to describe. The wonderful Dharma he expounds is not different in meaning from this [Dharma here], yet the Bodhisattva’s wonderful voice is clear, smooth, and harmonious; those who hear it forget their fatigue, and those who receive it are never satiated." More than forty li to the northwest of the old foundations of the lecture hall of Asaṅga (無著), one reaches an old monastery. It faces the Ganges (gaṅgā) River to the north and contains a brick stupa over a hundred feet high, marking the place where Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) first conceived the aspiration for the Mahayana. When Bodhisattva Vasubandhu arrived here from northern India, Bodhisattva Asaṅga ordered his disciples to go and welcome him. Upon arriving at this monastery, they met and gathered. A disciple of Asaṅga stopped outside the window and, after the middle of the night, recited the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (十地經). Having heard this, Vasubandhu became enlightened and filled with remorse, thinking, "This profound and wonderful Dharma is something I have never heard before. The fault of my slander originated from my tongue; since the tongue is the root of my offense, I should now cut it off." He immediately took up a sharp knife, intending to cut off his own tongue. Then he saw Asaṅga standing there, who told him, "The Mahayana teaching is the ultimate truth, praised by all Buddhas and revered by all sages. I wished to instruct you, and now you have realized it yourself. Since you have realized it at this time, what could be better? According to the holy teachings of the Buddhas, cutting off one's tongue is not repentance. In the past you used your tongue to revile the Mahayana, so now you should use your tongue to praise the Mahayana; to make amends and start anew is still a virtuous deed, but what benefit is there in remaining silent and speechless?" Having spoken these words, he suddenly disappeared. Vasubandhu followed the instruction and did not cut off his tongue. At dawn, he went to Asaṅga to consult him and receive the Mahayana. Thereupon, he refined his essence and pondered deeply, composing over a hundred Mahayana treatises, all of which were widely propagated and practiced.

t2087_text: 從此東行三百餘里，渡殑伽河，北至阿耶穆佉國（中印度境）。阿耶穆佉國，周二千四五百里。國大都城臨殑伽河，周二十餘里。其氣序土宜，同阿踰陀國。人淳俗質，勤學好福。伽藍五所，僧徒千餘人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠十餘所，異道雜居。城東南不遠，臨殑伽河岸，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺，是如來昔於此處三月說法。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪青石窣堵波。其側伽藍，僧徒二百餘人，佛像莊飾，威嚴如在。臺閣宏麗，奇製欝起，是昔佛陀馱婆（唐言覺使）論師於此製說一切有部《大毘婆沙論》。
translation: From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li and crossing the Ganges River (gaṅgā), one arrives north at the kingdom of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國) (within the borders of Central India). The kingdom of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom borders the Ganges River and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the kingdom of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and simple in their customs, diligent in study, and fond of meritorious deeds. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of various sects live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges River, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The towers and pavilions are magnificent, with unique structures rising high; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadāsa (佛陀馱婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Servant of the Buddha") formerly composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

t2087_text: 從此東南行七百餘里，渡殑伽河南、閻牟那河北，至鉢邏耶伽國（中印度境）。鉢邏耶伽國，周五千餘里。國大都城據兩河交，周二十餘里。稼穡滋盛，菓木扶疎。氣序和暢，風俗善順。好學藝，信外道。伽藍兩所，僧徒寡少，並皆習學小乘法教。天祠數百，異道寔多。大城西南瞻博迦華林中，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。基雖傾陷，尚百餘尺，在昔如來於此處降伏外道。其側則有髮、爪窣堵波、經行遺迹。髮、爪窣堵波側，有故伽藍，是提婆（唐言天受）菩薩作《廣百論》挫小乘、伏外道處。初，提婆菩薩自南印度至此伽藍，城中有外道婆羅門，高論有聞，辯才無礙，循名責實，反質窮辭。雅知提婆博究玄奧，欲挫其鋒，乃循名問曰：「汝為何名？」提婆曰：「名天。」外道曰：「天是誰？」提婆曰：「我。」外道曰：「我是誰？」提婆曰：「狗。」外道曰：「狗是誰？」提婆曰：「汝。」外道曰：「汝是誰？」提婆曰：「天。」外道曰：「天是誰？」提婆曰：「我。」外道曰：「我是誰？」提婆曰：「狗。」外道曰：「誰是狗？」提婆曰：「汝。」外道曰：「汝是誰？」提婆曰：「天。」如是循環，外道方悟。自時厥後，深敬風猷。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) and the north of the Yamunā, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢邏耶伽國) (in the territory of Central India). The country of Prayāga is more than five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is situated at the confluence of the two rivers and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant and lush, and the fruit trees are thick and spreading. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant. The people are fond of learning the arts and believe in non-Buddhist paths. There are two monasteries with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are several hundred deva temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous.  To the southwest of the great city, in a forest of Campaka (瞻博迦) flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still more than one hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued non-Buddhists at this place. Beside it are the stūpas of the hair and nails, as well as traces of his walking meditation. Beside the hair and nail stūpas is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Heaven-Received") composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to frustrate the Lesser Vehicle and subdue the non-Buddhists.  Formerly, when the Bodhisattva Deva came to this monastery from South India, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty arguments and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he would scrutinize names to demand their reality and use counter-interrogations to exhaust his opponents' words. Knowing that Deva was widely versed in profound mysteries and wishing to blunt his edge, he followed the name and asked, "What is your name?" Deva replied, "My name is Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." Through this cycle, the non-Buddhist finally attained realization. From that time forward, he deeply respected his noble conduct.
