t2087_text: 城中有天祠，瑩飾輪煥，靈異多端。依其典籍，此處是眾生殖福之勝地也，能於此祠捐捨一錢，功踰他所惠施千金。復能輕生，祠中斷命，受天福樂，悠永無窮。天祠堂前有一大樹，枝葉扶疎，陰影蒙密，有食人鬼依而棲宅，故其左右多有遺骸。若人至此祠中，無不輕捨身命，既怵邪說，又為神誘，自古迄今，習謬無替。近有婆羅門，族姓子也，闊達多智，明敏高才，來至祠中，謂眾人曰：「夫曲俗鄙志，難以導誘，吾方同事，然後攝化。」亦既登臨，俯謂友曰：「吾有死矣。昔謂詭妄，今驗真實，天仙伎樂依空接引，當從勝境捐此鄙形。」尋欲投身，自取殞絕，親友諫喻，其志不移。遂布衣服，遍周樹下，及其自投，得全軀命。久而醒曰：「唯見空中諸天召命，斯乃邪神所引，非得天樂也。」
translation: In the city there is a temple to a deity, adorned and resplendent, with many varied manifestations of spiritual power. According to its scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate a single coin at this temple yields merit exceeding a gift of a thousand gold pieces elsewhere. Furthermore, those who treat life lightly and end their existence within the temple receive heavenly bliss and joy, eternal and inexhaustible. In front of the temple hall stands a large tree with luxuriant branches and dense foliage, where a man-eating ghost (piśāca) has made its home; consequently, many skeletal remains lie scattered around it. When people come to this temple, they invariably throw away their lives, being both intimidated by perverse doctrines and enticed by the deity; from antiquity to the present, this erroneous practice has continued without change. Recently, there was a Brahmin, a son of a noble clan, who was magnanimous, wise, perceptive, and highly talented; he came to the temple and said to the crowd: "It is difficult to guide and transform those with crooked customs and base minds; I shall first join them in their actions and then lead them to conversion." Having ascended the tree, he looked down and said to his friends: "I am about to die. What I once considered a deception is now proven true; heavenly beings and celestial music are in the sky to receive me, and I shall abandon this base form to follow them to a superior realm." He immediately sought to cast himself down to end his life, and though his friends remonstrated with him, his resolve did not waver. He spread out his clothes all around beneath the tree, and when he threw himself down, he remained unharmed and his body was preserved. After a long while he regained consciousness and said: "I only saw various deities in the sky summoning me; this was the lure of evil spirits, not the attainment of heavenly bliss."

t2087_text: 大城東，兩河交，廣十餘里，土地爽塏，細沙彌漫。自古至今，諸王、豪族，凡有捨施，莫不至止，周給不計，號大施場。今戒日王者，聿修前緒，篤述惠施，五年積財，一旦傾捨，於其施場，多聚珍貨。初第一日，置大佛像，眾寶莊嚴，即持上妙奇珍，而以奉施；次常住僧；次見前眾；次高才碩學、博物多能；次外道學徒，隱淪肥遁；次鰥寡孤獨，貧窮乞人。備極珍玩，窮諸上饌，如是節級，莫不周施。府庫既傾，服玩都盡，髻中明珠，身諸瓔珞，次第施與，初無所悔。既捨施已，稱曰：「樂哉！凡吾所有，已入金剛堅固藏矣。」從此之後，諸國君王各獻珍服。嘗不踰旬，府庫充仞。大施場東合流口，日數百人自溺而死。彼俗以為欲求生天，當於此處絕粒自沈，沐浴中流，罪垢消滅。是以異國遠方，相趁萃止，七日斷食，然後絕命。至於山猨、野鹿，群遊水濱，或濯流而返，或絕食而死。當戒日王之大施也，有一獼猴，居河之濱，獨在樹下屏迹絕食，經數日後自餓而死。故諸外道修苦行者，於河中立高柱，日將旦也，便即昇之，一手一足執柱端，躡傍杙，一手一足虛懸外申，臨空不屈，延頸張目，視日右轉，逮乎曛暮，方乃下焉。若此者，其徒數十，冀斯勤苦，出離生死，或數十年未嘗懈息。
translation: To the east of the great city, where two rivers meet, the area is over ten *li* wide; the land is high and dry, covered with fine sand. From ancient times to the present, whenever kings and noble families have wished to perform acts of charity, they have all come to this place to distribute gifts without measure, and thus it is called the Grand Arena of Almsgiving (Mahādānapīṭha). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) continues the traditions of his predecessors and is devoted to the practice of charity; he accumulates wealth for five years and then, in a single day, empties his stores, gathering a vast quantity of precious goods at this arena. On the first day, a large statue of the Buddha is installed and adorned with various gems, and the most exquisite and rare treasures are offered to it. Next, offerings are made to the resident monks; then to the assembly present; then to those of high talent and profound learning, and those of broad knowledge and many skills; then to the disciples of non-Buddhist sects and those who live in seclusion; and finally to the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, and the poor and destitute. Every kind of precious object is prepared and the finest foods are exhausted; in this graded order, everyone is provided for. Once the treasury is emptied and all clothing and ornaments are exhausted, he gives away the lustrous pearl in his topknot and the various necklaces on his body one after another, without the slightest regret. Having completed the distribution, he declares: "How joyful! All that I possessed has now been deposited into the indestructible treasury of the Vajra." Following this, the kings of various countries each offer him precious garments, and within ten days, his treasury is filled once again. At the confluence of the rivers to the east of the Grand Arena of Almsgiving, several hundred people drown themselves every day. The local custom holds that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should abstain from food and drown themselves at this spot, for by bathing in the middle of the current, their sins and defilements will be eradicated. For this reason, people from distant foreign lands flock here, fasting for seven days before ending their lives. As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they roam in groups along the riverbank; some return after washing in the current, while others fast until they die. During the great almsgiving of King Śīlāditya (戒日王), there was a macaque that lived by the riverbank, remaining alone under a tree, isolating itself and fasting, until it died of starvation after several days. Therefore, the various non-Buddhist ascetics (外道) who practice austerities plant tall pillars in the river. At the approach of dawn, they climb them, grasping the top of the pillar with one hand and one foot while stepping on a side peg, with the other hand and foot suspended and stretched out into the void, held straight without bending. They crane their necks and stare with wide eyes, watching the sun as it rotates to the right, and only when dusk falls do they descend. There are dozens of such followers who, hoping through this diligent suffering to escape the cycle of birth and death, have never slackened for several decades.

t2087_text: 從此西南入大林中，惡獸、野象，群暴行旅，非多徒黨，難以經涉。行五百餘里，至憍賞彌國（舊曰拘睒彌國，訛也。中印度境）。憍賞彌國，周六千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土稱沃壤，地利豐植，粳稻多，甘蔗茂。氣序暑熱，風俗剛猛。好學典藝，崇樹福善。伽藍十餘所，傾頓荒蕪，僧徒三百餘人，學小乘教。天祠五十餘所，外道寔多。城內故宮中有大精舍，高六十餘尺，有刻檀佛像，上懸石蓋，鄔陀衍那王（唐言出愛。舊云優填王，訛也）之所作也。靈相間起，神光時照。諸國君王恃力欲舉，雖多人眾，莫能轉移。遂圖供養，俱言得真，語其源迹，即此像也。初，如來成正覺已，上昇天宮，為母說法，三月不還。其王思慕，願圖形像。乃請尊者沒特伽羅子，以神通力，接工人上天宮，親觀妙相，雕刻栴檀。如來自天宮還也，刻檀之像起迎世尊，世尊慰曰：「教化勞耶？開導末世，寔此為冀。」精舍東百餘步，有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。其側不遠，有如來井及浴室，井猶充汲，室以頹毀。
translation: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters ferocious beasts and wild elephants that attack travelers in herds; unless one has a large party, it is difficult to pass through. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) (formerly called the country of Kausāmbi, which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kauśāmbī is over six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much *śāli* rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) (in the language of the Tang, "Giving Rise to Love"; formerly called King Youtian (優填王), which is erroneous). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to move it, but although they brought many people, none could shift it. Consequently, they have had copies made for worship, each claiming to have obtained the true likeness; when one speaks of their origin, it is indeed this very image. Initially, after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, and for three months he did not return. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, who consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others? You are truly the hope for guiding those in the final age." More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

t2087_text: 城內東南隅，有故宅餘趾，是具史羅（舊云瞿師羅，訛也）長者故宅也，中有佛精舍及髮、爪窣堵波。復有故基，如來浴室也。城東南不遠，有故伽藍，具史羅長者舊園也。中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建立，高二百餘尺。如來於此數年說法。其側則有過去四佛座及經行遺迹之所，復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。伽藍東南重閣上有故塼室，世親菩薩嘗住此中作《唯識論》破斥小乘，難諸外道。伽藍東菴沒羅林中有故基，是無著菩薩於此作《顯揚聖教論》。城西南八九里，毒龍石窟。昔者如來伏此毒龍，於中留影，雖則傳記，今無所見。其側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺。傍有如來經行遺迹及髮、爪窣堵波，病苦之徒，求願多愈。釋迦法盡，此國最後，故上自君王，下及眾庶，入此國境，自然感傷，莫不飲泣，悲歎而歸。
translation: In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (具史羅) (formerly called Qushiluo (瞿師羅), which is erroneous). Within it are a Buddha-*vihāra* (佛精舍) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There are also old foundations that were the bathhouse of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed a treatise on consciousness-only (唯識論) to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery are old foundations where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa* (顯揚聖教論). Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of a poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, it cannot be seen today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign above down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country naturally feel a sense of sorrow, and there is no one who does not weep and return home with sighs of lamentation.

t2087_text: 龍窟東北大林中，行七百餘里，渡殑伽河，北至迦奢布羅城，周十餘里，居人富樂。城傍有故伽藍，唯餘基址，是昔護法菩薩伏外道處。此國先王扶於邪說，欲毀佛法，崇敬外道。外道眾中召一論師，聰敏高明達幽微者，作偽邪書千頌，凡三萬二千言，非毀佛法，扶正本宗。於是召集僧眾，令相摧論。外道有勝，當毀佛法；眾僧無負，斷舌以謝。是時僧徒懼有退負，集而議曰：「慧日已沈，法橋將毀，王黨外道，其可敵乎？事勢若斯，計將安出？」眾咸默然，無竪議者。護法菩薩年在幼稚，辯慧多聞，風範弘遠，在大眾中揚言贊曰：「愚雖不敏，請陳其略。誠宜以我疾應王命。高論得勝，斯靈祐也；徵議墮負，乃稚齒也。然則進退有辭，法、僧無咎。」僉曰：「允諧。」如其籌策。尋應王命，即昇論座。外道乃提頓綱網，抑揚辭義，誦其所執，待彼異論。護法菩薩納其言而笑曰：「吾得勝矣！將覆逆而誦耶？為亂辭而誦耶？」外道憮然而謂曰：「子無自高也。能領語盡，此則為勝，順受其文，後釋其義。」護法乃隨其聲調，述其文義，辭理不謬，氣韻無差。於是外道聞已，欲自斷舌。護法曰：「斷舌非謝，改執是悔。」即為說法，心信意悟。王捨邪道，遵崇正法。護法伏外道側，有窣堵波，無憂王所建也，基雖傾陷，尚高二百餘尺。是如來昔於此處六月說法。傍有經行之迹及髮、爪窣堵波。
translation: Traveling over seven hundred li through a great forest to the northeast of the dragon cave and crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura (迦奢布羅城), which is over ten li in circuit and whose inhabitants are wealthy and happy. Beside the city is an old monastery of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla once subdued the heretics. A former king of this country supported heterodox views and wished to destroy the Buddha-dharma while venerating the heretics. From among the heretics, he summoned a master of treatises who was intelligent, brilliant, and well-versed in subtle mysteries to compose a fallacious and heterodox work of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, to slander the Buddha-dharma and establish his own sect as the orthodox one. Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. If the heretics were victorious, the Buddha-dharma was to be destroyed; if the assembly of monks were not defeated, [the heretic] would cut out his tongue in atonement. At that time, the monks, fearing defeat, gathered and discussed the matter, saying, "The sun of wisdom has already set, and the bridge of the Dharma is about to be destroyed. The king sides with the heretics; how can we oppose them? With the situation as it is, what plan can we devise?" The assembly was silent, and no one could offer a suggestion. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was eloquent, wise, and widely learned, with a character of great breadth. He spoke out in the midst of the assembly, saying, "Although I am not clever, I ask to present a brief proposal. It is truly appropriate that I should quickly respond to the king's command. If I win the high debate, it will be a spiritual blessing; if I am defeated in the inquiry, it will be attributed to my tender age. In this way, there will be an explanation whether I advance or retreat, and the Dharma and the Sangha will be without fault." Everyone said, "This is acceptable." He followed his plan, immediately responded to the king's command, and ascended the debate seat. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) then laid out his main points, modulating his tone and meaning, and recited his own tenets, waiting for the opponent to raise objections. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) accepted his words and laughed, saying, "I have already won! Shall I recite it in reverse order? Or shall I recite it with the words jumbled?" The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said to him, "Do not be arrogant. If you can repeat the words in their entirety, that will be victory; accept the text as it is, and then explain its meaning." Dharmapāla then followed his intonation and recited the text and its meaning; his phrasing and logic were not in error, and his tone and rhythm were without discrepancy. Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhist wanted to cut out his own tongue. Dharmapāla said, "Cutting the tongue is not an apology; changing one's views is repentance." He then preached the Dharma for him, and his heart became faithful and his mind enlightened. The king abandoned his heterodox path and followed and honored the true Dharma. Beside the place where Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhist, there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has subsided, it is still over two hundred feet high. This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months. Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation (caṅkrama) and a stupa containing his hair and nails.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 自此北行百七八十里，至鞞索（山格反）迦國（中印度境）。鞞索迦國，周四千餘里。國大都城周十六里。穀稼殷盛，華果具繁。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。好學不倦，求福不回。伽藍二十餘所，僧眾三千餘人，並學小乘正量部法。天祠五十餘所，外道甚多。城南道左，有大伽藍。昔提婆設摩阿羅漢於此造《識身論》，說無我人；瞿波阿羅漢作《聖教要實論》，說有我人。因此法執，遂深諍論。又是護法菩薩於此七日中摧伏小乘一百論師。伽藍側有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王所建也。如來昔日，六年於此說法導化。說法側有奇樹，高六七尺，春秋遞代，常無增減。是如來昔嘗淨齒，棄其遺枝，因植根柢，繁茂至今。諸邪見人及外道眾競來殘伐，尋生如故。其側不遠，有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。靈基連隅，林沼交映。從此東北行五百餘里，至室羅伐悉底國（舊曰舍衛，訛也。中印度境）。
translation: Traveling northward from here for one hundred and seventy or eighty li, one arrives at the country of Viśākhā (鞞索迦國) (索 is read 山格反) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Viśākhā is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is sixteen li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are fond of learning without fatigue and are unswerving in their pursuit of merit. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. To the left of the road south of the city, there is a large saṃghārāma. In the past, the Arhat Devaśarman (提婆設摩) composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (識身論) here, which argues that there is no self or person; the Arhat Gopa (瞿波) composed the *Treatise on the Essential Truth of the Sacred Teaching* (聖教要實論), which argues that there is a self and a person. Because of this difference in doctrinal adherence, they engaged in deep debate. Furthermore, it was here that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) defeated one hundred masters of the Lesser Vehicle in seven days. Beside the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent six years here preaching the Dharma and guiding the people. Beside the place where he preached is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high; as spring and autumn succeed one another, it remains constant, neither increasing nor decreasing. It is said that the Tathāgata once cleaned his teeth here and discarded the twig, which then took root and has remained lush to this day. Various people of wrong views and followers of non-Buddhist paths have vied to cut it down, but it immediately grows back as it was before. Not far from there is the site of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The spiritual foundations are connected at the corners, and the woods and ponds reflect one another. Traveling northeast from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) (formerly called Shewei, which is an error; it is within the borders of Central India).
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 室羅伐悉底國，周六千餘里。都城荒頓，疆埸無紀。宮城故基周二十餘里，雖多荒圮，尚有居人。穀稼豐，氣序和。風俗淳質，篤學好福。伽藍數百，圮壞良多，僧徒寡少，學正量部。天祠百所，外道甚多。此則如來在世之時，鉢邏犀那恃多王（唐言勝軍。舊曰波斯匿，訛略也）所治國都也。故宮城內有故基，勝軍王殿餘趾也。次東不遠，有一故基，上建小窣堵波，昔勝軍王為如來所建大法堂也。法堂側不遠，故基上有窣堵波，是佛姨母鉢邏闍鉢底（唐言生主。舊云波闍波提，訛也）苾芻尼精舍，勝軍王之所建立。次東窣堵波，是蘇達多（唐言善施。舊曰須達，訛也）故宅也。善施長者宅側有大窣堵波，是鴦窶利摩羅（唐言指鬘。舊曰央掘摩羅，訛也）捨邪之處，鴦窶利摩羅者，室羅伐悉底之凶人也。作害生靈，為暴城國，殺人取指，冠首為鬘。將欲害母，以充指數。世尊悲愍，方行導化。遙見世尊，竊自喜曰：「我今生天必矣。先師有教，遺言在茲，害佛殺母，當生梵天。」謂其母曰：「老今且止，先當害彼大沙門。」尋即杖劍往逆世尊。如來於是徐行而退，凶人指鬘疾驅不逮。世尊謂曰：「何守鄙志，捨善本，激惡源？」時指鬘聞誨，悟所行非，因即歸命，求入法中，精勤不怠，證羅漢果。
translation: The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are honest and simple, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of merit. There are several hundred monasteries, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya (正量部) school. There are one hundred deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths.  This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王; in Chinese, Shengjun [Victorious Army]; the old term, Bosini (波斯匿), is a corruption and abbreviation) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Within the old palace city, there are old foundations, which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit. Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stupa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit formerly built for the Tathāgata. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stupa on old foundations; this is the nunnery of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底; in Chinese, Shengzhu [Lord of Life]; the old term, Bozhebotí (波闍波提), is a corruption), which was built by King Prasenajit. To the east of this is a stupa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (蘇達多; in Chinese, Shanshi [Well-Bestowing]; the old term, Xuda, is a corruption). Beside the residence of the elder Sudatta, there is a large stupa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅; in Chinese, Zhiman [Finger-Garland]; the old term, Yangjuemoluo (央掘摩羅), is a corruption) abandoned his evil ways. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and committed atrocities in the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers and wearing them on his head as a garland. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of his fingers. The World-honored One, moved by compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I am now certain to be reborn in heaven. My former teacher gave me instructions, and his legacy is here: by killing a Buddha and killing one's mother, one shall be reborn in the Brahmā heaven." He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-honored One said to him, "Why do you persist in your base intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then took refuge, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced diligently without slackening, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

城南五六里，有逝多林（唐言勝林。舊曰祇陀，訛也），是給孤獨園。勝軍王大臣善施為佛建精舍，昔為伽藍，今已荒廢。東門左右各建石柱，高七十餘尺，左柱鏤輪相於其端，右柱刻牛形於其上，並無憂王之所建也。室宇傾圮，唯餘故基，獨一甎室巋然獨在，中有佛像。昔者如來昇三十三天，為母說法之後，勝軍王聞出愛王刻檀像佛，乃造此像。善施長者仁而聰敏，積而能散，拯乏濟貧，哀孤恤老，時美其德，號給孤獨焉。聞佛功德，深生尊敬，願建精舍，請佛降臨。世尊命舍利子隨瞻揆焉，唯太子逝多園地爽塏。尋詣太子，具以情告。太子戲言：「金遍乃賣。」善施聞之，心豁如也，即出藏金，隨言布地。有少未滿，太子請留，曰：「佛誠良田，宜植善種。」即於空地，建立精舍。世尊即之，告阿難曰：「園地善施所買，林樹逝多所施，二人同心，式崇功業。自今已去，應謂此地為逝多林給孤獨園。」給孤獨園東北有窣堵波，是如來洗病苾芻處。昔如來之在世也，有病苾芻，含苦獨處。世尊見而問曰：「汝何所苦？汝何獨居？」曰：「我性疎嬾，不耐看病，故今嬰疾，無人瞻視。」如來是時愍而告曰：「善男子，我今看汝。」以手拊摩，病苦皆愈。扶出戶外，更易敷蓐，親為盥洗，改著新衣。佛語苾芻：「當自勤勵。」聞誨感恩，心悅身豫。給孤獨園西北有小窣堵波，是沒特伽羅子運神通力舉舍利子衣帶不動之處。昔佛在無熱惱池，人、天咸集，唯舍利子不時從會。佛命沒特伽羅往召來集。沒特伽羅承命而往，舍利子補護法衣。沒特伽羅曰：「世尊今在無熱惱池，命我召爾。」舍利子曰：「且止，須我補竟，與子偕行。」沒特伽羅曰：「若不速行，欲運神力，舉爾石室至大會所。」舍利子乃解衣帶置地，曰：「若舉此帶，我身或動。」時沒特伽羅運大神通，舉帶不動，地為之震。因以神足還詣佛所，見舍利子已在會坐。沒特伽羅俛而歎曰：「乃今以知，神通之力不如智慧之力矣。」舉帶窣堵波側不遠，有井。如來在世，汲充佛用。其側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，中有如來舍利。經行之迹，說法之處，並樹旌表，建窣堵波。冥祇警衛，靈瑞間起，或鼓天樂，或聞神香，景福之祥，難以備敘。伽藍後不遠，是外道梵志殺婬女以謗佛處。如來十力無畏，一切種智，人、天宗仰，聖賢遵奉。時諸外道共相議曰：「宜行詭詐，眾中謗辱。」乃誘雇婬女，詐為聽法，眾所知已，密而殺之，埋屍樹側，稱怨告王。王命求訪，於逝多園得其屍焉。是時外道高聲唱言：「喬答摩大沙門常稱戒忍，今私此女，殺而滅口。既婬既殺，何戒何忍？」諸天空中隨聲唱曰：「外道凶人為此謗耳。」伽藍東百餘步，有大深坑，是提婆達多欲以毒藥害佛，生身陷入地獄處。提婆達多（唐言天授），斛飯王之子也。精勤十二年，已誦持八萬法藏。後為利故，求學神通，親近惡友，共相議曰：「我相三十，減佛未幾；大眾圍繞，何異如來？」思惟是已，即事破僧。舍利子、沒特伽羅子奉佛指告，承佛威神，說法誨喻，僧復和合。提婆達多惡心不捨，以惡毒藥置指爪中，欲因作禮，以傷害佛。方行此謀，自遠而來，至於此也，地遂坼焉，生陷地獄。其南復有大坑，瞿伽梨苾芻毀謗如來，生身陷入地獄。瞿伽梨陷坑南八百餘步，有大深坑，是戰遮婆羅門女毀謗如來，生身陷入地獄之處。佛為人、天說諸法要，有外道弟子，遙見世尊大眾恭敬，便自念曰：「要於今日辱喬答摩，敗其善譽，當令我師獨擅芳聲。」乃懷繫木盂，至給孤獨園，於大眾中揚聲唱曰：「此說法人與我私通，腹中之子乃釋種也。」邪見者莫不信然，貞固者知為訕謗。時天帝釋欲除疑故，化為白鼠，齧斷盂系，系斷之聲震動大眾，凡諸見聞增深喜悅。眾中一人起持木盂，示彼女曰：「是汝兒耶？」是時也，地自開坼，全身墜陷，入無間獄，具受其殃。凡此三坑，洞無涯底，秋夏霖雨，溝池泛溢，而此深坑，嘗無水止。伽藍東六七十步，有一精舍，高六十餘尺，中有佛像，東面而坐。如來在昔，於此與諸外道論議。次東有天祠，量等精舍。日旦流光，天祠之影不蔽精舍；日將落照，精舍之陰遂覆天祠。影覆精舍東三四里，有窣堵波，是尊者舍利子與外道論議處。初，善施長者買逝多太子園，欲為如來建立精舍。時尊者舍利子隨長者而瞻揆，外道六師求角神力，舍利子隨事攝化，應物降伏。其側精舍前建窣堵波，如來於此摧諸外道，又受毘舍佉母請。受請窣堵波南，是毘盧釋迦王（舊曰毘琉離主，訛也）興甲兵誅釋種，至此見佛歸兵之處。毘盧釋迦王嗣位之後，追怨前辱，興甲兵，動大眾，部署已畢，申命方行。時有苾芻聞以白佛，世尊於是坐枯樹下。毘盧釋迦王遙見世尊，下乘禮敬，退立言曰：「茂樹扶疎，何故不坐？枯株朽櫱，而乃遊止？」世尊告曰：「宗族者，枝葉也。枝葉將危，庇蔭何在？」王曰：「世尊為宗親耳，可以迴駕。」於是覩聖感懷，還軍返國。還軍之側，有窣堵波，是釋女被戮處。毘盧釋迦王誅釋克勝，簡五百女，充實宮闈。釋女憤恚，怨言不遜，詈其王：「家人之子也。」王聞發怒，命令誅戮。執法者奉王教，刖其手足，投諸阬阱。時諸釋女含苦稱佛，世尊聖鑒，照其苦毒，告命苾芻，攝衣而往，為諸釋女說微妙法，所謂羈纏五欲，流轉三途，恩愛別離，生死長遠。時諸釋女聞佛指誨，遠塵離垢，得法眼淨，同時命終，俱生天上。時天帝釋化作婆羅門，收骸火葬，後人記焉。誅釋窣堵波側不遠，有大涸池，是毘盧釋迦王陷身入地獄處。世尊觀釋女已，還給孤獨園，告諸苾芻，今毘盧釋迦王却後七日，為火所燒。王聞佛記，甚懷惶懼。至第七日，安樂無危。王用歡慶，命諸宮女往至河側，娛遊樂飲。猶懼火起，鼓棹清流，隨波泛濫。熾焰飈發，焚輕舟，墜王身，入無間獄，備受諸苦。
translation: Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林; in the language of the Tang, "Victory Grove"; the old term "Qituo" (祇陀) is a corruption), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery, but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and intact, containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth only to distribute it, rescuing the needy, relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the aged. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada ("the Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of reverence and wished to build a vihāra and invite the Buddha to descend. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) was high and dry. He immediately went to the Prince and explained his intentions in full. The Prince jokingly said, "If you cover the ground with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had said. There was a small portion left uncovered, and the Prince requested to keep it, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds there." He then built the vihāra on the vacant land. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men were of one mind, and thus they jointly established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who was suffering and living alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "I am by nature lazy and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to look after me." At that time, the Tathāgata felt compassion and said to him, "Good man, I will now nurse you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent and exert yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) exercised his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the gathering. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt, and the earth shook because of it. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the stupa of the belt, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with signs and have stupas built upon them. Dark spirits guard and protect them, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes heavenly music is played, and sometimes divine incense is smelled. The auspicious omens of these blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the omniscience of all modes; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the assembly." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the assembly, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and complained to the king, claiming injury. The king ordered a search, and her body was found in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) always praises precepts and patience; now he has had illicit relations with this woman and killed her to silence her. Having committed both lechery and murder, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky responded in unison, saying: "The wicked non-Buddhists have fabricated this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta (in Chinese, "Heaven-bestowed") was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them: "My physical marks are thirty; they are not much less than the Buddha's. With the great assembly surrounding me, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, preached and admonished them, and the Sangha was reconciled. Devadatta did not abandon his evil heart; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the Bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. When the Buddha was preaching the essentials of the Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an external path saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama (喬答摩) today and ruin his good reputation, so that my teacher alone may possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her body and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those of evil views all believed it to be true, while those who were steadfast knew it to be a slander. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋), wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt their joy increase. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell into it, her whole body sinking into the Avīci (無間) hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions. These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows. Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a vihāra (精舍) over sixty feet high, in which there is an image of the Buddha seated facing east. In the past, the Tathāgata debated with various heretics here. To the east, there is a deva temple equal in size to the monastery. When the sun rises and sheds its light, the shadow of the deva temple does not cover the monastery; when the sun is about to set, the shadow of the monastery covers the deva temple. Three or four li to the east of the Shadow-covering Vihāra (影覆精舍), there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the heretics.  Initially, the elder Sudatta (善施長者) purchased the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) and wished to build a monastery for the Tathāgata. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accompanied the elder to survey the site. The teachers of the six heretical schools sought to compete in supernatural powers, but Śāriputra converted them according to the circumstances and subdued them in response to their challenges. Beside it, in front of a vihāra, a stūpa has been built; here the Tathāgata defeated the various heretics and also accepted the invitation of Mother Viśākhā.  To the south of the stūpa where he accepted the invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) (formerly called King Piliuli (毘琉離主), which is incorrect) raised an army to slaughter the Śākya clan, and where he saw the Buddha and turned his troops back. After King Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he pursued his resentment over a previous humiliation, raised an army, and mobilized the masses. Once the deployment was complete, he issued the order to march. At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and informed the Buddha. The World-Honored One then sat beneath a withered tree. King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar, dismounted to pay his respects, stood back, and said, "Lush trees are spreading and thick; why do you not sit under them, but instead stay by a withered stump and rotten branches?" The World-Honored One replied, "One's own kin are like the branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves are in danger, where is the shade?" The King said, "The World-Honored One is doing this for his kinsmen; I may turn back my carriage." Thereupon, seeing the Holy One and feeling moved, he returned his army to his country. Beside the place where the army turned back, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Śākya women were slaughtered. When King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he selected five hundred women to fill his palace. The Śākya women were filled with indignation and, speaking resentful and insolent words, cursed the King, saying, "You are the son of a domestic servant." When the King heard this, he became enraged and ordered them to be slaughtered. The executioners obeyed the King’s command, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that time, the Śākya women, enduring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy insight, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there. He preached the subtle Dharma to the Śākya women, explaining how they were bound by the five desires, wandering through the three evil paths, separated from those they loved, and caught in the long cycle of birth and death. When the Śākya women heard the Buddha’s instruction, they cast off the dust and removed the stains, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and at that same moment passed away and were all reborn in the heavens. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a Brahmin, collected their remains, and cremated them; later generations have commemorated this. Not far from the stūpa of the slaughtered Śākyas, there is a large dried-up pond, which is the place where King Virūḍhaka sank into the earth and fell into hell. After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya women, he returned to the Jetavana (給孤獨園) and told the bhikṣus, "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka will be consumed by fire." When the King heard the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with great fear and anxiety. When the seventh day arrived, he was safe and without danger. The king, feeling jubilant, ordered the palace maidens to go to the riverside to enjoy themselves with music and wine. Still fearing that a fire might break out, he rowed upon the clear currents and drifted along with the waves. Suddenly, a blazing fire erupted, consuming the light boat; the king’s body fell, and he entered the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering.

translation: Three or four li to the northwest of the monastery, one reaches the Wood of Regained Sight (Andhavana). There are traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and places where various sages practiced concentration, all marked by commemorative signs, with stūpas built. In the past, there was a band of five hundred bandits in this country who ran amok in the villages and acted lawlessly throughout the cities and states. King Prasenajit (勝軍王) captured them, gouged out their eyes, and abandoned them in the deep forest. The bandits, tormented by suffering, cried out in supplication to the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Jetavana Monastery (逝多精舍); hearing their cries of grief, he felt great compassion, and a gentle, cooling breeze blew medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains into their eyes, whereupon their sight was immediately restored. Upon seeing the World-Honored One standing before them, they conceived the resolve for enlightenment, bowed in joyful worship, and departed after casting down their staves, which then took root there.

translation: More than sixty li to the northwest of the great city, there is an ancient city; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. To the south of the city is a stūpa, which marks the place where he first met his father after attaining perfect enlightenment. To the north of the city is a stūpa containing the entire-body relics of the Buddha Kāśyapa. Both were built by King Aśoka (無憂王).

t2087_text: 從此東南行五百餘里，至劫比羅伐窣堵國（舊曰迦羅衛國，訛。中印度境）。劫比羅伐窣堵國，周四千餘里。空城十數，荒蕪已甚。王城頹圮，周量不詳。其內宮城周十四五里，壘甎而成，基跡峻固。空荒久遠，人里稀曠。無大君長，城各立主。土地良沃，稼穡時播。氣序無愆，風俗和暢。伽藍故基千有餘所，而宮城之側有一伽藍，僧徒三千餘人，習學小乘正量部教。天祠兩所，異道雜居。宮城內有故基，淨飯王正殿也。上建精舍，中作王像。其側不遠有故基，摩訶摩耶（唐言大術）夫人寢殿也。上建精舍，中作夫人之像。其側精舍，是釋迦菩薩降神母胎處，中作菩薩降神之像。上座部菩薩以嗢呾羅頞沙荼月三十日夜降神母胎，當此五月十五日；諸部則以此月二十三日夜降母胎，當此五月八日。菩薩降神東北，有窣堵波，阿私多仙相太子處。菩薩誕靈之日，嘉祥輻湊。時淨飯王召諸相師而告之曰：「此子生也，善惡何若？宜悉乃正，明言以對。」曰：「依先聖之記，考吉祥之應，在家作轉輪聖王，捨家當成等正覺。」是時阿私多仙自遠而至，叩門請見。王甚慶悅，躬迎禮敬，請就寶座，曰：「不意大仙今日降顧。」仙曰：「我在天宮安居宴坐，忽見諸天群從蹈舞，我時問言：『何悅豫之甚也？』曰：『大仙當知，贍部洲中釋種淨飯王第一夫人，今產太子，當證三菩提，圓明一切智。』我聞是語，故來瞻仰。所悲朽耄，不遭聖化。」城南門有窣堵波，是太子與諸釋角力擲象之處。太子伎藝多能，獨拔倫匹。淨飯大王懷慶將返，僕夫馭象，方欲出城。提婆達多素負強力，自外而入，問馭者曰：「嚴駕此象，其誰欲乘？」曰：「太子將還，故往奉馭。」提婆達多發憤引象，批其顙，蹴其臆，僵仆塞路，杜絕行途，無能轉移，人眾填塞。難陀後至，而問之曰：「誰死此象？」曰：「提婆達多。」即曳之避路。太子至，又問曰：「誰為不善，害此象耶？」曰：「提婆達多害以杜門，難陀引之開徑。」太子乃舉象高擲，越度城塹，其象墮地，為大深阬，土俗相傳為象墮阬也。其側精舍中作太子像。其側又有精舍，太子妃寢宮也，中作耶輸陀羅，并有羅怙羅像。宮側精舍作受業之像，太子學堂故基也。城東南隅有一精舍，中作太子乘白馬凌虛之像，是踰城處也。城四門外各有精舍，中作老、病、死人、沙門之像。是太子遊觀，覩相增懷，深厭塵俗，於此感悟，命僕迴駕。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kapilavastu (劫比羅伐窣堵國) (formerly called Jialuowei (迦羅衛國), which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kapilavastu is over four thousand *li* in circuit. There are more than ten empty cities, which are extremely desolate and overgrown. The royal city is in ruins, and its exact dimensions are unknown. The inner palace city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it was built of piled bricks, and its foundations remain high and solid. Having been desolate for a long time, the inhabited villages are sparse and wide apart. There is no great monarch; each city has its own ruler. The land is fertile and rich, and crops are sown at the proper times. The climate is regular, and the customs are harmonious and pleasant. There are more than a thousand old foundations of *saṃghārāmas*, and beside the palace city is one *saṃghārāma* with more than three thousand monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are two *deva* temples; followers of different sects live intermixed.  Inside the palace city are the old foundations of the main hall of King Śuddhodana. A vihāra (精舍) has been built upon it, containing a statue of the king. Not far to its side are the old foundations of the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā (which in Chinese means "Great Illusion"). A vihāra has been built upon it, containing a statue of the queen. The vihāra beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya descended into his mother’s womb; inside is a statue of the Bodhisattva descending into the womb. The Sthavira school holds that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month here; the other schools hold that he descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the twenty-third day of that month, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month here. To the northeast of the place where the Bodhisattva’s spirit descended, there is a stūpa at the site where the rishi Asita (阿私多) examined the physiognomy of the prince. On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious signs converged. At that time, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) summoned the various physiognomists and said to them: "This child has been born; what is his fortune, good or evil? You must examine him thoroughly and speak clearly in your reply." They said: "According to the records of the ancient sages and examining the auspicious omens, if he remains in household life, he will become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin); if he leaves the household life, he will attain equal and correct enlightenment (samyaksambodhi)." At this time, the rishi Asita arrived from afar and knocked at the gate to request an audience. The king was very joyful, personally welcomed and paid homage to him, and invited him to take a precious seat, saying: "I did not expect the great rishi to visit today." The rishi said: "I was dwelling in peace and sitting at ease in the heavenly palace when I suddenly saw the hosts of devas dancing. I then asked them: 'Why are you so extremely joyful?' They replied: 'Great rishi, you should know that in Jambudvīpa, the first wife of the Śākya King Śuddhodana has now given birth to a prince who shall attain *saṃbodhi* (三菩提) and perfect the light of all-knowing wisdom.' Having heard these words, I came to pay my respects. What I lament is my decrepitude, that I shall not encounter his holy transformation." At the south gate of the city, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the prince competed in strength with the other Śākyas and threw an elephant. The prince was highly skilled in many arts, standing alone and peerless. King Śuddhodana, feeling joy, was about to return when a servant was driving an elephant, just as they were about to exit the city. Devadatta, who had long prided himself on his great strength, was entering from outside and asked the driver, "You have prepared this elephant; who is to ride it?" He replied, "The prince is about to return, so I am going to serve as his driver." Devadatta, in a fit of anger, pulled the elephant, struck its forehead, and kicked its chest, causing it to fall dead and block the road, obstructing the path so that it could not be moved, and the crowd became congested. Nanda arrived later and asked, "Who killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta." He immediately dragged it aside to clear the path. When the prince arrived, he also asked, "Who committed this evil act and killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta killed it to block the gate, and Nanda dragged it away to open the path." The prince then lifted the elephant and flung it high, over the city moat. Where the elephant fell to the ground, it formed a large, deep pit, which local tradition calls the Pit of the Fallen Elephant. In a vihāra (精舍) beside it, a statue of the prince has been made. Beside that is another vihāra, which was the bedchamber of the prince's consort; inside are statues of Yaśodharā and Rāhula. In the vihāra beside the palace, a statue has been made in the posture of receiving instruction; this is the original site of the prince’s schoolroom. At the southeast corner of the city is a vihāra containing a statue of the prince riding a white horse through the air, marking the spot where he leaped over the city wall. Outside each of the four city gates is a vihāra containing statues of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a *śramaṇa*. These represent the prince’s excursions, where, upon seeing these signs, his anxiety increased and he became deeply weary of the mundane world; it was here that he was awakened [to renunciation] and ordered his servant to turn the carriage back.

translation: Traveling over fifty *li* south of the city, one reaches an ancient city containing a *stūpa*; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Krakucchanda (迦羅迦村馱佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. Not far to the south of the city is a *stūpa* marking the place where he met his father after attaining full enlightenment. To the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* containing the relics of that Tathāgata’s remains. In front of it stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, on top of which is carved the image of a lion, with an inscription on the side recording the events of his *parinirvāṇa*; it was erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

translation: Traveling more than thirty li northeast from the city of Krakucchanda Buddha (迦羅迦村馱佛), one reaches an ancient great city. Inside it is a stupa; this is the native city of Kanakamuni Buddha (迦諾迦牟尼佛) from the time in the Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was forty thousand years. Not far to the northeast is a stupa, which is the place where, having attained perfect enlightenment, he converted his father. To the north of this is a stupa containing the relics of that Tathagata’s physical body. In front of it stands a stone pillar over twenty feet high, with the image of a lion carved on top and an account of his nirvana inscribed on the side, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

t2087_text: 城東北四十餘里，有窣堵波，是太子坐樹陰，觀耕田，於此習定，而得離欲。淨飯王見太子坐樹陰，入寂定，日光逈照，樹影不移，心知靈聖，更深珍敬。大城西北，有數百千窣堵波，釋種誅死處也。毘盧釋迦王既克諸釋，虜其族類，得九千九百九十萬人，並從殺戮，積尸如莾，流血成池。天警人心，收骸瘞葬。誅釋西南，有四小窣堵波，四釋種拒軍處。初，勝軍王嗣位也，求婚釋種。釋種鄙其非類，謬以家人之女，重禮娉焉。勝軍王立為正后，其產子男，是為毘盧釋迦王。毘盧釋迦欲就舅氏請益受業，至此城南，見新講堂，即中憩駕。諸釋聞之，逐而詈曰：「卑賤婢子，敢居此室！此室諸釋建也，擬佛居焉。」毘盧釋迦嗣位之後，追復先辱，便興甲兵，至此屯軍。釋種四人躬耕畎畝，便即抗拒，兵寇退散，已而入城。族人以為承輪王之祚胤，為法王之宗子，敢行凶暴，安忍殺害，污辱宗門，絕親遠放。四人被逐，北趣雪山，一為烏仗那國王，一為梵衍那國王，一為呬摩呾羅國王，一為商彌國王，奕世傳業，苗裔不絕。
translation: More than forty li to the northeast of the city, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Prince sat in the shade of a tree, watched the plowing of the fields, and practiced meditation, thereby attaining freedom from desire. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) saw the Prince sitting in the shade of the tree, having entered into tranquil meditation, while the sunlight shone brightly yet the shadow of the tree did not move, he knew in his heart that the Prince was spiritually holy, and he cherished and respected him all the more.  To the northwest of the great city, there are several hundred thousand stūpas; these are the places where the Śākya clan were slaughtered. After King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) had conquered the Śākyas, he took their kin captive, obtaining ninety-nine million nine hundred thousand people, all of whom he put to death. The piled-up corpses were like a thicket, and the flowing blood formed a pond. Heaven stirred the hearts of men, and they gathered the remains and buried them.  To the southwest of the place where the Śākyas were slaughtered, there are four small stūpas; these are the places where four Śākya men resisted the army. Originally, when King Prasenajit (勝軍王) ascended the throne, he sought a marriage alliance with the Śākyas. The Śākyas, despising him as not being of their own kind, deceitfully gave him the daughter of a servant, yet they betrothed her with great ceremony. King Prasenajit established her as his principal queen, and she gave birth to a son, who was King Virūḍhaka.  When Virūḍhaka wished to go to his maternal uncles to request instruction and pursue his studies, he arrived south of this city and, seeing a new lecture hall, stopped his carriage to rest inside. When the Śākyas heard of this, they drove him out, cursing him: "You base-born slave, how dare you occupy this hall! This hall was built by the Śākyas, intended for the Buddha to reside in." After Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he sought to avenge this former humiliation, so he raised an army and marched to this place to encamp his troops. Four members of the Śākya clan, who were personally plowing the fields, immediately resisted them; the invading army retreated and dispersed, and the four men then entered the city. Their clansmen, believing that as descendants of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) and sons of the Dharma King, they should not have dared to commit acts of violence or heartlessly kill others, felt they had disgraced the clan; consequently, they severed ties with them and sent them into distant exile. After the four men were expelled, they fled north to the Snow Mountains; one became the king of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國), one the king of Bāmīyān (梵衍那國), one the king of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國), and one the king of Śami (商彌國). Their dynasties passed down the throne for generations, and their lineage remained unbroken.

t2087_text: 城南三四里尼拘律樹林，有窣堵波，無憂王建也。釋迦如來成正覺已，還國見父王，為說法處。淨飯王知如來降魔軍已，遊行化導，情懷渴仰，思得禮敬。乃命使請如來曰：「昔期成佛，當還本生。斯言在耳，時來降趾。」使至佛所，具宣王意。如來告曰：「却後七日，當還本生。」使臣還以白王，淨飯王乃告命臣庶，灑掃衢路，儲積華香，與諸群臣四十里外佇駕奉迎。是時如來與大眾俱，八金剛周衛，四天王前導，帝釋與欲界天侍左，梵王與色界天侍右，諸苾芻僧列在其後。維佛在眾，如月映星，威神動三界，光明踰七曜，步虛空，至生國。王與從臣禮敬已畢，俱共還國，止尼拘盧陀僧伽藍。其側不遠有窣堵波，是如來於大樹下，東面而坐，受姨母金縷袈裟。次此窣堵波，是如來於此度八王子及五百釋種。城東門內路左，有窣堵波，昔一切義成太子於此習諸技藝。門外有自在天祠，祠中石天像，危然起勢，是太子在襁褓中所入祠也。淨飯王自臘伐尼國迎太子還也，途次天祠。王曰：「此天祠多靈鑒，諸釋童稚求祐必効，宜將太子至彼修敬。」是時傅母抱而入祠，其石天像起迎太子。太子已出，天像復坐。城南門外路左，有窣堵波，是太子與諸釋角藝，射鐵鼓。
translation: Three or four li to the south of the city is a Nyagrodha (尼拘律) forest, where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is the place where the Śākya Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, returned to his home country to see his royal father and preach the Dharma. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) learned that the Tathāgata had already subdued the army of Māra and was traveling about to teach and guide others, his heart was filled with longing and he wished to pay his respects. He then commanded a messenger to invite the Tathāgata, saying: "Formerly you promised that upon attaining Buddhahood, you would return to your place of birth. These words are still in my ears; the time has come for you to arrive." The messenger reached the Buddha and fully conveyed the king's intent. The Tathāgata replied: "Seven days from now, I shall return to my place of birth." The messenger returned and reported this to the king. King Śuddhodana then ordered his officials and subjects to sprinkle and sweep the roads and to gather flowers and incense, and he went out forty li with his ministers to wait for the carriage and welcome him.  At that time, the Tathāgata was with the great assembly, surrounded by the eight Vajra-warriors, led by the Four Heavenly Kings, with Indra (帝釋) and the devas of the Desire Realm attending on the left, Brahmā (梵王) and the devas of the Form Realm attending on the right, and the congregation of bhikṣus following behind. As the Buddha stood among the assembly, he was like the moon reflecting among the stars; his majestic power moved the three realms, and his radiance surpassed the seven luminaries as he walked through the void to reach his birth country. After the king and his ministers had finished paying their respects, they all returned to the city together and stayed at the Nyagrodha (尼拘盧陀) monastery. Not far to the side of this is a stūpa, which is where the Tathāgata sat facing east under a large tree and accepted the golden-threaded monastic robe from his aunt. Next to this stūpa is another, where the Tathāgata converted the eight princes and five hundred members of the Śākya clan. Inside the east gate of the city, on the left side of the road, there is a stūpa where, in the past, the Bodhisattva Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成) practiced various arts. Outside the gate is a temple of Īśvara (自在天); inside the temple is a stone image of the deity in a towering, rising posture, which is the temple the Prince entered while still in his swaddling clothes. When King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) was escorting the Prince back from the country of Lumbinī (臘伐尼國), they passed by this celestial temple on their way. The King said, "This temple is known for its many spiritual manifestations; whenever the children of the Śākya clan seek protection here, their prayers are always answered; we should take the Prince there to pay his respects." At that time, the wet nurse carried the Prince into the temple, and the stone image of the deity rose to greet the Prince. Once the Prince had left, the image returned to its seated position. Outside the south gate of the city, on the left side of the road, there is a stūpa where the Prince competed in arts with the other Śākyas and shot through iron drums.

t2087_text: 從此東南三十餘里，有小窣堵波，其側有泉，泉流澄鏡，是太子與諸釋引強校能，弦矢既分，穿鼓過表，至池沒羽，因涌清流，時俗相傳，謂之箭泉。夫有疾病，飲沐多愈。遠方之人持泥以歸，隨其所苦，漬以塗額，靈神冥衛，多蒙痊愈。
translation: More than thirty *li* to the southeast from here is a small *stūpa*. Beside it is a spring with water as clear as a mirror. This is where the prince competed in strength and skill with the other Śākyas; when the arrow left the string, it pierced the drums, passed through the target, and buried its feathers in the pool, causing a clear stream to gush forth. Popular tradition calls it the Arrow Spring (Śarakūpa). Those who suffer from illnesses are often cured by drinking from it or bathing in it. People from distant lands take the mud home and, according to their afflictions, moisten it to apply to their foreheads; through the secret protection of the divine spirits, most of them are healed.

t2087_text: 箭泉東北行八九十里，至臘伐尼林，有釋種浴池，澄清皎鏡，雜華彌漫。其北二十四五步，有無憂華樹，今已枯悴，菩薩誕靈之處。菩薩以吠舍佉月後半八日，當此三月八日；上座部則曰以吠舍佉月後半十五日，當此三月十五日。次東窣堵波，無憂王所建，二龍浴太子處也。菩薩生已，不扶而行，於四方各七步，而自言曰：「天上、天下，唯我獨尊。今茲而往，生分已盡。」隨足所蹈，出大蓮花。二龍踊出，住虛空中，而各吐水，一冷一煖，以浴太子。浴太子窣堵波東，有二清泉，傍建二窣堵波，是二龍從地踊出之處。菩薩生已，支屬宗親莫不奔馳，求水盥浴。夫人之前，二泉涌出，一冷一煖，遂以浴洗。其南窣堵波，是天帝釋捧接菩薩處。菩薩初出胎也，天帝釋以妙天衣，跪接菩薩。次有四窣堵波，是四天王抱持菩薩處也。菩薩從右脇生已，四大天王以金色㲲衣，捧菩薩，置金机上。至母前曰：「夫人誕斯福子，誠可歡慶。諸天尚喜，況世人乎？」
translation: Traveling eighty or ninety *li* northeast from the Arrow Spring (Śarakūpa), one arrives at the Lumbinī Grove (臘伐尼林). There is a bathing pool of the Śākya clan, clear and bright as a mirror, with various flowers blooming in profusion. Twenty-four or twenty-five paces to its north is an Aśoka tree (無憂華樹), now withered and dry, which is the place where the Bodhisattva was born. The Bodhisattva was born on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month; the Sthavira school, however, says it was on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. To the east is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), the place where the two dragons bathed the prince. After the Bodhisattva was born, he walked seven paces in each of the four directions without assistance and declared, "In the heavens above and on earth below, I alone am the honored one. From this time forward, the cycle of birth is at an end." Wherever his feet stepped, a large lotus flower emerged. Two dragons leaped forth and remained in the void, each spitting out water—one cold and one warm—to bathe the prince. To the east of the stūpa marking the bathing of the prince are two clear springs, beside which two stūpas were built at the spot where the two dragons emerged from the earth. After the Bodhisattva was born, his relatives and kin all rushed about, seeking water for washing and bathing. In front of the Lady, two springs gushed forth, one cold and one warm, which were then used for the bathing. The stūpa to the south is the place where Śakra Devendra (天帝釋) received the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva first emerged from the womb, Śakra Devendra knelt and received the Bodhisattva with a wondrous heavenly garment. Next are four stūpas, which are the places where the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja) held the Bodhisattva. After the Bodhisattva was born from the right side, the Four Great Heavenly Kings received the Bodhisattva with a golden-colored fine cotton cloth and placed him on a golden table. They approached the Lady and said, "The Lady has given birth to this blessed child; it is truly a cause for rejoicing. Even the gods are joyful, how much more so should the people of the world be?"

translation: Not far from the side of the stupa where the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja) held the prince, there is a great stone pillar with the figure of a horse on top, which was erected by King Ashoka (Aśoka). Later, due to a thunderbolt caused by an evil dragon, the pillar was broken in the middle and fell to the ground. Beside it is a small river flowing southeast, which the local people call the Oil River. After Queen Māyā (Māyādevī) had given birth, the gods manifested this pond, its water glossy and pure, intending for the Queen to bathe in it to remove the wind-related infirmities. It has now changed into water, yet its current remains greasy.

t2087_text: 從此東行曠野荒林中二百餘里，至藍摩國（中印度境）。藍摩國，空荒歲久，疆埸無紀，城邑丘墟，居人稀曠。故城東南有甎窣堵波，高減百尺。昔者如來入寂滅已，此國先王分得舍利，持歸本國，式遵崇建，靈異間起，神光時燭。窣堵波側有一清池，龍每出遊，變形蛇服，右旋宛轉，繞窣堵波，野象群行，採花以散，冥力警察，初無間替。昔無憂王之分建窣堵波也，七國所建，咸已開發，至於此國，方欲興功，而此池龍恐見陵奪，乃變作婆羅門，前叩象曰：「大王情流佛法，廣樹福田，敢請紆駕，降臨我宅。」王曰：「爾家安在，為近遠乎？」婆羅門曰：「我，此池之龍王也。承大王欲建勝福，敢來請謁。」王受其請，遂入龍宮。坐久之，龍進曰：「我惟惡業，受此龍身，供養舍利，冀消罪咎，願王躬往，觀而禮敬。」無憂王見已，懼然謂曰：「凡諸供養之具，非人間所有也。」龍曰：「若然者，願無廢毀。」無憂王自度力非其疇，遂不開發。出池之所，今有封記。窣堵波側不遠，有一伽藍，僧眾尠矣，清肅皎然，而以沙彌總任眾務。遠方僧至，禮遇彌隆，必留三日，供養四事。聞諸先志曰：昔有苾芻，同志相召，自遠而至，禮窣堵波。見諸群象，相趨往來，或以牙芟草，或以鼻灑水，各持異華，共為供養。時眾見已，悲歎感懷。有一苾芻，便捨具戒，願留供養，與眾辭曰：「我惟多福，濫迹僧中，歲月亟淹，行業無紀。此窣堵波有佛舍利，聖德冥通，群象踐灑。遺身此地，甘與同群，得畢餘齡，誠為幸矣。」眾告之曰：「斯盛事也。吾等垢重，智不謀此。隨時自愛，無虧勝業。」亦既離群，重申誠願，歡然獨居，有終焉之志。於是葺茅為宇，引流成池，採掇時花，灑掃塋域。綿歷歲序，心事無殆。隣國諸王聞而雅尚，競捨財寶，共建伽藍，因而勸請，屈知僧務。自爾相踵，不泯元功，而以沙彌總知僧事。
translation: From here, traveling east through a wilderness and desolate forest for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Rāmagrāma (藍摩國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Rāmagrāma has been desolate for a long time; its borders are undefined, its cities and towns are in ruins, and its inhabitants are few and scattered. To the southeast of the old city, there is a brick *stūpa* slightly less than one hundred feet high. Formerly, after the Tathāgata entered *parinirvāṇa*, the former king of this country obtained a share of the relics, brought them back to his own country, and duly honored them by building [this structure]. Miraculous signs appeared from time to time, and divine light shone occasionally. Beside the *stūpa* is a clear pool; the dragon often emerges to wander, changing its form into that of a snake, circling the *stūpa* to the right in winding movements. Herds of wild elephants come to gather flowers and scatter them [as offerings]; this spiritual influence keeps watch, and there has never been any interruption. Formerly, when King Aśoka (無憂王) was distributing [relics] to build *stūpas*, those built by the seven [other] kingdoms had all been opened. When he arrived in this country and was about to begin the work, the dragon of this pool, fearing they would be seized and taken away, transformed into a Brahmin, approached the elephant, and said: "Your Majesty’s devotion flows toward the Buddha-dharma, and you have widely planted fields of merit; I venture to ask you to deign to visit my abode." The King said: "Where is your home? Is it near or far?" The Brahmin said: "I am the Dragon King of this pool. Having heard that Your Majesty wishes to build superior merit, I have ventured to come and invite you." The King accepted his invitation and thereupon entered the dragon palace. After sitting for a long time, the dragon approached and said: "Because of my evil karma, I have received this dragon body. I make offerings to the relics, hoping to eliminate my sins and faults. I wish for the King to go in person to observe and pay homage." When King Aśoka (無憂王) saw them, he said with trepidation: "All these implements of offering are not things of the human world." The dragon said: "If that is so, I hope you will not destroy or damage them." King Aśoka judged that his own power was not a match for theirs, and so he did not open them. The place where he emerged from the pool now has a marker.  Not far from the side of the stupa (窣堵波) is a monastery (伽藍); the community of monks is small, and the place is pure, solemn, and bright, with a novice (沙彌) in charge of all the affairs of the community. When monks from afar arrive, they are treated with great respect; they are always kept for three days and provided with the four requisites.  According to ancient records, there were once bhikṣus who, having invited one another, came from afar to pay homage at the stupa. They saw herds of elephants coming and going; some used their tusks to clear away grass, others used their trunks to sprinkle water, and each held different flowers to make offerings together. When the group saw this, they were moved to sadness and reflection. One bhikṣu then renounced his full precepts, wishing to remain and make offerings. He said to the group: "I have had much good fortune, but I have merely left traces among the sangha; years and months have passed quickly, yet my practice has no record. This stupa contains the Buddha’s relics, and his holy virtue reaches into the unseen, causing herds of elephants to tread and sprinkle it. To leave my body in this place and be willing to join this group, to be able to finish the remainder of my life here, would truly be a blessing." The group said to him: "This is a magnificent undertaking. We are heavy with defilements, and our wisdom does not reach this far. Take good care of yourself at all times, and do not fall short in this excellent work." Having parted from the group, he reaffirmed his sincere vow, lived alone in joy, and held the determination to remain there until the end of his days. He then thatched a hut for a dwelling, diverted a stream to form a pond, gathered seasonal flowers, and sprinkled and swept the burial area. As the years and months passed, his devotion never faltered. The kings of neighboring countries heard of this and held him in high esteem; they vied with one another to donate treasures to jointly build a monastery, and subsequently invited him to deign to oversee the monastic affairs. Since then, this tradition has been followed in succession so as not to let his original merit be forgotten, and a śrāmaṇera (沙彌) is always appointed to manage the affairs of the monastery.

t2087_text: 沙彌伽藍東，大林中行百餘里，至大窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。是太子踰城至此，解寶衣，去纓絡，命僕還處。太子夜半踰城，遲明至此，既允宿心，乃形言曰：「是我出籠樊，去羈鎖，最後釋駕之處也。」於天冠中解末尼寶，命僕夫曰：「汝持此寶，還白父王，今茲遠遁，非苟違離，欲斷無常，絕諸有漏。」闡鐸迦（舊曰車匿，訛也）曰：「詎有何心，空駕而返？」太子善言慰喻，感悟而還。迴駕窣堵波東，有贍部樹，枝葉雖凋，枯株尚在。其傍復有小窣堵波，太子以餘寶衣易鹿皮衣處。太子既斷髮易裳，雖去瓔珞，尚有天衣。曰：「斯服太侈，如何改易？」時淨居天化作獵人，服鹿皮衣，持弓負羽。太子舉其衣而謂曰：「欲相貿易，願見允從。」獵人曰：「善。」太子解其上服，授與獵人。獵人得已，還復天身，持所得衣，凌虛而去。太子易衣側不遠，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，是太子剃髮處。太子從闡鐸迦取刀，自斷其髮，天帝釋接上天宮，以為供養。時淨居天子化作剃髮人，執持銛刀，徐步而至。太子謂曰：「能剃髮乎？幸為我淨之。」化人受命，遂為剃髮。踰城出家時亦不定，或云菩薩年十九，或曰二十九，以吠舍佉月後半八日踰城出家，當此三月八日，或云以吠舍佉月後半十五日，當此三月十五日。
translation: To the east of the Śrāmaṇera Monastery, traveling more than one hundred *li* through a great forest, one reaches a large stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is the place where the Prince, having scaled the city walls and arrived here, took off his precious garments, removed his necklaces, and ordered his servant to return. The Prince had scaled the city walls at midnight and reached this place at dawn; having fulfilled his long-cherished wish, he spoke aloud, saying: "This is the place where I escape the cage, cast off the fetters, and finally unyoke my carriage." He took the *maṇi* jewel from his celestial crown and commanded his servant, saying: "Take this jewel and return to report to my father the King. My fleeing to this distant place is not out of a desire to abandon him, but to put an end to impermanence and sever all outflows." Chandaka (闡鐸迦) (The old term was Che-ni [車匿], which is incorrect) said: "How could I have the heart to return with an empty carriage?" The Prince comforted him with kind words, and he was moved to understanding and returned.  To the east of the "Returning Carriage" (迴駕) stūpa, there is a Jambu tree; although its branches and leaves have withered, the dead trunk still remains. Beside it is another small stūpa, marking the place where the Prince exchanged his remaining precious garments for a deerskin robe. After the Prince had cut his hair and changed his attire, although he had removed his necklaces, he still wore a celestial robe. He said: "This garment is too extravagant; how can I change it?" At that time, a Pure Abode Heaven (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) transformed into a hunter wearing a deerskin robe, carrying a bow and bearing feathers. The Prince raised his own garment and said to him: "I wish to trade with you; I hope you will consent." The hunter said: "Very well." The Prince took off his upper garment and handed it to the hunter. The hunter, having obtained it, resumed his celestial form, took the garment he had received, and ascended into the void to depart. Not far from where the Prince changed his clothes is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the Prince shaved his hair. The Prince took a blade from Chandaka (闡鐸迦) and cut off his own hair; Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋) caught it and took it to the heavenly palace to be venerated. At that time, a son of the Pure Abode Heaven (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) transformed into a barber, holding a sharp blade, and approached with slow steps. The Prince said to him, "Can you shave my hair? I would be grateful if you would clean it for me." The transformed being accepted the command and proceeded to shave his hair. The time when he climbed over the city wall to renounce the household life is also uncertain; some say the Bodhisattva was nineteen years old, while others say he was twenty-nine. He climbed over the city wall to renounce the household life on the eighth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month; others say it was on the fifteenth day of the latter half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month.

t2087_text: 太子剃髮窣堵波東南，曠野中行百八九十里，至尼拘盧陀林，有窣堵波，高三十餘尺。昔如來寂滅，舍利已分，諸婆羅門無所得獲，於涅疊般那（唐言焚燒。舊云闍維，訛也）地收餘灰炭，持至本國，建此靈基，而修供養。自茲已降，奇迹相仍，疾病之人，祈請多愈。灰炭窣堵波側，故伽藍中，有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。故伽藍左右，數百窣堵波。其一大者，無憂王所建也，崇基雖陷，高餘百尺。自此東北，大林中行，其路艱險，經途危阻，山牛、野象、群盜、獵師，伺求行旅，為害不絕。
translation: Southeast from the stupa where the prince had his hair shaved, traveling one hundred and eighty or ninety li through a wilderness, one reaches the Nyagrodha grove (尼拘盧陀林), where there is a stupa over thirty feet high. In the past, when the Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa and the relics had already been divided, the various Brahmins who had obtained none gathered the remaining ashes and charcoal at the place of the *niedie banna* (In Tang language this means cremation. The old term *shewei* is incorrect) and brought them to their own country, where they built this sacred foundation and performed offerings. From that time onward, miraculous signs have occurred in succession, and sick people who pray there are often healed. Beside the Ash Stupa, within an old monastery, there are sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Around this old monastery are several hundred stupas. One of them, which is large, was built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its lofty base has collapsed, it is over one hundred feet high. From here, traveling northeast through a great forest, the road is difficult and dangerous; the route is perilous and obstructed, and wild oxen, wild elephants, bands of robbers, and hunters lie in wait for travelers, causing ceaseless harm.

t2087_text: 出此林已，至拘尸那揭羅國（中印度境）。拘尸那揭羅國，城郭頹毀，邑里蕭條。故城甎基，周十餘里。居人稀曠，閭巷荒蕪。城內東北隅，有窣堵波，無憂王所建，准陀（舊曰純陀，訛也）之故宅也。宅中有井，將營獻供，方乃鑿焉。歲月雖淹，水猶清美。
translation: After emerging from this forest, I reached the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那揭羅國) (within the borders of Central India). In the country of Kuśinagara, the city walls are dilapidated and the towns and villages are desolate. The brick foundations of the old city measure more than ten li in circumference. The inhabitants are few and scattered, and the lanes and alleys are overgrown. In the northeast corner within the city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka on the site of the former residence of Cunda (准陀) (formerly called Chuntuo, which is a corruption). Inside the residence is a well; it was dug at the time he was preparing his offering. Although much time has passed, the water remains clear and sweet.
