t2087_text: 城西北三四里，渡阿恃多伐底河（唐言無勝，此世共稱耳。舊云阿利羅跋提河，訛也。典言謂之尸賴拏伐底河，譯曰有金河）。西岸不遠，至娑羅林。其樹類槲，而皮青白，葉甚光潤。四樹特高，如來寂滅之所也。其大甎精舍中作如來涅槃之像，北首而臥。傍有窣堵波，無憂王所建，基雖傾陷，尚高二百餘尺。前建石柱，以記如來寂滅之事，雖有文記，不書日月。聞諸先記曰：佛以生年八十，吠舍佉月後半十五日入般涅槃，當此三月十五日也。說一切有部則佛以迦剌底迦月後半八日入般涅槃，此當九月八日也。自佛涅槃，諸部異議，或云千二百餘年，或云千三百餘年，或云千五百餘年，或云已過九百，未滿千年。精舍側不遠，有窣堵波，是如來修菩薩行時，為群雉王救火之處。昔於此地有大茂林，毛群羽族巢居穴處。驚風四起，猛焰飈急。時有一雉，有懷傷愍，鼓濯清流，飛空奮灑。時天帝釋俯而告曰：「汝何守愚，虛勞羽翮？大火方起，焚燎林野，豈汝微軀所能撲滅？」雉曰：「說者為誰？」曰：「我天帝釋耳。」雉曰：「今天帝有大福力，無欲不遂，救災拯難，若指諸掌，反詰無功，其咎安在？猛火方熾，無得多言！」尋復奮飛，往趣流水。天帝遂以掬水泛灑其林，火滅煙消，生類全命，故今謂之救火窣堵波也。雉救火側不遠，有窣堵波，是如來修菩薩行時，為鹿救生之處。乃往古昔，此有大林，火炎中野，飛走窮窘，前有駛流之阨，後困猛火之難，莫不沈溺，喪棄身命。其鹿惻隱，身據橫流，穿皮斷骨，自強拯溺。蹇兔後至，忍疲苦而濟之。筋力既竭，溺水而死。諸天收骸，起窣堵波。鹿拯溺西不遠，有窣堵波，是蘇跋陀羅（唐言善賢。舊曰須跋陀羅，訛也）入寂滅之處。善賢者，本梵志師也。年百二十，耆舊多智。聞佛寂滅，至雙樹間，問阿難曰：「佛世尊將寂滅，我懷疑滯，願欲請問。」阿難曰：「佛將涅槃，幸無擾也。」曰：「吾聞佛世難遇，正法難聞，我有深疑，恐無所請。」善賢遂入，先問佛言：「有諸別眾，自稱為師，各有異法，垂訓導俗，喬答摩（舊曰瞿曇，訛略也）能盡知耶？」佛言：「吾悉深究。」乃為演說。善賢聞已，心淨信解，求入法中，受具足戒。如來告曰：「汝豈能耶？外道異學修梵行者，當試四歲，觀其行，察其性，威儀寂靜，辭語誠實，則可於我法中淨修梵行。在人行耳，斯何難哉！」善賢曰：「世尊悲愍，含濟無私，四歲試學，三業方順。」佛言：「我先已說，在人行耳！」於是善賢出家，即受具戒，勤勵修習，身心勇猛。已而於法無疑，自身作證。夜分未久，果證羅漢，諸漏已盡，梵行已立。不忍見佛入大涅槃，即於眾中入火界定，現神通事，而先寂滅。是為如來最後弟子，乃先滅度，即昔後渡蹇兔是也。善賢寂滅側，有窣堵波，是執金剛躄地之處。大悲世尊隨機利見，化功已畢，入寂滅樂，於雙樹間北首而臥。執金剛神密迹力士見佛滅度，悲慟唱言：「如來捨我入大涅槃，無歸依，無覆護，毒箭深入，愁火熾盛！」捨金剛杵，悶絕躄地。久而又起，悲哀戀慕，互相謂曰：「生死大海，誰作舟檝？無明長夜，誰為燈炬？」金剛躄地側，有窣堵波，是如來寂滅已七日供養之處。如來之將寂滅也，光明普照，人、天畢會，莫不悲感，更相謂曰：「大覺世尊今將寂滅，眾生福盡，世間無依。」如來右脇臥師子床，告諸大眾：「勿謂如來畢竟寂滅，法身常住，離諸變易，當棄懈怠，早求解脫。」諸苾芻等歔欷悲慟。時阿泥𢫫（盧骨反）陀（舊曰阿那律，訛也）告諸苾芻：「止，止，勿悲！諸天譏怪。」時末羅眾供養已訖，欲舉金棺，詣涅疊般那所。時阿泥𢫫陀告言：「且止！諸天欲留七日供養。」於是天眾持妙天華，遊虛空，讚聖德，各竭誠心，共興供養。停棺側有窣堵波，是摩訶摩耶夫人哭佛之處。如來寂滅，棺斂已畢，時阿泥𢫫陀上昇天宮，告摩耶夫人曰：「大聖法王今已寂滅。」摩耶聞已，悲哽悶絕，與諸天眾至雙樹間，見僧伽胝、鉢及錫杖，拊之號慟，絕而復聲曰：「人、天福盡，世間眼滅！今此諸物，空無有主。」如來聖力，金棺自開，放光明，合掌坐，慰問慈母：「遠來下降！諸行法爾，願勿深悲。」阿難銜哀而請佛曰：「後世問我，將何以對？」曰：「佛已涅槃，慈母摩耶自天宮降，至雙樹間，如來為諸不孝眾生，從金棺起，合掌說法。」
translation: Three or four *li* to the northwest of the city, one crosses the Ajitavatī River (阿恃多伐底河) (in the Tang language, "Invincible"; this is merely the common name in this world. The old name, Alilobati River (阿利羅跋提河), is a corruption. The classical language calls it the Hiraṇyavatī River, which translates as "River of Gold"). Not far from the west bank, one reaches the Sāla (娑羅) grove. The trees resemble the oak, but their bark is greenish-white and their leaves are very glossy and smooth. Four trees are particularly tall; this is the place where the Tathāgata attained extinction (parinirvāṇa). In the large brick vihāra (精舍) is an image of the Tathāgata in the state of *nirvāṇa*, lying with his head to the north. Beside it is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed and sunken, it is still over two hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar recording the event of the Tathāgata’s extinction; although there is an inscription, it does not record the year or month. I have heard from ancient records that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* at the age of eighty on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. The Sarvāstivāda school, however, holds that the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa* on the eighth day of the second half of the month of Kārttika, which corresponds to the eighth day of the ninth month. Since the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the various schools have held differing opinions: some say more than 1,200 years have passed, some say more than 1,300 years, some say more than 1,500 years, and others say more than 900 but less than 1,000 years. Not far from the side of the vihāra is a *stūpa* marking the place where the Tathāgata, when practicing the Bodhisattva path, acted as the king of a flock of pheasants to save them from a fire. Formerly, there was a great, dense forest in this place, where feathered and furred creatures nested and lived in burrows. Sudden winds arose from all directions, and the fierce flames surged rapidly. At that time, there was a pheasant who, moved by compassion, soaked its wings in a clear stream and flew into the air to sprinkle the water. The Heavenly Emperor Śakra (天帝釋) looked down and said to it, "Why are you so foolish, exhausting your wings in vain? A great fire has broken out, burning the forest and the wilderness; how could your tiny body possibly extinguish it?" The pheasant replied, "Who is it that speaks?" He said, "I am the Heavenly Emperor Śakra." The pheasant said, "Today, the Heavenly Emperor possesses great merit and power, and there is no desire he cannot fulfill; to relieve disasters and rescue those in distress should be as easy as pointing to one's own palm. Yet you instead question my lack of success—where does the blame truly lie? The fierce fire is currently raging; do not speak further!" It then flew off again to head toward the flowing water. The Heavenly Emperor then scooped up water with his hands and sprinkled it over the forest; the fire was extinguished and the smoke vanished, the lives of all creatures were saved, and thus it is now called the Fire-extinguishing Stūpa (救火窣堵波).  Not far from the side of the place where the pheasant extinguished the fire, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, saved lives as a deer. In the remote past, there was a great forest here; a fire broke out in the wilderness, and the birds and beasts were driven to desperation, facing the peril of a swift current in front and the hardship of a raging fire behind, such that none escaped drowning or losing their lives. The deer, moved by compassion, positioned its body across the current, its skin pierced and bones broken, forcing itself to rescue the drowning. A lame hare arrived last, and the deer, enduring its fatigue and pain, rescued it as well. When its strength was exhausted, it drowned and died. The devas gathered its remains and erected a stūpa. Not far to the west of where the deer rescued the drowning, there is a stūpa. This is the place where Subhadra (蘇跋陀羅) (in the Tang language, "Good and Virtuous" [善賢]; formerly called Xubatuoluo [須跋陀羅], which is incorrect) entered into extinction. This Good and Virtuous one was originally a Brahmin teacher. He was one hundred and twenty years old, an elder of great wisdom. Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter extinction, he arrived at the twin trees and asked Ānanda, "The Buddha, the World-honored One, is about to enter extinction. I have doubts and hesitations, and I wish to ask him questions." Ānanda said, "The Buddha is about to enter nirvāṇa; please do not disturb him." He replied, "I have heard that it is difficult to encounter a Buddha in the world and difficult to hear the true Dharma. I have deep doubts and fear that I will have no one to ask." Subhadra then entered and first asked the Buddha, "Are there various other groups who call themselves teachers, each having different doctrines, handing down instructions to guide the laity—can Gautama (formerly called Qutan [瞿曇], which is a corruption and abbreviation) know them all?" The Buddha said, "I have thoroughly investigated them all," and then he expounded them for him. Having heard this, Subhadra’s mind was purified and he gained faith and understanding. He requested to enter the Dharma and receive the full ordination. The Tathāgata said to him, "Are you able to do so? For those of other paths and different schools who wish to practice the holy life, they must be tested for four years. By observing their conduct and examining their nature—if their deportment is tranquil and their speech is truthful—then they may practice the holy life in my Dharma. It depends on the person's conduct; how could this be difficult?" Subhadra said, "The World-honored One is compassionate and merciful, bestowing salvation without partiality. If one is tested for four years, the three karmas will then be in accord." The Buddha said, "I have already said that it depends on the person's conduct!" Thereupon, Subhadra (善賢) renounced the household life, immediately received the full precepts, and diligently practiced with a courageous body and mind. Before long, he had no doubts regarding the Dharma and personally attained realization. Before the night was far advanced, he attained the fruit of an Arhat; all his outflows were exhausted, and his holy life was established. Unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter mahānirvāṇa, he entered the fire-element samādhi (火界定) amidst the assembly, manifested supernatural powers, and entered nirvana first. This was the Tathāgata's final disciple, who attained extinction first; he is the one who, in the past, was the hare that crossed the river last. Beside the spot where Subhadra entered nirvana, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Vajra-holder (執金剛) fell to the ground.  The Greatly Compassionate World-honored One, having appeared to benefit beings according to their capacities, finished his work of transformation and entered the joy of extinction, lying down with his head to the north between the twin trees. When the Vajra-holding deity, the Guhyapāda Malla (密迹力士), saw the Buddha enter nirvana, he cried out in bitter grief: "The Tathāgata has forsaken me and entered mahānirvāṇa; I have no refuge and no protection; the poisoned arrow has struck deep, and the fire of sorrow burns fiercely!" He cast aside his vajra-club and fell to the ground in a swoon. After a long time, he rose again, filled with sorrow and longing, and they said to one another: "In the great ocean of birth and death, who will serve as the boat and oar? In the long night of ignorance, who will serve as the lamp and torch?" Beside the spot where the Vajra-holder fell to the ground, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata was venerated for seven days after his nirvana. When the Tathāgata was about to enter nirvana, a brilliant light shone everywhere. Humans and devas gathered in full, all feeling deep sorrow and emotion, saying to one another: "The Great Awakened World-Honored One is now about to enter nirvana; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and the world is left without a refuge." The Tathāgata lay on his right side on a lion-couch and addressed the great assembly: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has entered final nirvana. The Dharma-body is eternally abiding and free from all change. You should abandon sloth and seek liberation early." The bhikṣus sobbed and grieved. At that time, Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) (𢫫 is read 盧骨反, i.e. *lu[t]*; formerly called Analü [阿那律], which is incorrect) told the bhikṣus: "Stop, stop! Do not grieve; the devas will mock and wonder at you." When the Malla people had finished their offerings and wished to lift the golden coffin to proceed to the cremation ground (涅疊般那), Aniruddha said: "Wait! The devas wish to keep it for seven days to make offerings." Thereupon, the host of devas held exquisite heavenly flowers, wandered through the void, praised the holy virtues, and each exhausted their sincere hearts to join in making offerings. Beside the place where the coffin rested, there is a stūpa; this is the spot where Lady Mahāmāyā wept for the Buddha. After the Tathāgata had entered nirvana and the encoffining was completed, Aniruddha ascended to the heavenly palace and informed Lady Mahāmāyā, saying: "The Great Holy Dharma King has now entered nirvana." Upon hearing this, Mahāmāyā was choked with grief and fainted. She went with the assembly of devas to the space between the twin trees, where she saw the saṃghāṭi (monastic robe), the pātra (alms bowl), and the khakkhara (pewter staff). Stroking them, she wailed in agony, fainting and then regaining her voice to cry out: "The merit of humans and devas is exhausted, and the Eye of the World is extinguished! Now these objects are empty and without a master." By the holy power of the Tathāgata, the golden coffin opened of its own accord, emitting a great light; he sat up with palms joined and consoled his compassionate mother: "You have descended from a great distance! All conditioned things are by nature such; I pray you, do not grieve so deeply." Ānanda, suppressing his sorrow, asked the Buddha: "If future generations ask me, how shall I answer them?" He replied: "Say that after the Buddha had entered nirvana, his compassionate mother Mahāmāyā descended from the heavenly palace to the space between the twin trees, and for the sake of unfilial sentient beings, the Tathāgata rose from his golden coffin and preached the Dharma with his palms joined."

t2087_text: 城北渡河三百餘步，有窣堵波，是如來焚身之處。地今黃黑，土雜灰炭，至誠求請，或得舍利。如來寂滅，人、天悲感，七寶為棺，千㲲纏身，設香華，建幡蓋，末羅之眾奉輿發引，前後導從，北渡金河，盛滿香油，積多香木，縱火以焚，二㲲不燒，一極𭣋身，一最覆外。為諸眾生分散舍利，唯有髮、爪儼然無損。焚身側有窣堵波，如來為大迦葉波現雙足處。如來金棺已下，香木已積，火燒不然，眾咸驚駭。阿泥𢫫陀言：「待迦葉波耳。」時大迦葉波與五百弟子自山林來，至拘尸城，問阿難曰：「世尊之身，可得見耶？」阿難曰：「千㲲纏絡，重棺周斂，香木已積，即事焚燒。」是時佛於棺內為出雙足，輪相之上，見有異色。問阿難曰：「何以有此？」曰：「佛初涅槃，人、天悲慟，眾淚迸染，致斯異色。」迦葉波作禮，旋繞興讚，香木自然，大火熾盛。故如來寂滅，三從棺出：初出臂，問阿難治路；次起坐，為母說法；後現雙足，示大迦葉波。現足側有窣堵波，無憂王所建也，是八王分舍利處。前建石柱，刻記其事。佛入涅槃，後涅疊般那已，諸八國王備四兵至，遣直性婆羅門謂拘尸力士曰：「天、人導師，此國寂滅，故自遠來，請分舍利。」力士曰：「如來降尊，即斯下土，滅世間明導，喪眾生慈父。如來舍利，自當供養，徒疲道路，終無得獲。」時諸大王遜辭以求，既不相允，重謂之曰：「禮請不從，兵威非遠。」直性婆羅門揚言曰：「念哉！大悲世尊忍修福善，彌歷曠劫，想所具聞，今欲相凌，此非宜也。今舍利在此，當均八分，各得供養，何至興兵？」諸力士依其言，即時均量，欲作八分。帝釋謂諸王曰：「天當有分，勿恃力競。」阿那婆答多龍王、文隣龍王、醫那鉢呾羅龍王復作是議：「無遺我曹。若以力者，眾非敵矣。」直性婆羅門曰：「勿諠諍也，宜共分之。」即作三分，一諸天，二龍眾，三留人間，八國重分。天、龍、人王，莫不悲感。
translation: Crossing the river more than three hundred paces to the north of the city, there is a stupa, which is the place where the Tathāgata (如來) was cremated. The ground is now yellow and black, the soil mixed with ash and charcoal; if one requests with utmost sincerity, one may obtain relics. When the Tathāgata entered into extinction, humans and devas were moved by grief; they made a coffin of the seven treasures and wrapped his body in a thousand layers of fine cotton, offered incense and flowers, and set up banners and canopies. The Malla (末羅) people then bore the hearse in a procession, with guides in front and followers behind, crossing the Gold River to the north, where they filled it with fragrant oil, piled up much scented wood, and set it ablaze. Two layers of the cotton did not burn: one that was closest to the body and one that covered the outermost layer. In order to distribute the relics for all sentient beings, only the hair and nails remained intact and undamaged. Beside the place of cremation is a stupa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata revealed his two feet to Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波). When the Tathāgata’s golden coffin had been lowered and the fragrant wood piled up, the fire would not ignite, and the assembly was filled with alarm. Aniruddha (阿泥𢫫陀) said, "We must wait for Kāśyapa." At that time, Mahākāśyapa, with five hundred disciples, came from the mountain forests and arrived at the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). He asked Ānanda, "Can the body of the World-Honored One still be seen?" Ānanda replied, "It is wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton, enclosed in heavy coffins, and the fragrant wood has already been piled up; the cremation is about to take place." At that moment, the Buddha, from within the coffin, revealed his two feet; upon the wheel-marks, a strange color was visible. He asked Ānanda, "Why is there this color?" He replied, "When the Buddha first entered parinirvāṇa, humans and devas were overcome with grief, and the tears of the multitude splashed and stained it, causing this strange color." Kāśyapa paid homage, circumambulated, and offered praises; the fragrant wood ignited spontaneously, and a great fire blazed fiercely. Thus, when the Tathāgata entered extinction, he emerged from the coffin three times: first, he extended his arm to ask Ānanda about the path; next, he sat up to preach the Dharma for his mother; finally, he revealed his two feet to show them to Mahākāśyapa. Beside the place where he revealed his feet is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the eight kings divided the relics. In front of it, a stone pillar was erected, inscribed with an account of the event. After the Buddha had entered nirvāṇa and the cremation was completed, the kings of eight countries arrived with their fourfold armies and dispatched a straightforward Brahmin to say to the Mallas of Kuśinagara (拘尸力士), "The Teacher of gods and men has entered extinction in this country; therefore, we have come from afar to request a share of the relics." The Mallas replied, "The Tathāgata descended in his majesty to this lower realm; here the bright guide of the world has been extinguished and we have lost the compassionate father of all living beings. The relics of the Tathāgata should naturally be worshipped by us alone; you have wearied yourselves on the road in vain, for you shall never obtain them." At that time, the various great kings requested them with humble words, but since they were not granted, they said again, "If polite requests are not followed, the might of our armies is not far off." The straightforward Brahmin spoke aloud, "Reflect! The Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One patiently cultivated merit and goodness throughout vast kalpas, as I presume you have all heard; it is not appropriate for you now to seek to oppress one another. Since the relics are here, they should be divided into eight equal portions so that each may receive them for worship; why go so far as to raise troops?" The Mallas followed his words and immediately measured the relics, intending to divide them into eight portions. Śakra (帝釋) said to the kings, "The heavens should have a share; do not rely on force to compete." The Nāga kings Anavatapta (阿那婆答多), Mucilinda (文隣), and Elāpattra (醫那鉢呾羅) also proposed, "Do not exclude us. If it comes to force, the masses are no match for us." The straightforward Brahmin said, "Do not clamor and contend; it is proper to divide them together." He immediately made three portions: first for the devas, second for the Nāga host, and third to remain among humans, which the eight kingdoms then subdivided. The devas, Nāgas, and human kings were all moved to sorrow.

t2087_text: 分舍利窣堵波西南行二百餘里，至大邑聚。有婆羅門，豪右巨富，確乎不雜，學究五明，敬崇三寶。接其居側，建立僧坊，窮諸資用，備盡珍飾，或有眾僧往來中路，慇懃請留，罄心供養，或止一宿，乃至七日。其後設賞迦王毀壞佛法，眾僧絕侶，歲月驟淹，而婆羅門每懷懇惻。經行之次，見一沙門，厖眉皓髮，杖錫而來。婆羅門馳往迎逆，問所從至，請入僧坊，備諸供養，旦以淳乳，煮粥進焉。沙門受已，纔一嚌齒，便即置鉢，沈吟長息。婆羅門持食，跪而問曰：「大德慧利隨緣，幸見臨顧，為夕不安耶？為粥不味乎？」沙門愍然告曰：「吾悲眾生福祐漸薄，斯言且置，食已方說。」沙門食訖，攝衣即語。婆羅門曰：「向許有說，今何無言？」沙門告曰：「吾非忘也。談不容易，事或致疑。必欲得聞，今當略說。吾向所歎，非薄汝粥。自數百年，不嘗此味。昔如來在世，我時預從，在王舍城竹林精舍，俯清流而滌器，或以澡漱，或以盥沐。嗟乎！今之淳乳，不及古之淡水，此乃人、天福滅使之然也。」婆羅門曰：「然則大德乃親見佛耶？」沙門曰：「然。汝豈不聞佛子羅怙羅者，我身是也。為護正法，未入寂滅。」說是語已，忽然不見。婆羅門遂以所宿之房，塗香灑掃，像設儀肅，其敬如在。復大林中行五百餘里，至婆羅痆（女黠反）斯國（舊曰波羅柰國，訛也。中印度境）。
translation: Traveling two hundred-odd *li* southwest from the relic stūpa, one arrives at a large town (大邑聚). There was a brāhmaṇa there, a man of great wealth and high standing, whose lineage was pure and unmixed, who had mastered the five sciences (pañcavidyā), and who deeply revered the Three Jewels. Adjacent to his residence, he established a monastery, exhausting his resources to provide it with every adornment. Whenever members of the saṅgha traveled along that road, he would earnestly invite them to stay, offering them his wholehearted support, whether they stopped for a single night or for as long as seven days. Later, when King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma, the saṅgha was dispersed and the years passed quickly, yet the brāhmaṇa remained filled with sincere sorrow. While walking in meditation, he saw a śramaṇa with bushy eyebrows and white hair approaching, leaning on a staff. The brāhmaṇa hurried to welcome him, asked where he had come from, and invited him into the monastery, where he prepared every kind of offering, including a morning meal of porridge cooked with pure milk. The śramaṇa accepted it, but after tasting only a morsel, he set down his bowl and sighed deeply. The brāhmaṇa, holding the food, knelt and asked, "Great Virtuous One, whose wisdom and merit follow conditions, I am fortunate to have your presence; were you uncomfortable during the night, or was the porridge not to your taste?" The śramaṇa replied with compassion, "I grieve that the merit and blessings of sentient beings are gradually thinning. Let that matter rest for now; I will speak after I have eaten." Once the śramaṇa had finished eating, he adjusted his robes and spoke. The brāhmaṇa said, "You previously promised to speak; why are you silent now?" The śramaṇa replied, "I have not forgotten. What I have to discuss is not easy, and the matter may invite doubt. If you truly wish to hear it, I shall now speak of it briefly." "What I sighed about just now was not to disparage your porridge. For several hundred years, I have not tasted such a flavor. Long ago, when the Tathāgata was in the world, I was in his retinue at the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) in the city of Rājagṛha, where I would lean over the clear stream to wash the vessels, or use the water for rinsing and bathing. Alas! The rich milk of today cannot compare to the plain water of old; this is because the merit of humans and devas has been exhausted." The brāhmaṇa asked, "In that case, does the Venerable One mean that you personally saw the Buddha?" The śramaṇa replied, "Indeed. Have you not heard of the Buddha’s son, Rāhula? I am he. To protect the True Dharma, I have not yet entered final extinction." Having said these words, he suddenly vanished. The brāhmaṇa then anointed and swept the room where he had stayed, set up an image with solemn ceremony, and paid his respects as if he were still present. Traveling further through the great forest for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) (痆 is read 女黠反; formerly called Poluonai, which is incorrect. It is in the region of Central India).

t2087_text: 婆羅痆斯國，周四千餘里。國大都城西臨殑伽河，長十八九里，廣五六里。閭閻櫛比，居人殷盛，家積巨萬，室盈奇貨。人性溫恭，俗重強學，多信外道，少敬佛法。氣序和，穀稼盛，果木扶疎，茂草靃靡。伽藍三十餘所，僧徒三千餘人，並學小乘正量部法。天祠百餘所，外道萬餘人，並多宗事大自在天，或斷髮，或椎髻，露形無服，塗身以灰，精勤苦行，求出生死。大城中天祠二十所，層臺祠宇，雕石文木，茂林相蔭，清流交帶，鍮石天像量減百尺，威嚴肅然，懍懍如在。
translation: The country of Vārāṇasī (婆羅痆斯國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River to the west; it is eighteen or nineteen li long and five or six li wide. The houses are arranged like the teeth of a comb, the inhabitants are prosperous, families possess vast wealth, and their rooms are filled with rare goods. The people are gentle and respectful by nature, and the customs value diligent study; many believe in non-Buddhist paths, and few respect the Buddha-dharma. The climate is temperate, cereal crops are abundant, fruit trees grow luxuriantly, and the grasses are lush and thick. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are over one hundred deva temples with more than ten thousand followers of other paths, most of whom worship Maheśvara; some cut their hair, others wear it in a topknot, they go naked without clothing and smear their bodies with ash, diligently practicing austerities to seek liberation from birth and death. Within the great city are twenty deva temples with multi-storied terraces and shrines made of carved stone and ornamented wood, shaded by luxuriant forests and encircled by clear streams; there is a brass statue of the deity nearly one hundred feet tall, solemn and majestic as if it were alive.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: 'Sthavira-Saṃmitīya school' → 小乘正量部 'Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle'; no Sthavira in the Chinese

translation: To the northeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Vāraṇā River (婆羅痆河), there is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In front of it stands a stone pillar, as bright and fresh as a mirror, with a lustrous surface like flowing liquid, in which the image of the Tathāgata (如來) frequently appears.

translation: Traveling northeast from the Varaṇā River (婆羅痆河) for more than ten li, one arrives at the Deer Park Monastery (Mṛgadāva 鹿野伽藍). The grounds are divided into eight sections, enclosed by a continuous wall, with multi-storied halls and pavilions of exquisite architectural splendor. There are one thousand five hundred monks, all studying the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. Within the great enclosure is a vihāra (精舍) over two hundred feet high, topped with a golden *āmra* fruit in relief; it has a stone foundation and steps, with brick niches arranged in tiers surrounding it in hundreds of levels, each containing a golden Buddha image in relief. Inside the vihāra is a brass statue of the Buddha, equal in size to the Tathāgata’s body, in the posture of turning the wheel of the Dharma.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 精舍西南有石窣堵波，無憂王建也，基雖傾陷，尚餘百尺。前建石柱，高七十餘尺。石含玉潤，鑒照映徹，慇懃祈請，影見眾像，善惡之相，時有見者。是如來成正覺已初轉法輪處也。其側不遠窣堵波，是阿若憍陳如等見菩薩捨苦行，遂不侍衛，來至於此，而自習定。其傍窣堵波，是五百獨覺同入涅槃處。又三窣堵波，過去三佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: To the southwest of the vihāra (精舍) is a stone *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has collapsed, it still remains one hundred feet high. In front of it stands a stone pillar, over seventy feet high. The stone is as lustrous as jade and as clear as a mirror; those who pray with sincere devotion may see various images reflected within it, and at times, signs of good and evil are revealed to the observer. This is the place where the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, first turned the wheel of the Dharma. Not far to its side is a *stūpa* marking the spot where Ājñātakauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the others, seeing the Bodhisattva abandon his ascetic practices, ceased to attend upon him and came here to practice meditation by themselves. Beside it is a *stūpa* marking the place where five hundred *pratyekabuddhas* entered *nirvāṇa* together. There are also three *stūpas* marking the sites where the three past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 三佛經行側有窣堵波，是梅呾麗耶（唐言慈，即姓也。舊曰彌勒，訛略也）菩薩受成佛記處。昔者如來在王舍城鷲峯山告諸苾芻：「當來之世，此贍部洲土地平正，人壽八萬歲，有婆羅門子慈氏者，身真金色，光明照朗，當捨家成正覺，廣為眾生三會說法。其濟度者，皆我遺法植福眾生也。其於三寶深敬一心，在家、出家，持戒、犯戒，皆蒙化導，證果解脫。三會說法之中，度我遺法之徒，然後乃化同緣善友。」是時慈氏菩薩聞佛此說，從坐起，白佛言：「願我作彼慈氏世尊。」如來告曰：「如汝所言，當證此果。如上所說，皆汝教化之儀也。」慈氏菩薩受記西有窣堵波，是釋迦菩薩受記之處。賢劫中人壽二萬歲，迦葉波佛出現於世，轉妙法輪，開化含識，授護明菩薩記曰：「是菩薩於當來世眾生壽命百歲之時，當得成佛，號釋迦牟尼。」釋迦菩薩受記南不遠，有過去四佛經行遺迹，長五十餘步，高可七尺，以青石積成，上作如來經行之像，像形傑異，威嚴肅然，肉髻之上特出鬚髮，靈相無隱，神鑒有徵。於其垣內，聖迹寔多，諸精舍、窣堵波數百餘所，略舉二三難用詳述。
translation: Beside the place where the three Buddhas walked in meditation, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Maitreya (梅呾麗耶; in Tang language *Ci* [Loving], which is his surname; formerly called *Mile* [彌勒], which is an erroneous abbreviation) received the prediction of his future Buddhahood. Long ago, the Tathāgata, while at Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) near the city of Rājagṛha, told the bhikṣus: "In a future age, when the land of this Jambudvīpa is level and even, and the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a Brahmin’s son named Maitreya. His body will be the color of pure gold, shining with brilliant light. He will leave his home to attain perfect enlightenment and will widely preach the Dharma for sentient beings in three assemblies. Those whom he saves will all be beings who planted roots of merit under my own dispensation. Whether lay or monastic, whether they kept the precepts or broke them, all who hold deep respect and a single mind toward the Three Jewels will receive his guidance and attain the fruit of liberation. Within these three assemblies of preaching, he will first save those who are followers of my dispensation, and only then will he transform those who are fellow-travelers with whom he shares a karmic connection." At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, having heard these words of the Buddha, rose from his seat and said to the Buddha: "I vow to become that Maitreya, the World-Honored One." The Tathāgata replied: "As you have said, you shall attain this fruit. All that has been described above is the manner of your teaching and transformation." To the west of the place where the Bodhisattva Maitreya received his prediction, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva Śākya received his own prediction. In the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, turned the wheel of the wonderful Dharma, and opened the way for sentient beings to be transformed, bestowing upon the Bodhisattva Prabhāpāla (護明菩薩) the prediction: "This Bodhisattva, in a future age when the lifespan of sentient beings is one hundred years, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni." Not far to the south of the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya received his prediction, there are the traces of the four past Buddhas walking to and fro. The site is over fifty paces long and about seven feet high, built of piled bluestone, and upon it is an image of the Tathāgata in the act of walking. The appearance of the image is extraordinary and solemn; from the top of the uṣṇīṣa, hair uniquely emerges, its spiritual features are fully revealed, and its divine intelligence is clearly evidenced. Within its enclosure, there are many sacred sites, including several hundred *vihāras* (精舍) and *stūpas*; I have briefly mentioned two or three, as it is difficult to describe them in detail.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 伽藍垣西有一清池，周二百餘步，如來嘗中盥浴。次西大池，周一百八十步，如來嘗中滌器。次北有池，周百五十步，如來嘗中浣衣。凡此三池，並有龍止。其水既深，其味又甘，澄淨皎潔，常無增減。有人慢心，濯此池者，金毘羅獸多為之害；若深恭敬，汲用無懼。浣衣池側大方石上，有如來袈裟之迹，其文明徹，煥如彫鏤，諸淨信者每來供養。外道凶人輕蹈此石，池中龍王便興風雨。池側不遠有窣堵波，是如來修菩薩行時，為六牙象王，獵人利其牙也，詐服袈裟，彎弧伺捕，象王為敬袈裟，遂捩牙而授焉。捩牙側不遠有窣堵波，是如來修菩薩行時，愍世無禮，示為鳥身，與彼獼猴、白象，於此相問，誰先見是尼拘律樹，各言事迹，遂編長幼，化漸遠近，人知上下，道俗歸依。其側不遠，大林中有窣堵波，是如來昔與提婆達多俱為鹿王斷事之處。昔於此處大林之中，有兩群鹿，各五百餘。時此國王畋遊原澤，菩薩鹿王前請王曰：「大王校獵中原，縱燎飛矢，凡我徒屬，命盡茲晨，不日腐臭，無所充膳。願欲次差，日輸一鹿。王有割鮮之膳，我延旦夕之命。」王善其言，迴駕而返。兩群之鹿，更次輸命。提婆群中有懷孕鹿，次當就死，白其王曰：「身雖應死，子未次也。」鹿王怒曰：「誰不寶命！」雌鹿歎曰：「吾王不仁，死無日矣。」乃告急菩薩鹿王。鹿王曰：「悲哉慈母之心，恩及未形之子！吾今代汝。」遂至王門。道路之人傳聲唱曰：「彼大鹿王今來入邑。」都人士庶莫不馳觀。王之聞也，以為不誠。門者白王，王乃信然。曰：「鹿王何遽來耶？」鹿曰：「有雌鹿當死，胎子未產，心不能忍，敢以身代。」王聞歎曰：「我人身鹿也，爾鹿身人也。」於是悉放諸鹿，不復輸命，即以其林為諸鹿藪，因而謂之施鹿林焉。鹿野之號，自此而興。
translation: To the west of the monastery enclosure is a clear pond, more than two hundred paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once bathed. Further west is a large pond, one hundred and eighty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his utensils. Further north is a pond, one hundred and fifty paces in circumference, where the Tathāgata once washed his robes. All three of these ponds are inhabited by dragons. Their water is deep and its taste is sweet; it is clear, pure, and bright, and it neither increases nor decreases. If someone with an arrogant mind washes in these ponds, the Kumbhīra (金毘羅) beasts often harm them; if one is deeply respectful, one may draw and use the water without fear. On a large square rock beside the robe-washing pond, there are traces of the Tathāgata’s robes; the patterns are clear and bright, as if carved or engraved, and the faithful often come here to make offerings. If wicked heretics tread contemptuously upon this stone, the dragon king in the pond immediately stirs up wind and rain. Not far from the pond is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was a six-tusked elephant king; a hunter, coveting his tusks, disguised himself in a monk’s robe and lay in wait with a drawn bow, but the elephant king, out of respect for the robe, broke off his tusks and gave them to him. Not far from the place where the tusks were broken is a stūpa, marking the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, felt pity for the world’s lack of propriety and manifested as a bird. Together with a monkey and a white elephant, he asked here who had first seen the Nyagrodha (尼拘律) tree. Each recounted their experiences, and they established seniority accordingly. Through this, the influence of the teaching gradually spread, people learned the order of precedence, and both the ordained and the laity took refuge. Not far from its side, in a great forest, there is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata, in the past, while he and Devadatta (提婆達多) were both deer kings, settled a matter. Formerly, in this great forest, there were two herds of deer, each numbering more than five hundred. At that time, the king of this country was hunting in the plains and marshes. The Bodhisattva deer king came forward and petitioned the king, saying: "Your Majesty is hunting across the plains, setting fires and loosing flying arrows. All my followers will lose their lives this morning; in a few days they will rot and stink, serving no purpose as food. I wish to arrange a rotation to deliver one deer each day. Your Majesty will have fresh meat for your meals, and I will prolong our lives for a little while." The king approved his words, turned his carriage around, and returned. The two herds of deer took turns delivering their lives. In Devadatta’s herd, there was a pregnant doe whose turn it was to die; she said to her king, "Although I am due to die, my unborn child’s turn has not yet come." The deer king replied angrily, "Who does not treasure their own life!" The doe sighed and said, "My king is inhumane; death is not far off." She then went to report her emergency to the Bodhisattva deer king. The deer king said, "How sorrowful is the heart of a compassionate mother, whose kindness extends even to her unborn child! I will now take your place." He then went to the king’s gate. People on the road passed the word along, calling out, "That great deer king is now entering the city." The city dwellers and commoners all rushed to watch. When the king heard of it, he thought it was not true. The gatekeeper reported it to the king, and the king then believed it. He said, "Why has the deer king come so suddenly?" The deer said, "There is a doe who is due to die, but her fetus has not yet been born; my heart cannot bear it, so I venture to offer my own body in her stead." Upon hearing this, the king sighed and said, "I am a deer in a human body; you are a human in a deer's body." Thereupon, he released all the deer and no longer required them to forfeit their lives, designating that forest as a sanctuary for the deer; thus, it was called the Forest Given to the Deer (Mr̥gadāva). The name "Deer Park" originated from this.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 伽藍西南二三里，有窣堵波，高三百餘尺，基趾廣峙，瑩飾奇珍，上無層龕，便置覆鉢，雖建表柱，而無輪鐸。其側有小窣堵波，是阿若憍陳如等五人棄制迎佛處也。初，薩婆曷剌他悉陀（唐言一切義成。舊曰悉達多，訛略也）太子踰城之後，棲山隱谷，忘身殉法。淨飯王乃命家族三人、舅氏二人曰：「我子一切義成捨家修學，孤遊山澤，獨處林藪，故命爾曹隨知所止。內則叔父、伯舅，外則既君且臣，凡厥動靜，宜知進止。」五人銜命，相望營衛，因即勤求，欲期出離。每相謂曰：「夫修道者，苦證耶？樂證耶？」二人曰：「安樂為道。」三人曰：「勤苦為道。」二三交爭，未有以明。於是太子思惟至理，為伏苦行外道，節麻米以支身。彼二人者見而言曰：「太子所行非真實法。夫道也者，樂以證之，今乃勤苦，非吾徒也。」捨而遠遁，思惟果證。太子六年苦行，未證菩提，欲驗苦行非真，受乳糜而證果。斯三人者聞而歎曰：「功垂成矣，今其退矣。六年苦行，一日捐功！」於是相從求訪二人，既相見已，匡坐高論，更相議曰：「昔見太子一切義成，出王宮，就荒谷，去珍服，披鹿皮，精勤勵志，貞節苦心，求深妙法，期無上果。今乃受牧女乳糜，敗道虧志，吾知之矣，無能為也。」彼二人曰：「君何見之晚歟？此猖蹶人耳。夫處乎深宮，安乎尊勝，不能靜志，遠迹山林，棄轉輪王位，為鄙賤人行，何可念哉？言增忉怛耳！」菩薩浴尼連河，坐菩提樹，成等正覺，號天人師，寂然宴默，惟察應度，曰：「彼欝頭藍子者，證非想定，堪受妙法。」空中諸天尋聲報曰：「欝頭藍子命終已來，經今七日。」如來歎惜：「如何不遇，垂聞妙法，遽從變化？」重更觀察，營求世界，有阿藍迦藍，得無所有處定，可授至理。諸天又曰：「終已五日。」如來再歎，愍其薄祐。又更諦觀，誰應受教？唯施鹿林中有五人者，可先誘導。如來爾時起菩提樹，趣鹿野園，威儀寂靜，神光晃曜，毫含玉彩，身真金色，安詳前進，導彼五人。斯五人遙見如來，互相謂曰：「一切義成，彼來者是。歲月遽淹，聖果不證，心期已退，故尋吾徒。宜各默然，勿起迎禮。」如來漸近，威神動物，五人忘制，拜迎問訊，侍從如儀。如來漸誘，示之妙理，兩安居畢，方獲果證。
translation: Two or three li to the southwest of the monastery, there is a stupa over three hundred feet high; its base is broad and imposing, adorned with lustrous and rare gems. It has no tiered niches on top, but is surmounted by an inverted bowl; although a central pillar was erected, it lacks the usual rings and bells. Beside it is a small stupa, marking the place where the five men, including Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如), abandoned their restraint to welcome the Buddha.  Previously, after the Prince Sarvārthasiddha (薩婆曷剌他悉陀; in Tang language, "Accomplished in All Meanings"; formerly called Siddhārtha, which is an abbreviated and inaccurate rendering) had climbed over the city wall, he dwelt in mountain valleys, forgetting his own body in his devotion to the Dharma. King Śuddhodana then commanded three members of the royal clan and two from the maternal side, saying: "My son, Accomplished in All Meanings, has left home to practice and learn; he wanders alone through mountains and marshes and dwells in isolation among the woods and thickets. Therefore, I order you to follow him and keep track of his whereabouts. Internally, you are his uncles and maternal uncles; externally, he is your lord and you are his subjects. In all his movements, you should know when to advance and when to stop."  The five men accepted the command and kept watch over him, providing protection. Consequently, they practiced diligently, hoping to attain liberation. They often said to one another, "Is the path to enlightenment attained through suffering, or is it attained through ease?" Two of them said, "Ease is the path." Three of them said, "Hardship and suffering are the path." The two and the three argued with each other, unable to reach a clear conclusion. Thereupon, the Prince contemplated the ultimate truth and, in order to subdue the non-Buddhist ascetics, he restricted himself to a few grains of hemp and rice to sustain his body. Those two men saw this and said, "What the Prince is practicing is not the true Dharma." "The Way is to be realized through ease; now he practices diligent suffering, so he is not one of our kind." They abandoned him and fled to a distance, contemplating the realization of the fruit. The Prince practiced asceticism for six years without realizing enlightenment; wishing to verify that asceticism was not the truth, he accepted milk gruel and attained the fruit. These three men heard of this and sighed, saying, "His merit was on the verge of completion, yet now he has retreated. Six years of asceticism, and in one day he has cast away his merit!" Thereupon, they followed one another to seek out the two men. Having met, they sat upright and engaged in lofty discourse, discussing further: "Formerly we saw the Prince, Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成), leave the royal palace, go to the desolate valleys, discard his precious garments, and don deerskin. He applied himself with diligent resolve and painstaking integrity to seek the profound and wonderful Dharma, aspiring to the supreme fruit. Now he has accepted milk gruel from a cowherd girl, ruining his path and compromising his resolve; I know him well, he is capable of nothing." Those two men said, "Why are you so late in seeing this? This is merely a reckless person. Dwelling in the deep palace, secure in his exalted status, he could not calm his mind; he fled to the mountain forests, abandoned the position of a wheel-turning king, and performed the acts of a base and lowly person—what is there to think about? Speaking of him only increases one's sorrow!" The Bodhisattva bathed in the Nairañjanā (尼連河) River, sat under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, attained perfect enlightenment, and was titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans. Remaining in silent tranquility, he observed those ready for deliverance and said, "That Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) has realized the meditative state of neither perception nor non-perception and is capable of receiving the wonderful Dharma." The devas in the sky heard his voice and replied, "It has been seven days since Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) passed away." The Tathāgata sighed with regret, "How unfortunate that he did not encounter this, for he was on the verge of hearing the wonderful Dharma, yet he has suddenly undergone transformation!" He observed the world again, seeking someone to teach, and found Ārāḍa Kālāma (阿藍迦藍), who had attained the meditative state of nothingness and could be taught the ultimate truth. The devas said again, "He passed away five days ago." The Tathāgata sighed once more, pitying his meager fortune. He observed carefully again: who was fit to receive instruction? Only the five men in the Deer Park (鹿林) could be guided first. At that time, the Tathāgata rose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree and headed for the Deer Park; his deportment was serene, his divine light shone brilliantly, his brow-hair possessed the luster of jade, and his body was the color of genuine gold as he proceeded composedly to guide those five men. When these five men saw the Tathāgata from afar, they said to one another, "Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成) is the one coming there. Much time has passed, he has not realized the holy fruit, and his aspirations have retreated, so he is coming to seek us. We should each remain silent and not rise to greet or pay homage to him." As the Tathāgata gradually approached, his divine power moved them; the five men, forgetting their resolve, bowed to welcome him with greetings and attended to him according to etiquette. The Tathāgata gradually guided them, revealing the wonderful truth to them, and after two retreats, they finally attained the realization of the fruit.

t2087_text: 施鹿林東行二三里，至窣堵波，傍有涸池，周八十餘步，一名救命，又謂烈士。聞諸先志曰：數百年前，有一隱士，於此池側結廬屏迹，博習伎術，究極神理，能使瓦礫為寶，人畜易形，但未能馭風雲，陪仙駕。閱圖考古，更求仙術。其方曰：「夫神仙者，長生之術也。將欲求學，先定其志，築建壇場，周一丈餘。命一烈士，信勇昭著，執長刀，立壇隅，屏息絕言，自昏達旦；求仙者中壇而坐，手按長刀，口誦神呪，收視反聽，遲明登仙。所執銛刀變為寶劍，凌虛履空，王諸仙侶，執劍指麾，所欲皆從，無衰無老，不病不死。」是人既得仙方，行訪烈士，營求曠歲，未諧心願。後於城中遇見一人，悲號逐路。隱士覩其相，心甚慶悅，即而慰問：「何至怨傷？」曰：「我以貧窶，傭力自濟。其主見知，特深信用，期滿五歲，當酬重賞。於是忍勤苦，忘艱辛。五年將周，一旦違失，既蒙笞辱，又無所得。以此為心，悲悼誰恤？」隱士命與同遊，來至草廬，以術力故，化具肴饌，已而令入池浴，服以新衣，又以五百金錢遺之，曰：「盡當來求，幸無外也。」自時厥後，數加重賂，潛行陰德，感激其心。烈士屢求効命，以報知己。隱士曰：「我求烈士，彌歷歲時，幸而會遇，奇貌應圖，非有他故，願一夕不聲耳。」烈士曰：「死尚不辭，豈徒屏息？」於是設壇場，受仙法，依方行事，坐待日曛。曛暮之後，各司其務，隱士誦神呪，烈士按銛刀。殆將曉矣，忽發聲叫。是時空中火下，煙焰雲蒸，隱士疾引此人，入池避難。已而問曰：「誡子無聲，何以驚叫？」烈士曰：「受命後，至夜分，惛然若夢，變異更起。見昔事主躬來慰謝，感荷厚恩，忍不報語；彼人震怒，遂見殺害。受中陰身，顧屍歎惜，猶願歷世不言，以報厚德。遂見託生南印度大婆羅門家，乃至受胎出胎，備經苦厄，荷恩荷德，嘗不出聲。洎乎受業、冠、婚、喪親、生子，每念前恩，忍而不語，宗親戚屬咸見怪異。年過六十有五，我妻謂曰：『汝可言矣！若不語者，當殺汝子。』我時惟念，已隔生世，自顧衰老，唯此稚子，因止其妻，令無殺害。遂發此聲耳。」隱士曰：「我之過也！此魔嬈耳。」烈士感恩，悲事不成，憤恚而死。免火災難，故曰救命；感恩而死，又謂烈士池。烈士池西有三獸窣堵波，是如來修菩薩行時燒身之處。劫初時，於此林野，有狐、兔、猨，異類相悅。時天帝釋欲驗修菩薩行者，降靈應化為一老夫，謂三獸曰：「二三子善安隱乎？無驚懼耶？」曰：「涉豐草，遊茂林，異類同歡，既安且樂。」老夫曰：「聞二三子情厚意密，忘其老弊，故此遠尋。今正飢乏，何以饋食？」曰：「幸少留此，我躬馳訪。」於是同心虛己，分路營求。狐沿水濱，銜一鮮鯉，猨於林樹，採異華菓，俱來至止，同進老夫。唯免空還，遊躍左右。老夫謂曰：「以吾觀之，爾曹未和。猨狐同志，各能役心，唯兔空返，獨無相饋。以此言之，誠可知也。」兔聞譏議，謂狐、猨曰：「多聚樵蘇，方有所作。」狐、猨競馳，銜草曳木，既已蘊崇，猛焰將熾。兔曰：「仁者，我身卑劣，所求難遂，敢以微躬，充此一䬸。」辭畢入火，尋即致死。是時老夫復帝釋身，除燼收骸，傷歎良久，謂狐、猨曰：「一何至此！吾感其心，不泯其迹，寄之月輪，傳乎後世。」故彼咸言，月中之兔，自斯而有。後人於此建窣堵波。
translation: Going two or three li east from the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), one reaches a stūpa. Beside it is a dried-up pond, more than eighty paces in circumference, known as "Life-saving" (Jīvitatrāṇa) and also called "Hero" (Vīra). According to the local records: several hundred years ago, there was a hermit who built a hut and lived in seclusion beside this pond. He was extensively learned in the arts and had mastered the ultimate divine principles, being able to turn rubble into jewels and change the forms of humans and animals, yet he was not yet able to ride the winds and clouds or join the company of the immortals. He examined the diagrams and studied the ancients, seeking further for the arts of immortality. The formula stated: "Immortality is the art of long life. If one wishes to seek this study, one must first settle one's resolve and build an altar more than one zhang in circumference. Command a man of mettle, renowned for his loyalty and courage, to hold a long sword and stand at the corner of the altar, holding his breath and remaining silent from dusk until dawn. The seeker of immortality shall sit in the center of the altar, hand resting on the long sword, chanting divine incantations, withdrawing his vision and turning his hearing inward; by daybreak, he shall ascend to immortality. The sharp sword he holds will turn into a precious blade; he will soar through the void and tread upon the air, reigning over the company of immortals, and with the sword in hand, he will command, and all he desires will be fulfilled, without decline or aging, without sickness or death." Having obtained this formula for immortality, the man traveled in search of a man of mettle, but despite seeking for many years, he could not find anyone to satisfy his wish. Later, in the city, he encountered a man wailing as he walked along the road. The hermit observed his appearance and was greatly delighted; he approached him and asked with concern, "Why are you so aggrieved and wounded?" The man replied, "I am poor and destitute, and I labor to support myself." His master had recognized his worth and placed deep trust in him, promising that when five years were completed, he would be rewarded with a heavy bounty. Consequently, he endured toil and hardship, forgetting his suffering. As the five years were about to conclude, he made a single mistake, and for this he was not only whipped and humiliated but also received nothing. "With this weighing on my heart, who is there to pity my grief?" The hermit bade him travel together, and they arrived at a thatched hut. By the power of his arts, the hermit conjured a spread of food and drink; afterwards, he ordered him to bathe in the pond, dressed him in new clothes, and presented him with five hundred gold coins, saying, "When these are exhausted, come and ask for more; pray do not treat me as an outsider." From that time on, the hermit repeatedly bestowed heavy gifts upon him, secretly performing acts of kindness to stir his heart. The hero (烈士) repeatedly sought to offer his life in service to repay the one who understood him. The hermit said, "I have sought a hero for many years; fortunately we have met, and your singular appearance matches the prophecies. I have no other motive; I only wish for you to remain silent for a single night." The hero replied, "I would not even refuse death, so how could I not merely hold my breath?" Thereupon, they set up an altar, received the immortal method, and followed the instructions to perform the rites, sitting and waiting for the sun to set. After dusk, each attended to his duties: the hermit recited divine incantations, while the hero gripped his sharp blade. When it was almost dawn, he suddenly let out a cry. At that moment, fire descended from the sky, and smoke and flames billowed like clouds. The hermit quickly pulled the man into the pond to escape the danger. Afterwards, he asked, "I warned you to remain silent; why did you cry out in alarm?" The hero replied, "After receiving your instructions, when midnight came, I fell into a trance-like dream, and strange transformations began to arise." I saw my former master come in person to comfort and thank me; moved by his great kindness, I restrained myself and did not respond. He became furious and killed me. I entered the intermediate state (antarābhava) and, looking back at my corpse, sighed with regret, yet I still wished to remain silent throughout my lives to repay his great virtue. I was then reborn into a great Brahmin family in South India; from conception to birth and through all manner of hardships, I bore your grace and virtue in mind and never made a sound. Even when I reached the stages of schooling, capping, marriage, mourning my parents, and fathering a son, I always remembered your past kindness and endured in silence, though my kinsmen and relatives all found it strange. When I was over sixty-five years old, my wife said to me, "You must speak! If you do not speak, I shall kill your son." At that moment, I thought that since I had already passed through a lifetime and was now old and frail, this young son was all I had; therefore, I stopped my wife to prevent her from killing him. That is why I let out this cry." The hermit said, "It is my fault! This was the harassment of a demon." The hero, moved by gratitude but grieved that the task was not accomplished, died in a fit of indignation. Because he escaped the disaster of fire, it is called the Life-Saving Pond; because he died out of gratitude, it is also called the Hero's Pond (烈士池). West of the Hero's Pond is the Three-Beast Stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata, while practicing the bodhisattva path, burned his body. At the beginning of the kalpa, in this wilderness, there lived a fox, a rabbit, and a monkey who lived together in harmony despite their different species. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to test the one practicing the bodhisattva path, manifested his spirit as an old man and said to the three beasts, "Are you three well and at peace?" "Are you free from fear and alarm?" They replied, "We roam through lush grasses and wander in dense forests; though of different species, we share the same joy, and are both peaceful and happy." The old man said, "I have heard that you two or three are deeply affectionate and close in spirit, and forgetting my own old age and infirmity, I have sought you out from afar. Now, I am truly hungry and weak; what do you have to offer me for food?" They replied, "Please stay here a while; we will personally hasten to seek some." Thereupon, with one heart and humble intent, they went their separate ways to search. The fox went along the riverbank and caught a fresh carp in its mouth, while the ape went among the forest trees and gathered rare flowers and fruits; they both returned to the spot and presented them together to the old man. Only the hare returned empty-handed, leaping about to the left and right. The old man said to them, "In my view, you are not in harmony. The ape and the fox share the same intent and each exerted their minds, yet only the hare returned empty-handed, offering nothing at all. Judging by this, the truth is clear." Having heard this derisive remark, the hare said to the fox and the ape, "Gather plenty of firewood and grass, for I am about to do something." The fox and the ape raced to do so, carrying grass in their mouths and dragging wood; once they had piled it high, the fierce flames were about to blaze. The hare said, "O Benevolent One, my body is lowly and base, and what I sought was difficult to achieve; I venture to offer my humble self to provide this one meal." Having finished speaking, it entered the fire and immediately died. At that time, the old man resumed his form as Śakra (帝釋), cleared away the embers to collect the remains, and after sighing in grief for a long while, said to the fox and the ape, "How could it have come to this! I am moved by its heart and shall not let its traces vanish; I will entrust it to the lunar disk to be passed down to future generations." Therefore, everyone says that the hare in the moon has existed from that time onward. People of later times built a stūpa at this site.

t2087_text: 從此順殑伽河流，東行三百餘里，至戰主國（中印度境）。戰主國，周二千餘里，都城臨殑伽河，周十餘里。居人豐樂，邑里相隣。土地膏腴，稼穡時播。氣序和暢，風俗淳質，人性獷烈，邪正兼信。伽藍十餘所，僧徒減千人。並皆遵習小乘教法。天祠二十，異道雜居。大城西北伽藍中窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。《印度記》曰：「此中有如來舍利一斗。」昔者世尊嘗於此處，七日之中，為天、人眾顯說妙法。其側則有過去三佛坐及經行遺迹之處。隣此復有慈氏菩薩像，形量雖小，威神嶷然，靈鑒潛通，奇迹間起。
translation: From here, following the Ganges (gaṅgā) River and traveling east for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Yuddhapati (戰主國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Yuddhapati is more than two thousand li in circuit, and its capital city, which borders the Ganges River, is more than ten li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and the towns and villages are adjacent to one another. The land is fertile, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is mild and pleasant, the customs are simple and honest, and the temperament of the people is fierce and impetuous; they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries, with fewer than one thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. In a monastery to the northwest of the great city, there is a stupa built by King Aśoka. The *Record of India* states: "Within this there is one dou of the relics of the Tathāgata." In the past, the World-Honored One once stayed in this place for seven days, manifesting and expounding the wonderful Dharma for the sake of the assemblies of gods and men. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Adjacent to this, there is also a statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya; although its size is small, its majestic spirit is imposing, its spiritual perception is subtly connected, and miraculous signs occur from time to time.

t2087_text: 大城東行二百餘里，至阿避陀羯剌拏僧伽藍（唐言不穿耳）。周垣不廣，彫飾甚工，花池交影，臺閣連甍，僧徒肅穆，眾儀庠序。聞諸先志曰：昔大雪山北覩貨邏國有樂學沙門，二三同志禮誦餘閑，每相謂曰：「妙理幽玄，非言談所究；聖迹昭著，可足趾所尋。宜詢莫逆，親觀聖迹。」於是二三交友，杖錫同遊。既至印度，寓諸伽藍，輕其邊鄙，莫之見舍。外迫風露，內累口腹，顏色憔悴，形容枯槁。時此國王出遊近郊，見諸客僧，怪而問曰：「何方乞士？何所因來？耳既不穿，衣又垢弊。」沙門對曰：「我，覩貨邏國人也。恭承遺教，高蹈俗塵，率其同好，觀禮聖迹。慨以薄福，眾所同棄，印度沙門，莫顧羈旅。欲還本土，巡禮未周，雖迫勤苦，心遂後已。」王聞其說，用增悲感，即斯勝地，建立伽藍，白㲲題書，為之制曰：「我惟尊居世上，貴極人中，斯皆三寶之靈祐也。既為人王，受佛付囑，凡厥染衣，吾當惠濟。建此伽藍，式招羈旅。自今已來，諸穿耳僧，我此伽藍不得止舍。」因其事迹，故以名焉。
translation: Going eastward from the great city for more than two hundred li, one reaches the Aviddhakarṇa Monastery (阿避陀羯剌拏僧伽藍) (which in the language of the Tang means "Unpierced Ears"). Its surrounding walls are not extensive, but the carvings and decorations are most exquisite; the flower ponds reflect one another, the terraces and pavilions stand with connected roofs, the monks are solemn and grave, and the community conducts its rituals in an orderly manner.  According to the records of former times: Long ago, in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) north of the Great Snowy Mountains, there were śramaṇas who delighted in learning. In their leisure time after chanting and recitation, two or three like-minded companions would often say to one another, "The wonderful principles are profound and mysterious, and cannot be fully investigated through mere talk; the sacred sites are clearly manifest, and can be sought out by the soles of one's feet. We should consult with those of like mind and personally visit the sacred sites."  Thereupon, these two or three friends took up their staves and traveled together. Upon arriving in India, they lodged at various monasteries, but because they were looked down upon as being from a borderland, no one would provide them with shelter. Exposed to the wind and dew outdoors and burdened by hunger and thirst within, their complexions became haggard and their bodies grew emaciated.  At that time, the king of this country was traveling in the suburbs and, seeing these visiting monks, was surprised and asked, "From what region are you mendicants? For what reason have you come? Your ears are not pierced, and your robes are dirty and tattered."  The śramaṇas replied, "We are people from the country of Tukhāra. Respectfully upholding the legacy of the teachings, we have transcended worldly dust. I led my like-minded companions to visit and pay homage to the sacred sites. Regrettably, due to our meager merit, we have been forsaken by all; the Indian monks show no concern for us travelers. We wish to return to our native land, but our pilgrimage is not yet complete; although we are pressed by hardship, our hearts are reluctant to give up." Upon hearing their account, the king’s pity and sorrow were further increased. He immediately established a monastery at this excellent site and, writing a decree on white cotton cloth, declared: "That I dwell as the most honored in the world and the noblest among men is entirely due to the spiritual protection of the Triple Gem. Since I am a king of men and have received the Buddha’s entrustment, I shall provide relief and aid to all those who wear the dyed robes. This monastery has been constructed to provide hospitality for travelers. From this time forward, no monks with pierced ears shall be allowed to stay in this monastery of mine." Because of these events, it was so named.

t2087_text: 阿避陀羯剌拏伽藍東南行百餘里，南渡殑伽河，至摩訶娑羅邑，並婆羅門種，不遵佛法。然見沙門，先訪學業，知其強識，方深禮敬。
translation: Traveling southeast from the Aviddhakarṇa (阿避陀羯剌拏) Monastery for more than one hundred li, one crosses the Gaṅgā (殑伽) River to the south and arrives at the town of Mahāsāla (摩訶娑羅邑). The inhabitants are all of the Brahman caste and do not follow the Buddha-dharma. However, when they see a śramaṇa, they first inquire about his learning; only when they know he possesses a retentive memory do they then pay him deep respect.

translation: To the north of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, there is a temple of Nārāyaṇa (那羅延天祠). It has multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, which are vast and exquisitely adorned. The images of the various devas are carved from stone; the craftsmanship exhausts human ingenuity, and their spiritual responses are difficult to fathom.

t2087_text: 那羅延天祠東行三十餘里，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，太半陷地。前建石柱，高餘二丈，上作師子之像，刻記伏鬼之事。昔於此處有曠野鬼，恃大威力，噉人血肉，作害生靈，肆極妖祟。如來愍諸眾生不得其死，以神通力誘化諸鬼，導以歸依之敬，齊以不殺之戒。諸鬼承教，奉以周旋。於是舉石請佛安坐，願聞正法，克念護持。自時厥後，無信之徒競共推移鬼置石座，動以千數，莫之能轉。茂林清池，周基左右，人至其側，無不心懼。伏鬼側不遠，有數伽藍，雖多傾毀，尚有僧徒，並皆遵習大乘教法。
translation: Traveling more than thirty *li* east of the Nārāyaṇa (那羅延天祠) temple, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, more than half of which has sunk into the ground. In front of it stands a stone pillar over two *zhang* high, topped with the figure of a lion and inscribed with a record of the subduing of demons. Formerly, there were demons of the wilderness at this place who, relying on their great power, devoured human flesh and blood, harming living beings and committing the most extreme atrocities. The Tathāgata, pitying the living beings who were meeting untimely deaths, used his supernatural powers to convert the demons, leading them to take refuge with reverence and bringing them into order with the precept against killing. The demons accepted his teaching and followed him in his rounds. Thereupon, they raised a stone to invite the Buddha to sit, wishing to hear the true Dharma and sincerely vowing to protect and uphold it. From that time onward, non-believers vied with one another to push and move the stone seat placed by the demons, but even with thousands of people, none could budge it. Dense forests and clear ponds surround the base; those who come near it are all filled with fear. Not far from the place of the subduing of the demons are several *saṃghārāma*s; although many are in ruins, there are still monks residing there, all of whom follow and study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

t2087_text: 從此東南行百餘里，至一窣堵波，基已傾陷，餘高數丈。昔者如來寂滅之後，八國大王分舍利也，量舍利婆羅門蜜塗瓶內，分授諸王，而婆羅門持瓶以歸，既得所粘舍利，遂建窣堵波，并瓶置內，因以名焉。後無憂王開取舍利瓶，改建大窣堵波，或至齋日，時燭光明。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for over a hundred li, one arrives at a stūpa whose foundation has already collapsed and sunk, with the remaining portion standing several tens of feet high. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had entered extinction, the great kings of the eight nations divided the relics. The Brahmin who measured the relics smeared the inside of a vessel with honey to distribute the portions to the various kings. The Brahmin then took the vessel and returned home; having obtained the relics that adhered to it, he built a stūpa and placed the vessel inside, hence it was named accordingly. Later, King Aśoka (無憂王) opened it to take the relic vessel and rebuilt it into a great stūpa; occasionally on fast days, it radiates a brilliant light.

t2087_text: 從此東北度殑伽河，行百四五十里，至吠舍釐國（舊曰毘舍離國，訛也。中印度境）。吠舍釐國，周五千餘里。土地沃壤，花菓茂盛，菴沒羅菓、茂遮菓既多且貴。氣序和暢，風俗淳質，好福重學，邪正雜信。伽藍數百，多已圮壞，存者三五，僧徒稀少。天祠數十，異道雜居，露形之徒，寔繁其黨。吠舍釐城已甚傾頹，其故基趾周六七十里，宮城周四五里，少有居人。
translation: From here, crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the northeast and traveling one hundred forty or fifty li, one reaches the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國) (formerly called Piśālī [毘舍離國], which is an error; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Vaiśālī is more than five thousand li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and flowers and fruits are abundant; mangoes (菴沒羅菓) and plantains (茂遮菓) are both plentiful and highly valued. The climate is pleasant and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people love merit and value learning, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated; only three or five remain, and the number of monks is small. There are several dozen Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together; the followers of the naked ascetics are particularly numerous among them. The city of Vaiśālī is already in a state of extreme ruin; its old foundations are sixty or seventy li in circuit, and the palace city is four or five li in circuit, with very few inhabitants.

translation: Five or six li to the northwest of the palace city, one arrives at a monastery where the community of monks is small and studies the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. Beside it is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra (毘摩羅詰經) and where the elder’s son Ratnākara (寶積) and others offered precious parasols. To its east is a stūpa where Śāriputra and others attained the fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).

t2087_text: 舍利子證果東南有窣堵波，是吠舍釐王之所建也。佛涅槃後，此國先王分得舍利，式修崇建。《印度記》曰：「此中舊有如來舍利一斛，無憂王開取九斗，唯留一斗。」後有國王復欲開取，方事興功，尋則地震，遂不敢開。
translation: To the southeast of the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) attained the fruit, there is a stūpa built by the king of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐). After the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, a former king of this country received a share of the relics and respectfully constructed this monument. The *Record of India* (印度記) states: "Originally, there was one *hu* of the Tathāgata’s relics here; King Aśoka (無憂王) opened it and took out nine *dou*, leaving only one *dou* behind." Later, another king wished to open it again and had just begun the work when the earth shook, so he dared not open it.

t2087_text: 其西北有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。傍有石柱，高五六十尺，上作師子之像。石柱南有池，是群獼猴為佛穿也。在昔如來曾住於此。池西不遠有窣堵波，諸獼猴持如來鉢上樹取蜜之處；池南不遠有窣堵波，是諸獼猴奉佛蜜處；池西北隅猶有獼猴形像。
translation: To the northwest of this there is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Beside it is a stone pillar, fifty or sixty feet high, with the figure of a lion fashioned on top. To the south of the stone pillar is a pond, which was dug for the Buddha by a troop of monkeys. In the past, the Tathāgata once resided here. Not far to the west of the pond is a stūpa, the place where the monkeys took the Tathāgata’s bowl and climbed a tree to gather honey; not far to the south of the pond is a stūpa, which is the place where the monkeys offered honey to the Buddha; in the northwest corner of the pond, there still remains an image of a monkey.

t2087_text: 伽藍東北三里有窣堵波，是毘摩羅詰（唐言無垢稱。舊曰淨名，然淨則無垢，名則是稱，義雖取同，名乃有異。舊曰維摩詰，訛略也）故宅基趾，多有靈異。去此不遠有一神舍，其狀壘甎，傳云積石，即無垢稱長者現疾說法之處。去此不遠有窣堵波，長者子寶積之故宅也。去此不遠有窣堵波，是菴沒羅女故宅，佛姨母等諸苾芻尼於此證入涅槃。
translation: Three li to the northeast of the monastery is a stūpa, which is the site of the former residence of Vimalakīrti (in Chinese, Wugoucheng [Stainless Reputation]; formerly it was called Jingming [Pure Name], but "pure" means "stainless" and "name" means "reputation"; although the meaning is the same, the terms differ. The former name, Weimojie, was an abbreviated corruption). There are many miraculous occurrences there. Not far from this place is a spirit shrine, built of piled bricks—tradition says it is piled stone—which is the place where the elder Wugoucheng manifested illness and expounded the Dharma. Not far from here is a stūpa, which is the former residence of the elder’s son, Ratnākara (Baoji). Not far from here is a stūpa, which is the former residence of the woman Āmrapālī, where the Buddha’s maternal aunt and other bhikṣuṇīs attained parinirvāṇa.

t2087_text: 伽藍北三四里有窣堵波，是如來將往拘尸那國入般涅槃，人與非人隨從世尊，至此佇立。次西北不遠有窣堵波，是佛於此最後觀吠舍釐城。其南不遠有精舍，前建窣堵波，是菴沒羅女園持以施佛。菴沒羅園側有窣堵波，是如來告涅槃處。佛昔在此告阿難曰：「其得四神足者，能住壽一劫。如來今者，當壽幾何？」如是再三，阿難不對，天魔迷惑故也。阿難從坐而起，林中宴默。時魔來請佛曰：「如來在世教化已久，蒙濟流轉，數如塵沙，寂滅之樂，今其時矣。」世尊以少土置爪上，而告魔曰：「地土多耶？爪土多耶？」對曰：「地土多也。」佛言：「所度者如爪上土，未度者如大地土。却後三月，吾當涅槃。」魔聞歡喜而退。阿難林中忽感異夢，來白佛言：「我在林間，夢見大樹，枝葉茂盛，蔭影蒙密，驚風忽起，摧散無餘。將非世尊欲入寂滅？我心懷懼，故來請問。」佛告阿難：「吾先告汝，汝為魔蔽，不時請留。魔王勸我早入涅槃，已許之期，斯夢是也。」告涅槃期側不遠有窣堵波，千子見父母處也。昔有仙人，隱居巖谷，仲春之月，鼓濯清流，麀鹿隨飲，感生女子，姿貌過人，唯脚似鹿，仙人見已，收而養焉。其後命令求火，至餘仙廬，足所履地，迹有蓮華。彼仙見已，深以奇之，令其繞廬，方乃得火。鹿女依命，得火而還。時梵豫王畋遊見華，尋迹以求，悅其奇怪，同載而返。相師占言，當生千子。餘婦聞之，莫不圖計。日月既滿，生一蓮花，花有千葉，葉坐一子。餘婦誣罔，咸稱不祥，投殑伽河，隨波泛濫。烏耆延王下流遊觀，見黃雲蓋乘波而來，取以開視，乃有千子，乳養成立，有大力焉。恃有千子，拓境四方，兵威乘勝，將次此國。時梵豫王聞之，甚懷震懼，兵力不敵，計無所出矣。是時鹿女心知其子，乃謂王曰：「今寇戎臨境，上下離心，賤妾愚忠，能敗強敵。」王未之信也，憂懼良深。鹿女乃昇城樓，以待寇至。千子將兵，圍城已匝，鹿女告曰：「莫為逆事！我是汝母，汝是我子。」千子謂曰：「何言之謬？」鹿女手按兩乳，流注千岐，天性所感，咸入其口。於是解甲歸宗，釋兵返族，兩國交歡，百姓安樂。千子歸宗側不遠有窣堵波，是如來行經舊迹，指告眾曰：「昔吾於此歸宗見親。欲知千子，即賢劫千佛是也。」述本生東有故基，上建窣堵波，光明時燭，祈請或遂，是如來說《普門陀羅尼》等經重閣講堂餘趾也。講堂側不遠有窣堵波，中有阿難半身舍利。去此不遠有數百窣堵波，欲定其數，未有克知，是千獨覺入寂滅處。吠舍釐城內外周隍，聖迹繁多，難以具舉。形勝故墟，魚鱗間峙，歲月驟改，炎涼亟移，林既摧殘，池亦枯涸，朽株餘迹，其詳驗焉。
translation: Three or four *li* to the north of the monastery is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where humans and non-humans followed the World-Honored One and stood still as the Tathāgata was proceeding to the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國) to enter *parinirvāṇa*. Not far to the northwest is a *stūpa*, marking the spot where the Buddha last gazed upon the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). Not far to its south is a vihāra (精舍), with a *stūpa* built in front, marking the site of the Āmrapālī-vana (菴沒羅女園) which she held and offered to the Buddha. Beside the Āmrapālī-vana is a *stūpa*, marking the place where the Tathāgata announced his *nirvāṇa*. Formerly, the Buddha was here and said to Ānanda, "Those who have attained the four bases of psychic power (*catvāraḥ ṛddhi-pādāḥ*) are able to remain for an aeon. The Tathāgata now, how long shall he remain?" In this way he asked three times, but Ānanda did not respond, for he was deluded by the heavenly Māra. Ānanda rose from his seat and went into the forest to meditate in silence. At that time, Māra came to request the Buddha, saying, "The Tathāgata has been in the world teaching and transforming for a long time; those who have been saved from transmigration are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The joy of extinction—now is the time for it." The World-Honored One placed a small amount of soil on his fingernail and said to Māra, "Is the soil of the earth more, or is the soil on my fingernail more?" He replied, "The soil of the earth is more." The Buddha said, "Those whom I have saved are like the soil on my fingernail, while those who have not been saved are like the soil of the great earth. Three months from now, I shall enter *nirvāṇa*." Hearing this, Māra was joyful and withdrew. Ānanda suddenly had a strange dream while in the woods and came to report it to the Buddha, saying: "While I was in the woods, I dreamed of a great tree with luxuriant branches and leaves and dense shade; a violent wind suddenly arose and scattered it until nothing remained. Could it be that the World-Honored One is about to enter extinction? My heart is filled with fear, so I have come to ask." The Buddha told Ānanda: "I told you before that you were obscured by Māra and did not request me to remain at the proper time. The Demon King urged me to enter *nirvāṇa* early, and I have already granted him the date; this dream is the sign of that."  Not far from the place where he announced the time of his *nirvāṇa* is a *stūpa* (窣堵波), which is the place where the thousand sons saw their parents. Long ago, there was a *ṛṣi* (仙人) living in seclusion in a rocky valley. In the second month of spring, while he was bathing in a clear stream, a doe followed him to drink and was moved to give birth to a girl. Her appearance was superior to others, but her feet resembled those of a deer. The *ṛṣi* saw her, took her in, and raised her. Later, he ordered her to seek fire. When she reached the hermitage of another *ṛṣi*, lotus flowers appeared in the tracks where her feet stepped. That *ṛṣi* saw this and, deeply amazed, ordered her to walk around his hermitage before she could obtain the fire. The deer-girl followed his instructions, obtained the fire, and returned.  At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) was hunting and saw the flowers. He followed the tracks to search for their source, was delighted by their strangeness, and took her back with him in his carriage. A physiognomist predicted that she would give birth to a thousand sons. The other wives heard of this and all began to plot against her. When the months and days were full, she gave birth to a single lotus flower. The flower had a thousand petals, and on each petal sat a son. The other wives slandered her, all claiming it was an inauspicious omen, and threw them into the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, where they drifted away with the waves. King Ujjayana (烏耆延王) was sightseeing in the lower reaches of the river when he saw a yellow cloud-like canopy floating on the waves; he took it and opened it to find a thousand sons, whom he nursed and raised until they grew up to possess great strength. Relying on his thousand sons, he expanded his territory in all directions, and riding on the momentum of his military victories, he was about to invade this country. At that time, King Brahmadatta (梵豫王) heard of this and was filled with great fear; his military strength was no match for them, and he could think of no solution. At that moment, the Deer Woman (鹿女) knew in her heart that they were her sons, so she said to the King: "Now that the invaders are at our borders and the people are divided, I, your humble servant, in my simple loyalty, can defeat the powerful enemy." The King did not believe her and remained deeply worried and afraid. The Deer Woman then ascended the city tower to await the arrival of the invaders. The thousand sons led their troops and completely surrounded the city, whereupon the Deer Woman called out to them, "Do not commit such a rebellious act! I am your mother, and you are my sons." The thousand sons replied, "What is this absurd talk?" The Deer Woman pressed her two breasts with her hands, and the milk flowed out in a thousand streams; moved by their natural bond, the milk entered each of their mouths. Thereupon, they took off their armor and returned to their lineage, released their weapons and returned to their kin; the two countries rejoiced together, and the common people were at peace. Not far from where the thousand sons returned to their lineage is a stūpa (窣堵波), which marks the old site where the Tathāgata (如來) once walked. He pointed it out to the assembly and said, "In the past, I returned to my lineage here and saw my relatives. If you wish to know who the thousand sons are, they are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫)." To the east of the place where he narrated his former lives, there is an old foundation upon which a stūpa (窣堵波) is built. It occasionally glows with light, and prayers offered there are sometimes granted; these are the remains of the multi-storied lecture hall where the Tathāgata (如來) preached the *Samantamukha-dhāraṇī* (普門陀羅尼) and other sūtras. Not far from the side of the lecture hall is a stūpa containing the relics of half of Ānanda’s body. Not far from here are several hundred stūpas, and though one might wish to determine their exact number, it has never been known; this is the place where a thousand Pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered into extinction (寂滅). Within and surrounding the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐), there are numerous sacred sites, which are difficult to enumerate in full. The old ruins at these scenic and strategic locations stand as thick as fish scales, but as the years have suddenly changed and the seasons have rapidly shifted, the forests have been destroyed and the ponds have dried up; only decayed stumps and remaining traces are left to be examined in detail.

t2087_text: 大城西北行五六十里，至大窣堵波，栗呫（昌葉反）婆子（舊云離車子，訛也）別如來處。如來自吠舍釐城趣拘尸那國，諸栗呫婆子聞佛將入寂滅，相從悲號送。世尊既見哀慕，非言可喻，即以神力化作大河，崖岸深絕，波流迅急，諸栗呫婆悲慟以止，如來留鉢，為作追念。
translation: Traveling fifty or sixty li to the northwest of the great city, one reaches a great stūpa at the place where the Licchavis (栗呫婆子; 呫 read with the initial of 昌 and the final of 葉; formerly called Lichezi [離車子], which is an error) bade farewell to the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata was proceeding from the city of Vaiśālī toward the country of Kuśinagara, the Licchavis, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, followed him, wailing and lamenting as they saw him off. Seeing that their sorrow and longing were so deep as to be beyond words, the World-honored One used his supernatural powers to create a great river with steep, precipitous banks and a rapid, rushing current. The Licchavis were stopped there in their bitter grief, and the Tathāgata left his almsbowl as a memento for them.

t2087_text: 吠舍釐城西北減二百里，有故城，荒蕪歲久，居人曠少。中有窣堵波，是佛在昔為諸菩薩、人、天大眾，引說本生，修菩薩行，曾於此城為轉輪王，號曰摩訶提婆（唐言大天）。有七寶應，王四天下，覩衰變之相，體無常之理，冥懷高蹈，忘情大位，捨國出家，染衣修學。
translation: Less than two hundred li to the northwest of the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城), there is an old city that has been desolate for a long time and has few inhabitants. Within it is a stūpa, which is where the Buddha in the past, for the sake of an assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, recounted his former births and his cultivation of bodhisattva deeds, having once been a wheel-turning king in this city named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆; in Chinese, "Great Deva"). He possessed the seven treasures and ruled over the four continents. Upon observing the signs of decay and change and realizing the principle of impermanence, he became deeply contemplative and sought a higher path, renouncing his attachment to his exalted position, abandoning his kingdom to go forth into homelessness, and donning the dyed robes to engage in study and practice.

t2087_text: 城東南行十四五里，至大窣堵波，是七百賢聖重結集處。佛涅槃後百一十年，吠舍釐城有諸苾芻，遠離佛法，謬行戒律。時長老耶舍陀住憍薩羅國，長老三菩伽住秣兔羅國，長老釐波多住韓若國，長老沙羅住吠舍釐國，長老富闍蘇彌羅住娑羅梨弗國。諸大羅漢心得自在，持三藏，得三明，有大名稱，眾所知識，皆是尊者阿難弟子。時耶舍陀遣使告諸賢聖，皆可集吠舍釐城。猶少一人，未滿七百。是時富闍蘇彌羅以天眼見諸大賢聖集議法事，運神足至法會。時三菩伽於大眾中右袒長跪，揚言曰：「眾無譁！欽哉，念哉！昔大聖法王善權寂滅，歲月雖淹，言教尚在。吠舍釐城懈怠苾芻謬於戒律，有十事出，違十力教。今諸賢者深明持犯，俱承大德阿難指誨，念報佛恩，重宣聖旨。」時諸大眾莫不悲感，即召集諸苾芻，依毘柰耶，訶責制止，削除謬法，宣明聖教。
translation: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stūpa, which is the place where the seven hundred sages and saints performed the second council. One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, there were *bhikṣus* in the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國) who had strayed from the Buddha-dharma and were practicing the disciplinary rules erroneously. At that time, the Elder Yaśoda was residing in the kingdom of Kosala (憍薩羅國), the Elder Sambhūta was residing in the kingdom of Mathurā (秣兔羅國), the Elder Revata was residing in the kingdom of Sahajāti (韓若國), the Elder Sālha was residing in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, and the Elder Kubjashobhita was residing in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra (娑羅梨弗國). These great *arhats* had attained mastery of mind, were keepers of the *tripiṭaka*, had attained the three knowledges, possessed great renown, were known to the masses, and were all disciples of the Venerable Ānanda. At that time, Yaśoda sent messengers to inform the various noble sages that they should all assemble in the city of Vaiśālī. There was still one person missing, and the number of seven hundred was not yet complete. At that time, Kubjashobhita, using his heavenly eye, saw the great noble sages gathering to discuss matters of the Dharma and employed his spiritual foot-power to arrive at the assembly. Then Sambhūta, in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt on one knee, and proclaimed aloud: "Let the assembly be silent! Listen with reverence, attend with care! Long ago, the Great Sage, the Dharma King, skillfully and expediently entered *nirvāṇa*; although much time has passed, his verbal teachings still remain. The negligent *bhikṣus* of the city of Vaiśālī have erred regarding the disciplinary rules; ten matters have arisen that violate the teachings of Him who possesses the Ten Powers. Now, you noble ones, who deeply understand what is to be upheld and what is to be avoided, all having received the instructions of the great virtuous Ānanda, remember to repay the Buddha’s kindness and once again proclaim the holy decree." At that time, the great assembly was moved with grief; they immediately summoned the *bhikṣus* and, in accordance with the *Vinaya* (毘柰耶), reproached and restrained them, eliminated the erroneous practices, and clarified the holy teachings.

t2087_text: 七百賢聖結集南行八九十里，至濕吠多補羅僧伽藍，層臺輪煥，重閣翬飛，僧眾清肅，並學大乘。其傍則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之處。其側窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔南趣摩揭陀國，北顧吠舍釐城，中途止息遺迹之處。
translation: Traveling eighty or ninety li south from the place where the seven hundred sages and saints held their assembly, one arrives at the Śvetapura Monastery (濕吠多補羅僧伽藍), where the tiered terraces are magnificent and the multi-storied pavilions soar like birds in flight; the community of monks is pure and solemn, and they all study the Mahayana. Beside it are the sites of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Next to these is a stupa built by King Aśoka. This is the site where the Tathāgata, in the past, stopped to rest while traveling south to the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and looking back north toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城).

t2087_text: 濕吠多補羅伽藍東南行三十餘里，殑伽河南北岸各有一窣堵波，是尊者阿難陀分身與二國處。阿難陀者，如來之從父弟也，多聞總持，博物強識，佛去世後繼大迦葉住持正法，導進學人。在摩揭陀國，於林中經行，見一沙彌諷誦佛經，章句錯謬，文字紛亂。阿難聞已，感慕增懷，徐詣其所，提撕指授。沙彌笑曰：「大德耄矣，所言謬矣！我師高明，春秋鼎盛，親承示誨，誠無所誤。」阿難默然，退而歎曰：「我年雖邁，為諸眾生，欲久住世，住持正法。然眾生垢重，難以誨語，久留無利，可速滅度。」於是去摩揭陀國，趣吠舍釐城，度殑伽河，泛舟中流。摩揭陀王聞阿難去，情深戀德，即嚴戎駕，疾驅追請，數百千眾營軍南岸。吠舍釐王聞阿難來，悲喜盈心，亦治軍旅，奔馳迎候，數百千眾屯集北岸。兩軍相對，旌旗翳日。阿難恐鬪其兵，更相殺害，從舟中起，上昇虛空，示現神變，即入寂滅，化火焚骸，骸又中折，一墮南岸，一墮北岸。於是二王各得一分，舉軍號慟，俱還本國，起窣堵波，而修供養。
translation: Traveling more than thirty li southeast from the Śvetapura (濕吠多補羅) Monastery, there is a stūpa on both the north and south banks of the Gaṅgā (殑伽) River; these are the places where the Venerable Ānanda divided his body between the two countries. Ānanda was the paternal cousin of the Tathāgata; he was learned and possessed of total retention, broad in his knowledge and strong in his memory. After the Buddha passed away, he succeeded Mahākāśyapa in upholding the True Dharma and guiding those who were advancing in their studies. While in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國), he was walking in a forest when he saw a novice monk reciting a Buddhist scripture with erroneous chapters and sentences, and confused wording. Upon hearing this, Ānanda felt a growing sense of sympathy and longing; he slowly approached the novice and offered to correct and instruct him. The novice laughed and said, "The Great Virtuous one is senile; what you say is wrong! My teacher is brilliant and in the prime of his life; having received his instructions personally, there is certainly no error." Ānanda remained silent, withdrew, and sighed, saying, "Although I am aged, I have wished to remain in the world for a long time for the sake of all sentient beings, to uphold the True Dharma. However, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy, and it is difficult to instruct them with words; remaining for a long time is of no benefit, so I may as well quickly enter parinirvāṇa." Thereupon, he left the country of Magadha and headed for the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城), crossing the Gaṅgā River and sailing in a boat midstream. When the King of Magadha heard that Ānanda was departing, his heart was filled with deep attachment to his virtue; he immediately prepared his military carriages and drove rapidly in pursuit to invite him back, with hundreds of thousands of people camping as an army on the southern bank. When the King of Vaiśālī heard that Ānanda was coming, his heart was filled with both grief and joy; he also mobilized his troops and raced to welcome him, with hundreds of thousands of people stationed as an army on the northern bank. The two armies faced each other, their banners and flags obscuring the sun. Ānanda, fearing that their troops would clash and kill one another, rose from the boat and ascended into the void. He manifested supernatural transformations and immediately entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa); he transformed into fire to consume his remains, and the remains then split in two, one part falling on the southern bank and one part falling on the northern bank. Thereupon, the two kings each obtained a portion; their entire armies wailed in grief, and they both returned to their respective countries to erect stūpas and perform offerings.
