菩提樹東有精舍，高百六七十尺，下基面廣二十餘步，壘以青甎，塗以石灰，層龕皆有金像，四壁鏤作奇製，或連珠形，或天仙像，上置金銅阿摩落迦果（亦謂寶瓶，又稱寶臺）。東面接為重閣，檐宇特起三層，榱柱棟梁，戶扉寮牖，金銀彫鏤以飾之，珠玉廁錯以填之，奧室邃宇，洞戶三重。外門左右各有龕室，左則觀自在菩薩像，右則慈氏菩薩像，白銀鑄成，高十餘尺。精舍故地，無憂王先建小精舍，後有婆羅門更廣建焉。初，有婆羅門，不信佛法，事大自在天，傳聞天神在雪山中，遂與其弟往求願焉。天曰：「凡諸願求，有福方果。非汝所祈，非我能遂。」婆羅門曰：「修何福可以遂心？」天曰：「欲植善種，求勝福田，菩提樹者，證佛果處也。宜時速反，往菩提樹，建大精舍，穿大水池，興諸供養，所願當遂。」婆羅門受天命，發大信心，相率而返，兄建精舍，弟鑿水池，於是廣修供養，勤求心願，後皆果遂，為王大臣，凡得祿賞，皆入檀捨。精舍既成，招募工人，欲圖如來初成佛像。曠以歲月，無人應召。久之，有婆羅門來告眾曰：「我善圖寫如來妙相。」眾曰：「今將造像，夫何所須？」曰：「香泥耳。宜置精舍之中，并一燈照，我入已，堅閉其戶，六月後乃可開門。」時諸僧眾皆如其命。尚餘四日，未滿六月，眾咸駭異，開以觀之。見精舍內佛像儼然，結加趺坐，右足居上，左手斂，右手垂，東面而坐，肅然如在。座高四尺二寸，廣丈二尺五寸，像高丈一尺五寸，兩膝相去八尺八寸，兩肩六尺二寸，相好具足，慈顏若真，唯右乳上圖瑩未周。既不見人，方驗神鑒，眾咸悲歎，慇懃請知。有一沙門，宿心淳質，乃感夢見往婆羅門而告曰：「我是慈氏菩薩，恐工人之思不測聖容，故我躬來圖寫佛像。垂右手者，昔如來之將證佛果，天魔來嬈，地神告至，其一先出，助佛降魔，如來告曰：『汝勿憂怖，吾以忍力，降彼必矣。』魔王曰：『誰為明證？』如來乃垂手指地，言：『此有證。』是時第二地神踊出作證，故今像手倣昔下垂。」眾知靈鑒，莫不悲感。於是乳上未周，填廁眾寶，珠瓔寶冠，奇珍交飾。設賞迦王伐菩提樹已，欲毀此像，既覩慈顏，心不安忍，迴駕將返，命宰臣曰：「宜除此佛像，置大自在天形。」宰臣受旨，懼而歎曰：「毀佛像則歷劫招殃，違王命乃喪身滅族，進退若此，何所宜行！」乃召信心以為役使，遂於像前橫壘甎壁，心慚冥闇，又置明燈，甎壁之前畫自在天。功成報命，王聞心懼，舉身生皰，肌膚攫裂，居未久之，便喪沒矣。宰臣馳返，毀除障壁，時經多日，燈猶不滅。像今尚在，神工不虧。既處奧室，燈炬相繼，欲覩慈顏，莫由審察，必於晨朝持大明鏡，引光內照，乃覩靈相。夫有見者，自增悲感。如來以印度吠舍佉月後半八日成等正覺，當此三月八日也。上座部則吠舍佉月後半十五日成等正覺，當此三月十五日也。是時如來年三十矣。或曰年三十五矣。菩提樹北有佛經行之處。如來成正覺已，不起于座，七日寂定。其起也，至菩提樹北，七日經行，東西往來，行十餘步，異華隨迹十有八文。後人於此壘甎為基，高餘三尺。聞諸先志曰：此聖迹基，表人命之脩短也，先發誠願，後乃度量，隨壽脩短，數有增減。經行基北，道右，盤石上，大精舍中，有佛像，舉目上望。昔者，如來於此七日觀菩提樹，目不暫捨。為報樹恩，故此瞻望。菩提樹西不遠，大精舍中，有鍮石佛像，飾以奇珍，東面而立。前有青石，奇文異采，是昔如來初成正覺，梵王起七寶堂，帝釋建七寶座，佛於其上七日思惟，放異光明，照菩提樹。去聖悠遠，寶變為石。菩提樹南不遠，有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。菩薩既濯尼連河，將趣菩提樹，竊自思念何以為座？尋自發明當須淨草。天帝釋化其身為刈草人，荷而逐路。菩薩謂曰：「所荷之草頗能惠耶？」化人聞命，恭以草奉，菩薩受已，執而前進。受草東北不遠，有窣堵波，是菩薩將證佛果，青雀、群鹿呈祥之處。印度休徵，斯為嘉應，故淨居天隨順世間，群從飛繞，効靈顯聖。菩提樹東，大路左右，各一窣堵波，是魔王嬈菩薩處也。菩薩將證佛果，魔王勸受輪王，策說不行，殷憂而返。魔王之女請往誘焉，菩薩威神，衰變冶容，扶羸策杖，相携而退。菩提樹西北，精舍中，有迦葉波佛像，既稱靈聖，時燭光明。聞諸先記曰：若人至誠，旋繞七周，在所生處，得宿命智。迦葉波佛精舍西北二甎室，各有地神之像。昔者如來將成正覺，一報魔至，一為佛證。後人念功，圖形旌德。菩提樹垣西不遠，有窣堵波，謂欝金香，高四十餘尺，漕炬吒國商主之所建也。昔漕炬吒國有大商主，宗事天神，祠求福利，輕蔑佛法，不信因果。其後將諸商侶，貿遷有無，泛舟南海，遭風失路，波濤飄浪，時經三歲，資糧罄竭，糊口不充。同舟之人，朝不謀夕，勠力同志，念所事天，心慮已勞，冥功不濟。俄見大山，崇崖峻嶺，兩日聯暉，重明照朗。時諸商侶更相慰曰：「我曹有福，過此大山，宜於中止，得安樂。」商主曰：「非山也，乃摩竭魚耳。崇崖峻嶺，鬚鬣也；兩日聯暉，眼光也。」言聲未靜，舟帆飄湊。於是商主告諸侶曰：「我聞觀自在菩薩於諸危厄能施安樂，宜各至誠，稱其名字。」遂即同聲，歸命稱念。崇山既隱，兩日亦沒。俄見沙門，威儀庠序，杖錫凌虛，而來拯溺，不踰時而至本國矣。因即信心貞固，求福不回，建窣堵波，式修供養，以欝金香泥而周塗上下。既發信心，率其同志，躬禮聖迹，觀菩提樹。未暇言歸，已淹晦朔。商侶同遊，更相謂曰：「山川悠間，鄉國遼遠，昔所建立窣堵波者，我曹在此，誰其灑掃？」言訖，旋繞至此，忽見窣堵波，駭其由致，即前瞻察，乃本國所建窣堵波也。故今印度因以欝金為名。菩提樹垣東南隅，尼拘律樹側，窣堵波傍有精舍，中作佛坐像。昔如來初證佛果，大梵天王於此勸請轉妙法輪。菩提樹垣內，四隅皆有大窣堵波。在昔如來受吉祥草已，趣菩提樹，先歷四隅，大地震動，至金剛座，方得安靜。樹垣之內，聖迹鱗次，羌難遍舉。菩提樹垣外，西南窣堵波，奉乳糜二牧女故宅。其側窣堵波，牧女於此煮糜。次此窣堵波，如來受糜處也。菩提樹垣南門外有大池，周七百餘步，清瀾澄鏡，龍魚潛宅，婆羅門兄弟承大自在天命之所鑿也。次南一池，在昔如來初成正覺，方欲浣濯，天帝釋為佛化成池。西有大石，佛浣衣已，方欲曝曬，天帝釋自大雪山持來也。其側窣堵波，如來於此納故衣。次南林中窣堵波，如來受貧老母施故衣處。
translation: To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is a vihāra (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings. At the top is placed a golden-copper āmalaka fruit (also called a treasure vase, or a treasure terrace). The eastern side is connected to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate are niche chambers; on the left is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and on the right is an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and over ten feet high. On the original site of the vihāra, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihāra, which was later expanded by a Brahmin. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are fulfilled only when one has merit. What you pray for is not something I can grant." The Brahmin asked, "What merit should I cultivate to fulfill my heart's desire?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi, build a great vihāra, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihāra (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their heart’s desires, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihāra was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihāra, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door firmly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihāra looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed with sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and an earth deity announced his arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, knowing of this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying, "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying, "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated. In such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was terrified; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hurried back and destroyed the wall that had served as a barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Since it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one who wishes to behold the compassionate countenance cannot examine it clearly; one must hold a large, bright mirror in the morning to reflect light inside, and only then can the sacred image be seen. Those who see it naturally feel an increase in sorrow and reverence.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footprints, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of the meditation foundation, on the right side of the path, upon a large rock, there is a great shrine (精舍) containing a Buddha image that is looking upward with its eyes raised. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) without once averting his eyes. He did this to repay the tree for its kindness, and thus he kept it in his view. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree, in a great shrine (精舍), there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing and facing east. In front of it is a blue stone with wonderful patterns and extraordinary colors; this is where, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the Brahma King (Brahmā) built a hall of seven treasures and Lord Indra (Śakra) constructed a throne of seven treasures, upon which the Buddha meditated for seven days, emitting a wondrous light that illuminated the Mahā-bodhi tree. As the time since the Sage’s passing is long, the treasures have turned into stone.  Not far to the south of the Mahā-bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When the Bodhisattva had bathed in the Nairañjanā River and was about to proceed to the Mahā-bodhi tree, he secretly pondered what he should use for a seat. He soon realized that he required clean grass. Lord Indra (天帝釋) transformed himself into a grass-cutter, carrying grass and following the path. The Bodhisattva said to him, "Could you bestow upon me some of the grass you are carrying?" The transformed being, hearing this request, respectfully offered the grass, which the Bodhisattva accepted, holding it as he proceeded forward.  Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa, which marks the place where bluebirds and herds of deer presented auspicious omens when the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In India, such signs are considered favorable omens; therefore, the gods of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) conformed to the ways of the world, and the flocks followed, flying and circling to manifest their spiritual power and reveal the holiness of the site. To the east of the Mahā-bodhi tree, on either side of the main road, there is a stūpa; these are the places where the King of Māras disturbed the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the King of Māras urged him to accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King; when his entreaties failed, he returned in deep sorrow. The daughters of the King of Māras requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s divine power, their beautiful appearances withered and changed; they withdrew supporting one another, frail and leaning on staves. To the northwest of the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), inside a shrine (精舍), there is an image of Kāśyapa Buddha; it is renowned for its spiritual efficacy and frequently emits a brilliant light. According to ancient records, if a person with utmost sincerity circumambulates it seven times, they will attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are reborn. To the northwest of the Kāśyapa Buddha shrine are two brick chambers, each containing an image of an earth deity. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one reported the arrival of Māra, and the other served as a witness for the Buddha. Later generations, mindful of their service, depicted their forms to honor their virtue. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree enclosure, there is a stūpa called the Saffron (郁金香) Stūpa, over forty feet high, which was built by a merchant lord of the country of Jāguḍa (漕炬吒國). Formerly, in the country of Jāguḍa, there was a great merchant lord who worshiped heavenly deities and offered sacrifices to seek blessings, while holding the Buddha’s teachings in contempt and disbelieving in cause and effect. Later, he led a group of merchants to trade goods, sailing on the southern sea, when they encountered a storm and lost their way. Drifting on the waves for three years, their provisions were exhausted and they could not even secure enough food to survive. The people on the ship, unable to plan for the next day, joined their efforts and shared their resolve, calling upon the deities they served; yet, though their minds were weary with anxiety, their secret prayers were not answered. Suddenly, they saw a great mountain with towering cliffs and steep ridges, where two suns shone together, casting a brilliant, double light. At that time, the merchants comforted one another, saying, "We are fortunate; having passed this great mountain, we should stop here and find peace and happiness." The merchant leader said, "It is not a mountain, but a makara-fish. The towering cliffs and steep ridges are its whiskers and mane, and the two suns shining together are the light of its eyes." Before his voice had faded, the ship drifted toward it. Thereupon, the merchant leader told his companions, "I have heard that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara can bestow peace and happiness in the midst of all dangers and difficulties; we should each, with utmost sincerity, call upon his name." They immediately joined their voices in unison, taking refuge and reciting his name. The towering mountain then vanished, and the two suns also disappeared. Suddenly, they saw a śramaṇa, dignified and composed, holding a staff and walking through the void, who came to rescue them from drowning; before long, they arrived at their own country.  Because of this, their faith became firm and steadfast, and they sought merit without wavering. They built a stūpa and performed offerings, coating it from top to bottom with saffron-scented mud. Having developed this faith, they led their companions to personally pay homage to the sacred sites and view the Mahā-bodhi tree. Before they had time to return home, a month had already passed. As the merchants traveled together, they said to one another, "The mountains and rivers are vast and our homeland is far away; since we are here, who is there to sweep and clean the stūpa we previously built?" Having said this, they circled around to this spot and suddenly saw the stūpa. Astonished at how this could be, they went forward to examine it and found it was the very stūpa built by their own country. Therefore, in India today, it is known by the name of Saffron. At the southeast corner of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹), beside a banyan tree (nyagrodha), there is a vihāra (精舍) next to a stūpa, containing a statue of the Buddha in a seated posture. In the past, when the Tathāgata first attained the fruit of Buddhahood, the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmā-devarāja) here entreated him to turn the wheel of the wonderful Dharma. Within the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, there are large stūpas at each of the four corners. In the past, after the Tathāgata had received the auspicious grass (kuśa), he proceeded toward the Mahā-bodhi; he first passed by the four corners, and the great earth shook, only becoming still when he reached the Vajrāsana (金剛座). Within the enclosure of the tree, sacred sites are arranged like the scales of a fish, and it is difficult to enumerate them all.  Outside the enclosure of the Mahā-bodhi, to the southwest, there is a stūpa marking the former residence of the two milkmaids who offered the milk gruel. Beside it is a stūpa where the milkmaids boiled the gruel. Next to this stūpa is the place where the Tathāgata received the gruel. Outside the south gate of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is a large pond, over seven hundred paces in circumference, with clear, mirror-like waves where dragons and fish dwell; it was excavated by two Brahmin brothers acting under the command of Maheśvara (大自在天). To the south of this is another pond; in the past, when the Tathāgata had first attained perfect enlightenment and wished to bathe, Śakra-devānām-indra (天帝釋) manifested this pond for the Buddha. To the west is a large stone; after the Buddha had washed his robes and wished to dry them, Śakra-devānām-indra brought it from the Great Snow Mountains (Himālaya). Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata put on an old garment. Further to the south, in the forest, is a stūpa marking the place where the Tathāgata accepted the offering of an old garment from a poor elderly woman.

t2087_text: 帝釋化池東，林中有目支隣陀龍王池，其水清黑，其味甘美。西岸有小精舍，中作佛像。昔如來初成正覺，於此宴坐，七日入定。時此龍王警衛如來，即以其身繞佛七匝，化出多頭，俯垂為蓋，故池東岸有其室焉。目支隣陀龍池東，林中精舍有佛羸瘦之像。其側有經行之所，長七十餘步，南北各有卑鉢羅樹。故今土俗，諸有嬰疾，香油塗像，多蒙除差。是菩薩修苦行處。如來為伏外道，又受魔請，於是苦行六年，日食一麻一麥，形容憔悴，膚體羸瘠，經行往來，攀樹後起。菩薩苦行卑鉢羅樹側有窣堵波，是阿若憍陳如等五人住處。初，太子之捨家也，彷徨山澤，棲息林泉，時淨飯王乃命五人隨瞻侍焉。太子既修苦行，憍陳如等亦即勤求。
translation: To the east of the pool created by Śakra (帝釋), in a forest, is the pool of the Dragon King Mucilinda (目支隣陀); its water is clear and dark, and its taste is sweet and delicious. On the west bank is a small shrine (精舍) containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, when the Tathāgata had first attained supreme enlightenment, he sat here in meditation for seven days. At that time, this dragon king guarded the Tathāgata by coiling his body around the Buddha seven times and manifesting many heads that bowed down to form a canopy; therefore, his dwelling is located on the east bank of the pool.  To the east of the Mucilinda Dragon Pool, in a forest shrine, there is an image of the Buddha in an emaciated state. Beside it is a place for walking meditation, more than seventy paces long, with a pippala (卑鉢羅) tree at both the north and south ends. Therefore, among the local people today, those who are afflicted with illness often apply scented oil to the image and frequently receive relief and recovery.  This is the place where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities. In order to subdue the non-Buddhists and also because he accepted the request of Māra, the Tathāgata practiced austerities for six years, eating one hemp seed and one grain of wheat per day. His appearance became haggard and his body became emaciated; when walking back and forth, he would grasp the trees to rise. Beside the pippala tree where the Bodhisattva practiced austerities, there is a stūpa; this is the place where Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya (阿若憍陳如) and the other four men resided. Initially, when the prince renounced his home, wandering through mountains and marshes and resting in forests and by springs, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) ordered these five men to follow and attend to him. Once the prince practiced austerities, Kauṇḍinya and the others also diligently sought the way.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 憍陳如等住處東南有窣堵波，菩薩入尼連禪那河沐浴之處。河側不遠，菩薩於此受食乳糜。其側窣堵波，二長者獻麨蜜處。佛在樹下結加趺坐，寂然宴默，受解脫樂，過七日後，方從定起。時二商主行次林外，而彼林神告商主曰：「釋種太子今在此中，初證佛果，心凝寂定，四十九日未有所食，隨有奉上，獲大善利。」時二商主各持行資麨蜜奉上，世尊納受。長者獻麨側有窣堵波，四天奉鉢處。商主既獻麨蜜，世尊思以何器受之。時四天從四方來，各持金鉢，而以奉上。世尊默然，而不納受，以為出家不宜此器。四天王捨金鉢，奉銀鉢，乃至頗胝、琉璃、馬腦、車渠、真珠等鉢，世尊如是皆不為受。四天王各還宮，奉持石鉢，紺青映徹，重以進獻。世尊斷彼此故，而總受之，次第重疊，按為一鉢，故其外則有四隆焉。四天王獻鉢側不遠，有窣堵波，如來為母說法處也。如來既成正覺，稱天人師，其母摩耶自天宮降於此處，世尊隨機示教利喜。其側涸池岸有窣堵波，在昔如來見諸神變化有緣處。現神變側有窣堵波，如來度優樓頻螺迦葉波三兄弟及千門人處。如來方垂善道，隨應降伏，時優樓頻螺迦葉波五百門人請受佛教，迦葉波曰：「吾亦與爾俱返迷途。」於是相從來至佛所。如來告曰：「棄鹿皮衣，捨祭火具。」時諸梵志恭承聖教，以其服用投尼連河。捺地迦葉波見諸祭器隨流漂泛，與其門人候兄動靜，既見改轍，亦隨染衣。伽耶迦葉波二百門人。聞其兄之捨法也，亦至佛所，願修梵行。度迦葉波兄弟西北窣堵波，是如來伏迦葉波所事火龍處。如來將化其人，克伏所宗，乃止梵志火龍之室。夜分已後，龍吐煙焰，佛既入定，亦起火光，其室洞然，猛焰炎熾。諸梵志師恐火害佛，莫不奔赴，悲號愍惜。優樓頻螺迦葉波謂其徒曰：「以今觀之，未必火也，當是沙門伏火龍耳。」如來乃以火龍盛置鉢中，清旦持示外道門人。其側窣堵波，五百獨覺同入涅槃處也。目支隣陀龍池南窣堵波，迦葉波救如來溺水處也。迦葉兄弟時推神通，遠近仰德，黎庶歸心。世尊方導迷徒，大權攝化，興布密雲，降澍暴雨，周佛所居，令獨無水。迦葉是時見此雲雨，謂門人曰：「沙門住處將不漂溺？」泛舟來救，乃見世尊履水如地，蹈河中流，水分沙現。迦葉見已，心伏而退。
translation: Southeast of the place where Kauṇḍinya and his companions resided, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Bodhisattva entered the Nairañjanā River to bathe. Not far from the riverbank is the place where the Bodhisattva received the milk-rice. Beside that is a stūpa marking the place where the two elders offered parched grain and honey. The Buddha sat under a tree in the cross-legged position, silent and still, experiencing the joy of liberation; after seven days had passed, he finally arose from meditation. At that time, two merchant leaders were passing by the edge of the forest, and the deity of that forest told the merchant leaders, "The Prince of the Śākya clan is now within this wood; he has just attained the fruit of Buddhahood and his mind is concentrated in silent meditation. He has not eaten for forty-nine days; if you offer him whatever you have, you will obtain great and wholesome benefit." The two merchant leaders then each took their travel provisions of parched grain and honey to offer to him, and the World-Honored One accepted them. Beside the place where the elders offered the parched grain, there is a stūpa marking the spot where the Four Heavenly Kings offered alms bowls. After the merchant leaders had offered the parched grain and honey, the World-Honored One considered what vessel he should use to receive them. At that time, the four heavenly kings came from the four directions, each holding a golden bowl to offer to him. The World-Honored One remained silent and did not accept them, thinking that such vessels were not appropriate for one who has left the household life. The four heavenly kings set aside the golden bowls and offered silver ones, and even bowls of crystal, lapis lazuli, agate, musaragalva, and pearl, but the World-Honored One would not accept any of them. The four heavenly kings each returned to their palaces and brought back stone bowls, dark blue and translucent, which they presented again. To avoid favoring one over the others, the World-Honored One accepted them all, stacked them in sequence, and pressed them into a single bowl; therefore, on the outside, there are four ridges. Not far from the place where the four heavenly kings offered the bowls, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for his mother. After the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment and was acclaimed as the teacher of gods and men, his mother, Māyā, descended from the heavenly palace to this place, and the World-Honored One, according to her capacity, manifested teachings to bring her benefit and joy. Beside it, on the bank of a dried-up pond, there is a stūpa; this is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata displayed miracles to convert those with whom he had affinity. Beside the place where he manifested divine transformations, there is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata converted the three brothers Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) and the others, together with their one thousand disciples. As the Tathāgata was setting forth the good path and subduing them according to their dispositions, the five hundred disciples of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa requested to receive the Buddha’s teaching. Kāśyapa said, "I shall also return from the path of delusion along with you." Thereupon, they followed one another and came to the place of the Buddha. The Tathāgata told them, "Discard your deer-skin garments and abandon your fire-worship implements." At that time, the Brahmins respectfully accepted the holy teaching and cast their robes and implements into the Nairañjanā River. Nadī-Kāśyapa (捺地迦葉波) saw the sacrificial vessels floating down the current and, together with his disciples, waited to see what his elder brother would do; having seen him change his course, he also followed suit and dyed his robes. Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波) with his two hundred disciples, hearing that his elder brother had abandoned his former practice, also came to the place of the Buddha and wished to practice the holy life. To the northwest of the place where the Kāśyapa brothers were converted is a stūpa; this is the place where the Tathāgata subdued the fire dragon that the Kāśyapas worshipped. When the Tathāgata was about to convert those people and overcome what they revered, he stayed in the chamber of the Brahmins' fire dragon. After midnight, the dragon exhaled smoke and flames. The Buddha, having entered into samādhi, also emitted a fiery light, so that the chamber was brightly illuminated with fierce and blazing flames. The Brahmin masters, fearing the fire would harm the Buddha, all rushed toward it, crying out in sorrow and pity. Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa (優樓頻螺迦葉波) said to his disciples, "Looking at it now, this may not be a fire; it must be that the Śramaṇa has subdued the fire dragon." The Tathāgata then placed the fire dragon into his alms bowl and, at dawn, held it up to show the disciples of the non-Buddhists. The stūpa beside this is the place where five hundred pratyekabuddhas (獨覺) entered nirvāṇa together. The stūpa to the south of the Mucilinda (目支隣陀) Dragon Pool is the place where Kāśyapa rescued the Tathāgata from drowning. At that time, the Kāśyapa brothers were esteemed for their supernatural powers, and people from far and near admired their virtue, with the masses turning their hearts toward them. The World-honored One, intending to guide the deluded disciples, employed great skillful means to transform them; he raised dense clouds and caused a violent rain to fall, which surrounded the place where the Buddha resided, leaving it alone without water. Seeing this cloud and rain, Kāśyapa said to his disciples, "Will the Śramaṇa’s dwelling not be flooded?" He set out in a boat to rescue him, only to see the World-honored One walking on the water as if it were dry land; as he stepped into the middle of the river, the waters parted and the sand appeared. Having seen this, Kāśyapa’s heart was subdued and he withdrew.

t2087_text: 菩提樹垣東門外二三里，有盲龍室。此龍者，殃累宿積，報受生盲。如來自前正覺山欲趣菩提樹，途次室側，龍眼忽明，乃見菩薩將趣佛樹，謂菩薩曰：「仁今不久當成正覺。我眼盲冥，于茲已久，有佛興世，我眼輒明。賢劫之中，過去三佛出興世時，已得明視。仁今至此，我眼忽開，以故知之，當成佛矣。」菩提樹垣東門側有窣堵波，魔王怖菩薩之處。初，魔王知菩薩將成正覺也，誘亂不遂，憂惶無賴，集諸神眾，齊整魔軍，治兵振旅，將脅菩薩。於是風雨飄注，雷電晦冥，縱火飛煙，揚沙激石，備矛楯之具，極弦矢之用。菩薩於是入大慈定，凡厥兵杖變為蓮華。魔軍怖駭，奔馳退散。其側不遠有二窣堵波，帝釋、梵王之所建也。
translation: Two or three li outside the east gate of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree is the cave of the blind dragon. This dragon, due to the accumulation of past misdeeds, was born blind as retribution. When the Tathāgata was traveling from Mount Prāgbodhi (正覺山) toward the Mahā-bodhi tree, he passed by the side of this cave, and the dragon’s eyes suddenly became clear. Seeing the Bodhisattva approaching the tree of the Buddha, he said to the Bodhisattva, "Kind sir, you shall soon attain Perfect Enlightenment. My eyes have been blind and dark for a long time; whenever a Buddha arises in the world, my eyes immediately become clear. During this Bhadrakalpa (賢劫), when the three past Buddhas arose in the world, I already gained clear vision. Now that you have come here, my eyes have suddenly opened; therefore I know that you shall surely become a Buddha."  Beside the east gate of the wall surrounding the Mahā-bodhi tree is a stūpa, the place where the King of Māras (魔王) frightened the Bodhisattva. At first, when the King of Māras knew that the Bodhisattva was about to attain Perfect Enlightenment, he tried to seduce and disturb him but failed. Worried and helpless, he gathered his divine hosts, marshaled his demonic army, and prepared his troops and equipment to threaten the Bodhisattva. Thereupon, wind and rain poured down, thunder and lightning darkened the sky, fires were set and smoke flew, and sand was raised and stones were hurled. They prepared spears and shields and made full use of bows and arrows. The Bodhisattva then entered the samādhi of great compassion, and all their weapons turned into lotus flowers. The demonic army was terrified and fled in a rout. Not far from there are two stūpas, which were built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王).

t2087_text: 菩提樹北門外摩訶菩提僧伽藍，其先僧伽羅國王之所建也。庭宇六院，觀閣三層，周堵垣牆高三四丈，極工人之妙，窮丹青之飾。至於佛像，鑄以金銀，凡厥莊嚴，廁以珍寶。諸窣堵波高廣妙飾，中有如來舍利，其骨舍利大如手指節。光潤鮮白皎徹中外。其肉舍利如大真珠，色帶紅縹。每歲至如來大神變月滿之日，出示眾（即印度十二月三十日，當此正月十五日也）。此時也，或放光，或雨花。僧徒減千人，習學大乘、上座部法，律儀清肅，戒行貞明。昔者，南海僧伽羅國，其王淳信佛法，發自天然。有族弟出家，想佛聖迹，遠遊印度，寓諸伽藍，咸輕邊鄙。於是返迹本國，王躬遠迎，沙門悲耿，似若不能言。王曰：「將何所負，若此殷憂？」沙門曰：「憑恃國威，遊方問道，羈旅異域，載罹寒暑，動遭凌辱，語見譏誚。負斯憂恥，詎得歡心？」曰：「若是者何謂也？」曰：「誠願大王福田為意，於諸印度建立伽藍，既旌聖迹，又擅高名，福資先王，恩及後嗣。」曰：「斯事甚美，聞之何晚？」於是以國中寶獻印度王。王既納貢，義存懷遠，謂使臣曰：「我今將何持報來命？」使臣曰：「僧伽羅王稽首印度大吉祥王！威德遠振，惠澤遐被，下土沙門，欽風慕化，敢遊上國，展敬聖迹，寓諸伽藍，莫之見館，艱辛已極，蒙恥而歸。竊圖遠謀，貽範來葉，於諸印度建此伽藍，使客遊乞士，息肩有所，兩國交歡，行人無替。」王曰：「如來潛化，遺風斯在，聖迹之所，任取一焉。」使者奉辭報命，群臣拜賀，遂乃集諸沙門，評議建立。沙門曰：「菩提樹者，去來諸佛咸此證聖，考之異議，無出此謀。」於是捨國珍寶，建此伽藍，以其國僧而修供養，乃刻銅為記曰：「夫周給無私，諸佛至教；慧濟有緣，先聖明訓。今我小子，丕承王業，式建伽藍，用旌聖迹，福資祖考，惠被黎元。唯我國僧而得自在，及有國人亦同僧例。傳之後嗣，永永無窮。」故此伽藍多執師子國僧也。菩提樹南十餘里，聖迹相隣，難以備舉。每歲比丘解安居，四方法俗百千萬眾，七日七夜，持香花，鼓音樂，遍遊林中，禮拜供養。印度僧徒依佛聖教，皆以室羅伐拏月前半一日入兩安居，當此五月十六日；以頞濕縛庾闍月後半十五日解兩安居，當此八月十五日。印度月名，依星而建，古今不易，諸部無差。良以方言未融，傳譯有謬，分時計月，致斯乖異，故以四月十六日入安居，七月十五日解安居也。
translation: Outside the north gate of the Bodhi tree is the Mahābodhi Monastery (摩訶菩提僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國). It has six courtyards and three-storied pavilions, surrounded by walls thirty to forty feet high; the workmanship is of the utmost ingenuity, and the painted decorations are exquisite. As for the Buddha images, they are cast in gold and silver, and all their adornments are inlaid with precious gems. The various stupas are lofty, spacious, and exquisitely decorated, containing the relics of the Tathāgata; the bone relics are as large as a finger joint, lustrous, pure white, and translucent inside and out. The flesh relics are like large pearls, with a color tinged with reddish-blue. Every year, on the full moon day of the month of the Tathāgata’s great spiritual manifestations, they are displayed to the public (This is the thirtieth day of the twelfth month in India, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the first month here). At this time, they sometimes emit light or rain down flowers. The community of monks numbers nearly one thousand; they study the teachings of the Mahāyāna and the Sthavira school, their monastic discipline is pure and strict, and their conduct is upright and bright. Formerly, in the southern sea, there was the country of Siṃhala, whose king was purely devoted to the Buddha-dharma, a faith arising from his own nature. He had a younger cousin who became a monk and, longing to see the sacred sites of the Buddha, traveled far to India. He stayed in various monasteries, but all of them treated him with contempt as a border-dweller. He then returned to his own country, and the king personally went out to welcome him. The śramaṇa was sorrowful and distressed, as if he were unable to speak. The king said, "What burden do you carry that causes such deep melancholy?" The śramaṇa said, "Relying on the prestige of the state, I traveled to distant lands to inquire after the Way. Living as a stranger in foreign territories, I endured the cold and the heat, and at every turn I encountered humiliation and was mocked for my speech. Bearing such sorrow and shame, how could I be happy?" The king asked, "What do you mean by this?" He replied, "I sincerely wish that Your Majesty would take the field of merit to heart and establish a monastery (saṃghārāma) in India. This would both honor the holy sites and bring you great fame, while the resulting merit would support the late king and its blessings would reach your descendants." The king said, "This is a wonderful idea; why did I not hear of it sooner?" He then sent the treasures of his country as an offering to the King of India.  Having accepted the tribute and wishing to show kindness to those from afar, the King of India said to the envoy, "What should I now give as a return gift for your mission?" The envoy said, "The King of Siṃhala (僧伽羅) bows his head to the Great Auspicious King of India! Your majesty’s prestige and virtue extend far, and your benevolent grace reaches to distant places. The śramaṇas of our lowly land, admiring your influence and transformation, dared to travel to your superior kingdom to pay their respects at the holy sites. Yet, when they stayed in the monasteries, they were not provided with lodging; they suffered extreme hardship and returned home having endured shame. I humbly propose a far-reaching plan to set an example for future generations: to build this monastery in India so that traveling mendicants may have a place to rest, the two countries may enjoy friendly relations, and travelers may pass between them without end." The king said, "The Tathāgata’s subtle influence has passed, but his legacy remains; you may choose any one of the holy sites." The envoy accepted the command and returned to report the mission. The ministers offered their congratulations, and the king then gathered the śramaṇas to deliberate on the construction. The śramaṇas said, "The Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where all Buddhas of the past and future attain holiness; having examined the various opinions, there is no better plan than this." Thereupon, the king gave up the treasures of his country and built this monastery, assigning monks from his own country to perform the offerings, and he engraved a copper plate as a record, which stated: "To provide for all without partiality is the supreme teaching of the Buddhas; to aid those with affinity through wisdom is the clear instruction of the ancient sages. Now I, this humble person, having inherited the great royal undertaking, have built this monastery to commemorate the holy site, so that the resulting merit may benefit my ancestors and its grace may extend to the common people. Only monks from my own country shall have authority here, and any of my countrymen shall be treated the same as the monks. May this be passed down to descendants, forever and ever without end." For this reason, this monastery is mostly occupied by monks from the country of Siṃhala (師子國).  More than ten li south of the Mahā-bodhi, holy sites are adjacent to one another, and it is difficult to list them all. Every year, when the bhikṣus conclude the rains retreat (vārṣika), clergy and laity from the four directions, numbering hundreds of thousands,, for seven days and seven nights, carry incense and flowers, play music, and travel throughout the forest to pay homage and make offerings. According to the holy teachings of the Buddha, the monks of India all enter the two-part rains retreat on the first day of the first half of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which corresponds to the sixteenth day of the fifth month here; they conclude the two-part rains retreat on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Aśvayuja, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the eighth month here. The names of the Indian months are based on the stars and have remained unchanged from ancient times to the present; among all the schools, there is no discrepancy. It is because the local dialects were not fully reconciled and there were errors in translation regarding the division of time and the calculation of months that these discrepancies have arisen; therefore, the retreat is entered on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and concluded on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 菩提樹東渡尼連禪那河，大林中有窣堵波。其北有池，香象侍母處也。如來在昔修菩薩行，為香象子，居北山中，遊此池側。其母盲也，採藕根，汲清水，恭行孝養，與時推移。屬有一人，遊林迷路，彷徨往來，悲號慟哭。象子聞而愍焉，導之以示歸路。是人既還，遂白王曰：「我知香象遊舍林藪，此奇貨也，可往捕之。」王納其言，興兵往狩，是人前導，指象示王，即時兩臂墮落，若有斬截者。其王雖驚此異，仍縛象子以歸。象子既已維縶多時，而不食水草，典廐者以聞，王遂親問之。象子曰：「我母盲冥，累日飢餓，今見幽厄，詎能甘食？」王愍其情也，故遂放之。其側窣堵波，前建石柱，是昔迦葉波佛於此宴坐。其側有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: East of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, crossing the Nairañjanā River, there is a stūpa in a great forest. To its north is a pond, which is the place where a fragrant elephant (gandhahastin) attended to his mother. In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a young fragrant elephant living in the northern mountains, who would roam by the side of this pond. His mother was blind, and he would gather lotus roots and draw clear water, respectfully performing his filial duties and adapting to the changing seasons. It happened that a man, wandering in the forest and losing his way, paced back and forth, wailing and crying in distress. The young elephant heard him and, feeling compassion, guided him to show him the way home. Once the man had returned, he reported to the king, saying, "I know of a fragrant elephant wandering in the forest thickets; this is a rare treasure, and you may go to capture it." The king accepted his words and raised an army to go hunting. The man acted as a guide, but the moment he pointed out the elephant to the king, both his arms fell off as if they had been severed. Although the king was startled by this strange event, he still bound the young elephant and brought him back. After the young elephant had been tied up for a long time, he would not eat grass or drink water. The stable keeper reported this to the king, who then went in person to question him. The young elephant said, "My mother is blind and has been starving for days; now that I am suffering in captivity, how could I find food sweet?" The king, feeling compassion for his situation, released him. Beside this is a stūpa, with a stone pillar erected in front, which is the place where the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) once sat in meditation. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 四佛坐東渡莫訶河，至大林中，有石柱，是外道入定發惡願處。昔有外道欝頭藍子者，志逸煙霞，身遺草澤，於此法林栖神匿迹。既具五神通，得第一有定。摩揭陀王特深宗敬，每至中時，請就宮食。欝頭藍子凌虛履空，往來無替。摩揭陀王候時瞻望，亦既至已，捧接置座。王將出遊，欲委留事，簡擢中宮，無堪承命。有少息女，淑慎令儀，既親且賢，無出其右，摩揭陀王召而命曰：「吾方遠遊，將有所委，爾宜悉心，慎終其事。彼欝頭藍仙，宿所宗敬，時至來飯，如我所奉。」勅誡既已，便即巡覽。少女承旨，瞻候如儀，大仙至已，捧而置座。欝頭藍子既觸女人，起欲界染，退失神通，飯訖言歸，不得虛遊。中心愧恥，詭謂女曰：「吾比修道業，入定怡神，凌虛往來，略無暇景，國人願覩，聞之久矣。然先達垂訓，利物為務，豈守獨善，忘其兼濟？今欲從門而出，履地而往，使夫覩見之徒，咸蒙福利。」王女聞已，宣告遠近。是時人以馳競，灑掃衢路，百千萬眾，佇望來儀。欝頭藍子步自王宮，至彼法林，宴坐入定，心馳外境，棲林則烏鳥嚶囀，臨池乃魚鼈諠聲，情散心亂，失神廢定。乃生忿恚，即發惡願：「願我當來為暴惡獸，狸身鳥翼，搏食生類，身廣三千里，兩翅各廣千五百里，投林噉諸羽族，入流食彼水生。」發願既已，忿心漸息，勤求頃之，復得本定。不久命終，生第一有天，壽八萬劫。如來記之，天壽畢已，當果昔願，得此弊身。從是流轉惡道，未期出離。
translation: To the east of where the four Buddhas sat, one crosses the Mahā (莫訶河) River and arrives in a great forest, where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist practitioner entered into meditation and made an evil vow. In the past, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子), whose aspirations transcended the mists and clouds, and whose body abandoned the marshes and thickets; he dwelt in this forest of the Dharma, hiding his spirit and concealing his traces. Having attained the five supernatural powers, he achieved the meditation of the peak of existence (bhavāgra). The King of Magadha (摩揭陀王) held him in particularly deep respect and, every day at noon, invited him to the palace for a meal. Udraka Rāmaputra would soar through the void and walk upon the air, coming and going without fail. The King of Magadha would watch and wait for the appointed time; once he arrived, the king would personally receive him and escort him to his seat.  When the king was about to depart on a tour and wished to entrust his affairs to someone, he examined those in the inner palace, but found no one capable of undertaking the command. He had a young daughter of virtuous and prudent character; she was both close to him and wise, with none surpassing her, so the King of Magadha summoned her and commanded: "I am about to travel far and have something to entrust to you; you should be diligent and see this matter through to the end with care. That immortal Udraka Rāmaputra is one whom I have long held in respect; when the time comes for him to arrive for his meal, treat him just as I have done."  Having given these instructions, the king departed on his tour. The young lady accepted the command and waited upon him according to the rites; when the great immortal arrived, she supported him and assisted him to his seat. Once Udraka Rāmaputra had touched the woman, desire for the realm of sense-objects arose, and he regressed, losing his supernatural powers. When he had finished his meal and spoke of returning, he was unable to soar through the void. Feeling ashamed and humiliated in his heart, he deceitfully said to the woman: "I have recently been cultivating the path, entering into meditation to soothe my spirit, and have been soaring through the void to come and go, having almost no leisure time. I have long heard that the people of the country wish to see this. However, the sages of old have left us instructions that benefiting others is our primary duty; how could I remain content with my own virtue and forget the need to assist others? I now wish to depart through the gate and travel by treading upon the ground, so that all those who see me may receive blessings and benefit." Having heard this, the king’s daughter made the announcement far and near. At that time, people rushed to compete, sweeping and cleaning the roads, and hundreds of thousands of people stood waiting to see his arrival. Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) walked from the royal palace to that religious forest and sat in meditation, but his mind wandered to external environments; when he stayed in the forest, the birds chirped, and when he approached the pond, the fish and turtles made noise, so that his feelings were distracted and his mind disturbed, causing him to lose his concentration and abandon his meditation. He then gave rise to anger and immediately made an evil vow: "May I in the future become a fierce and wicked beast with the body of a wildcat and the wings of a bird to seize and eat living creatures; let my body be three thousand li wide, with two wings each fifteen hundred li wide, so that I may enter the forests to devour the feathered tribes and enter the currents to eat the aquatic beings." Having made this vow, his anger gradually subsided, and after practicing diligently for a while, he regained his original concentration. Not long after, he passed away and was born in the Heaven of the First Existence (第一有天), with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas. The Tathāgata predicted that once his heavenly lifespan was exhausted, he would fulfill his former vow and obtain this wretched body. From that point on, he would wander through the evil paths, with no time set for his liberation.

t2087_text: 莫訶河東入大林野，行百餘里，至屈屈（居勿反）吒播陀山（唐言雞足），亦謂窶盧播陀山（唐言尊足）。高巒陗，無極深，壑洞無涯，山麓谿㵎，喬林羅谷，岡岑嶺嶂，繁草被巖，峻起三峯，傍挺絕崿，氣將天接，形與雲同。其後尊者大迦葉波居中寂滅，不敢指言，故云尊足。摩訶迦葉波者，聲聞弟子也，得六神通，具八解脫。如來化緣斯畢，垂將涅槃，告迦葉波曰：「我於曠劫勤修苦行，為諸眾生求無上法，昔所願期，今已果滿。我今將欲入大涅槃，以諸法藏囑累於汝，住持宣布，勿有失墜。姨母所獻金縷袈裟，慈氏成佛，留以傳付。我遺法中諸修行者，若比丘、比丘尼、鄔波索迦、（唐言近事男。舊曰伊蒱塞，又曰優波塞，又曰優婆塞，皆訛也）、鄔波斯迦（唐言近事女。舊曰優婆斯，又曰優婆夷，皆訛也），皆先濟渡，令離流轉。」迦葉承旨，住持正法。結集既已，至第二十年，厭世無常，將入寂滅。乃往雞足山，山陰而上，屈盤取路，至西南岡。山峯險阻，崖徑槃薄，乃以錫扣，剖之如割。山徑既開，逐路而進，槃紆曲折，迴互斜通，至于山頂，東北面出，既入三峯之中，捧佛袈裟而立，以願力故，三峯斂覆，故今此山三脊隆起。當來慈氏世尊之興世也，三會說法之後，餘有無量憍慢眾生，將登此山，至迦葉所。慈氏彈指，山峯自開，彼諸眾生既見迦葉，更增憍慢。時大迦葉授衣致辭，禮敬已畢，身昇虛空，示諸神變，化火焚身，遂入寂滅。時眾瞻仰，憍慢心除，因而感悟，皆證聖果。故今山上建窣堵波，靜夜遠望，或見明炬，及有登山，遂無所覩。
translation: Going east from the Mahā River, one enters a great forest wilderness and, after traveling over a hundred li, reaches Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (屈屈吒播陀山) (屈 pronounced 居勿反) (translated into Chinese as Jizu, "Cock's Foot"), also called Gurupāda Mountain (translated into Chinese as Zunzu, "Venerable Foot"). The high peaks are steep and the ravines infinitely deep; the caverns are boundless, and at the foot of the mountain by the mountain streams, tall trees fill the valleys, while ridges and cliffs are covered with lush grass. Three peaks rise sharply with sheer precipices standing at their sides, their atmosphere joining with the heavens and their forms merging with the clouds. Because the Venerable Mahākāśyapa later entered nirvana in its midst, people did not dare to refer to him directly by name, and thus it is called "Venerable Foot."  Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波) is a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle who attained the six supernatural powers and possesses the eight liberations. When the Tathāgata had finished his work of transformation and was about to enter nirvana, he told Kāśyapa: "Throughout vast eons I have diligently practiced austerities, seeking the supreme Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. The vows I made in the past have now been fulfilled. I am now about to enter the great nirvana, and I entrust the entire treasury of the Dharma to you. Maintain and proclaim it; do not let it be lost or fall into ruin. The golden-threaded robe offered by my aunt is to be kept and passed on to Maitreya when he attains buddhahood. Among the practitioners within my bequeathed Dharma—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣunīs, upāsakas (鄔波索迦) (in the Tang language, 'laymen who serve'; formerly called yipusai 伊蒱塞, also youposai 優波塞, also youposai 優婆塞, all of which are erroneous), or upāsikās (鄔波斯迦) (in the Tang language, 'laywomen who serve'; formerly called youposi 優婆斯, also youpoyi 優婆夷, all of which are erroneous)—all of them are to be liberated first, causing them to depart from the cycle of transmigration." Kāśyapa accepted the command to uphold the True Dharma. Once the compilation was finished, in the twentieth year, he grew weary of the world and its impermanence and was about to enter final extinction. He then went to Mount Kukkutapāda (雞足山), ascended from the northern side of the mountain, and took a winding path to the southwest ridge. The mountain peaks were steep and obstructed, and the cliff paths were rugged; he struck them with his staff, and they split open as if cut. Once the mountain path was opened, he proceeded along the way, winding and turning through crisscrossing passages until he reached the summit and emerged on the northeast side. Having entered the midst of the three peaks, he stood holding the Buddha’s robe, and by the power of his vow, the three peaks closed over him, which is why the mountain now has three protruding ridges. When the future Maitreya, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and completes his three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, there will remain countless arrogant sentient beings who shall ascend this mountain and come to the place of Kāśyapa. When Maitreya snaps his fingers, the mountain peaks will open of their own accord; yet when those sentient beings see Kāśyapa, their arrogance will increase even further. At that time, the Great Kāśyapa will present the robe and deliver a discourse; once they have finished paying their respects, he will ascend into the void, manifest various spiritual transformations, transform into fire to consume his body, and thus enter final extinction. At that time, the assembly will gaze up in reverence, their arrogant minds will be dispelled, and through this realization, they will all attain the holy fruits. Therefore, a stūpa has been built on the mountain; on quiet nights, one may see a bright torch from afar, but upon ascending the mountain, nothing can be seen.

t2087_text: 鷄足山東北行百餘里，至佛陀伐那山。峯崖崇峻，巘崿隱嶙，巖間石室，佛嘗降止。傍有盤石，帝釋、梵王摩牛頭栴檀塗飾如來，今其石上餘香郁烈。五百羅漢潛靈於此，諸有感遇，或得覩見，時作沙彌之形，入里乞食，隱顯靈奇之迹，羌難以述。
translation: Traveling more than one hundred li northeast from Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (鷄足山), one reaches the mountain of Buddhavana (佛陀伐那山). Its peaks and cliffs are lofty and steep, with jagged and towering ridges; among the rocks is a stone chamber where the Buddha once descended and stayed. Beside it is a flat rock where Śakra (帝釋) and the Brahmā King (梵王) ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Tathāgata; even now, a strong fragrance remains upon the stone. Five hundred arhats conceal their spirits here, and those who have a spiritual resonance may sometimes see them; they occasionally take the form of śrāmaṇeras to enter villages and beg for food, and their miraculous traces, appearing and disappearing, are truly difficult to describe.

t2087_text: 佛陀伐那山空谷中東行三十餘里，至洩（移結反）瑟知林（唐言杖林）。林竹修篠，被山滿谷。其先有婆羅門，聞釋迦佛身長丈六，常懷疑惑，未之信也，乃以丈六竹杖，欲量佛身。恒於杖端出過丈六，如是增高，莫能窮實，遂投杖而去，因植根焉。中有大窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔，於此七日為諸天、人現大神通，說深妙法。杖林中近有鄔波索迦闍耶犀那者（唐言勝軍），西印度剎帝利種也，志尚夷簡，情悅山林，迹居幻境，心遊真際，內外典籍，窮究幽微，辭論清高，儀範閑雅。諸沙門、婆羅門、外道、異學、國王、大臣、長者、豪右，相趨通謁，伏膺請益。受業門人，十室而六。年漸七十，耽讀不倦，餘藝捐廢，唯習佛經，策勵身心，不舍晝夜。印度之法，香末為泥，作小窣堵波，高五六寸，書寫經文，以置其中，謂之法舍利也；數漸盈積，建大窣堵波，總聚於內，常修供養。故勝軍之為業也，口則宣說妙法，導誘學人，手乃作窣堵波，式崇勝福，夜又經行禮誦，宴坐思惟，寢食不遑，晝夜無怠。年百歲矣，志業不衰。三十年間，凡作七拘胝（唐言億）法舍利窣堵波。每滿一拘胝，建大窣堵波，而總置中，盛修供養，請諸僧眾，法會稱慶，其時神光燭曜，靈異昭彰，自茲厥後，時放光明。
translation: Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of Buddhavana Mountain (Skt. *buddha-vana*), one reaches Yaṣṭivana (洩瑟知林) (洩 is pronounced y[i] + [j]ie) (in the language of Tang, this means "Staff Forest"). The forest’s bamboo is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall; he constantly harbored doubts and, unable to believe it, took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. The staff always extended beyond the sixteen-foot mark at its tip; as it continued to grow taller in this way, he could never reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, and it subsequently took root. Within the forest is a large *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and humans, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an *upāsaka* named Jayasena (in the language of Tang, this means "Victorious Army"), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces remained in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He had thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, possessing noble eloquence and elegant manners. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Of every ten households, six had sent disciples to receive his instruction. Now approaching seventy years of age, he studied with tireless devotion; having abandoned all other arts, he practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make small stupas five or six inches high; scriptures are written and placed inside them, which are called Dharma relics. As the number gradually accumulates, a large stupa is built to house them all within, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was as follows: his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stupas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice circumambulation, chanting, and seated meditation, never finding time for sleep or food, and working day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis (in the Tang language, *yi* [億]) of Dharma-relic stupas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stupa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.

translation: More than ten *li* to the southwest of the Stick Wood (Yaṣṭivana), on the southern slope of a great mountain, there are two hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested this water and bathed therein. They still exist today with their clear flow undiminished; people from near and far all come to bathe in them, and there are none among those with chronic illnesses or old ailments who are not cured. Beside them is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata once walked.

In front of a transverse ridge stands a stone stupa where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma to humans and devas for two or three months. At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王), wishing to come and hear the Dharma, cleared the mountain and piled up stones to build a staircase for his ascent, measuring over twenty paces in width and three or four li in length.

t2087_text: 孤山東北四五里，有小孤山，山壁石室廣袤可坐千餘人矣，如來在昔於此三月說法。石室上有大磐石，帝釋、梵王摩牛頭栴檀塗飾佛身，石上餘香，于今郁烈。石室西南隅有巖岫，印度謂之阿素洛（舊曰阿修羅，又曰阿須倫，又曰阿修羅，皆訛也）宮也。往有好事者，深閑呪術，顧儔命侶，十有四人，約契同志，入此巖岫。行三四十里，廓然大明，乃見城邑臺觀，皆是金銀琉璃。是人至已，有諸少女佇立門側，歡喜迎接，甚加禮遇。於是漸進至內城門，有二婢使各捧金盤，盛滿花香，而來迎候。謂諸人曰：「宜就池浴，塗冠香花，已而後入，斯為美矣。唯彼術士，宜時速進。」餘十三人遂即沐浴，既入池已，恍若有忘，乃坐稻田中，去此之北平川中，已三四十里矣。石室側有棧道，廣十餘步，長四五里。昔頻毘娑羅王將往佛所，乃斬石通谷，疏崖填川，或壘石，或鑿巖，作為階級，以至佛所。
translation: Four or five li to the northeast of the Isolated Hill is the Small Isolated Hill. In the cliffside of the mountain is a stone chamber, vast and spacious, capable of seating over a thousand people; here the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma for three months. Above the stone chamber is a large flat rock where Śakra and Brahmā ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Buddha’s body; the lingering fragrance on the rock remains potent to this day. In the southwest corner of the stone chamber is a rocky grotto, which in India is called the palace of the *asura* (阿素洛) (formerly called *axiuluo* [阿修羅], also *axulun* [阿須倫], also *axiuluo*; all are erroneous). In the past, there was a curious man, deeply skilled in spells, who gathered companions, fourteen people in all, and having made a pact to share the same purpose, entered this grotto. After traveling thirty or forty li, it suddenly became brightly illuminated, and they beheld cities, towers, and pavilions, all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Once these people arrived, there were various young maidens standing by the gates who joyfully welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy. Proceeding gradually to the inner city gate, there were two maidservants, each holding a golden basin filled with flowers and incense, who came to greet them. They said to the group, "It is fitting to go to the pool to bathe, to apply perfumes and wear flower garlands, and only after that to enter; this would be most excellent. Only that sorcerer should proceed quickly." The other thirteen people then bathed, but as soon as they entered the pool, they felt as if they had forgotten everything, and they found themselves sitting in a rice paddy on a level plain to the north of this place, already thirty or forty li away. Beside the stone chamber is a plank road, more than ten paces wide and four or five li long. In the past, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was about to go to the place of the Buddha, he had rocks cut to open the valley and cliffs leveled to fill the ravines; he either piled up stones or excavated the cliffs to create steps, in order to reach the place of the Buddha.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 從此大山中東行六十餘里，至矩奢揭羅補羅城（唐言上茅宮城）。上茅宮城，摩揭陀國之正中，古先君王之所都，多出勝上吉祥香茅，以故謂之上茅城也。崇山四周，以為外郭，西通峽徑，北闢山門，東西長，南北狹，周一百五十餘里。內城餘趾周三十餘里。羯尼迦樹遍諸蹊徑，花含殊馥，色爛黃金，暮春之月，林皆金色。宮城北門外有窣堵波，是提婆達多與未生怨王共為親友，乃放護財醉象，欲害如來。如來指端出五師子，醉象於此馴伏而前。伏醉象東北有窣堵波，是舍利子聞阿濕婆恃比丘（唐言馬勝）說法證果之處。初，舍利子在家也，高才雅量，見重當時，門生學徒，傳以受業。此時將入王舍大城，馬勝比丘亦方乞食。時舍利子遙見馬勝，謂門生曰：「彼來者甚庠序，不證聖果，豈斯調寂？宜少佇待，觀其進趣。」馬勝比丘已證羅漢，心得自在，容止和雅，振錫來儀。舍利子曰：「長老善安樂耶？師何人，證何法，若此之悅豫乎？」馬勝謂曰：「爾不知耶，淨飯王太子，捨轉輪王位，悲愍六趣，苦行六年，證三菩提，具一切智，是吾師也。夫法者，非有非空，難用銓緒，唯佛與佛乃能究述，豈伊愚昧所能詳議？」因為頌說，稱讚佛法。舍利子聞已，便獲果證。舍利子證果北不遠，有大深坑，傍建窣堵波，是室利毱多（唐言勝密）以火坑、毒飯欲害佛處。勝密者，宗信外道，深著邪見。諸梵志曰：「喬答摩國人尊敬，遂令我徒無所恃賴，汝今可請至家飯會，門穿大坑，滿中縱火，棧以朽木，覆以燥土。凡諸飲食，皆雜毒藥，若免火坑，當遭毒食。」勝密承命，便設毒會。城中之人皆知勝密於世尊所起惡害心，咸皆勸請，願佛勿往。世尊告曰：「無得懷憂。如來之身，物莫能害。」於是受請而往。足履門閫，火坑成池，清瀾澄鑒，蓮花彌漫。勝密見已，憂惶無措，謂其徒曰：「以術免火，尚有毒食。」世尊飯食已訖，為說妙法，勝密聞已，謝咎歸依。
translation: Traveling east from these great mountains for more than sixty li, one reaches the city of Kuśāgrapura (矩奢揭羅補羅城; in the language of Tang, the City of Superior Thatch Palaces). The City of Superior Thatch Palaces is located in the center of the kingdom of Magadha and was the capital of ancient kings; because it produces an abundance of excellent and auspicious fragrant thatch, it is called the City of Superior Thatch. Lofty mountains surround it, serving as an outer wall; to the west it connects to a mountain pass, and to the north a mountain gate opens. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty li. The remaining foundations of the inner city measure more than thirty li in circumference. *Karṇikāra* (羯尼迦) trees cover all the paths; their flowers contain a unique fragrance and their color is as brilliant as gold, so that in the month of late spring, the forests are all golden.  Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, marking the place where Devadatta, having become an intimate friend of King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王), released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla (護財) in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata. From the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, five lions emerged, and the intoxicated elephant was subdued and bowed down here. To the northeast of the place where the intoxicated elephant was subdued is a stūpa, marking the place where Śāriputra heard the bhikṣu Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃) (in the language of Tang, "Horse Victory" [馬勝]) preach the Dharma and attained the fruit of sainthood.   Formerly, when Śāriputra was a householder, he possessed high talent and elegant bearing, and was esteemed by his contemporaries; students and disciples came to him to receive instruction. At this time, he was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Aśvajit was also just then begging for food. At that time, Śāriputra saw Aśvajit from afar and said to his disciples, "That person coming here is very composed and dignified; if he has not attained the holy fruit, how could he be so calm and tranquil?" "We should wait a moment and observe his demeanor." The bhikṣu Aśvajit had already attained the state of an arhat; his mind was at ease, his bearing was gentle and refined, and he approached with the ringing of his khakkhara. Śāriputra said, "Elder, are you well and at peace? Who is your teacher, and what Dharma have you realized, that you are so joyful?" Aśvajit replied, "Do you not know? The crown prince of King Śuddhodana, who renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch, out of compassion for the six destinies, practiced austerities for six years, realized perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*), and possesses omniscience—he is my teacher. As for the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is difficult to define or explain. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully describe it; how could one as ignorant as I discuss it in detail?" He then recited a verse in praise of the Buddha’s Dharma. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained the fruit.  Not far to the north of where Śāriputra attained the fruit, there is a large, deep pit with a stūpa built beside it; this is the place where Śrīgupta (室利毱多) (in the language of Tang, "Victorious Secret" [勝密]) attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned food. This Śrīgupta followed the teachings of the non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to erroneous views. The various Brahmins said to him, "Gautama is respected by the people of the country, which has left our followers with nothing to rely on. You should now invite him to your home for a feast; dig a large pit at the gate, fill it with fire, bridge it with rotten wood, and cover it with dry earth. All the food and drink should be mixed with poison; if he escapes the fire pit, he will surely encounter the poisoned food." Śrīgupta accepted their command and prepared the poisoned feast. The people in the city all knew that Śrīgupta (勝密) harbored evil and harmful intentions toward the World-Honored One, and they all urged and pleaded with the Buddha not to go. The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor anxiety. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be harmed by anything." Thereupon, he accepted the invitation and went. As his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the fire pit turned into a pool, its clear waters reflecting like a mirror and filled with blooming lotuses. Having seen this, Śrīgupta was filled with panic and confusion, and said to his disciples, "He used magic to escape the fire, but there is still the poisoned food." After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he preached the wonderful Dharma for him; having heard this, Śrīgupta confessed his faults and took refuge.

translation: To the northeast of the fire pit of Śrīgupta (勝密), at a bend in the mountain city, there is a stūpa. This is where the great physician Jīvaka (時縛迦; formerly called Qipo [耆婆], which is incorrect) built a preaching hall for the Buddha. He planted flowers and fruit trees around its surrounding walls, and the remains of the foundations and the stumps of the trees can still be seen. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often stayed here. Beside it are the former residence of Jīvaka, the remains of the foundations, an old well, and the hollows of the ruins, which still exist.

t2087_text: 宮城東北行十四五里，至姞栗陀羅矩吒山（唐言鷲峯，亦謂鷲臺。舊曰耆闍崛山，訛也）。接北山之陽，孤摽特起，既棲鷲鳥，又類高臺，空翠相映，濃淡分色。如來御世垂五十年，多居此山，廣說妙法。頻毘娑羅王為聞法故，興發人徒，自山麓至峯岑，跨谷凌巖，編石為階，廣十餘步，長五六里。中路有二小窣堵波，一謂下乘，即王至此徒行以進；一謂退凡，即簡凡人不令同往。其山頂則東西長，南北狹。
translation: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain (in the language of Tang, this means Vulture Peak, and it is also called Vulture Terrace; the old name, Qidujue Mountain, is incorrect). It adjoins the southern slope of the North Mountain and rises solitary and steep; it is a place where vultures dwell and it resembles a lofty terrace, with the verdant peaks reflecting against the sky in varying shades of color. For nearly fifty years, while the Tathāgata presided over the world, he resided mostly on this mountain, extensively expounding the subtle Dharma. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra mobilized laborers to build a path from the foot of the mountain to the summit, spanning valleys and scaling rocks, laying stones to form steps more than ten paces wide and five or six *li* in length. Midway along the path are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting," marking the spot where the king would proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary," marking the spot where he would screen out ordinary people and not allow them to accompany him further. The summit of the mountain is long from east to west and narrow from north to south.

t2087_text: 臨崖西埵有甎精舍，高廣奇製，東闢其戶，如來在昔多居說法，今作說法之像，量等如來之身。精舍東有長石，如來經行所履也。傍有大石，高丈四五尺，周三十餘步，是提婆達多遙擲擊佛處也。其南崖下有窣堵波，在昔如來於此說《法花經》。精舍南山崖側有大石室，如來在昔於此入定。佛石室西北，石室前有大磐石，阿難為魔怖處也。尊者阿難於此入定，魔王化作鷲鳥，於黑月夜分據其大石，奮翼驚鳴，以怖尊者。尊者是時驚懼無措，如來鑒見，伸手安慰，通過石壁，摩阿難頂，以大慈言而告之曰：「魔所變化，宜無怖懼。」阿難蒙慰，身心安樂。石上鳥迹、崖中通穴，歲月雖久，于今尚存。精舍側有數石室，舍利子等諸大羅漢於此入定。舍利子石室前有一大井，枯涸無水，墟坎猶存。精舍東北石㵎中有大磐石，是如來曬袈裟之處，衣文明徹，皎如彫刻。其傍石上有佛脚迹，輪文雖暗，規摸可察。北山頂有窣堵波，是如來望摩揭陀城，於此七日說法。
translation: On the western edge of the cliff stands a brick vihara (精舍), of lofty and spacious, extraordinary construction, with its door opening to the east. In the past, the Tathāgata often resided here to expound the Dharma; today, there is an image of him expounding the Dharma, equal in measure to the body of the Tathāgata. To the east of the vihara is a long stone, which is where the Tathāgata walked during his meditative perambulations. Beside it is a large stone, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces in circumference; this is the place where Devadatta threw a rock from afar to strike the Buddha. Below the cliff to the south is a stūpa where, in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (法花經). On the side of the mountain cliff to the south of the vihara is a large stone chamber where the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration in the past. To the northwest of the Buddha’s stone chamber, in front of a cave, is a large flat rock; this is the place where Ānanda was terrified by Māra. While the Venerable Ānanda was in meditative concentration here, the Demon King transformed himself into a vulture; during the dark phase of the moon, it perched upon the large rock, flapping its wings and shrieking to frighten the Venerable One. At that time, the Venerable One was terrified and at a loss. The Tathāgata, perceiving this, reached out his hand to comfort him, passing through the stone wall to stroke Ānanda’s head, and addressed him with words of great compassion: "This is a transformation by Māra; you should have no fear." Having received this comfort, Ānanda’s body and mind became peaceful and joyful. The bird’s tracks on the stone and the hole through the cliff, though much time has passed, still remain today. Beside the vihara are several stone chambers where Śāriputra and other great Arhats entered into meditative concentration. In front of Śāriputra’s stone chamber is a large well; though it is dried up and waterless, its ruins and hollow still remain. In the stony gully to the northeast of the vihara is a large flat rock, which is the place where the Tathāgata dried his kaṣāya; the patterns of the robe are clear and distinct, as bright as if they were carved. Beside it, on the rock, are the footprints of the Buddha; although the wheel markings are faint, their shape and form can still be discerned. On the summit of the north mountain is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata gazed toward the city of Magadha (摩揭陀城) and preached the Dharma for seven days.

t2087_text: 山城北門西有毘布羅山，聞之土俗曰：山西南崖陰，昔有五百溫泉，今者數十而已，然猶有冷有暖，未盡溫也。其泉源發雪山之南無熱惱池，潛流至此，水甚清美，味同本池。流經五百枝小熱地獄，火熱上炎，致斯溫熱。泉流之口，並皆彫石，或作師子、白象之首，或作石筒懸流之道，下乃編石為池。諸方異域咸來此浴，浴者宿疾多差。溫泉左右諸窣堵波及精舍，基址鱗次，並是過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。此處既山水相帶，仁智攸居，隱淪之士蓋亦多矣。
translation: To the west of the north gate of the mountain city is Mount Vipula (毘布羅山). According to local tradition, on the shaded cliff to the southwest of the mountain, there were formerly five hundred hot springs; today, only several dozen remain, and they are still a mixture of cold and warm, not all of them being hot. The source of these springs originates from Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池) to the south of the Snowy Mountains (雪山), flowing underground to this location; the water is exceptionally clear and fine, with a taste identical to that of the original lake. The water flows through five hundred branch minor hot hells, where the fiery heat rises upward, causing this warmth. The mouths of the springs are all carved from stone, some fashioned into the heads of lions or white elephants, others forming stone conduits for the cascading water, which flows down into pools constructed of layered stone. People from various regions and foreign lands all come here to bathe, and those who bathe often find their chronic illnesses cured. To the left and right of the hot springs, the foundations of various stūpas and monasteries (精舍) are arranged like fish scales; these are all sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Since this place is bordered by mountains and rivers, serving as a dwelling for the benevolent and the wise, there are indeed many recluses living here in seclusion.

t2087_text: 溫泉西有卑鉢羅石室，世尊在昔恒居其中。後壁洞穴是阿素洛宮也。習定比丘多居此室。時出怪異龍、蛇、師子之形，見之者心發狂亂。然斯勝地，靈聖所止，躡迹欽風，忘其災禍。近有比丘，戒行貞潔，心樂幽寂，欲於此室匿迹習定。或有諫曰：「勿往彼也。彼多災異，為害不少，既難取定，亦恐喪身。宜鑒前事，勿貽後悔。」比丘曰：「不然。我方志求佛果，摧伏天魔，若此之害，夫何足言？」便即振錫而往室焉。於是設壇場，誦禁呪。旬日之後，穴出少女，謂比丘曰：「尊者染衣守戒，為含識歸依；修慧習定，作生靈善導。而今居此，驚懼我曹。如來之教，豈若是耶？」比丘曰：「我守淨戒，遵聖教也。匿迹山谷，遠諠雜也。忽此見譏，其咎安在？」對曰：「尊者誦呪聲發，火從外入，燒我居室，苦我枝屬。唯願悲愍，勿復誦呪。」比丘曰：「誦呪自護，非欲害物。往者，行人居此習定，期於聖果，以濟幽塗，覩怪驚懼，喪棄身命，汝之辜也，其何辭乎？」對曰：「罪障既重，智慧斯淺。自今已來，屏居守分，亦願尊者勿誦神呪。」比丘於是修定如初，安靜無害。毘布羅山上有窣堵波，昔者如來說法之處。今有露形外道，多依此住，修習苦行，夙夜匪懈，自旦至昏，旋轉觀察。
translation: To the west of the hot springs is the Pippala (卑鉢羅) stone cave, where the World-Honored One used to dwell constantly in the past. The cavern in the rear wall is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛). Many bhikṣus who practice meditation reside in this chamber. At times, strange and monstrous forms of dragons, snakes, and lions appear; those who see them become mentally deranged. However, because this is a superior site where the holy and sagely have dwelt, those who follow in their footsteps and admire their influence forget the disasters and calamities associated with it. Recently, there was a bhikṣu of pure conduct who delighted in quiet seclusion and wished to hide away in this chamber to practice meditation. Someone cautioned him, saying, "Do not go there. It is full of disasters and strange occurrences, causing no small amount of harm. It is difficult to attain concentration there, and I fear you will lose your life. You should take warning from past events and not leave cause for later regret." The bhikṣu replied, "That is not so. I am determined to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and to subdue the heavenly demons; if this is the harm you speak of, how is it worth mentioning?" He then shook his khakkhara-staff and went to the chamber. There, he set up an altar and recited protective mantras. After ten days, a young woman emerged from the cavern and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable one, you wear the dyed robes and keep the precepts, serving as a refuge for sentient beings; you cultivate wisdom and practice meditation, acting as a virtuous guide for living creatures. Yet now you dwell here and terrify us. Is this the teaching of the Tathāgata?" The bhikṣu replied, "I observe the pure precepts and follow the holy teachings. I hide my tracks in the mountain valleys to stay far from noise and confusion. Why do you suddenly reproach me for this?" She replied, "When you recite your mantras, the sound goes forth, and fire enters from outside, burning my dwelling and afflicting my kin. I only pray that you have compassion and do not recite the mantras again." The bhikṣu said, "I recite the mantras for self-protection, not because I wish to harm living beings. In the past, when practitioners dwelt here to practice meditation, hoping to attain the holy fruit to save those in the dark paths, they saw your monstrosity and were terrified, losing their lives; this was your fault, so what excuse do you have?" She replied, "My karmic obstructions are heavy and my wisdom is shallow. From now on, I shall live in seclusion and keep to my place; I also hope that you, Venerable Sir, will not recite the divine mantras." The bhikṣu then practiced meditation as before, in peace and without harm. On Mount Vipula (毘布羅山) there is a stūpa, the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma in the past. Nowadays, many naked heretics (nirgrantha) reside here, practicing austerities without negligence day or night; from dawn until dusk, they turn around and observe the sun.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: the woman's speech ("When you recite… do not recite the mantras again") is split into two quotations by a stray quote mark — one speech in the Chinese

t2087_text: 山城北門左，南崖陰，東行二三里，至大石室，昔提婆達多於此入定。石室東不遠，磐石上有班采，狀血染，傍建窣堵波，是習定比丘自害證果之處。昔有比丘，勤勵心身，屏居修定，歲月逾遠，不證聖果。退而自咎，竊復歎曰：「無學之果，終不時證；有累之身，徒生何益！」便就此石自刺其頸，是時即證阿羅漢果，上昇虛空，示現神變，化火焚身，而入寂滅。美其雅操，建以記功。比丘證果東石崖上，有石窣堵波，習定比丘投崖證果之處。昔在佛世，有一比丘，宴坐山林，修證果定，精勤已久，不得果證，晝夜繼念，無忘靜定。如來知其根機將發也，遂往彼而成之，自竹林園至山崖下，彈指而召，佇立以待。此比丘遙覩聖眾，身意勇悅，投崖而下，猶其淨心，敬信佛語，未至于地，已獲果證。世尊告曰：「宜知是時。」即昇虛空，示現神變。用彰淨信，故斯封記。
translation: To the left of the north gate of the mountain city, on the shaded side of the southern cliff, traveling east for two or three li, one arrives at a great stone chamber; in the past, Devadatta entered into meditation here. Not far to the east of the stone chamber, there are colored streaks on a flat rock that appear as if stained with blood, and beside it stands a stūpa built at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation took his own life and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who exerted his mind and body, living in seclusion to practice meditation; as the years passed, he did not attain the holy fruit. Retiring and blaming himself, he sighed privately, saying: "The fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) is not attained in time; what is the use of living in this body burdened with defilements!" He then went to this rock and stabbed his own neck; at that moment, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, rose into the void, manifested spiritual transformations, transformed into fire to consume his body, and entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa). Admiring his noble conduct, they built this to record his merit. On the cliff to the east of where the bhikṣu attained the fruit, there is a stone stūpa at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation threw himself from the cliff and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in the mountain forests practicing the meditation for attaining the fruit; though he had been diligent for a long time, he could not realize the fruit, yet he continued his contemplation day and night without forgetting his tranquil meditation. The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were about to ripen, went there to bring it to completion; he traveled from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the foot of the mountain cliff, snapped his fingers to summon him, and stood waiting. Seeing the Holy One from afar, the bhikṣu felt great joy in body and mind and threw himself from the cliff; because of his pure heart and his respectful faith in the Buddha's words, he attained the fruit of sainthood before reaching the ground. The World-Honored One said, "You should know that now is the time." He then ascended into the void and manifested miraculous transformations. This was to make manifest his pure faith, and therefore this memorial was established.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 山城北門行一里餘，至迦蘭陀竹園。今有精舍，石基甎室，東闢其戶。如來在世，多居此中，說法開化，導凡拯俗。今作如來之身。初，此城中有大長者迦蘭陀，時稱豪貴，以大竹園施諸外道。及見如來，聞法淨信，追昔竹園居彼異眾，今天人師無以館舍。時諸神鬼感其誠心，斥逐外道，而告之曰：「長者迦蘭陀當以竹園起佛精舍，汝宜速去，得免危厄。」外道憤恚，含怒而去。長者於此建立精舍，功成事畢，躬往請佛，如來是時遂受其施。
translation: Traveling more than one *li* from the north gate of the mountain city, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden (迦蘭陀竹園; Skt. Veṇuvana-kalandakanivāpa). There is now a vihāra (精舍) here with a stone foundation and brick chambers, with its entrance opening to the east. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often resided here, expounding the Dharma and transforming beings, guiding the ordinary and rescuing the worldly. Now, an image of the Tathāgata’s body has been made.  Formerly, there was a great elder in this city named Kalandaka, who was renowned for his wealth and nobility at that time. He had donated a large bamboo grove to the non-Buddhists. When he saw the Tathāgata and heard the Dharma, he developed pure faith. He reflected on how he had previously allowed the bamboo grove to be occupied by those of other sects, while the Teacher of Gods and Men now had no place to lodge. At that time, various spirits and deities, moved by his sincerity, expelled the non-Buddhists and told them, "The elder Kalandaka intends to build a Buddhist monastery in the bamboo grove; you should depart quickly to avoid danger and calamity." The non-Buddhists were resentful and departed in anger. The elder then established the monastery here; once the work was completed, he went in person to invite the Buddha, and the Tathāgata thereupon accepted his offering.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 迦蘭陀竹園東有窣堵波，阿闍多設咄路王（唐言未生怨，舊曰阿闍世，訛略也）之所建也。如來涅槃之後，諸王共分舍利，未生怨王得以持歸，式遵崇建，而修供養。無憂王之發信心也，開取舍利，建窣堵波，尚有遺餘，時燭光景。未生怨王窣堵波，有尊者阿難半身舍利。昔尊者將寂滅也，去摩揭陀國，趣吠舍釐城。兩國交爭，欲興兵甲。尊者傷愍，遂分其身，摩揭陀王奉歸供養，即斯勝地，式修崇建。其傍則有如來經行之處。次此不遠有窣堵波，是舍利子及沒特伽羅子等安居之所。
translation: To the east of the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove (迦蘭陀竹園) is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru (阿闍多設咄路王; translated in the Tang language as "Unborn Enemy" [未生怨], formerly called Ajāśatru [阿闍世], which is an erroneous abbreviation). After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the various kings divided the relics among themselves. King Ajātaśatru obtained his share and brought them back, where he formally observed the rites of construction and performed offerings. When King Aśoka (無憂王) developed faith, he opened the stūpa to retrieve the relics and built [new] stūpas; some relics still remain, and from time to time they shine with light.  In the stūpa of King Ajātaśatru, there are relics of half the body of the Venerable Ānanda. Formerly, when the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and headed toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). The two countries were in conflict and intended to raise an army. The Venerable One felt compassion and therefore divided his body; the King of Magadha received his portion and brought it back for veneration, and at this very sacred site, he formally performed the rites of construction. Beside it is a place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) and others resided during the rainy season.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
