t2087_text: 竹林園西南行五六里，南山之陰，大竹林中，有大石室，是尊者摩訶迦葉在此與九百九十大阿羅漢，如來涅槃後結集三藏。前有故基，未生怨王為集法藏諸大羅漢建此堂宇。初，大迦葉宴坐山林，忽燭光明，又覩地震，曰：「是何祥變，若此之異？」以天眼觀，見佛世尊於雙樹林間入般涅槃，尋命徒屬趣拘尸城。路逢梵志，手執天花。迦葉問曰：「汝從何來？知我大師今在何處？」梵志對曰：「我適從彼拘尸城來，見汝大師已入涅槃，天、人大眾咸興供養，我所持花，自彼得也。」迦葉聞已，謂其徒曰：「慧日淪照，世界闇冥，善導遐棄，眾生顛墜。」懈怠比丘更相賀曰：「如來寂滅，我曹安樂，若有所犯，誰能訶制？」迦葉聞已，深更感傷，思集法藏，據教治犯。遂至雙樹，觀化禮敬。既而法王去世，人、天無導，諸大羅漢亦取滅度。時大迦葉作是思惟：「承順佛教，宜集法藏。」於是登蘇迷盧山，擊大揵稚，唱如是言：「今王舍城將有法事，諸證果人宜時速集！」揵稚聲中傳迦葉教，遍至三千大千世界，得神通者聞皆集會。是時迦葉告諸眾曰：「如來寂滅，世界空虛，當集法藏，用報佛恩。今將集法，務從簡靜，豈恃群居，不成勝業？其有具三明，得六通，聞持不謬，辯才無礙，如斯上人，可應結集。自餘果學，各歸其居。」於是得九百九十人，除阿難在學地，大迦葉召而謂曰：「汝未盡漏，宜出聖眾。」曰：「隨侍如來，多歷年所，每有法議，曾未棄遺。今將結集，而見擯斥，法王寂滅，失所依怙。」迦葉告曰：「勿懷憂惱。汝親侍佛，誠復多聞，然愛惑未盡，習結未斷。」阿難辭屈而出，至空寂處，欲取無學，勤求不證。既已疲怠，便欲假寐，未及伏枕，遂證羅漢。往結集所，叩門白至。迦葉問曰：「汝結盡耶？宜運神通，非門而入。」阿難承命，從鑰隙入，禮僧已畢，退而復坐。是時安居初十五日也。於是迦葉揚言曰：「念哉諦聽！阿難聞持，如來稱讚，集素呾纜（舊曰修多羅，訛也）藏。優波釐持律明究，眾所知識，集毘奈耶（舊曰毘那耶，訛也）藏。我迦葉波集阿毘達磨藏。」兩三月盡，集三藏訖。以大迦葉僧中上座，因而謂之上座部焉。大迦葉波結集西北，有窣堵波，是阿難受僧訶責，不預結集，至此宴坐，證羅漢果。證果之後，方乃預焉。
translation: Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, "What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?" Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?" The Brahman replied, "I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there."  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, "The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin." Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, "The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?" Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply saddened and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away, leaving humans and gods without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is appropriate to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭā (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with haste!" The sound of the ghaṇṭā carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm, and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how could we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), are endowed with perfect retention (聞持) without error, and possess unobstructed eloquence (辯才)—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. All the rest, those who hold a fruit and those still in training, should return to their respective dwellings."  Thus, he obtained nine hundred and ninety people, excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning. Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows (漏); you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. Although you have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed learned, your attachments and delusions have not yet been exhausted, and your habitual bonds have not yet been severed." Ānanda, silenced, withdrew and went to a quiet, secluded place, desiring to attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he did not attain it. Having become exhausted and weary, he intended to lie down for a moment; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and then withdrew to sit down. This was on the fifteenth day, the beginning of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (素呾纜藏) (formerly called *xiuduoluo* [修多羅], which is erroneous). Upāli, who is clear and thorough in upholding the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (毘奈耶藏) (formerly called *pinaye* [毘那耶], which is erroneous). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka." After two or three months had passed, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, it was consequently called the Sthavira school (Sthaviravāda).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa; this is where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

t2087_text: 阿難證果西行二十餘里，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，大眾部結集之處。諸學、無學數百千人，不預大迦葉結集之眾，而來至此，更相謂曰：「如來在世，同一師學，法王寂滅，簡異我曹。欲報佛恩，當集法藏。」於是凡、聖咸會，賢智畢萃，復集素呾纜藏、毘柰耶藏、阿毘達磨藏、雜集藏、禁呪藏，別為五藏。而此結集，凡、聖同會，因而謂之大眾部。
translation: Traveling more than twenty *li* west from the place where Ānanda attained the fruit, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the Mahāsāṃghika (大眾部) held their assembly. Hundreds of thousands of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), not having participated in the assembly of Mahākāśyapa, came to this place and said to one another: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, we studied under the same teacher. Now that the Dharma King has passed into extinction, they have excluded us. Wishing to repay the Buddha’s kindness, we must compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, the ordinary and the saintly all gathered, and the wise and the virtuous fully assembled. They compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Saṃyukta Piṭaka), and the Dhāraṇī Piṭaka (禁呪藏), forming five separate collections. Because both ordinary people and sages assembled for this compilation, it was therefore called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) school.

t2087_text: 石柱東北不遠，至曷羅闍姞利呬城（唐言王舍）。外郭已壞，無復遺堵，內城雖毀，基址猶峻，周二十餘里，面有一門。初，頻毘娑羅王都在上宮城也，編戶之家頻遭火害。一家縱逸，四隣罹災，防火不暇，資產廢業，眾庶嗟怨，不安其居。王曰：「我以不德，下民罹患，修何德可以禳之？」群臣曰：「大王德化邕穆，政教明察，今茲細民不謹，致此火災，宜制嚴科，以清後犯，若有火起，窮究先發，罰其首惡，遷之寒林。寒林者，棄屍之所，俗謂不祥之地，人絕遊往之迹。今遷於彼，同夫棄屍。既恥陋居，當自謹護。」王曰：「善，宜遍宣告居。」頃之，王宮中先自失火。謂諸臣曰：「我其遷矣。」乃命太子監攝留事，欲清國憲，故遷居焉。時吠舍釐王聞頻毘娑羅王野處寒林，整集戎旅，欲襲不虞。邊候以聞，乃建城邑。以王先舍於此，故稱王舍城也。官屬、士、庶咸徙家焉。或云：至未生怨王乃築此城，未生怨太子既嗣王位，因遂都之。逮無憂王遷都波吒釐城，以王舍城施婆羅門，故今城中無復凡民，唯婆羅門減千家耳。宮城西南隅有二小伽藍，諸國客僧往來此止，是佛昔日說法之所。次此西北有窣堵波，珠底色迦（唐言星曆。舊曰樹提伽，訛也）長者本生故里。城南門外，道左有窣堵波，如來於此說法及度羅怙羅。
translation: Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬城) (in the language of Tang, "King's Abode" [王舍]). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring over twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side.   Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fires. It is appropriate to establish strict regulations to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it, punish the primary culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)."   The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people avoid traveling there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as treating them like a corpse. Since they will be ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border guards reported this, and he then built a city. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he then made it his capital. By the time King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city are two small saṃghārāmas where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly expounded the Dharma. To the northwest of this is a stūpa, the former birthplace of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦) (in the language of Tang, "Star Calendar" [星曆]; formerly called Shutijia [樹提伽], which is erroneous). Outside the south gate of the city, to the left of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma and converted Rāhula.

t2087_text: 從此北行三十餘里，至那爛陀（唐言施無厭）僧伽藍。聞之耆舊曰：此伽藍南菴沒羅林中有池，其龍名那爛陀，傍建伽藍，因取為稱。從其實議，是如來在昔修菩薩行，為大國王，建都此地，悲愍眾生，好樂周給，時美其德，號施無厭，由是伽藍因以為稱。其地本菴沒羅園，五百商人以十億金錢買以施佛，佛於此處三月說法，諸商人等亦證聖果。佛涅槃後未久，此國先王鑠迦羅阿逸多（唐言帝日），敬重一乘，遵崇三寶，式占福地，建此伽藍。初興功也，穿傷龍身，時有善占尼乾外道，見而記曰：「斯勝地也，建立伽藍，當必昌盛，為五印度之軌則，逾千載而彌隆，後進學人易以成業，然多歐血，傷龍故也。」其子佛陀毱多王（唐言覺護），繼體承統，聿遵勝業，次此之南，又建伽藍。呾他揭多毱多王（唐言如來），篤修前緒，次此之東，又建伽藍。婆羅阿迭多（唐言幼日）王之嗣位也，次此東北，又建伽藍。功成事畢，福會稱慶，輸誠幽顯，延請凡聖。其會也，五印度僧萬里雲集，眾坐已定，二僧後至，引上第三重閣。或有問曰：「王將設會，先請凡聖，大德何方，最後而至？」曰：「我至那國也，和上嬰疹，飯已方行，受王遠請，故來赴會。」問者驚駭，遽以白王。王心知聖也，躬往問焉，遲上重閣，莫知所去。王更深信，捨國出家。出家既已，位居僧末，心常怏怏，懷不自安：「我昔為王，尊居最上；今者出家，卑在眾末。」尋往白僧，自述情事。於是眾僧和合，令未受戒者以年齒為次，故此伽藍獨有斯制。其王之子代闍羅（唐言金剛），嗣位之後，信心貞固，復於此西建立伽藍。其後中印度王此北復建大伽藍。於是周垣峻峙，同為一門，既歷代君王繼世興建，窮諸剞劂，誠壯觀也。帝曰本大伽藍者，今置佛像，眾中日差四十僧就此而食，以報施主之恩。僧徒數千，並俊才高學也，德重當時，聲馳異域者，數百餘矣。戒行清白，律儀淳粹，僧有嚴制，眾咸貞素，印度諸國皆仰則焉。請益談玄，竭日不足，夙夜警誡，少長相成，其有不談三藏幽旨者，則形影自愧矣。故異域學人欲馳聲問，咸來稽疑，方流雅譽。是以竊名而遊，咸得禮重。殊方異域欲入談議，門者詰難，多屈而還；學深今古，乃得入焉。於是客遊後進，詳論藝能，其退飛者固十七八矣。二三博物，眾中次詰，莫不挫其銳、頹其名。若其高才博物，強識多能，明德哲人，聯暉繼軌。至如護法、護月，振芳塵於遺教；德慧、堅慧，流雅譽於當時；光友之清論；勝友之高談；智月則風鑒明敏；戒賢乃至德幽邃。若此上人，眾所知識，德隆先達，學貫舊章，述作論釋各十數部，並盛流通，見珍當世。伽藍四周，聖迹百數，舉其二三，可略言矣。
translation: From here, traveling north for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā (translated into Chinese as "Giving Without Weariness") monastery. I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond; a dragon named Nālandā lived there, and because the monastery was built beside it, it took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, it is because the Tathāgata, in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at the time, people praised his virtue and called him "Giving Without Weariness," and thus the monastery took this as its name. The land was originally a mango grove; five hundred merchants bought it with ten billion gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and the merchants all attained the fruits of sainthood. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as "Emperor Sun" [帝日]) deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem; he selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When the work first began, they pierced and injured the body of the dragon. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination who saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will grow even more prosperous after a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here. However, there will be much coughing of blood, because the dragon was injured." His son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as "Protector of Awakening"), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (translated into Chinese as "Thus-Come") earnestly followed the noble legacy and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (translated into Chinese as "Young Sun") succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the ceremonies finished, he held a celebratory feast of merit, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both the ordinary and the holy. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand miles away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third-story pavilion. Someone asked, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited the ordinary and the holy; from what place do you venerable ones come, that you arrive last?" They replied, "We have come from the country of Cīna (至那國); our teacher was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King, knowing in his heart that they were sages, went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am ranked at the very end of the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and recounted his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who have not yet received the full precepts shall be ranked according to their age; thus, this monastery alone possesses this rule. The King’s son, Vajra (translated into Chinese as "Diamond"), possessed a firm and steadfast faith; after succeeding to the throne, he built another monastery to the west of this site. Afterward, the King of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this one. Thereupon, the surrounding walls were raised high, and they were joined into a single gate; since successive kings have built them generation after generation, exhausting all the arts of carving and joinery, it is truly a magnificent sight. In the original great monastery of Śakrāditya (帝日), a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donors. The number of monks is several thousand, all of whom are men of outstanding talent and high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed in the present age and whose fame has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct in the precepts is pure and white, and their monastic discipline is refined and perfect; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth. For this reason, even those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, when visiting scholars and newcomers discuss their arts and abilities in detail, those who are forced to retreat are certainly seven or eight out of every ten. As for the few who are broadly learned, they are questioned in turn by the assembly, and there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty discussions of Jinamitra (勝友); Candrakīrti (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.

t2087_text: 伽藍西不遠有精舍，在昔如來三月止此，為諸天、人廣說妙法。南百餘步小窣堵波，遠方比丘見佛處。昔有比丘自遠方來，至此遇見如來聖眾，內發敬心，五體投地，便即發願求輪王位。如來見已，告諸眾曰：「彼比丘者甚可愍惜。福德深遠，信心堅固，若求佛果，不久當證。今其發願求轉輪王，於當來世必受此報。身體投地下至金輪，其中所有微塵之數，一一塵是一輪王報也。既耽世樂，聖果斯遠。」其南則有觀自在菩薩立像。或見執香爐往佛精舍，周旋右繞。觀自在菩薩像南窣堵波中，有如來三月之間剃剪髮、爪。有嬰疾病，旋繞多愈。其西垣外池側窣堵波，是外道執雀於此問佛死生之事。次東南垣內五十餘步，有奇樹，高八九尺，其幹兩披，在昔如來嚼楊枝棄地，因植根柢，歲月雖久，初無增減。次東大精舍，高二百餘尺，如來在昔於此四月說諸妙法。次北百餘步精舍中，有觀自在菩薩像，淨信之徒興供養者所見不同，莫定其所，或立門側，或出簷前，諸國法俗咸來供養。觀自在菩薩精舍北有大精舍，高三百餘尺，婆羅阿迭多王之所建也，莊嚴度量及中佛像，同菩提樹下大精舍。其東北窣堵波，在昔如來於此七日演說妙法。西北則有過去四佛坐處。其南鍮石精舍，戒日王之所建立，功雖未畢，然其圖量十丈而後成之。次東二百餘步垣外，有銅立佛像，高八十餘尺，重閣六層，乃得彌覆，昔滿胄王之所作也。滿胄王銅佛像北二三里，甎精舍中，有多羅菩薩像。其量既高，其靈甚察。每歲元日，盛興供養，隣境國王、大臣、豪族，齎妙香花，持寶旛蓋，金石遞奏，絲竹相和，七日之中，建斯法會。其垣南門內有大井。昔在佛世，有大商侶，熱渴逼迫，來至佛所。世尊指其地，以可得水。商主乃以車軸築地，地既為陷，水遂泉涌。飲已聞法，皆悟聖果。
translation: Not far to the west of the monastery (saṃghārāma) is a vihāra (精舍). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for three months, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the devas and humans. More than one hundred paces to the south is a small stupa, the place where a bhikṣu from a distant land saw the Buddha. Long ago, a bhikṣu came from a distant land and, upon arriving here, encountered the Tathāgata and his holy assembly. Internally giving rise to a heart of reverence, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and immediately made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Having seen this, the Tathāgata told the assembly: "That bhikṣu is truly to be pitied. His merit and virtue are deep and far-reaching, and his faith is firm; if he were to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he would soon attain it. Now, however, he has made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king, and in a future life, he will certainly receive this reward. From the place where his body touched the ground down to the golden wheel, the number of all the minute dust particles contained therein—each and every dust particle represents the reward of a wheel-turning king. Since he indulges in worldly pleasures, the holy fruit is far off." To the south of this is a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Sometimes he is seen holding an incense burner, going toward the Buddha’s vihāra, and circling it to the right. In the stupa to the south of the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are the hair and fingernails of the Tathāgata, shorn and clipped during those three months. Those who are afflicted with illness often recover by circumambulating it. The stupa by the side of the pond outside the western wall is where a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), holding a bird, questioned the Buddha about the matter of life and death. More than fifty paces to the southeast, within the enclosure, is a marvelous tree eight or nine feet high with its trunk divided into two; in the past, the Tathāgata chewed a willow twig and threw it on the ground, where it took root, and although a long time has passed, it has neither increased nor decreased. To the east is a great vihara, over two hundred feet high, where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for four months. To the north, one hundred and some paces away, is a vihara containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). Those of pure faith who come to make offerings see it differently, and its position cannot be fixed; sometimes it stands by the side of the door, and sometimes it appears before the eaves. The clergy and laity of various countries all come to make offerings. To the north of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vihara is a great vihara, over three hundred feet high, built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王); its ornamentation, dimensions, and the Buddha image within are the same as those of the great vihara under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree. To its northeast is a stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for seven days. To the northwest is the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihara built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet finished, according to its plans and measurements, it will be one hundred feet high when completed. To the east, two hundred and some paces outside the enclosure, is a standing copper Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which required a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in the past by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王). Two or three li north of the copper Buddha image of King Pūrṇavarman, inside a brick vihara, is an image of the Bodhisattva Tārā (多羅菩薩). Its stature is lofty, and its spiritual efficacy is very manifest. Every year on the first day of the year, grand offerings are made; kings of neighboring regions, ministers, and noble families bring wonderful incense and flowers, hold precious banners and canopies, play metal and stone instruments in succession, and harmonize them with string and bamboo instruments, holding this Dharma assembly for seven days. Inside the south gate of the enclosure, there is a large well. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, a large company of merchants, pressed by heat and thirst, came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One pointed to the ground, indicating that water could be obtained there. The leader of the merchants then struck the ground with a cart axle; once the ground was indented, water gushed forth like a spring. Having drunk and heard the Dharma, they all realized the holy fruit.

t2087_text: 伽藍西南行八九里，至拘理迦邑，中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，是尊者沒特伽羅子本生故里。傍有窣堵波，尊者於此入無餘涅槃，其中則有遺身舍利。尊者，大婆羅門種，與舍利子少為親友。舍利子以才明見貴，尊者以精鑒延譽，才智相比，動止必俱，結要終始，契同去就，相與厭俗，共求捨家，遂師珊闍耶焉。舍利子遇馬勝阿羅漢，聞法悟聖，還為尊者重述，聞而悟法，遂證初果。與其徒二百五十人俱到佛所，世尊遙見，指告眾曰：「彼來者，我弟子中神足第一。」既至佛所，請入法中。世尊告曰：「善來，比丘，淨修梵行，得離苦際。」聞是語時，鬚髮落，俗裳變，戒品淨，威儀調順。經七日，結漏盡，證羅漢果，得神通力。沒特伽羅子故里東行三四里，有窣堵波，頻毘娑羅王迎見佛處。如來初證佛果，知摩揭陀國人心渴仰，受頻毘娑羅王請，於晨朝時，著衣持鉢，與千比丘左右圍繞，皆是耆舊螺髻梵志，慕法染衣，前後羽從，入王舍城。時帝釋天王變為摩那婆，首冠螺髻，左手執金瓶，右手持寶杖，足蹈空虛，離地四指，在大眾中前導佛路。時摩揭陀國頻毘娑羅王與其國內諸婆羅門、長者、居士，百千萬眾，前後導從，出王舍城奉迎聖眾。
translation: Traveling eight or nine li southwest from the monastery, one reaches the town of Kolika (拘理迦邑), where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the native village of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子). Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where the Venerable One entered the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), and it contains his bodily relics. The Venerable One was of a great Brahmin lineage and had been a close friend of Śāriputra since youth. Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while the Venerable One was renowned for his profound discernment; they were equals in wisdom, always together in their movements, bound by a lifelong pact to share the same path, and together they grew weary of the secular world and sought to leave the householder's life, eventually taking Sañjaya as their teacher. Śāriputra encountered the arhat Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained realization; he returned and recounted it to the Venerable One, who, upon hearing and realizing the Dharma, attained the first fruit. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out to the assembly, said: "Those who are coming are the foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples." Upon arriving at the place of the Buddha, they requested to enter the Dharma. The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, monks; practice the holy life purely to reach the end of suffering." Upon hearing these words, their hair and beards fell away, their secular garments changed, their precepts became pure, and their deportment became harmonious. After seven days, their defilements were exhausted, they attained the fruit of arhatship, and they gained supernatural powers. Three or four li to the east of the native village of Maudgalyāyana, there is a stūpa at the place where King Bimbisāra went to meet and see the Buddha. When the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of buddhahood, he knew that the hearts of the people in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) were thirsting with longing. He accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) and, in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl. Surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were elder brahmans with shell-shaped topknots who had donned dyed robes out of admiration for the Dharma, following him in his retinue—he entered the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, the heavenly king Śakra (帝釋天王) transformed himself into a māṇava (摩那婆) with a shell-shaped topknot on his head. Holding a golden vase in his left hand and a precious staff in his right, his feet treading on empty space four finger-widths above the ground, he led the way for the Buddha amidst the assembly. Then King Bimbisāra of the country of Magadha, together with the various brahmans, elders, and laypeople of his kingdom—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—came out of the city of Rājagṛha in a procession to welcome the holy assembly.

t2087_text: 頻毘娑羅王迎佛東南行二十餘里，至迦羅臂拏迦邑，中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。是尊者舍利子本生故里，井今尚在。傍有窣堵波，尊者於此寂滅，其中則有遺身舍利。尊者，大婆羅門種。其父高才博識，深鑒精微，凡諸典籍莫不究習。其妻感夢，具告夫曰：「吾昨宵寐，夢感異人，身被鎧甲，手執金剛，摧破諸山，退立一山之下。」夫曰：「夢甚善。汝當生男，達學貫世，摧諸論師，破其宗致，唯不如一人，為作弟子。」果而有娠，母忽聰明，高論劇談，言無屈滯。尊者年始八歲，名擅四方，其性淳質，其心慈悲，朽壞結縛，成就智慧。與沒特伽羅子少而相友，深厭塵俗，未有所歸，於是與沒特伽羅子於珊闍耶外道所而修習焉。乃相謂曰：「斯非究竟之理，未能窮苦際也。各求明導，先嘗甘露，必同其味。」時大阿羅漢馬勝執持應器，入城乞食。舍利子見其威儀閑雅，即而問曰：「汝師是誰？」曰：「釋種太子厭世出家，成等正覺。是我師也。」舍利子曰：「所說何法，可得聞乎？」曰：「我初受教，未達深義。」舍利子曰：「願說所聞。」馬勝乃隨宜演說，舍利子聞已，即證初果。遂與其徒二百五十人往詣佛所，世尊遙見，指告眾曰：「我弟子中智慧第一。」至已頂禮，願從佛法。世尊告曰：「善來，比丘。」聞是語時，戒品具足。過半月後，聞佛為長爪梵志說法，聞餘論而感悟，遂證羅漢之果。其後阿難承佛告寂滅期，展轉相語，各懷悲感，舍利子深增戀仰，不忍見佛入般涅槃，遂請世尊，先入寂滅。世尊告曰：「宜知是時。」告謝門人，至本生里，侍者沙彌遍告城邑。未生怨王及其國人莫不風馳，皆悉雲會。舍利子廣為說法，聞已而去。於後夜分，正意繫心，入滅盡定，從定起已而寂滅焉。迦羅臂挐迦邑東南四五里，有窣堵波，是尊者舍利子門人入涅槃處。或曰：迦葉波佛在世時，有三拘胝（拘胝者，唐言億）大阿羅漢同於此地無餘寂滅。
translation: From the place where King Bimbisāra welcomed the Buddha, traveling more than twenty *li* to the southeast, one arrives at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became brilliant, engaging in high-level discussions and intense debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) had been friends since youth and were deeply weary of the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate principle, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share its flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and refined demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have heard." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out, told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the ground and wished to follow the Buddha’s dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha preaching to the Long-nailed Brahmacārin (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha’s announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow and grief. Śāriputra’s longing and reverence deepened, and, unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and the people of his country all rushed there like the wind, gathering like clouds. Śāriputra (舍利子) preached the Dharma extensively, and having heard him, the people departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he entered final extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha (迦葉波佛) was in the world, three koṭis (*koṭi* is, in the language of Tang, *yi* [億]) of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

t2087_text: 舍利子門人窣堵波東行三十餘里，至因陀羅勢羅窶訶山（唐言帝釋窟）。其山巖谷杳冥，花林蓊欝，嶺有兩峯，岌然特起。西峯南巖間有大石室，廣而不高，昔如來嘗於中止。時時天帝釋以四十二疑事畫石請問，佛為演釋，其迹猶在。今作此像，擬昔聖儀，入中禮敬者，莫不肅然驚懼。山巖上有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。東峯上有伽藍，聞諸土俗曰：其中僧眾，或於夜分，望見西峯石室佛像前每有燈炬，常為照燭。因陀羅勢羅窶訶山東峯伽藍前有窣堵波，謂亘（許贈反）娑（唐言雁）。昔此伽藍習翫小乘，小乘漸教也，故開三淨之食，而此伽藍遵而不墜。其後三淨求不時獲。有比丘經行，忽見群雁飛翔，戲言曰：「今日眾僧中食不充，摩訶薩埵宜知是時。」言聲未絕，一雁退飛，當其僧前，投身自殞。比丘見已，具白眾僧，聞者悲感，咸相謂曰：「如來設法，導誘隨機；我等守愚，遵行漸教。大乘者，正理也，宜改先執，務從聖旨。此雁垂誡，誠為明導，宜旌厚德，傳記終古。」於是建窣堵波，式昭遺烈，以彼死雁瘞其下焉。
translation: Going thirty-some *li* to the east of the stupa of the disciples of Śāriputra, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (Indra-śaila-guhā; in the language of Tang, "Cave of Śakra"). The mountain’s rocky valleys are deep and dark, and its flowering forests are lush and dense; on the ridge are two peaks that rise prominently and steeply. Between the southern cliffs of the western peak is a large stone chamber, wide but not high, where the Tathāgata once stayed. From time to time, the Heavenly Lord Śakra would carve forty-two questions of doubt onto the stone to ask [the Buddha], and the Buddha would explain them; those traces still remain. Today, an image has been made there to emulate the sacred appearance of the past, and those who enter to pay homage are all filled with awe and trepidation. On the mountain cliffs are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. On the eastern peak is a monastery; I heard from the local people that the monks there sometimes see, during the night, lamps and torches shining as constant illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber of the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of Indraśailaguhā Mountain is a stupa called Haṃsa (亘娑) (亘 is pronounced x[u] + [z]eng) (in the language of Tang, "Goose"). Formerly, this monastery practiced the Lesser Vehicle; the Lesser Vehicle is a gradual teaching, and therefore permitted the consumption of the three pure meats, a practice this monastery followed and did not abandon. Later, the three pure meats were not always obtainable. A monk who was walking in meditation suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and jokingly said, "Today the midday meal for the monks is insufficient; the Mahāsattvas should know the time." Before his words had ceased, one goose flew back, landed before the monk, and cast its body down to die. After the bhikṣu saw this, he reported it fully to the assembly of monks. Those who heard were moved with grief and said to one another, "The Tathāgata established the Dharma to guide and entice according to the capacity of the individual; we have clung to our ignorance and followed the gradual teachings. The Mahāyāna is the true principle; we should change our former attachments and strive to follow the holy will. This goose has handed down a warning and is truly a bright guide; we should commemorate its great virtue and transmit this record for all eternity." Thereupon, they built a stūpa to manifest its heroic legacy, burying the dead goose beneath it.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 因陀羅勢羅窶訶山東北行百五六十里，至迦布德迦（唐言鴿）伽藍，僧徒二百餘人，學說一切有部。伽藍東有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。昔佛於此為諸大眾一宿說法。時有羅者於此林中網捕羽族，一日不獲，遂作是言：「我惟薄福，恒為弊事。」來至佛所，揚言唱曰：「今日如來於此說法，令我網捕都無所得，妻孥飢餓，其計安出？」如來告曰：「汝應蘊火，當與汝食。」如來是時化作大鴿，投火而死，羅者持歸，妻孥共食。其後重往佛所，如來方便攝化，羅者聞法，悔過自新，捨家修學，便證聖果。因名所建為鴿伽藍。
translation: Traveling northeast from the Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶) Mountain for one hundred and fifty or sixty li, one reaches the Kapotaka (迦布德迦; in Chinese, "pigeon") Monastery, where there are over two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the east of the monastery is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Buddha stayed here for one night to preach the Dharma to the great assembly. At that time, a fowler was netting birds in this forest; having caught nothing all day, he said, "I have but little merit and am always met with misfortune." He came to where the Buddha was and cried out, "Today the Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma here, causing me to catch nothing in my nets; my wife and children are starving, so what plan can I devise?" The Tathāgata replied, "You should kindle a fire, and I will provide you with food." The Tathāgata then transformed himself into a large pigeon and threw himself into the fire to die; the fowler took it home, and he and his wife and children ate it together. Afterward, he returned to the Buddha, who guided and transformed him through skillful means. The fowler heard the Dharma, repented of his faults, renewed himself, left home to study, and subsequently attained the holy fruit. For this reason, the monastery that was built there was named the Pigeon Monastery.

t2087_text: 迦布德迦伽藍南二三里，至孤山。其山崇峻，樹林欝茂，名花清流，被崖緣壑。上多精舍靈廟，頗極剞劂之工。正中精舍有觀自在菩薩像，軀量雖小，威神感肅，手執蓮花，頂戴佛像。常有數人，斷食要心，求見菩薩，七日、二七日、乃至一月，其有感者，見觀自在菩薩，妙相莊嚴，威光赫奕，從像中出，慰喻其人。昔南海僧伽羅國王清旦以鏡照面，不見其身，乃覩贍部洲摩揭陀國多羅林中小山上有此菩薩像，王深感慶，圖以營求。既至此山，寔唯肖似，因建精舍，興諸供養。自後諸王尚想遺風，遂於其側建立精舍靈廟，香花伎樂供養不絕。
translation: Two or three li south of the Kapotaka monastery (迦布德迦伽藍), one arrives at an isolated hill (孤山). The mountain is lofty and steep, with lush forests, famous flowers, and clear streams covering the cliffs and lining the ravines. Above, there are many vihāras (精舍) and sacred temples, which are extremely refined in their craftsmanship. In the central vihāra is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); although small in size, its spiritual majesty inspires awe, as it holds a lotus in its hand and bears a Buddha figure upon its crown. There are often people who fast and focus their minds, seeking a vision of the Bodhisattva for seven days, fourteen days, or even a full month; those who receive a response see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, in all his solemn and wondrous beauty and brilliant radiance, emerge from the statue to comfort and exhort them. Long ago, the king of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea looked into a mirror at dawn and saw not his own reflection, but rather this Bodhisattva statue atop a small hill in the Tāla forest of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in Jambudvīpa (贍部洲); the king, deeply moved and joyful, sought to find it. When he arrived at this hill, he found the statue to be exactly as he had seen, so he built a vihāra and established various offerings. Since then, subsequent kings, admiring this legacy, have built vihāras and sacred temples alongside it, and offerings of incense, flowers, and music have never ceased.

translation: Traveling southeast for more than forty li from the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) on the isolated hill (孤山), one reaches a monastery where there are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. In front of the monastery is a great stūpa, which possesses many miraculous qualities; it is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days to the Brahmadeva-rāja and others. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the three past Buddhas.

translation: From here, traveling east into the mountains and forests for more than one hundred li, one reaches the village of Luobanniluo (Röhinila). In front of the monastery is a great stupa built by King Ashoka (Aśoka), where the Buddha once stayed for three months to preach the Dharma. Two or three li to the north of this place is a large pond, more than thirty li in circumference, where four-colored lotus flowers bloom in all four seasons. From here, traveling east into the great mountains and forests for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Yilannabafaduo (Hiraṇyaparvata) (within the borders of Central India).

t2087_text: 伊爛拏鉢伐多國，周三千餘里。國大都城北臨殑伽河，周二十餘里。稼穡滋植，花菓具繁。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。伽藍十餘所，僧徒四千餘人，多學小乘正量部法。天祠二十餘所，異道雜居。近有隣王廢其國君，以大都城持施眾僧。於此城中建二伽藍，各減千僧，並學小乘教說一切有部。大城側，臨殑伽河，有伊爛拏山，含吐烟霞，蔽虧日月，古今仙聖繼踵棲神，今有天祠尚遵遺則。在昔如來亦嘗居此，為諸天、人廣說妙法。大城南有窣堵波，如來於此三月說法。其傍則有過去三佛坐及經行遺迹之所。三佛經行西不遠，有窣堵波，是室縷多頻設底拘胝（唐言聞二百億。舊譯曰億耳，謬也）苾芻生處。昔此城有長者，豪貴巨富，晚有繼嗣，時有報者，輒賜金錢二百億，因名其子聞二百億。洎乎成立，未曾履地，故其足跖毛長尺餘，光潤細軟，色若黃金。珍愛此兒，備諸玩好，自其居家以至雪山，亭傳連隅，僮僕交路，凡須妙藥，遞相告語，轉而以授，曾不踰時，其豪富如此。世尊知其善根將發，也命沒特伽羅子而往化焉。既至門下，莫由自通。長者家祠日天，每晨朝時東向以拜。是時尊者以神通力，從日輪中降立於前。長者子疑日天也，因施香飯而歸，其飯香氣遍王舍城。時頻毘娑羅王駭其異馥，命使歷問，乃竹林精舍沒特伽羅子自長者家持來，因知長者子有此奇異，乃使召焉。長者承命，思何安步？泛舟鼓棹，有風波之危；乘車馭象，懼蹶躓之患。於是自其居家，至王舍城，鑿渠通漕，流滿芥子，御舟安止，長縆以引。至王舍城，先禮世尊。世尊告曰：「頻毘娑羅王命使召汝，無過欲見足下毛耳。王欲觀者，宜結跏坐。伸脚向王，國法當死。」長者子受誨而往，引入廷謁。王欲視毛，乃跏趺坐，王善其有禮，特深珍愛。亦既得歸，還至佛所。如來是時說法誨喻，聞而感悟，遂即出家。於是精勤修習，思求果證，經行不捨，足遂流血。世尊告曰：「汝善男子，在家之時知鼓琴耶？」曰：「知。」「若然者，以此為喻。絃急則聲不合韻，絃緩則調不和雅，非急非緩，其聲乃和。夫修行者亦然。急則身疲心怠，緩則情舒志逸。」承佛指教，奉以周旋，如是不久，便獲果證。
translation: The country of Īraṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國) is over three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā River to the north and is over twenty *li* in circuit. The crops are lush and productive, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox sects live together. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and bestowed the capital city upon the community of monks. Within this city, two monasteries were built, each housing nearly one thousand monks, both of which study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school.  Beside the great city, overlooking the Gaṅgā River, is Mount Īraṇa, which exhales mists and clouds that obscure the sun and the moon. From ancient times to the present, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell there in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here and preached the profound Dharma extensively for devas and humans. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Not far to the west of the walking paths of the three Buddhas is a stūpa; this is the birthplace of the bhikṣu Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (室縷多頻設底拘胝) (in Chinese, "Heard of Two Hundred Koṭis" [聞二百億]; the old translation "Koṭikarṇa" [億耳, "Koṭi-Ear"] is wrong). In the past, there was a wealthy and noble elder in this city who had a child late in life. to the one who then brought him the news he at once gave two hundred koṭis of gold coins, and thus he named his son Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (He who heard of two hundred koṭis). By the time he reached adulthood, he had never once walked upon the ground, and thus the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, with a color like yellow gold. Cherishing this child, his parents provided him with every kind of luxury; from his residence all the way to the Snow Mountains, post-stations were linked together and servants lined the roads, so that whenever a rare medicine was required, the word was passed along and the item delivered in succession, arriving in no time at all—such was the extent of his great wealth. The World-Honored One, knowing that his roots of goodness were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) to go and convert him. Upon arriving at his gate, he found no way to announce himself. The elder’s family worshipped the Sun Deity, and every morning they would face east to bow. At that time, the Venerable One used his supernatural powers to descend from the solar disc and stand before them. The elder’s son, suspecting he was the Sun Deity, offered him fragrant rice; the Venerable One then returned, and the aroma of the rice filled the entire city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was astonished by the extraordinary fragrance and ordered a messenger to investigate; it was discovered that Maudgalyāyana of the Bamboo Grove Monastery (竹林精舍) had brought the rice from the elder's house, and thus, learning that the elder's son possessed such a wonder, the king summoned him. The elder accepted the command, but pondered how to travel safely. To travel by boat and ply the oars carried the danger of wind and waves; to ride in a carriage or on an elephant brought the fear of stumbling or falling. Thereupon, from his residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he excavated a canal for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, so that the boat could rest securely and be towed along by a long rope. Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said to him, "King Bimbisāra has ordered a messenger to summon you for no other reason than to see the hair on the soles of your feet. If the king wishes to see them, you should sit in the cross-legged position. To extend your feet toward the king is a capital offense according to the laws of the country." The elder's son accepted this instruction and went to the court, where he was led in to have an audience. When the king wished to see the hair, he sat in the cross-legged position; the king praised his courtesy and came to cherish him deeply. Once he was able to return, he went back to the place of the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma and offered him instruction; upon hearing it, he was moved to realization and immediately renounced the household life. Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking to realize the fruits of enlightenment; he engaged in walking meditation without rest until his feet began to bleed. The World-Honored One said to him, "Good man, when you were at home as a layman, did you know how to play the lute?" He replied, "I did." "If that is so, take this as an analogy. If the strings are too tight, the sound will not be in harmony; if the strings are too loose, the melody will not be refined. Neither too tight nor too loose, the sound is then harmonious. The practitioner of the path is also like this. If one is too urgent, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too lax, the passions expand and the will becomes dissipated." Having received the Buddha's instruction, he followed it faithfully, and before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

t2087_text: 國西界殑伽河南，至小孤山，重巘嶜崟，昔佛於此三月安居，降薄句羅藥叉。山東南巖下大石上，有佛坐跡，入石寸餘，長五尺二寸，廣二尺一寸，其上則建窣堵波焉。次南石上則有佛置捃稚迦（即澡瓶也。舊曰軍持，訛略也）跡，深寸餘，作八出花文。佛坐跡東南不遠，有薄句羅藥叉脚跡，長尺五六寸，廣七八寸，深減二寸。藥叉跡後有石佛坐像，高六七尺。次西不遠有佛經行之處。其山頂上有藥叉故室。次北有佛足跡，長尺有八寸，廣餘六寸，深可半寸，其跡上有窣堵波。如來昔日降伏藥叉，令不殺人食肉，敬受佛戒，後得生天。此西有溫泉六七所，其水極熱。國南界大山林中多諸野象，其形偉大。
translation: At the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one reaches the Small Isolated Hill (小孤山). Its layered peaks are lofty and precipitous. In the past, the Buddha spent three months of the rainy season retreat here, subduing the yakṣa Bakula (薄句羅). On a large rock below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which penetrates the stone by more than an inch; it is five feet two inches long and two feet one inch wide, and a stūpa has been built upon it. Next, to the south on the stone, there is a trace where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (捃稚迦) (that is, a water-jar for washing; formerly called *kundī* [軍持], erroneous and abbreviated), which is more than an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled flower design. Not far to the southeast of the Buddha’s sitting trace is the footprint of the yakṣa Bakula, which is one foot five or six inches long, seven or eight inches wide, and slightly less than two inches deep. Behind the yakṣa’s footprint is a stone seated image of the Buddha, six or seven feet high. Not far to the west is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. On the summit of the mountain is the former dwelling of the yakṣa. Next, to the north, is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long, over six inches wide, and about half an inch deep; there is a stūpa above this trace. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the yakṣa, causing him to stop killing people and eating meat, and to respectfully receive the Buddha’s precepts, after which he was reborn in the heavens. To the west of this are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the great mountain forests at the southern border of the country, there are many wild elephants, which are immense in size.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 從此順殑伽河南岸東行三百餘里，至瞻波國（中印度境）。瞻波國，周四千餘里。國大都城北背殑伽河，周四十餘里。土地墊濕，稼穡滋盛。氣序溫暑，風俗淳質。伽藍數十所，多有傾毀，僧徒二百餘人，習小乘教。天祠二十餘所，異道雜居。都城壘甎，其高數丈，基址崇峻，却敵高險。在昔劫初，人物伊始，野居穴處，未知宮室。後有天女，降迹人中，遊殑伽河，濯流自媚，感靈有娠，生四子焉。分贍部洲，各擅區宇，建都築邑，封畺畫界，此則一子之國都，贍部洲諸城之始也。
translation: From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li along the southern bank of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Campā is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country has the Ganges River to its north and is more than forty li in circuit. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with more than two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The walls of the capital city are built of brick, several chang high, with lofty and steep foundations and high, precipitous battlements. In the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first appeared, they lived in the wild and dwelt in caves, not yet knowing of palaces or houses. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and, while wandering by the Ganges and bathing in its currents to please herself, she was spiritually moved and became pregnant, eventually giving birth to four sons. They divided Jambudvīpa among themselves, each ruling over a region, building capitals and constructing towns, and marking out boundaries and borders. This city was the capital of one of those sons, and it was the beginning of all the cities in Jambudvīpa.

translation: One hundred forty or fifty li to the east of the city, south of the Ganges (gaṅgā), water surrounds a solitary islet with lofty and precipitous cliffs; atop it stands a deva temple where the deity manifests many miracles. Chambers have been carved into the cliffs and water channeled to form ponds; with its flowery groves, exotic trees, massive rocks, and perilous peaks, it is an abode for the benevolent and wise, so beautiful that visitors forget to return. In the mountains and forests of the country's southern border, wild elephants and fierce beasts roam in herds numbering in the thousands.

t2087_text: 自此東行四百餘里，至羯朱嗢祇羅國（彼俗或謂羯蠅揭羅國。中印度境）。羯朱嗢祇羅國，周二千餘里。土地泉濕，稼穡豐盛，氣序溫，風俗順。敦尚高才，崇貴學藝。伽藍六七所，僧徒三百餘人。天祠十所，異道雜居。自數百年，王族絕嗣，役屬隣國，所以城郭丘墟，多居村邑。故戒日王遊東印度，於此築宮，理諸國務，至則葺茅為宇，去則縱火焚燒。國南境多野象。
translation: Traveling east from here for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Kajaṅgala (羯朱嗢祇羅國) (the local people sometimes call it the country of Kayaṅghara [羯蠅揭羅國]; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kajaṅgala is more than two thousand li in circuit. The land is moist and marshy, the crops are abundant, the climate is temperate, and the customs are agreeable. The people value high talent and esteem learning and the arts. There are six or seven saṃghārāmas with more than three hundred monks. There are ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. For several hundred years, the royal line has been extinct and the country has been subject to neighboring states; for this reason, the walled cities are in ruins, and the people mostly dwell in villages and towns. Therefore, when King Śīlāditya (戒日王) traveled to East India, he built a palace here to manage the affairs of the various states; when he arrived, he thatched a building with grass, and when he departed, he set fire to it. In the southern borders of the country, there are many wild elephants.

t2087_text: 自此東渡殑伽河，行六百餘里，至奔那伐彈那國（中印度境）。奔那伐彈那國，周四千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。居人殷盛，池館花林往往相間。土地卑濕，稼穡滋茂。般核娑菓既多且貴，其菓大如冬瓜，熟則黃赤，剖之中有數十小菓，大如鶴卵，又更破之，其汁黃赤，其味甘美。或在樹枝，如眾菓之結實，或在樹根，若伏苓之在土。氣序調暢，風俗好學。伽藍二十餘所，僧徒三千餘人，大小二乘，兼功綜習。天祠百所，異道雜居，露形尼乾寔繁其黨。
translation: From here, crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east and traveling over six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Puṇḍravardhana (奔那伐彈那國) (within the territory of Central India). The country of Puṇḍravardhana is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and ponds, pavilions, and flower groves are interspersed throughout. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The *panasa* (般核娑) fruit is both plentiful and highly valued; the fruit is as large as a winter melon, and when ripe, it turns yellowish-red. When sliced open, it contains several dozen smaller fruits as large as crane eggs, and when these are further broken, they yield a yellowish-red juice with a sweet and delicious taste. Some grow on the tree branches like the fruits of other trees, while others grow from the roots, like *fuling* (伏苓) in the soil. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs favor learning. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over three thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are one hundred deva temples, where followers of various heterodox sects dwell together, and the Nirgrantha (尼乾) ascetics, who go naked, are particularly numerous among their groups.

translation: More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibhā Monastery (跋始婆僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its terraces and pavilions are lofty. There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; most of the eminent scholars and renowned monks of East India reside here. Not far to its side is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka. This is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata spent three months preaching the Dharma for the devas and humans; on fast days, it sometimes emits a brilliant light. To its side are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation paths of the four Buddhas. Not far from here is another shrine (精舍), in which is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Its spiritual insight is all-revealing and its divine responses are manifest, so that people from far and near fast and pray before it.

t2087_text: 自此東行九百餘里，渡大河，至迦摩縷波國（東印度境）。迦摩縷波國，周萬餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土地泉濕，稼穡時播。般核娑菓、那羅雞羅菓，其樹雖多，彌復珍貴。河流湖陂，交帶城邑。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。人形卑小，容貌釐黑。語言少異中印度。性甚獷暴，志存強學。宗事天神，不信佛法。故自佛興以迄于今，尚未建立伽藍，招集僧侶。其有淨信之徒，但竊念而已。天祠數百，異道數萬。今王本那羅延天之祚胤，婆羅門之種也，字婆塞羯羅伐摩（唐言日胄），號拘摩羅（唐言童子）。自據畺土，奕葉君臨，逮於今王，歷千世矣。君上好學，眾庶從化，遠方高才，慕義客遊，雖不淳信佛法，然敬高學沙門。初，聞有至那國沙門在摩揭陀那爛陀僧伽藍，自遠方來，學佛深法，殷勤往復者再三，未從來命。時尸羅跋陀羅論師曰：「欲報佛恩，當弘正法，子其行矣，勿憚遠涉。拘摩羅王世宗外道，今請沙門，斯善事也，因茲改轍，福利弘遠。子昔起廣大心，發弘誓，願孤遊異域，遺身求法，普濟含靈，豈徒鄉國？宜忘得喪，勿拘榮辱，宣揚聖教，開導群迷，先物後身，忘名弘法。」於是辭不獲免，遂與使偕行，而會見焉。拘摩羅王曰：「雖則不才，常慕高學，聞名雅尚，敢事延請。」曰：「寡能褊智，猥蒙流聽。」拘摩羅王曰：「善哉！慕法好學，顧身若浮，踰越重險，遠遊異域。斯則王化所由，國風尚學。今印度諸國多有歌頌摩訶至那國《秦王破陣樂》者，聞之久矣，豈大德之鄉國耶？」曰：「然，此歌者，美我君之德也。」拘摩羅王曰：「不意大德是此國人，常慕風化，東望已久，山川道阻，無由自致。」曰：「我大君聖德遠洽，仁化遐被，殊俗異域拜闕稱臣者眾矣。」拘摩羅王曰：「覆載若斯，心冀朝貢。今戒日王在羯朱嗢祇羅國，將設大施，崇樹福慧，五印度沙門、婆羅門有學業者，莫不召集。今遣使來請，願與同行。」於是遂往焉。此國東山阜連接，無大國都，境接西南夷，故其人類蠻獠矣。詳問土俗，可兩月行，入蜀西南之境，然山川險阻，嶂氣氛沴，毒蛇毒草，為害滋甚。國之東南野象群暴，故此國中象軍特盛。
translation: From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li and crossing a great river, one reaches the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國) (in the territory of East India). The country of Kāmarūpa is over ten thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit. The land is low and moist, and crops are sown at the proper seasons. Although there are many *panasa* (般核娑 - jackfruit) and *nārikela* (那羅雞羅 - coconut) trees, they are considered very precious. Rivers, lakes, and ponds encircle the cities and towns. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are short in stature and dark in complexion. Their language differs slightly from that of Central India. Their nature is very fierce and impetuous, but they are determined to study diligently. They revere and serve the heavenly gods and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, from the time the Buddha appeared until the present, no monasteries have been built to gather monks. Those who have pure faith only pay homage in secret. There are several hundred deva temples and tens of thousands of non-Buddhists. The reigning king is a descendant of the god Nārāyaṇa and belongs to the Brahman caste; his name is Bhāskaravarman (婆塞羯羅伐摩) (in the language of Tang, "Sun-Armor"), and his title is Kumāra (拘摩羅) (in the language of Tang, "Youth"). Since he first occupied this territory, his family has ruled for a thousand generations down to the present king. The king is fond of learning, and the common people follow his example; men of high talent from distant lands, admiring his righteousness, come to travel as his guests. Although he does not sincerely believe in the Buddha-dharma, he respects learned śramaṇas. Previously, having heard that a śramaṇa from the country of Cīna (至那國) was at the Nālandā (那爛陀) Monastery in Magadha, having come from afar to study the profound Dharma of the Buddha, the king sent cordial invitations back and forth three times, but the monk had not yet complied with the request. At that time, the Master of Treatises Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) said, "If you wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness, you must propagate the True Dharma. You should go; do not fear the long journey. The family of King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) has followed non-Buddhist paths for generations, and his invitation to a śramaṇa is a virtuous deed. If he changes his course because of this, the benefits will be vast and far-reaching. You previously aroused a great mind and made a grand vow, wishing to travel alone to foreign lands, casting aside your body to seek the Dharma and universally save all sentient beings—how could this be limited to your own country? You should forget about gain and loss, disregard honor and disgrace, propagate the holy teachings, enlighten the deluded, put others before yourself, and forget personal fame to spread the Dharma."  Thereupon, being unable to decline, he accompanied the envoy and went to meet him. King Kumāra said, "Although I am without talent, I have always admired those of high learning. Having heard of your fame and noble character, I ventured to invite you." He replied, "I am of little ability and narrow wisdom, yet I have undeservedly received your attention."  King Kumāra said, "Excellent! You admire the Dharma and love learning, regarding your own body as light as a feather, crossing heavy dangers to travel far to foreign lands. This is the source of royal transformation and the reason why the customs of your country value learning. Now, in all the countries of India, there are many who sing the 'Music of the King of Qin Breaking the Battle Lines' (秦王破陣樂) of the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國); I have heard it for a long time. Is this not the country of the Great Virtuous One?" He replied, "Indeed, this song praises the virtues of my sovereign."  King Kumāra said, "I did not realize that you, Great Virtuous One, were a man of this country. I have always admired its refined culture and have long looked toward the East, but as the mountains and rivers block the way, I have had no means to go there myself." I replied, "The sacred virtues of our great monarch spread far and wide, and his benevolent influence reaches distant lands; those from foreign regions with different customs who come to the imperial palace to pay homage and declare themselves subjects are numerous indeed." King Kumāra said, "Since his grace covers all like heaven and earth, I have long hoped to send tribute. Now King Śīlāditya (戒日王) is in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國), where he is about to hold a great almsgiving to cultivate merit and wisdom; all the Śramaṇas and Brahmins of the five Indias who possess learning have been summoned to assemble. He has now sent an envoy to invite me, and I wish for you to travel with me." I therefore went with him.  In the eastern part of this country, mountains and hills are interconnected, and there are no large capital cities; as its borders adjoin the Southwest Yi (西南夷), its people resemble the Man (蠻) and Lao (獠) tribes. I inquired in detail about the local customs and learned that one could reach the southwestern borders of Shu (蜀) in about two months' travel; however, the mountains and rivers are treacherous and obstructed, the mountain mists are noxious, and poisonous snakes and herbs cause great harm. In the southeast of the country, wild elephants roam in violent herds, which is why the elephant corps of this country is particularly numerous.

t2087_text: 從此南行千二三百里，至三摩呾吒國（東印度境）。三摩呾吒國，周三千餘里。濱近大海，地遂卑濕。國大都城周二十餘里。稼穡滋植，花菓繁茂。氣序和，風俗順。人性剛烈，形卑色黑，好學勤勵，邪正兼信。伽藍三十餘所，僧徒二千餘人，並皆遵習上座部學。天祠百所，異道雜居，露形尼乾，其徒甚盛。去城不遠有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。昔者如來為諸天、人於此七日說深妙法。傍有四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。去此不遠，伽藍中有青玉佛像，其高八尺，相好圓備，靈應時効。從此東北大海濱山谷中，有室利差呾羅國。次東南大海隅有迦摩浪迦國。次東有墮羅鉢底國。次東有伊賞那補羅國。次東有摩訶瞻波國，即此云林邑是也。次西南有閻摩那洲國。凡此六國，山川道阻，不入其境，然風俗壤，界聲聞可知。
translation: From here, traveling south for one thousand two hundred or one thousand three hundred li, one reaches the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) (in the territory of eastern India). The country of Samataṭa is more than three thousand li in circuit. It borders the great ocean, and the land is low and damp. The great capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are lush and the flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is temperate and the customs are harmonious. The people are fierce by nature, short in stature, and dark in complexion; they are diligent in learning and believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over two thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together, and the naked Nirgrantha ascetics are particularly numerous. Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the profound and wonderful Dharma here for seven days for the sake of devas and humans. Nearby are the sites of the four Buddhas' sitting and walking meditation. Not far from this, in a saṃghārāma, there is a green jade Buddha image eight feet high, with all the physical marks perfectly complete, which frequently manifests miraculous responses.  From here, to the northeast, in a valley by the seaside, is the country of Śrīkṣetra (室利差呾羅國). Next, to the southeast, in a corner of the great ocean, is the country of Kamalāṅkā (迦摩浪迦國). Next, to the east, is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國). Next, to the east, is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國). Next, to the east, is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國), which is what is called Linyi (林邑) here. Next, to the southwest, is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the mountains and rivers make the roads difficult, so I did not enter their borders; however, their customs and territories can be known by hearsay.

t2087_text: 自三摩呾吒國西行九百餘里，至耽摩栗底國（東印度境）。耽摩栗底國，周千四五百里。國大都城周十餘里。濱近海垂，土地卑濕。稼穡時播，花菓茂盛。氣序溫暑，風俗躁烈。人性剛勇，邪正兼信。伽藍十餘所，僧眾千餘人。天祠五十餘所，異道雜居。國濱海隅，水陸交會，奇珍異寶，多聚此國，故其國人大抵殷富。城側窣堵波，無憂王所建也。其傍則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: Traveling west from the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) for over nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Tāmraliptī (耽摩栗底國) (within the borders of East India). The country of Tāmraliptī is about one thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. It is situated near the edge of the sea; the land is low and damp. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are courageous and brave, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas and over one thousand monks. There are more than fifty deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. As the country is situated on a sea corner where water and land routes meet, rare and precious treasures are gathered here in abundance, and for this reason, the people of the country are generally wealthy. Beside the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

t2087_text: 自此西北行七百餘里，至羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國（東印度境）。羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國，周四千四五百里。國大都城周二十餘里。居人殷盛，家室富饒。土地下濕，稼穡時播，眾花滋茂，珍菓繁植。氣序調暢，風俗淳和。好尚學藝，邪正兼信。伽藍十餘所，僧徒二千餘人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠五十餘所，異道寔多。別有三伽藍，不食乳酪，遵提婆達多遺訓也。
translation: From here, traveling northwest for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) (in the territory of East India). The country of Karṇasuvarṇa is four thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and the households are wealthy. The land is low and damp; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and various flowers and precious fruits grow in abundance. The climate is temperate and the customs are honest and harmonious. The people value learning and the arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. There are more than fifty Deva temples, and the number of non-Buddhists is very large. Separately, there are three monasteries where the monks do not consume milk or cream, following the legacy of Devadatta.

t2087_text: 大城側有絡多未知僧伽藍（唐言赤泥）。庭宇顯敞，臺閣崇峻。國中高才達學、聰敏有聞者，咸集其中，警誡相成，琢磨道德。初，此國未信佛法時，南印度有一外道，腹錮銅鍱，首戴明炬，杖策高步，來入此城，振擊論鼓，求欲談議。或者問曰：「首腹何異？」曰：「吾學藝多能，恐腹拆裂；悲諸愚闇，所以持照。」時經旬日，人無問者，詢訪髦彥，莫有異人。王曰：「合境之內，豈無明哲？客難不酬，為國深恥。宜更營求，訪諸幽隱。」或曰：「大林中有異人，其自稱曰沙門，強學是務，今屏居幽寂，久矣于茲，非夫體法合德，何能若此者乎？」王聞之，躬往請焉。沙門對曰：「我，南印度人也，客遊止此，學業膚淺，恐黜所聞。敢承來旨，不復固辭。論議無負，請建伽藍，招集僧徒，光讚佛法。」王曰：「敬聞，不敢忘德。」沙門受請，往赴論場。外道於是誦其宗致，三萬餘言。其義遠，其文約，苞含名相，網羅視聽。沙門一聞究覽，辭義無謬，以數百言，辯而釋之，因問宗致。外道辭窮理屈，杜口不酬。既折其名，負恥而退。王深敬德，建此伽藍，自時厥後，方弘法教。伽藍側不遠有窣堵波，無憂王所建也，在昔如來於此七日說法開導。其側精舍，過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。有數窣堵波，並是如來說法之處，無憂王之所建也。
translation: Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttikā Monastery (絡多未知僧伽藍) (in Chinese, "Red Clay"). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its towers and pavilions are lofty and steep. The highly talented and profoundly learned scholars of the country, as well as those of renowned intelligence, all assemble therein to assist one another through mutual admonition and to cultivate their morality and virtue.  Formerly, before this country believed in the Buddha-dharma, there was a heretic from South India who bound his belly with copper plates, wore a bright torch upon his head, and, leaning on a staff, walked with proud strides into this city, where he struck the drum of debate and sought to engage in discussion. Someone asked him, "Why do you wear a torch on your head and plates on your belly?" He replied, "My learning and skills are so vast that I fear my belly might burst; I pity the ignorance of others, which is why I carry this light."  Ten days passed, and no one came to question him. They inquired among the eminent and wise, but there was no one who could match him. The king said, "Within the borders of this realm, can there be no wise and enlightened men? To leave a guest's challenge unanswered is a deep shame for the country. We should search further and inquire among those living in seclusion."  Someone said, "In the great forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa; he is dedicated to arduous study and has lived here in quiet seclusion for a long time. Were he not one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he live like this?"  The king heard this and went in person to invite him. The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man of South India staying here as a traveler; my learning is superficial, and I fear I may fall short of what you have heard. However, I dare to accept your command and will no longer firmly decline. If I am not defeated in the debate, I request that you build a monastery, gather monks together, and glorify and promote the Buddha-dharma." The king said, "I respectfully hear your words and dare not forget your virtue." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to the site of the debate. The non-Buddhist then recited his tenets, totaling more than thirty thousand words. Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, capturing the sight and hearing of the audience. The śramaṇa, having heard them once, comprehended them completely, without error in wording or meaning, and with a few hundred words, he debated and refuted them, then questioned the non-Buddhist on his tenets. The non-Buddhist, his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, sealed his mouth and could not respond. Having been refuted in his reputation, he retreated in shame. The king deeply respected the śramaṇa’s virtue and built this monastery; from that time thereafter, the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated. Not far from the side of the monastery is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王); in the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. Beside it is a *vihāra* (精舍), the place where the past four Buddhas left traces of sitting and walking in meditation. There are several stūpas, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and they were built by King Aśoka.

translation: Traveling southwest from here for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Uḍra (烏荼國) (in the region of East India). The country of Uḍra is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit. The land is rich and fertile, and the crops and grains grow luxuriantly; all kinds of fruits are much larger than in other countries, and the exotic grasses and famous flowers are difficult to describe. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and impetuous. The people are tall and robust in appearance, and their complexions are dark. Their speech and mannerisms differ from those of Central India. They are diligent in learning and mostly believe in the Buddhadharma; there are more than one hundred saṃghārāmas and over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are fifty deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are more than ten stūpas in total, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and were built by King Aśoka.

translation: In the great mountains on the southwestern border of the kingdom is the Puṣpagiri (補澁波祇釐) monastery. Its stone stūpa possesses many spiritual anomalies; sometimes, on fast days, it emits a bright light. Therefore, the pure-hearted faithful, from both near and far, all gather there, holding exquisite flower canopies and vying to perform offerings. Below the dew-receiving basin and above the inverted-bowl structure, if one places the handle of a flower canopy, it remains fixed there as if a magnet were attracting a needle.

translation: On the southeastern border of the country, facing the coast of the great ocean, is the city of Caritra (折利呾羅城; translated in Chinese as "Departure"). It is over twenty *li* in circuit and serves as a thoroughfare and stopping place for seafaring merchants and travelers from distant lands. The city is solid and steep, and it contains many rare treasures. Outside the city, five monasteries stand in a row; their terraces and pavilions are lofty, and the sacred images are exquisitely crafted. To the south, the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over twenty thousand *li* away; gazing into the distance on a quiet night, one can see the light of the precious pearl atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa of that land, shining clearly like a torch suspended in the air.

t2087_text: 自此西南大林中行千二百餘里，至恭御陀國（東印度境）。恭御陀國，周千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。濱近海隅，山阜隱軫，土地墊濕，稼穡時播。氣序溫暑，風俗勇烈。其形偉，其貌黑。粗有禮義，不甚欺詐。至於文字，同中印度，語言風調，頗有異焉。崇敬外道，不信佛法。天祠百餘所，異道萬餘人。國境之內，數十小城，接山嶺，據海交，城既堅峻，兵又敢勇，威雄隣境，遂無強敵。國臨海濱，多有奇寶，螺貝珠璣，斯為貨用。出大青象，超乘致遠。
translation: From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than one thousand two hundred li, one reaches the country of Koṅgoda (恭御陀國) (in the region of East India). The country of Koṅgoda is more than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. It borders the seashore; the mountains and hills are rugged and undulating, the land is low and damp, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are bold and fierce. Their stature is large, and their complexion is black. They possess a rough sense of propriety and righteousness, and are not very deceitful. As for their writing, it is the same as that of Central India, but their language and manner of speech differ considerably. They revere non-Buddhist sects and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. There are more than one hundred Deva temples and over ten thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. Within the borders of the country, there are several dozen small towns situated near mountain ranges and occupying the junctions of sea routes. The city walls are strong and steep, and the soldiers are brave and daring; their power dominates the neighboring lands, and thus they have no formidable enemies. The country borders the sea, and there are many rare treasures; conch shells, pearls, and precious stones are used as currency. They produce large dark-colored elephants, which are capable of traveling long distances when ridden.

t2087_text: 從此西南入大荒野，深林巨木，干霄蔽日，行千四五百里，至羯𩜁（力甑反）伽國（南印度境）。羯𩜁伽國，周五千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。稼穡時播，花果具繁，林藪聯綿，動數百里。出青野象，隣國所奇。氣序暑熱，風俗躁暴，性多狷獷，志存信義。言語輕捷，音調質正，辭旨風則，頗與中印度異焉。少信正法，多遵外道，伽藍十餘所，僧徒五百餘人，習學大乘上座部法。天祠百餘所，異道甚眾，多是尼乾之徒也。羯𩜁伽國在昔之時，民俗殷盛，肩摩轂擊，舉袂成帷。有五通仙棲巖養素，人或陵觸，退失神通，以惡呪術殘害國人，少長無遺，賢愚俱喪。人煙斷絕，多歷年所，頗漸遷居，猶未充實，故今此國人戶尚少。城南不遠有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。傍有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: From here, traveling southwest into a vast wilderness with deep forests and giant trees that reached the sky and obscured the sun, one proceeds for one thousand four or five hundred *li* to the country of Kaliṅga (羯𩜁伽國) (𩜁 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 力甑) (in the region of South India). The country of Kaliṅga is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant; forests and marshes stretch continuously for hundreds of *li*. It produces dark wild elephants, which are prized by neighboring countries. The climate is hot, and the customs are impetuous and violent; the people are by nature impatient and fierce, yet they value faith and righteousness. Their speech is rapid and light, their tone is simple and direct, and their diction and style are quite different from those of Central India. Few believe in the true Dharma, and most follow non-Buddhist paths. There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than one hundred *deva* temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is very great, most of whom are followers of the Nirgrantha. In former times, the country of Kaliṅga was prosperous and densely populated, with shoulders rubbing and wheel hubs clashing, and the raising of sleeves would form a curtain. A sage possessing the five supernatural powers was dwelling in the rocks and cultivating purity; because people insulted and provoked him, he lost his supernatural powers and used evil spells to slaughter the people of the country, leaving no one, young or old, and destroying both the wise and the foolish. Human habitation was cut off for many years. Gradually, people have moved back, but it is still not fully populated; therefore, the number of households in this country is currently small. Not far south of the city is a *stūpa* more than one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas.
