t2087_text: 自此西北山林中行千八百餘里，至憍薩羅國（中印度境）。憍薩羅國，周六千餘里，山嶺周境，林藪連接。國大都城周四十餘里。土壤膏腴，地利滋盛。邑里相望，人戶殷實。其形偉，其色黑。風俗剛猛，人性勇烈。邪正兼信，學藝高明。王，剎帝利也。崇敬佛法，仁慈深遠。伽藍百餘所，僧徒減萬人，並皆習學大乘法教。天祠七十餘所，異道雜居。城南不遠有故伽藍，傍有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。昔者，如來曾於此處現大神通，摧伏外道。後龍猛菩薩止此伽藍，時此國王號娑多婆訶（唐言引正）。珍敬龍猛，周衛門廬。時提婆菩薩自執師子國來求論義，謂門者曰：「幸為通謁。」時門者遂為白。龍猛雅知其名，盛滿鉢水，命弟子曰：「汝持是水，示彼提婆。」提婆見水，默而投針。弟子持鉢，懷疑而返。龍猛曰：「彼何辭乎？」對曰：「默無所說，但投針於水而已。」龍猛曰：「智矣哉，若人也！知幾其神，察微亞聖，盛德若此，宜速命入。」對曰：「何謂也？無言妙辯，斯之是歟？」曰：「夫水也者，隨器方圓，逐物清濁，彌漫無間，澄湛莫測。滿而示之，比我學之智周也；彼乃投針，遂窮其極。此非常人，宜速召進。」而龍猛風範懍然肅物，言談者皆伏抑首。提婆素挹風徽，久希請益，方欲受業，先騁機神，雅懼威嚴，昇堂僻坐，談玄永日，辭義清高。龍猛曰：「後學冠世，妙辯光前，我惟衰耄，遇斯俊彥，誠乃寫瓶有寄，傳燈不絕，法教弘揚，伊人是賴。幸能前席，雅談玄奧。」提婆聞命，心獨自負，將開義府，先遊辯囿，提振辭端，仰視質義。忽覩威顏，忘言杜口，避坐引責，遂請受業。龍猛曰：「復坐，今將授子至真妙理，法王誠教。」提婆五體投地，一心歸命，曰：「而今而後，敢聞命矣。」龍猛菩薩善閑藥術，飡餌養生，壽年數百，志貌不衰。引正王既得妙藥，壽亦數百。王有稚子，謂其母曰：「如我何時得嗣王位？」母曰：「以今觀之，未有期也。父王年壽已數百歲，子孫老終者蓋亦多矣。斯皆龍猛福力所加，藥術所致。菩薩寂滅，王必殂落。夫龍猛菩薩智慧弘遠，慈悲深厚，周給群有，身命若遺。汝宜往彼，試從乞頭，若遂此志，當果所願。」王子恭承母命，來至伽藍，門者敬懼，故得入焉。時龍猛菩薩方讚誦經行，忽見王子，佇而謂曰：「今夕何因，降跡僧坊，若危若懼，疾驅而至？」對曰：「我承慈母餘論，語及行捨之士，以為含生寶命，經語格言，未有輕捨報身，施諸求欲。我慈母曰：『不然。十方善逝，三世如來，在昔發心，逮乎證果，勤求佛道，修習戒忍。或投身𩚅獸，或割肌救鴿，月光王施婆羅門頭，慈力王飲餓藥叉血，諸若此類，羌難備舉。求之先覺，何代無人？』今龍猛菩薩篤斯高志，我有所求，人頭為用，招募累歲，未之有捨。欲行暴劫殺，則罪累尤多，虐害無辜，穢德彰顯。惟菩薩修習聖道，遠期佛果，慈霑有識，惠及無邊，輕生若浮，賤身如朽，不違本願，垂允所求！」龍猛曰：「俞，誠哉是言也！我求佛聖果，我學佛能捨，是身如響，是身如泡，流轉四生，去來六趣，宿契弘誓，不違物欲。然王子！有一不可者，其將若何？我身既終，汝父亦喪，顧斯為意，誰能濟之？」龍猛俳佪顧視，求所絕命，以乾茅葉自刎其頸，若利劍斷割，身首異處。王子見已，驚奔而去。門者上白，具陳始末，王聞哀感，果亦命終。
translation: From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for over 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Kosala is over 6,000 li in circumference, with mountain ranges encircling its borders and forests and marshes connected throughout. The capital city of the country is over 40 li in circumference. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is highly productive. Villages and hamlets look out upon one another, and the households are prosperous and substantial. The people are large in stature and dark in complexion. Their customs are fierce and impetuous, and their nature is brave and violent. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they are highly skilled in the arts. The king is a Kṣatriya. He reveres the Buddha-Dharma and is deeply compassionate and far-reaching in his benevolence. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, and the number of monks is just under ten thousand; all of them study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are over seventy Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this place to subdue non-Buddhists. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶) (in Chinese, "Leading the Righteous"). He cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, and he guarded the gates of his residence. At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) to seek a debate, and he said to the gatekeeper, "I would be grateful if you would announce my visit." The gatekeeper then went to report this. Nāgārjuna, already well aware of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and instructed his disciple, saying, "Take this water and show it to that Deva." When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it. The disciple took the bowl and returned, feeling puzzled. Nāgārjuna asked, "What did he say?" The disciple replied, "He said nothing, but merely dropped a needle into the water." Nāgārjuna said, "How wise he is, this man! To know the subtle is divine; to perceive the minute is to be second only to a sage. With such great virtue, he should be invited in immediately." The disciple asked, "What does this mean? Is this what you call the marvelous eloquence of silence?" Nāgārjuna said, "Water takes the shape of its container, whether square or round; it adapts to the purity or turbidity of its surroundings; it permeates everywhere without gaps, and its clarity is unfathomable. I showed him the bowl filled to the brim to signify that my learning is complete; he dropped a needle into it, thereby exhausting its depths. This is no ordinary person; he should be summoned at once." Nāgārjuna’s demeanor was awe-inspiring and commanded respect; all who spoke with him would bow their heads in submission. Deva had long admired his reputation and had long hoped to request instruction. Just as he was about to become a student, he first wished to display his own keen intellect, yet he was also intimidated by Nāgārjuna’s majesty. He ascended the hall, sat to one side, and they discussed the profound mysteries all day long, their discourse clear and lofty. Nāgārjuna said, "Your scholarship surpasses the world and your brilliant eloquence outshines your predecessors. I am but a feeble old man, and meeting such a talented youth truly allows me to pour the contents of my vessel into another and keep the lamp of transmission burning without end; the propagation of the Dharma depends on such a person. I hope you will move to the front seat so that we may discuss the profound mysteries." Upon hearing this command, Deva, who had been confident in his own mind, prepared to open the storehouse of his arguments and first roam the garden of debate. He raised his points and looked up to challenge the meaning, but suddenly catching sight of Nāgārjuna’s majestic countenance, he forgot his words and fell silent. He moved his seat back, acknowledged his fault, and requested to become his student. Nāgārjuna said, "Sit down again. I shall now bestow upon you the most perfect and wonderful truth, the authentic teaching of the Dharma King." Deva prostrated himself, his five limbs touching the ground, and with a single mind surrendered his life, saying, "From this moment on, I dare to follow your instructions." Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was well-versed in the arts of medicine; by consuming elixirs to nourish his life, he lived for several hundred years, his spirit and appearance showing no signs of decline. The king, Sātavāhana (引正王), having obtained the wonderful medicine, also lived for several hundred years. The king had a young son who said to his mother, "At this rate, when will I ever be able to succeed to the throne?" His mother replied, "Judging by the present situation, there is no prospect. Your father the king has already lived for several hundred years, and many of his descendants have already grown old and died. This is all due to the power of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medical arts. If the Bodhisattva were to pass away, the king would surely perish. Now, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva possesses vast wisdom and profound compassion; he provides for all living beings and regards his own life as something to be cast aside. You should go to him and try to beg for his head. If you can fulfill this intention, your wish will be granted." The prince respectfully obeyed his mother’s command and came to the monastery; the gatekeepers were awestruck and fearful, so he was able to enter. At that time, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was chanting and walking in meditation. Suddenly seeing the prince, he stopped and asked, "For what reason have you come to the monastery this evening, appearing so anxious and fearful, and rushing here in such haste?" The prince replied, "I have received the words of my compassionate mother, which touched upon those who practice the virtue of giving. I had thought that for all living beings, life is a precious treasure, and that in the words and maxims of the scriptures, there has never been anyone who lightly cast aside their physical body to bestow it upon those who seek it. But my compassionate mother said: 'It is not so. The Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three ages, from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced the precepts and forbearance. Some threw their bodies to feed hungry beasts, some cut their flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin, and King Maitrībala gave his blood to satisfy hungry Yakṣas; examples such as these are truly difficult to enumerate fully. In seeking the sages of the past, what age has been without such people?' Now, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) is firm in his noble ambitions. I have a request for a human head to use, but though I have sought one for many years, no one has yet offered theirs. If I were to commit a violent robbery and murder, the burden of my sins would be all the greater; to cruelly harm the innocent would make my defiled virtue manifest. Only you, Bodhisattva, who practice the holy path and look toward the distant fruit of Buddhahood, whose compassion moistens all sentient beings and whose kindness reaches the boundless, treat life as lightly as a floating bubble and hold your body as cheaply as rotten wood. Do not violate your original vow, but grant what I request!" Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are indeed true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood and I learn from the Buddha the ability to renounce all. This body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble; it circulates through the four types of birth and comes and goes through the six realms. Bound by a long-standing great vow, I will not oppose the desires of living beings. However, Prince, there is one thing that is not possible; what shall be done about it? Once my body is finished, your father will also perish. Considering this, who could save him?" Nāgārjuna paced about and looked around, seeking a way to end his life. He cut his own throat with a blade of dry cogon grass as if with a sharp sword, and his head was severed from his body. Seeing this, the prince was terrified and fled. The gatekeeper went up and reported the matter, detailing the beginning and the end; upon hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and, as a result, he also passed away.

t2087_text: 國西南三百餘里至跋邏末羅耆釐山（唐言黑蜂）。岌然特起，峯巖峭險，既無崖谷，宛如全石。引正王為龍猛菩薩鑿此山中，建立伽藍。去山十數里，鑿開孔道，當其山下，仰鑿疏石。其中則長廊步簷，崇臺重閣，閣有五層，層有四院，竝建精舍，各鑄金像，量等佛身，妙窮工思，自餘莊嚴，唯飾金寶。從山高峯臨注飛泉，周流重閣，交帶廊廡。疎寮外穴，明燭中宇。初，引正王建此伽藍也，人力疲竭，府庫空虛，功猶未半，心甚憂慼。龍猛謂曰：「大王何故若有憂負？」王曰：「輒運大心，敢樹勝福，期之永固，待至慈氏。功績未成，財用已竭，每懷此恨，坐而待旦。」龍猛曰：「勿憂。崇福勝善，其利不窮，有興弘願，無憂不濟。今日還宮，當極歡樂，後晨出遊，歷覽山野，已而至此，平議營建。」王既受誨，奉以周旋。龍猛菩薩以神妙藥，滴諸大石，竝變為金。王遊見金，心口相賀，迴駕至龍猛所曰：「今日畋遊，神鬼所惑，山林之中，時見金聚。」龍猛曰：「非鬼惑也。至誠所感，故有此金，宜時取用，濟成勝業。」遂以營建，功畢有餘。於是五層之中，各鑄四大金像，餘尚盈積，充諸帑藏。招集千僧，居中禮誦。龍猛菩薩以釋迦佛所宣教法，及諸菩薩所演述論，鳩集部別，藏在其中。故上第一層唯置佛像及諸經論，下第五層居止淨人、資產、什物，中間三層僧徒所舍。聞諸先志曰：引正王營建已畢，計工人所食鹽價，用九拘胝（拘胝者，唐言億）金錢。其後僧徒忿諍，就王平議。時諸淨人更相謂曰：「僧徒諍起，言議相乖，凶人伺隙，毀壞伽藍。」於是重閣反拒，以擯僧徒。自爾已來，無復僧眾。遠矚山巖，莫知門徑。時引善醫方者入中療疾，蒙面入出，不識其路。
translation: Three hundred or more li southwest of the country, one arrives at the mountain of Bhramaragiri (跋邏末羅耆釐山) (in Chinese, "Black Bee"). It rises abruptly and loftily, with precipitous peaks and cliffs; having neither slopes nor valleys, it appears to be a single solid rock. King Sātavāhana (引正王) excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) to establish a monastery (saṃghārāma). Ten or more li from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated; directly beneath the mountain, they carved upward into the rock. Within it are long corridors and eaves, lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions; the pavilions have five tiers, and each tier has four courtyards, all containing shrines (精舍) where golden images of the Buddha's size have been cast with exquisite craftsmanship, while the remaining decorations consist entirely of gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, a waterfall pours down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and verandas. Windows open through to the outside, letting light illuminate the interior. Initially, when King Sātavāhana was building this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; with the work not yet half finished, his heart was filled with deep sorrow. Nāgārjuna said to him, "Great King, why are you so burdened with worry?" The king replied, "I have given rise to a great aspiration and ventured to establish a supreme field of merit, hoping it would remain firm forever until the coming of Maitreya (慈氏). With the work not yet finished and the financial resources exhausted, I am constantly filled with this regret, sitting and waiting for the dawn." Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry. The merit of cultivating such supreme goodness is inexhaustible; if one has raised a vast vow, there is no worry that it will not be fulfilled. Return to the palace today and enjoy yourself to the fullest; tomorrow morning, go out for an excursion, travel through the mountains and fields, and then come here to discuss the construction." The king, having received these instructions, followed them accordingly. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) used a miraculous medicine, dripping it onto large rocks, which all turned into gold. When the king saw the gold during his excursion, he rejoiced in his heart and words; he drove his carriage back to Nāgārjuna’s place and said, "During my outing today, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts, for I repeatedly saw heaps of gold amidst the mountains and forests." Nāgārjuna replied, "It was not a delusion of ghosts. It is the result of your utmost sincerity that this gold has appeared. You should take and use it immediately to complete your noble undertaking." He then proceeded with the construction, and when the work was finished, there was still a surplus. Thereupon, in each of the five tiers, he cast four large golden statues, and the remainder was still abundant, filling the treasuries. He summoned one thousand monks to reside within and perform rites and recitations. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected and classified the teachings proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha and the treatises composed by various Bodhisattvas, storing them within. Thus, the first tier at the top housed only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the fifth tier at the bottom was for the residence of lay servants (淨人) and the storage of property and miscellaneous goods; and the three middle tiers were the lodgings for the monks. I have heard from the records of former sages that after King Sātavāhana had completed the construction, the cost of salt consumed by the workers was calculated to be nine koṭis (koṭi is, in Chinese, 億, a hundred million) of gold coins. Thereafter, the monks fell into disputes and went to the king to seek arbitration. At that time, the lay servants said to one another, "Since a quarrel has arisen among the monks and their arguments are contradictory, evil men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery." Consequently, they barred the heavy doors to exclude the monks. From that time on, there has been no monastic community there. Looking at the mountain cliffs from afar, one cannot discern any gate or path. At times, those skilled in medical arts were brought inside to treat illnesses; they were blindfolded upon entering and exiting, and thus did not recognize the route.

t2087_text: 從此大林中南行九百餘里，至案達羅國（南印度境）。案達羅國，周三千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里，號瓶耆羅。土地良沃，稼穡豐盛。氣序溫暑，風俗猛暴。語言辭調異中印度，至於文字，軌則大同。伽藍二十餘所，僧徒三千餘人。天祠三十餘所，異道寔多。瓶耆羅城側不遠有大伽藍，重閣層臺，製窮剞劂，佛像聖容，麗極工思。伽藍前有石窣堵波，高數百尺，並阿折羅（唐言所行）阿羅漢之所建也。所行羅漢伽藍西南不遠有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，如來在昔於此說法，現大神通，度無量眾。
translation: From here, traveling south through a great forest for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the country of Āndhra (案達羅國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Āndhra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit and is named Vengīpura (瓶耆羅). The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of Central India, but as for their written characters, the rules are largely the same. There are more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks. There are more than thirty Deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous. Not far from the side of Vengīpura city is a large monastery with multi-storied pavilions and layered terraces, the craftsmanship of which exhausts the possibilities of carving; the sacred images of the Buddhas are of exquisite and ingenious design. In front of the monastery is a stone stūpa, several hundred feet high; both were built by the Arhat Ācāra (阿折羅) (in Chinese, "Conduct"). Not far to the southwest of the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 所行羅漢伽藍西南行二十餘里，至孤山，山嶺有石窣堵波，陳那（唐言授）菩薩於此作《因明論》。陳那菩薩者，佛去世後，承風染衣。智願廣大，慧力深固，愍世無依，思弘聖教。以為因明之論，言深理廣，學者虛功，難以成業，乃匿迹幽巖，拪神寂定，觀述作之利害，審文義之繁約。是時崖谷震響，煙雲變釆，山神捧菩薩高數百尺，唱如是言：「昔佛世尊善權導物，以慈悲心，說《因明論》，綜括妙理，深究微言。如來寂滅，大義泯絕。今者，陳那菩薩福智悠遠，深達聖旨，因明之論，重弘茲日。」菩薩乃放大光明，照燭幽昧。時此國王深生尊敬，見此光明相，疑入金剛定，因請菩薩證無生果。陳那曰：「吾入定觀察，欲釋深經，心期正覺，非願無生果也。」王曰：「無生之果，眾聖欣仰，斷三界欲，洞三明智，斯盛事也，願疾證之。」陳那是時心悅王請，方欲證受無學聖果。時妙吉祥菩薩知而惜焉，欲相警誡，乃彈指悟之，而告曰：「惜哉！如何捨廣大心，為狹劣志，從獨善之懷，棄兼濟之願？欲為善利，當廣傳說慈氏菩薩所製《瑜伽師地論》，導誘後學，為利甚大。」陳那菩薩敬受指誨，奉以周旋。於是覃思沈研，廣因明論。猶恐學者懼其文微辭約也，乃舉其大義，綜其微言，作《因門論》，以導後進。自茲已後，宣暢瑜伽，盛業門人，有知當世。
translation: Traveling more than twenty *li* southwest from the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra, one reaches a solitary hill. On the mountain ridge is a stone *stūpa* where the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) (in Chinese, "Bestowed") composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic). As for the Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed away, he followed the tradition and donned the dyed robes. His wisdom and vows were vast and great, and his power of discernment was deep and firm. Pitying the world for having no refuge, he contemplated how to propagate the sacred teachings. Considering that the treatises on logic were profound in language and extensive in reasoning, such that students labored in vain and found it difficult to achieve success, he hid his traces in secluded cliffs and settled his spirit in silent meditation, examining the merits and demerits of past works and scrutinizing the verbosity and conciseness of their meanings. At that time, the cliffs and valleys shook and echoed, the mist and clouds changed color, and a mountain god lifted the Bodhisattva up several hundred feet, proclaiming: "In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guided sentient beings through skillful means and, with a compassionate heart, preached the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, encompassing wonderful principles and investigating subtle words to their depths. Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the great meaning has been cut off. Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, and who deeply understands the sacred intent, shall once again propagate the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* on this day." The Bodhisattva then emitted a great light, illuminating the darkness. At that time, the king of this country felt deep respect; seeing this manifestation of light, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the *vajra-samādhi* and therefore requested that the Bodhisattva certify the fruit of non-arising. Dignāga said: "I have entered meditation to observe and wish to explain the profound scriptures; my heart is set on perfect enlightenment, not on the fruit of non-arising." The king said: "The fruit of non-arising is something all sages admire; it severs the desires of the three realms and provides mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge—this is a magnificent achievement, and I hope you will realize it quickly." At that time, Dignāga (陳那) was pleased by the king’s request and was about to realize and accept the holy fruit of the *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning). At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (妙吉祥菩薩) knew of this and felt it was a pity; wishing to warn him, he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said: "What a pity! How can you abandon the vast and great mind for a narrow and inferior intention, following a desire for individual salvation while discarding the vow to benefit others? If you wish to perform a virtuous benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論) composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) to guide and encourage later students; the benefit of this is truly great." The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction and followed it faithfully. Thereupon, he pondered deeply and researched extensively the treatises on *hetuvidyā* (logic). Fearing that students might be intimidated by the subtlety of the text and the conciseness of the language, he extracted the essential meanings and synthesized the profound words to compose the *Nyāyamukha* (因門論) in order to guide those who would come after. From this time forward, he propagated the *Yogācāra* (瑜伽), and his flourishing work and disciples were known throughout the world.

translation: From this forest and wilderness, traveling south for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Dhānakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國; also called the Great Andhra country; it is within the borders of South India). The country of Dhānakaṭaka is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than forty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. There is much wilderness and few settlements. The climate is warm and hot, and the people are dark in complexion. Their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they are fond of learning the arts. The monasteries are arranged like the scales of a fish, but they are already very desolate; those that remain number more than twenty, with over a thousand monks, all of whom mostly study the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There are more than a hundred Deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.

t2087_text: 城東據山有弗婆勢羅（唐言東山）僧伽藍，城西據山有阿伐羅勢羅（唐言西山）僧伽藍，此國先王為佛建焉。奠川通徑，疏崖峙閣，長廊步簷，枕巖接岫，靈神警衛，聖賢遊息。自佛寂滅，千年之內，每歲有千凡夫僧同入安居，其解安居日，皆證羅漢，以神通力凌虛而去；千年之後，凡、聖同居；自百餘年，無復僧侶，而山神易形，或作豺狼，或為猨狖，驚恐行人，以故空荒，閴無僧眾。
translation: To the east of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (弗婆勢羅) (in Chinese, "Eastern Mountain") Monastery; to the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) (in Chinese, "Western Mountain") Monastery. These were built for the Buddha by a former king of this country. The streams were regulated and paths opened, with pavilions perched upon cleared cliffs, and long corridors and covered walkways resting against the rocks and joining the peaks; they are guarded by divine spirits and frequented by sages and saints. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would gather each year to enter the summer retreat; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the air through their supernatural powers. After the millennium, ordinary and holy monks lived there together. For over a hundred years, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals and wolves, other times as apes and monkeys—to terrify travelers; for this reason, the place is desolate and devoid of any monastic community.

t2087_text: 城西據山有阿伐羅勢羅（唐言西山）僧伽藍，此國先王為佛建焉。奠川通徑，疏崖峙閣，長廊步簷，枕巖接岫，靈神警衛，聖賢遊息。自佛寂滅，千年之內，每歲有千凡夫僧同入安居，其解安居日，皆證羅漢，以神通力凌虛而去；千年之後，凡、聖同居；自百餘年，無復僧侶，而山神易形，或作豺狼，或為猨狖，驚恐行人，以故空荒，閴無僧眾。
translation: To the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) (in Chinese, "West Mountain") Monastery, which a former king of this country built for the Buddha. The stream was regulated and paths opened, with cliffs cleared to support pavilions, long corridors, and covered walkways, all resting against the crags and joining the peaks; divine spirits guard and protect it, and sages and saints have frequented it to rest. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would enter the summer retreat there together each year; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the void through their supernatural powers. After that millennium, ordinary monks and holy ones lived there together. For the past hundred years or so, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals or wolves, other times as apes or monkeys—to terrify travelers. For this reason, the place has become desolate and is devoid of any monastic community.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 城南不遠有大山巖，婆毘吠伽（唐言清辯）論師住阿素洛宮待見慈氏菩薩成佛之處。論師雅量弘遠，至德深邃，外示僧佉之服，內弘龍猛之學。聞摩揭陀國護法菩薩宣揚法教，學徒數千，有懷談議，杖錫而往。至波吒釐城，知護法菩薩在菩提樹，論師乃命門人曰：「汝行詣菩提樹護法菩薩所，如我辭曰：『菩薩宣揚遺教，導誘迷徒，仰德虛心，為日已久。然以宿願未果，遂乖禮謁。菩提樹者，誓不空見，見當有證，稱天人師。』」護法菩薩謂其使曰：「人世如幻，身命若浮，渴日勤誠，未遑談議。」人信往復，竟不會見。論師既還本土，靜而思曰：「非慈氏成佛，誰決我疑？」於觀自在菩薩像前誦《隨心陀羅尼》，絕粒飲水，時歷三歲。觀自在菩薩乃現妙色身，謂論師曰：「何所志乎？」對曰：「願留此身，待見慈氏。」觀自在菩薩曰：「人命危脆，世間浮幻，宜修勝善願，生覩史多天，於斯禮覲，尚速待見。」論師曰：「志不可奪，心不可貳。」菩薩曰：「若然者，宜往馱那羯磔迦國城南山巖執金剛神所，至誠誦持《執金剛陀羅尼》者，當遂此願。」論師於是往而誦焉。三歲之後，神乃謂曰：「伊何所願，若此勤勵？」論師曰：「願留此身，待見慈氏。觀自在菩薩指遣來請，成我願者，其在神乎？」神乃授祕方，而謂之曰：「此巖石內有阿素洛宮，如法行請，石壁當開，開即入中，可以待見。」論師曰：「幽居無覩，詎知佛興？」執金剛曰：「慈氏出世，我當相報。」論師受命，專精誦持，復歷三歲，初無異想，呪芥子以擊石，巖壁豁而洞開。是時百千萬眾觀覩忘返，論師跨其戶而告眾曰：「吾久祈請，待見慈氏，聖靈警祐，大願斯遂，宜可入此，同見佛興。」聞者怖駭，莫敢履戶，謂是毒蛇之窟，恐喪身命。再三告語，唯有六人從入。論師顧謝時眾，從容而入，入之既已，石壁還合，眾皆怨嗟，恨前言之過也。
translation: Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain crag, the place where the master of treatises Bhāviveka (婆毘吠伽) (in Chinese, Qingbian, "Clear Discrimination") resided in the palace of the Asuras, awaiting the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood. The master of treatises possessed a refined character that was vast and far-reaching, and his supreme virtue was profound and deep; outwardly he displayed the attire of the Sāṃkhya, while inwardly he promoted the teachings of Nāgārjuna. Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla in the country of Magadha was propagating the teachings of the Dharma and had several thousand students, he felt a desire to engage in discussion, so he took up his staff and set out. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi Tree. The master of treatises then instructed his disciple, saying: "Go to the place of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi Tree and convey my words as follows: 'The Bodhisattva propagates the bequeathed teachings and guides the deluded; I have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind. However, because my past vows have not yet been fulfilled, I have missed the opportunity to pay my respects. As for the Bodhi Tree, I vow not to see it in vain; when I see it, I shall attain realization and be called the Teacher of gods and men.'" The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger: "The human world is like an illusion, and life is like a floating bubble; all day long I strive earnestly and have no time for discussion." Messengers went back and forth, but they never met. After the master of treatises returned to his native land, he reflected in silence: "If Maitreya does not attain Buddhahood, who can resolve my doubts?" Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (隨心陀羅尼), abstaining from grain and drinking only water for a period of three years. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master of treatises: "What is your aspiration?" He replied, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya (慈氏)." Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "Human life is precarious and fragile, and the world is a floating illusion; you should cultivate superior and virtuous vows to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天), where you may pay homage and meet him more quickly." The master of treatises said, "My will cannot be swayed, and my heart cannot be divided." The Bodhisattva said, "If that is the case, you should go to the mountain cave south of the city of the country of Dhānyakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國) to the abode of the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛) deity; if you recite the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* (執金剛陀羅尼) with utmost sincerity, this vow shall be fulfilled." The master of treatises then went there and recited it. After three years, the deity asked him, "What is your wish, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The master of treatises said, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva directed me to come and request your aid; is it not in your power to fulfill my vow?" The deity then bestowed a secret method upon him and said, "Inside this rock is the Asura Palace (阿素洛宮); if you perform the ritual according to the Dharma and make your request, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, you may enter and wait there to see him." The master of treatises said, "If I dwell in seclusion and see nothing, how will I know when the Buddha has arisen?" The Vajrapāṇi deity replied, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you." The master of treatises accepted this instruction and practiced the recitation with focused intensity. After another three years had passed, without ever having a different thought, he enchanted mustard seeds and struck the rock with them; the stone wall suddenly split open. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched, forgetting to return home. The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd, "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏); through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step through the entrance, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

t2087_text: 自此西南行千餘里，至珠利耶國（南印度境）。珠利耶國，周二千四五百里。國大都城周十餘里。土野空曠，藪澤荒蕪。居戶寡少，群盜公行。氣序溫暑，風俗姦宄。人性獷烈，崇信外道。伽藍頹毀，粗有僧徒。天祠數十所，多露形外道也。城東南不遠有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔曾於此處現大神通，說深妙法，摧伏外道，度諸天人。城西不遠有故伽藍，提婆菩薩與羅漢論議之處。初，提婆菩薩聞此伽藍有嗢呾羅（唐言上）阿羅漢，得六神通，具八解脫，遂來遠尋，觀其風範。既至伽藍，投羅漢宿。羅漢少欲知足，唯置一床。提婆既至，無以為席，乃聚落葉，指令就坐。羅漢入定，夜分方出。提婆於是陳疑請決，羅漢隨難為釋，提婆尋聲重質，第七轉已，杜口不酬，竊運神通力，往覩史多天請問慈氏。慈氏為釋，因而告曰：「彼提婆者，曠劫修行，賢劫之中，當紹佛位，非爾所知，宜深禮敬。」如彈指頃，還復本座，乃復抑揚妙義，剖析微言。提婆謂曰：「此慈氏菩薩聖智之釋也，豈仁者所能詳究哉？」羅漢曰：「然，如來旨。」於是避席禮謝，深加敬歎。
translation: From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Cuḷya (珠利耶國) (in the region of South India). The country of Cuḷya is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference. The land is wild and desolate, with marshes and wastes. The population is sparse, and bands of robbers operate openly. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are treacherous. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. The monasteries are dilapidated, with only a few monks. There are several dozen *deva* temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. Not far to the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested great supernatural powers at this place, preached the profound and subtle Dharma, subdued the non-Buddhists, and saved various heavenly beings and humans. Not far to the west of the city is an old monastery, the place where the Bodhisattva Deva debated with an Arhat. Initially, the Bodhisattva Deva heard that there was an Arhat in this monastery named Uttara (*Uttara* is translated as "Superior" in Chinese), who had attained the six supernatural powers and was endowed with the eight emancipations; he therefore came from afar to seek him out and observe his demeanor. Upon arriving at the monastery, he requested to stay with the Arhat. The Arhat was of few desires and knew contentment, possessing only one bed. When Deva arrived, there was nothing to use as a seat, so he gathered fallen leaves and instructed him to sit upon them. The Arhat entered into meditation and did not emerge until midnight. Deva then presented his doubts and requested resolutions; the Arhat explained each difficulty as it was raised. Deva followed his words with repeated questioning, and by the seventh round, the Arhat remained silent and could not respond, so he secretly exercised his supernatural powers to go to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya. Maitreya (慈氏) provided the explanation and told him: "That Deva (提婆) has practiced for vast kalpas and shall succeed to the Buddha's throne during the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫); this is beyond your knowledge, and you should pay him deep respect." In the space of a finger-snap, he returned to his original seat, whereupon he expounded the wonderful meanings and analyzed the subtle words. Deva said to him: "This is the explanation from the holy wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva; how could it be something you have investigated thoroughly on your own?" The Arhat replied: "Indeed, it is the intent of the Tathāgata." Thereupon, he left his seat to offer thanks and expressed deep reverence and admiration.

t2087_text: 從此南入林野中，行千五六百里，至達羅毘荼國（南印度境）。達羅毘荼國，周六千餘里，國大都城號逮志補羅，周三十餘里。土地沃壤，稼穡豐盛，多花菓，出寶物。氣序溫暑，風俗勇烈。深篤信義，高尚博識，而語言、文字少異中印度。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，皆遵學上座部法。天祠八十餘所，多露形外道也。如來在世，數遊此國，說法度人，故無憂王於諸聖迹皆建窣堵波。逮志補羅城者，即達磨波羅（唐言護法）菩薩本生之城。菩薩，此國大臣之長子也。幼懷雅量，長而弘遠。年方弱冠，王姬下降。禮筵之夕，憂心慘悽，對佛像前殷懃祈請。至誠所感，神負遠遁，去此數百里，至山伽藍，坐佛堂中。有僧開戶，見此少年，疑其盜也，更詰問之，菩薩具懷指告，因請出家。眾咸驚異，遂允其志。王乃宣命，推求遐邇，乃知菩薩神負遠塵。王之知也，增深敬異。自染衣已，篤學精勤，令問風範，語在前記。城南不遠有大伽藍，國中聰叡同類萃止。有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王所建也。如來在昔於此說法，摧伏外道，廣度人、天。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
translation: From here, traveling south into the wilderness for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Draviḍa is over six thousand li in circumference, and its capital city, called Kāñcīpura (逮志補羅), is over thirty li in circumference. The land is fertile and rich, with abundant crops, many flowers and fruits, and it produces precious treasures. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are brave and fierce. They are deeply devoted to faith and righteousness, and are noble and learned, though their language and script differ slightly from those of Central India. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are over eighty Deva temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and save people, and for this reason, King Aśoka (無憂王) built stūpas at all the sacred sites. The city of Kāñcīpura is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (達磨波羅) (in Tang language, "Protector of the Dharma"). The Bodhisattva was the eldest son of a high minister of this country. In his youth, he possessed a refined character, and as he grew, his aspirations became vast. When he reached the age of twenty, a princess was betrothed to him. On the evening of the wedding ceremony, he felt deeply distressed and prayed earnestly before an image of the Buddha. Moved by his utmost sincerity, a deity carried him far away to a mountain saṃghārāma several hundred li from there, where he sat within the Buddha hall. A monk opened the door and, seeing this youth, suspected him of being a thief and questioned him further. The Bodhisattva explained his situation in full and requested to leave the household life. The assembly was astonished and subsequently granted his wish. The king then issued a decree to search far and near, and thus learned that the Bodhisattva had been carried away to a distant land by a deity. Upon learning this, the king’s respect and wonder increased all the more. After the Bodhisattva had dyed his robes (i.e., entered the monastic life), he studied with diligent sincerity, and his excellent reputation and conduct are described in the preceding record. Not far to the south of the city is a large saṃghārāma where the wise and learned of the country gather and reside. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, subduing the followers of external paths and extensively saving humans and devas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

t2087_text: 自此南行三千餘里，至秣羅矩吒國（亦謂枳秣羅國。南印度境）。秣羅矩吒國，周五千餘里。國大都城周四十餘里。土田舃鹵，地利不滋。海渚諸珍，多聚此國。氣序炎熱，人多釐黑。志性剛烈，邪正兼崇。不尚遊藝，唯善逐利。伽藍故基，寔多餘址，存者既少，僧徒亦寡。天祠數百，外道甚眾，多露形之徒也。城東不遠有故伽藍，庭宇荒蕪，基址尚在，無憂王弟大帝之所建也。其東有窣堵波，崇基已陷，覆鉢猶存，無憂王之所建立。在昔如來於此說法，現大神通，度無量眾，用彰聖迹，故此標建。歲久彌神，祈願或遂。
translation: From here, traveling south for more than three thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Malakūṭa (秣羅矩吒國) (also called the country of Kumārī (枳秣羅國); it is within the borders of South India). The country of Malakūṭa is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than forty *li* in circuit. The soil is salty and barren, and the land is not fertile. Many precious items from the islands of the sea are gathered in this country. The climate is hot, and the people are mostly dark-skinned. Their dispositions are fierce and unyielding, and they revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings. They do not value the arts, but are skilled only in the pursuit of profit. There are many ruins of old monasteries, but few remain standing, and the monks are also scarce. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous, many of whom are ascetics who go naked. Not far to the east of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, but the foundations still remain, having been built by the Great King (Mahendra), the younger brother of King Aśoka. To its east is a *stūpa* whose high foundation has sunk, though the inverted-bowl dome still exists, established by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes; this was built to mark these sacred traces. As time has passed, it has become increasingly miraculous, and prayers are sometimes fulfilled.

t2087_text: 國南濱海有秣剌耶山，崇崖峻嶺，洞谷深㵎。其中則有白檀香樹、栴檀儞婆樹。樹類白檀，不可以別，唯於盛夏，登高遠瞻，其有大蛇縈者，於是知之。猶其木性涼冷，故蛇盤也。既望見已，射箭為記，冬蟄之後，方乃採伐。羯布羅香樹松身異葉，花菓斯別，初採既濕，尚未有香，木乾之後，循理而析，其中有香，狀若雲母，色如氷雪，此所謂龍腦香也。
translation: To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs, steep ridges, deep caverns, and mountain torrents. Among them are white sandalwood trees and candaneva trees (栴檀儞婆樹). The latter resemble white sandalwood and cannot be distinguished from them, except in the height of summer, when one climbs to a high place and looks out from afar; those entwined by large snakes are known to be such. Because the nature of this wood is cool and cold, the snakes coil around it. Once they have been sighted, arrows are shot to mark them, and only after the snakes have hibernated in winter are the trees harvested. The camphor tree (羯布羅香樹; Skt. karpūra) has a trunk like a pine but different leaves, and its flowers and fruits are also distinct. When first harvested and still moist, it has no fragrance, but after the wood dries, it is split along the grain to reveal a fragrant substance within, shaped like mica and colored like ice or snow; this is what is called camphor (龍腦香).

t2087_text: 秣剌耶山東有布呾洛迦山，山徑危險，巖谷敧傾，山頂有池，其水澄鏡，流出大河，周流繞山二十匝，入南海。池側有石天宮，觀自在菩薩往來遊舍。其有願見菩薩者，不顧身命，厲水登山，忘其艱險，能達之者，蓋亦寡矣。而山下居人，祈心請見，或作自在天形，或為塗灰外道，慰喻其人，果遂其願。
translation: To the east of the Malaya (秣剌耶) Mountains is Mount Potalaka (布呾洛迦山). The mountain paths are perilous, and the cliffs and valleys are precipitous. On the summit of the mountain is a lake with water as clear as a mirror, from which flows a great river that circles the mountain twenty times before entering the South Sea. Beside the lake is a stone celestial palace where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) comes and goes to dwell. Those who wish to see the Bodhisattva disregard their own lives, wading through waters and climbing the mountain, forgetting all hardships and dangers; yet those who are able to reach it are few indeed. As for the inhabitants at the foot of the mountain who pray with a sincere heart to see him, the Bodhisattva may appear in the form of Maheśvara (自在天) or as an ash-smearing ascetic (塗灰外道) to console them and fulfill their wishes.

僧伽羅國，周七千餘里。國大都城周四十餘里。土地沃壤，氣序溫暑，稼穡時播，花果具繁。人戶殷盛，家產富饒。其形卑黑，其性獷烈。好學尚德，崇善勤福。此國本寶渚也，多有珍寶，棲止鬼神。其後南印度有一國王，女娉隣國，吉日送歸，路逢師子，侍衛之徒棄女逃難，女居輿中，心甘喪命。時師子王負女而去，入深山，處幽谷，捕鹿採菓，以時資給，既積歲月，遂孕男女，形貌同人，性種畜也。男漸長大，力格猛獸。年方弱冠，人智斯發，謂其母曰：「我何謂乎？父則野獸，母乃是人，既非族類，如何配偶？」母乃述昔事以告其子，曰：「人畜殊途，宜速逃逝。」母曰：「我先已逃，不能自濟。」其子於後逐師子父，登山踰嶺，察其遊止，可以逃難。伺父去已，遂擔負母妹，下趨人里。母曰：「宜各慎密，勿說事源，人或知聞，輕鄙我等。」於是至父本國，國非家族，宗祀已滅。投寄邑人，人謂之曰：「爾曹何國人也？」曰：「我本此國，流離異域，子母相携，來歸故里。」人皆哀愍，更共資給。其師子王還無所見，追戀男女，憤恚既發，便出山谷，往來村邑，咆哮震吼，暴害人物，殘毒生類，邑人輒出，遂取而殺。擊鼓吹貝，負弩持矛，群從成旅，然後免害。其王懼仁化之不洽也，乃縱獵者，期於擒獲。王躬率四兵，眾以萬計，掩薄林藪，彌跨山谷。師子震吼，人畜僻易。既不擒獲，尋復招募，其有擒執師子除國患者，當酬重賞，式旌茂績。其子聞王之令，乃謂母曰：「飢寒已甚，宜可應募，或有所得，以相撫育。」母曰：「言不可若是！彼雖畜也，猶謂父焉，豈以艱辛，而興逆害？」子曰：「人畜異類，禮義安在？既以違阻，此心何冀？」乃袖小刀，出應招募。是時千眾萬騎，雲屯霧合，師子踞在林中，人莫敢近。子即其前，父遂馴伏，於是乎親愛忘怒，乃剚刃於腹中，尚懷慈愛，猶無忿毒，乃至刳腹，含苦而死。王曰：「斯何人哉，若此之異也？」誘之以福利，震之以威禍，然後具陳始末，備述情事。王曰：「逆哉！父而尚害，況非親乎？畜種難馴，兇情易動。除民之害，其功大矣；斷父之命，其心逆矣。重賞以酬其功，遠放以誅其逆。則國典不虧，王言不二。」於是裝二大船，多儲糧糗。母留在國，周給賞功，子女各從一舟，隨波飄蕩。其男船泛海至此寶渚，見豐珍玉，便於中止。其後商人採寶，復至渚中，乃殺其商主，留其子女。如是繁息，子孫眾多，遂立君臣，以位上下，建都築邑，據有疆域，以其先祖擒執師子，因舉元功，而為國號。其女船者，泛至波剌斯西，神鬼所魅，產育群女，故今西大女國是也。故師子國人形貌卑黑，方頤大顙，情性獷烈，安忍鴆毒，斯亦猛獸遺種，故其人多勇健。斯一說也。佛法所記，則曰：昔此寶洲大鐵城中，五百羅剎女之所居也。城樓之上竪二高幢，表吉凶之相，有吉事吉幢動，有凶事凶幢動。恒伺商人至寶洲者，便變為美女，持香華，奏音樂，出迎慰問，誘入鐵城，樂讌會已，而置鐵牢中，漸取食之。時贍部洲有大商主僧伽者，其子字僧伽羅。父既年老，代知家務，與五百商人入海採寶，風波飄蕩，遇至寶洲。時羅剎女望吉幢動，便齎香華，鼓奏音樂，相携迎候，誘入鐵城。商主於是對羅剎女王歡娛樂會，自餘商侶，各相配合，彌歷歲時，皆生一子。諸羅剎女情疎故人，欲幽之鐵牢，更伺商侶。時僧伽羅夜感惡夢，知非吉祥，竊求歸路，遇至鐵牢，乃聞悲號之聲，遂昇高樹，問曰：「誰相拘縶，而此怨傷？」曰：「爾不知耶？城中諸女，並是羅剎，昔誘我曹入城娛樂。君既將至，幽牢我曹，漸充所食，今已太半，君等不久亦遭此禍。」僧伽羅曰：「當圖何計，可免危難？」對曰：「我聞海濱有一天馬，至誠祈請，必相濟渡。」僧伽羅聞已，竊告商侶，共望海濱，專精求救。是時天馬來告人曰：「爾輩各執我毛鬣，不回顧者，我濟汝曹，越海免難，至贍部洲，吉達鄉國。」諸商人奉指告，專一無二，執其髦鬣，天馬乃騰驤雲路，越濟海岸。諸羅剎女忽覺夫逃，遞相告語，異其所去，各携稚子凌虛往來。知諸商人將出海濱，遂相召命，飛行遠訪。嘗未踰時，遇諸商侶，悲憙俱至，涕淚交流，各掩泣而言曰：「我惟感遇，幸會良人，室家有慶，恩愛已久，而今遠棄，妻子孤遺，悠悠此心，誰其能忍？幸願留顧，相與還城。」商人之心未肯回慮，諸羅剎女策說無功，遂縱妖媚，備行矯惑。商侶愛戀，情難堪忍，心疑去留，身皆退墮。羅剎諸女更相拜賀，與彼商人携持而去。僧伽羅者，智慧深固，心無滯累，得越大海，免斯危難。時羅剎女王空還鐵城，諸女謂曰：「汝無智略，為夫所棄，既寡藝能，宜勿居此。」時羅剎女王持所生子，飛至僧伽羅前，縱極媚惑，誘請令還。僧伽羅口誦神呪，手揮利劍，叱而告曰：「汝是羅剎，我乃是人，人鬼異路，非其匹合。若苦相逼，當斷汝命。」羅剎女知誘惑之不遂也，凌虛而去，至僧伽羅家，詐其父僧伽曰：「我是某國王女，僧伽羅娶我為妻，生一子矣，齎持寶貨，來還鄉國。泛海遭風，舟楫漂沒，唯我子母及僧伽羅，僅而獲濟。山川道阻，凍餧艱辛，一言忤意，遂見棄遺，詈言不遜，罵為羅剎。歸則家國遼遠，止則孤遺覊旅。進退無依，敢陳情事。」僧伽曰：「誠如所言，宜時即入室。」居未久，僧伽羅至。父謂之曰：「何重財寶，而輕妻子？」僧伽羅曰：「此羅剎女也。」則以先事具白父母，而親宗戚屬咸事驅逐。時羅剎女遂以訴王，王欲罪僧伽羅。僧伽羅曰：「羅剎之女，情多妖惑。」王以為不誠也，而情悅其淑美，謂僧伽羅曰：「必棄此女，今留後宮。」僧伽羅曰：「恐為災禍。斯既羅剎，食唯血肉。」王不聽僧伽羅之言，遂納為妻。其後夜分，飛還寶渚，召餘五百羅剎鬼女共至王宮，以毒呪術殘害宮中，凡諸人畜，食肉飲血，持其餘屍，還歸寶渚。旦日群臣朝集，王門閉而不開，候聽久之，不聞人語。於是排其戶，闢其門，相從趨進，遂至宮庭，閴其無人，唯有骸骨。群官僚佐相顧失圖，悲號慟哭，莫測禍源。僧伽羅具告始末，臣庶信然，禍自招矣。於是國輔、老臣、群官、宿將，歷問明德，推據崇高，咸仰僧伽羅之福智也，乃相議曰：「夫君人者，豈苟且哉？先資福智，次體明哲，非福智無以享寶位，非明哲何以理機務？僧伽羅者，斯其人矣。夢察禍機，感應天馬，忠以諫主，智足謀身。曆運在茲，惟新成詠。」眾庶樂推，尊立為王。僧伽羅辭不獲免，允執其中，恭揖群官，遂即王位。於是沿革前弊，表式賢良。乃下令曰：「吾先商侶在羅剎國，死生莫測，善惡不分。今將救難，宜整兵甲，拯危恤患，國之福也；收珍藏寶，國之利也。」於是治兵，浮海而往。時鐵城上凶幢遂動，諸羅剎女覩而惶怖，便縱妖媚，出迎誘誑。王素知其詐，令諸兵士口誦神呪，身奮武威。諸羅剎女蹎墜退敗，或逃隱孤島，或沈溺洪流。於是毀鐵城，破鐵牢，救得商人，多獲珠寶。招募黎庶，遷居寶洲，建都築邑，遂有國焉。因以王名而為國號。僧伽羅者，則釋迦如來本生之事也。僧伽羅國先時唯宗淫祀。佛去世後第一百年，無憂王弟摩醯因陀羅捨離欲愛，志求聖果，得六神通，具八解脫，足步虛空，來遊此國，弘宣正法，流布遺教。自茲已降，風俗淳信。伽藍數百所，僧徒二萬餘人，遵行大乘上座部法。佛教至後二百餘年，各擅專門，分成二部：一曰摩訶毘訶羅住部，斥大乘，習小教。二曰阿跋耶祇釐住部，學兼二乘，弘演三藏。僧徒乃戒行貞潔，定慧凝明，儀範可師，濟濟如也。王宮側有佛牙精舍，高數百尺，瑩以珠珍，飾之奇寶。精舍上建表柱，置鉢曇摩羅加大寶，寶光赫奕，聯暉照曜，晝夜遠望，爛若明星。王以佛牙日三灌洗，香水香末，或濯或焚，務極珍奇，式修供養。佛牙精舍側有小精舍，亦以眾寶而為瑩飾。中有金佛像，此國先王等身而鑄，肉髻則貴寶飾焉。其後有盜，伺欲竊取，而重門周檻，衛守清切。盜乃鑿通孔道，入精舍而穴之，遂欲取寶，像漸高遠。其盜既不果求，退而歎曰：「如來在昔修菩薩行，起廣大心，發弘誓願，上自身命，下至國城，悲愍四生，周給一切。今者，如何遺像悋寶？靜言於此，不明昔行。」像乃俯首而授寶焉。是盜得已，尋持貨賣，人或見者，咸謂之曰：「此寶乃先王金佛像頂髻寶也。爾從何獲，來此鬻賣？」遂擒以白王。王問所從得，盜曰：「佛自與我，我非盜也。」王以為不誠，命使觀驗，像猶俯首。王覩聖靈，信心淳固，不罪其人，重贖其寶，莊嚴像髻，重置頂焉。像因俯首，以至於今。王宮側建大厨，日營萬八千僧食。食時既至，僧徒持鉢受饌，既得食已，各還其居。自佛教流被，建斯供養，子孫承統，繼業至今。十數年來，國中政亂，未有定主，乃廢斯業。國濱海隅，地產珍寶，王親祠祭，神呈奇貨，都人士子，往來求採，稱其福報，所獲不同。隨得珠璣，賦稅有科。
translation: The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how could they have mated?" His mother then recounted the past to her son. He said, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at her father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept his children. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) are short and dark in appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match. If you press me hard, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them. The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (佛牙精舍), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel?" "Reflecting on this, I do not understand the past conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.

t2087_text: 那羅稽羅洲西浮海數千里，孤島東崖有石佛像，高百餘尺，東面坐，以月愛珠為肉髻，月將回照，水即懸流，滂霈崖嶺，臨注谿壑。時有商侶，遭風飄浪，隨波泛濫，遂至孤島，海鹹不可以飲，渴乏者久之。是時月十五日也，像頂流水，眾皆獲濟，以為至誠所感，靈聖拯之。於即留停，遂經數日，每月隱高巖，其水不流。時商主曰：「未必為濟我曹而流水也。嘗聞月愛珠月光照即水流注耳，將非佛像頂上有此寶耶？」遂登崖而視之，乃以月愛珠為像肉髻。當見其人，說其始末。
translation: Sailing several thousand *li* west across the sea from the country of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲), on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha statue over a hundred feet high, seated facing east. It has a moonstone (*candrakānta*) as its *uṣṇīṣa*; when the moon shines upon it, water flows down, drenching the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the mountain ravines. At one time, a group of merchants, having encountered a storm and drifted with the waves, arrived at this solitary island. The sea water was salty and undrinkable, and they suffered from thirst for a long time. It happened to be the fifteenth day of the month, and water flowed from the top of the statue, by which the entire group was saved; they believed that their utmost sincerity had moved the divine sage to rescue them. They remained there for several days, but whenever the moon was hidden behind the high cliffs, the water would not flow. The leader of the merchants then said, "It is not necessarily the case that it flows to save us. I have heard that when moonlight shines upon a moonstone, water will flow; could it be that there is such a gem atop the head of the Buddha statue?" They then climbed the cliff to look at it and found that the *uṣṇīṣa* of the image was indeed made of moonstone. When they met the people there, they told them the whole story from beginning to end.

translation: To the west of the country, sailing several thousand li across the sea, one reaches the Great Treasure Island (Mahāratnadvīpa), which is uninhabited by humans and serves only as an abode for deities. In the quiet of the night, looking from afar, its light illuminates the mountains and waters. Many merchants have traveled there, but all have returned without obtaining anything.

t2087_text: 自達羅毘荼國北入林野中，歷孤城，過小邑，凶人結黨，作害覊旅。行二千餘里，至荼建那補羅國（南印度境）。荼建那補羅國，周五千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土地膏腴，稼穡滋盛。氣序溫暑，風俗躁烈。形貌黧黑，情性獷暴。好學業，尚德藝。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，大小二乘，兼功綜習。天祠數百，異道雜居。王宮城側有大伽藍，僧徒三百餘人，寔唯俊彥也。其伽藍大精舍高百餘尺，中有一切義成太子寶冠，高減二尺，飾以寶珍，盛以寶函。每至齋日，出置高座，香花供養，時放光明。城側大伽藍中有精舍，高五十餘尺，中有刻檀慈氏菩薩像，高十餘尺，或至齋日，神光照燭，是聞二百億羅漢之所造也。城北不遠有多羅樹林，周三十餘里，其葉長廣，其色光潤，諸國書寫，莫不採用。林中有窣堵波，是過去四佛坐及經行遺跡之所。其側則有聞二百億羅漢遺身舍利窣堵波也。城東不遠有窣堵波，基已傾陷，餘高三丈。聞諸先志曰：此中有如來舍利，或至齋日，時燭靈光。在昔如來於此說法，現神通力，度諸群生。城西南不遠有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。是聞二百億羅漢於此現大神通，化度眾生。傍有伽藍，唯餘基趾，是彼羅漢之所建也。
translation: From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns where bands of brigands harm travelers, one journeys over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國) (in the region of South India). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their temperaments are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the royal palace is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly men of outstanding talent. In the great *vihāra* (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a jeweled casket. Whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, and at times it emits a brilliant light. Beside the city, in a large monastery, there is a *vihāra* over fifty feet high, containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet tall. On fast days, it sometimes shines with a divine light; it was made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (聞二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, over thirty *li* in circuit. Its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth; all the various countries use them for writing. In the forest there is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi. Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. According to ancient records, it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes shines with a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is here that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a monastery, of which only the foundations remain, which was built by that Arhat.

t2087_text: 從此西北入大林野，猛獸暴害，群盜兇殘。行二千四五百里，至摩訶剌侘國（南印度境）。摩訶剌侘國，周六千餘里。國大都城西臨大河，周三十餘里。土地沃壤，稼穡殷盛。氣序溫暑，風俗淳質。其形偉大，其性傲逸，有恩必報，有怨必復，人或陵辱，殉命以讎，窘急投分，忘身以濟。將復怨也，必先告之，各被堅甲，然後爭鋒。臨陣逐北，不殺已降。兵將失利，無所刑罰，賜之女服，感激自死。國養勇士，有數百人，每將決戰，飲酒酣醉，一人摧鋒，萬夫挫銳。遇人肆害，國刑不加，每出遊行，擊鼓前導。復𩚅暴象，凡數百頭，將欲陣戰，亦先飲酒，群馳蹈踐，前無堅敵。其王恃此人象，輕陵隣國。王，剎帝利種也，名補羅稽舍。謀猷弘遠，仁慈廣被，臣下事之，盡其忠矣。今戒日大王東征西伐，遠賓邇肅，唯此國人獨不臣伏，屢率五印度甲兵，及募召諸國烈將，躬往討伐，猶未克勝。其兵也如此，其俗也如彼。人知好學，邪正兼崇。伽藍百餘所，僧徒五千餘人，大小二乘，兼功綜習。天祠百數，異道甚多。大城內外，五窣堵波，並過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所，無憂王建也。自餘石甎諸窣堵波，其數甚多，難用備舉。城南不遠有故伽藍，中有觀自在菩薩石像，靈鑒潛被，願求多果。
translation: From here, traveling northwest into a great forest and wilderness, one encounters ferocious beasts and cruel bands of robbers. After traveling two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Mahārāṣṭra (摩訶剌侘國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Mahārāṣṭra is over six thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders a great river on the west and is over thirty li in circumference. The soil is fertile and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are tall and sturdy in stature and proud and carefree by nature; they never fail to repay a kindness or avenge a grievance. If someone insults them, they will risk their lives to take vengeance; if someone is in desperate straits and seeks their aid, they will forget their own safety to assist them. When they intend to take revenge, they must first notify their opponent; both sides then don sturdy armor before engaging in battle. When pursuing a retreating enemy on the battlefield, they do not kill those who have surrendered. If a general or soldier suffers a defeat, he is not punished; instead, he is presented with women’s clothing, and, feeling ashamed, he will take his own life. The state maintains several hundred warriors. Whenever they are about to engage in a decisive battle, they drink until they are intoxicated; a single one of these men can break the vanguard, causing ten thousand men to lose their edge. If they happen to harm someone, the state does not impose punishment; whenever they go out, they have drums beaten to lead the way. Furthermore, they keep several hundred ferocious elephants. When they are about to engage in battle, these elephants are also given wine to drink; they then charge in a group, trampling everything, with no firm enemy able to stand before them. The king relies on these men and elephants to lightly treat and bully neighboring countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya (剎帝利) caste and is named Pulakeśin (補羅稽舍). His strategies and plans are far-reaching, and his benevolence is widely extended; his subjects serve him with the utmost loyalty. Currently, the great King Śīlāditya (戒日大王) campaigns from the east to the west, bringing distant lands to submission and near lands to order; only the people of this country alone refuse to acknowledge his suzerainty. Although he has repeatedly led the armored troops of the Five Indias and summoned the heroic generals of many nations to personally lead an invasion, he has yet to achieve victory. Such is their military, and such are their customs. The people are known for their love of learning, and they revere both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are hundreds of Deva temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. Inside and outside the great city, there are five stūpas (窣堵波), all of which are sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). As for the other stone and brick stūpas, their number is so great that it is difficult to enumerate them all. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, in which there is a stone image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and those who pray for wishes often see them fulfilled.

t2087_text: 國東境有大山，疊嶺連障，重巒絕巘。爰有伽藍，基于幽谷，高堂邃宇，疏崖枕峯，重閣層臺，背巖面𭐋，阿折羅（唐言所行）阿羅漢所建。羅漢，西印度人也，其母既終，觀生何趣，見於此國受女人身，羅漢遂來至此，將欲導化，隨機攝受。入里乞食，至母生家，女子持食來施，乳便流汁，親屬既見，以為不祥。羅漢說本因緣，女子便證聖果。羅漢感生育之恩，懷業緣之致，將酬厚德，建此伽藍。伽藍大精舍高百餘尺，中有石佛像，高七十餘尺。上有石蓋七重，虛懸無綴，蓋間相去各三尺餘。聞諸先志曰：斯乃羅漢願力之所持也；或曰神通之力；或曰藥術之功。考厥實錄，未詳其致。精舍四周彫鏤石壁，作如來在昔修菩薩行諸因地事。證聖果之禎祥，入寂滅之靈應，巨細無遺，備盡鐫鏤。伽藍門外，南、北、左、右各一石象。聞之土俗曰：此象時大聲吼，地為震動。昔陳那菩薩多止此伽藍。
translation: On the eastern border of the country is a great mountain with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. There is a monastery situated in a deep valley, with lofty halls and spacious chambers built against the cliffs and peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rocks and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Ācāra (which means "the one who acts" in the language of the Tang). The Arhat was a man from West India. After his mother passed away, he observed where she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman's body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the girl brought food to offer as alms, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and cherishing the karmic conditions that brought it about, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue. The great vihāra (精舍) of the monastery is over a hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue more than seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any attachments, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of those before me that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is by the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses upon his entry into nirvana are all carved in detail, leaving nothing out. Outside the gate of the monastery, there is a stone elephant at each of the four positions: south, north, left, and right. According to the local people, these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 自此西行千餘里，渡耐秣陀河，至跋祿羯呫（昌葉反）婆國（南印度境）。跋祿羯呫婆國，周二千四五百里。國大都城周二十餘里。土地鹹鹵，草木稀疎。煮海為鹽，利海為業。氣序暑熱，回風颷起。土俗澆薄，人性詭詐。不知學藝，邪正兼信。伽藍十餘所，僧徒三百餘人，習學大乘上座部法。天祠十餘所，異道雜居。
translation: From here, traveling west for over a thousand li and crossing the Narmada River (耐秣陀河), one reaches the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國) (呫 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 昌葉) (in the region of South India). The country of Bharukacchapa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The land is saline and barren, with sparse vegetation. The people boil seawater to make salt and rely on the sea for their livelihood. The climate is hot, and swirling winds rise up frequently. The local customs are mean and thin, and the people’s nature is deceitful and cunning. They do not study arts or crafts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
