t2087_text: 城西二百餘里，至大山。山氣巃嵸，觸石興雲，崖隒崢嶸，將崩未墜。其巔窣堵波，欝然奇制也。聞諸土俗曰：數百年前，山崖崩圮，中有苾芻，瞑目而坐，軀量偉大，形容枯槁，鬚髮下垂，被肩蒙面。有田獵者見已白王，王躬觀禮。都人士子，不召而至，焚香散花，競修供養。王曰：「斯何人哉？若此偉也！」有苾芻對曰：「此鬚髮垂長而被服袈裟，乃入滅心定阿羅漢也。夫入滅心定者，先有期限，或言聞揵稚聲，或言待日光照，有茲警察，便從定起；若無警察，寂然不動，定力持身，遂無壞滅。段食之體，出定便謝。宜以蘇油灌注，令得滋潤，然後鼓擊，警悟定心。」王曰：「俞乎？」乃擊揵稚。其聲纔振，而此羅漢豁然高視，久之，乃曰：「爾輩何人？形容卑劣，被服袈裟？」對曰：「我苾芻也。」曰：「然，我師迦葉波如來今何所在？」對曰：「入大涅槃，其來已久。」聞而閉目，悵若有懷，尋重問曰：「釋迦如來出興世耶？」對曰：「誕靈導世，已從寂滅。」聞復俯首，久之乃起，昇虛空，現神變，化火焚身，遺骸墜地。王收其骨起窣堵波。
translation: Two hundred or more *li* west of the city, one arrives at a great mountain. The mountain’s atmosphere is dense and swirling; clouds rise where it touches the rocks, and the cliffs and precipices are jagged and steep, as if about to collapse yet not falling. On its summit is a stūpa of imposing and extraordinary construction. According to local tradition, several hundred years ago, a mountain cliff collapsed, and within it was a bhikṣu sitting with eyes closed. His body was of great stature, his appearance emaciated, and his beard and hair hung down, covering his shoulders and face. A hunter saw him and reported it to the king, who went in person to pay his respects. The city’s inhabitants and scholars arrived without being summoned, burning incense and scattering flowers, vying to offer worship. The king asked, "Who is this person? He is so magnificent!" A bhikṣu replied, "This person with long, hanging hair and beard, clad in a kaṣāya robe, is an arhat who has entered the samādhi of mental extinction (nirodha-samāpatti). Those who enter the samādhi of mental extinction set a prior time limit; some say they will arise upon hearing the sound of a ghaṇṭā, others say they will wait for the sunlight to shine. With such an alert, they arise from their meditation; if there is no alert, they remain silent and motionless, the power of their meditation sustaining their body so that it does not decay. The physical body, sustained by morsel food, would perish upon emerging from meditation. It is proper to pour in ghee to provide nourishment and moisture, and only then strike the ghaṇṭā to awaken his meditative mind." The king said, "Is that so?" He then struck the ghaṇṭā. The sound had barely vibrated when the arhat suddenly opened his eyes and looked up. After a long while, he said, "Who are you people? Your appearance is base and inferior, yet you wear the kaṣāya robes?" They replied, "We are bhikṣus." He asked, "Is that so? Where is my teacher, Kāśyapa Tathāgata (迦葉波如來), now?" They replied, "He entered mahānirvāṇa a long time ago." Upon hearing this, he closed his eyes, looking dejected as if lost in thought. Shortly after, he asked again, "Has Śākya Tathāgata (釋迦如來) appeared in the world?" They replied, "The holy one who guided the world has already passed into extinction." Hearing this, he bowed his head again, and after a long while, he rose, ascended into the void, manifested supernatural transformations, and transformed into fire to consume his body, his remains falling to the ground. The king collected his bones and erected a stūpa (窣堵波) over them.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 從此北行，山磧曠野五百餘里，至佉沙國（舊謂疏勒者，乃稱其城號也。正音宜云室利訖栗多底。疏勒之言，猶為訛也）。佉沙國，周五千餘里。多沙磧，少壤土。稼穡殷盛，花菓繁茂。出細氈褐，工織細㲲氍毺。氣候和暢，風雨順序。人性獷暴，俗多詭詐，禮義輕薄，學藝膚淺。其俗生子，押頭匾㔸，容貌麁鄙，文身綠睛。而其文字，取則印度，雖有刪訛，頗存體勢。語言辭調，異於諸國。淳信佛法，勤營福利。伽藍數百所，僧徒萬餘人，習學小乘教說一切有部。不究其理，多諷其文，故誦通三藏及《毘婆沙》者多矣。
translation: Traveling north from here for over five hundred li across mountains, gravelly plains, and wilderness, one arrives at the country of Khāsa (佉沙國) (What was formerly called Shule (疏勒) is actually the name of its capital city. The correct pronunciation should be Śrī-kṛtati; the term Shule is a corruption). The country of Khāsa is over five thousand li in circumference. There is much gravel and sand, and little fertile soil. Agriculture is flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It produces fine felt and coarse wool, and they are skilled at weaving fine cotton cloth and woollen rugs. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and their customs are full of deceit; they treat ritual and righteousness lightly, and their learning and arts are superficial. It is their custom to compress the heads of newborn children to make them flat; their appearance is coarse and vulgar, and they have tattooed bodies and green eyes. Their writing system is modeled after that of India; although there have been deletions and corruptions, it still retains the original structure. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of other countries. They are sincerely devoted to the Buddha-dharma and diligently engage in meritorious works. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with over ten thousand monks, who study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. They do not delve deeply into the principles but mostly recite the texts; therefore, many have mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal

t2087_text: 從此東南行五百餘里，濟徙多河，踰大沙嶺，至斫句迦國（舊曰沮渠）。斫句迦國，周千餘里。國大都城周十餘里，堅峻險固，編戶殷盛。山阜連屬，礫石彌漫，臨帶兩河，頗以耕植。蒲陶、梨、柰，其菓寔繁。時風寒，人躁暴。俗唯詭詐，公行劫盜。文字同瞿薩旦那國，言語有異。禮義輕薄，學藝淺近。淳信三寶，好樂福利。伽藍數十，毀壞已多，僧徒百餘人，習學大乘教。
translation: From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, I crossed the Sītā River, passed over a great sandy range, and reached the country of Cukuka (formerly called Juqu). The country of Cukuka is more than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circuit; it is solid, steep, and secure, and the households are numerous and prosperous. The hills and mounds are connected, and the ground is covered with gravel and stones. It borders two rivers and is quite suitable for cultivation. Grapes, pears, and crabapples—these fruits are abundant. The climate is cold, and the people are impetuous and violent. Their customs are characterized by deceit and trickery, and they practice robbery openly. Their script is the same as that of the country of Gostāna (瞿薩旦那國), though their spoken language is different. Their sense of propriety and righteousness is slight, and their learning and arts are shallow. They are sincerely devoted to the Three Jewels and take pleasure in performing meritorious deeds. There are several dozen sanghārāmas, though many are in ruins, and there are more than one hundred monks who study the teachings of the Great Vehicle.

mz_other_views: Stein, 黄文弼 attempted no identification
t2087_text: 國南境有大山，崖嶺嵯峨，峯巒重疊；草木凌寒，春秋一觀；谿㵎浚瀨，飛流四注；崖龕石室，棋布巖林。印度果人，多運神通，輕舉遠遊，棲止於此。諸阿羅漢寂滅者眾，以故多有窣堵波也，今猶現有三阿羅漢居巖穴中，入滅心定，形若羸人，鬚髮恒長，故諸沙門時往為剃。而此國中大乘經典部數尤多，佛法至處，莫斯為盛也。十萬頌為部者，凡有十數；自茲已降，其流寔廣。
translation: On the southern border of the country is a great mountain, with craggy cliffs and ridges and overlapping peaks. The vegetation defies the cold, looking the same in spring and autumn. Deep ravines and rushing torrents flow in all directions, and cliff niches and stone chambers are scattered like chess pieces throughout the rocky forests. Many people from India who have attained the fruits of enlightenment employ their supernatural powers to travel far and alight here to dwell. Because many Arhats have entered nirvana here, there are numerous stupas. Even now, three Arhats remain in the mountain caves, having entered the samadhi of mental extinction; their forms appear like those of emaciated men, and their hair and beards grow continuously, so monks periodically go there to shave them. In this country, the number of Mahayana scriptures is particularly large; of all the places where the Buddha’s teachings have spread, none is more flourishing than this. There are over ten works consisting of one hundred thousand stanzas each, and from this size on down, their circulation is truly vast.
translation_source: DharmaMitra, corrected against Mizutani and Beal
translation_issues: a great mountain (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text; presenting a singular sight in both spring and autumn → 春秋一觀: looking the same in spring and autumn (evergreen)

t2087_text: 從此而東，踰嶺越谷，行八百餘里，至瞿薩旦那國（唐言地乳，即其俗之雅言也。俗語謂之渙那國，匈奴謂之于遁，諸胡謂之谿旦，印度謂之屈丹。舊曰于闐，訛也）。瞿薩旦那國，周四千餘里。沙磧太半，壤土隘狹。宜穀稼，多眾菓。出氍毺、細氈，工紡績絁紬。又產白玉、黳玉。氣序和暢，飄風飛埃。俗知禮義，人性溫恭。好學典藝，博達技能。眾庶富樂，編戶安業。國尚樂音，人好歌舞。少服毛褐氈裘，多衣絁紬白㲲。儀形有禮，風則有紀。文字憲章，聿尊印度，微改體勢，粗有沿革。語異諸國。崇尚佛法。伽藍百有餘所，僧徒五千餘人，並多習學大乘法教。王甚驍武，敬重佛法，自云毘沙門天之祚胤也。昔者，此國虛曠無人，毘沙門天於此棲止。無憂王太子在呾叉始羅國被抉目已，無憂王怒譴輔佐，遷其豪族，出雪山北，居荒谷間。遷人逐物，至此西界，推舉酋豪，尊立為王。當是時也，東土帝子蒙譴流徙，居此東界，群下勸進，又自稱王。歲月已積，風教不通。各因田獵，遇會荒澤，更問宗緒，因而爭長。忿形辭語，便欲交兵。或有諫曰：「今何遽乎？因獵決戰，未盡兵鋒。宜歸治兵，期而後集。」於是迴駕而返，各歸其國，校習戎馬，督勵士卒。至期兵會，旗鼓相望。旦日合戰，西主不利，因而逐北，遂斬其首。東主乘勝，撫集亡國，遷都中地，方建城郭。憂其無土，恐難成功，宣告遠近，誰識地理。時有塗灰外道，負大瓠，盛滿水，而自進曰：「我知地理。」遂以其水屈曲遺流，周而復始，因即疾驅，忽而不見。依彼水迹，峙其基堵，遂得興功，即斯國治，今王所都於此城也。城非崇峻，攻擊難剋，自古已來，未能有勝。其王遷都作邑，建國安人，功績已成，齒耋云暮，未有胤嗣，恐絕宗緒。乃往毘沙門天神所祈禱請嗣，神像額上，剖出嬰孩，捧以回駕，國人稱慶。既不飲乳，恐其不壽，尋詣神祠，重請育養。神前之地忽然隆起，其狀如乳，神童飲吮，遂至成立。智勇光前，風教遐被，遂營神祠，宗先祖也。自茲已降，奕世相承，傳國君臨，不失其緒。故今神廟多諸珍寶，拜祠享祭，無替於時。地乳所育，因為國號。
translation: Going eastward from here, crossing mountains and valleys for more than eight hundred li, one reaches the country of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) (in the language of Tang, this means "Earth-Nipple," which is the elegant form of the local name. In the vulgar tongue it is called the country of Huanna; the Xiongnu call it Yudun; the various Hu peoples call it Qidan; and in India it is called Qudan. The old name, Yutian (于闐), is erroneous). The country of Gostana is more than four thousand li in circumference. More than half of it is sand and gravel, and the arable land is narrow and restricted. It is suitable for grain crops and produces many kinds of fruit. It produces rugs and fine felt, and the people are skilled at spinning and weaving silk and pongee. It also produces white jade and black jade. The climate is mild and pleasant, though there are drifting winds and flying dust. The customs value propriety and righteousness, and the people are gentle and respectful by nature. They are fond of learning the arts and are broadly proficient in various skills. The populace is wealthy and happy, and the households are settled in their occupations. The country prizes musical sounds, and the people are fond of singing and dancing. Few wear coarse wool, felt, or furs; most clothe themselves in silk, pongee, and white cotton. Their deportment is refined, and their customs are well-ordered. Their writing and laws are modeled after those of India, though they have slightly altered the style and form, having undergone some evolution. Their language differs from that of other countries. They revere and uphold the Buddha-dharma. There are more than one hundred sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The king is very brave and martial, respects the Buddha-dharma, and claims to be a descendant of the deity Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天). In ancient times, this country was empty and uninhabited, and the deity Vaiśravaṇa resided here. After the crown prince of King Aśoka (無憂王) had his eyes gouged out in the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), the king angrily rebuked his ministers and exiled the powerful families to the north of the Snow Mountains to dwell among the desolate valleys. These exiles followed their herds and reached the western border of this land, where they elected their leader and established him as king. At that time, a prince from the eastern lands had been banished and had migrated to dwell on the eastern border of this region; his subordinates urged him to assume the throne, and he too proclaimed himself king. As years and months accumulated, their customs and teachings remained disconnected. Each group, while out hunting, encountered the other in the desolate marshes; they inquired about each other’s lineage and consequently disputed who was superior. Anger manifested in their words, and they were about to engage in battle. Someone advised them, saying, "Why be so hasty now? To decide the battle while hunting does not fully display the sharpness of our weapons. It is better to return and prepare our troops, and gather at an appointed time." Thereupon, they turned their carriages and returned, each going back to his own country to drill their horses and soldiers and encourage their troops. When the appointed time arrived, the armies met, and their banners and drums faced one another. The next day they joined battle, and the Western Lord was disadvantaged; consequently, he was pursued in his retreat and his head was cut off. The Eastern Lord, riding the momentum of his victory, pacified and gathered the people of the defeated country, moved his capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. Worried that he lacked land and fearing that he might not succeed, he made a proclamation far and near, asking who knew the geography. At that time, there was an ash-smeared outsider (tīrthika) who carried a large gourd filled with water and stepped forward, saying, "I know the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, returning to where it started, and then he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully completed; this became the seat of government, and it is in this city that the current king has established his capital. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome by attack, and from ancient times until now, no one has been able to conquer it. By the time the king had moved the capital to build this city, established the state, and settled the people, his achievements were complete and he was in the twilight of his old age; yet he had no heir and feared the end of his ancestral line. He then went to the place of the god Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天神) to pray for an heir. From the forehead of the god’s statue, an infant was produced; the king took him in his arms and returned to his palace, and the people of the country celebrated. Since the baby would not drink milk, the king feared he would not live long, so he soon returned to the divine shrine to pray again for a way to nourish him. The ground in front of the deity suddenly rose up in the shape of a breast, and the divine child suckled from it until he grew to adulthood. His wisdom and courage surpassed his predecessors, and his moral influence spread far and wide; he then built a divine shrine to honor his ancestor. From that time on, the throne has been passed down through generations, and the kings have ruled the country without the line being broken. Therefore, the divine temple today contains many precious treasures, and offerings and sacrifices are made there without fail. Because he was nourished by the earth-breast, this became the name of the country.

t2087_text: 王城南十餘里有大伽藍，此國先王為毘盧折那（唐言遍照）阿羅漢建也。昔者，此國佛法未被，而阿羅漢自迦濕彌羅國至此林中，宴坐習定。時有見者，駭其容服，具以其狀上白於王。王遂躬往，觀其容止，曰：「爾何人乎，獨在幽林？」羅漢曰：「我，如來弟子，閑居習定。王宜樹福，弘讚佛教，建伽藍，召僧眾。」王曰：「如來者，有何德，有何神，而汝鳥棲，勤苦奉教？」曰：「如來慈愍四生，誘導三界，或顯或隱，示生示滅。遵其法者，出離生死，迷其教者，羈纏愛網。」王曰：「誠如所說，事高言議，既云大聖，為我現形；既得瞻仰，當為建立，罄心歸信，弘揚教法。」羅漢曰：「王建伽藍，功成感應。」王苟從其請，建僧伽藍，遠近咸集，法會稱慶，而未有揵稚扣擊召集。王謂羅漢曰：「伽藍已成，佛在何所？」羅漢曰：「當至誠，聖鑒不遠。」王遂禮請，忽見空中佛像下降，授王揵稚，因即誠信，弘揚佛教。
translation: More than ten li to the south of the royal city is a great monastery, which was built by a former king of this country for the Arhat Vairocana (meaning "Universal Shining" in Chinese). In the past, the Buddha’s teaching had not yet reached this country, but the Arhat came from the country of Kaśmīra to this forest, where he sat in quietude to practice meditation. At that time, those who saw him were startled by his appearance and attire, and they reported his condition in detail to the king. The king then went in person to observe his demeanor and said, "Who are you, staying alone in this secluded forest?" The Arhat replied, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, living in seclusion to practice meditation. Your Majesty should cultivate merit, propagate the Buddha’s teaching, build a monastery, and assemble the monkhood." The king asked, "What virtues and divine powers does the Tathāgata possess that you would dwell like a bird in the woods and so diligently follow his teachings?" He replied, "The Tathāgata compassionately cares for the four types of birth and guides the three realms; he sometimes manifests and sometimes remains hidden, demonstrating birth and demonstrating extinction. Those who follow his teaching escape birth and death; those who are confused by his teaching remain entangled in the net of desire." The king said, "If it is truly as you say, the matter transcends words and discussion. Since you speak of a Great Sage, manifest his form for me; once I have been able to gaze upon him, I shall build [a monastery], devote my heart to faith, and propagate the teaching." The Arhat said, "If the king builds a monastery, the merit will bring about a response." The king followed his request and built a sanghārāma; people from far and near gathered to celebrate the dharma assembly, but they lacked a ghaṇṭā to strike for summoning the assembly. The king said to the Arhat, "The monastery (saṃghārāma) is now completed, but where is the Buddha?" The Arhat replied, "You must be perfectly sincere; the Sage’s observation is not far off." The king then performed rites of petition, and suddenly he saw an image of the Buddha descend from the air and bestow upon the king a ghaṇṭā (揵稚). Because of this, he became sincerely faithful and propagated the Buddha’s teaching.

t2087_text: 王城西南二十餘里，有瞿室𩜁伽山（唐言牛角）。山峯兩起，巖隒四絕，於崖谷間建一伽藍，其中佛像時燭光明。昔如來曾至此處，為諸天、人略說法要，懸記此地當建國土，敬崇遺法，遵習大乘。牛角山巖有大石室，中有阿羅漢，入滅心定，待慈氏佛，數百年間，供養無替。近者崖崩，掩塞門徑，國王興兵欲除崩石，即黑蜂群飛，毒螫人眾，以故至今石門不開。
translation: More than twenty li to the southwest of the royal city is the mountain of Gośṛṅga (瞿室𩜁伽山; in the language of Tang, "Cow Horn"). Two peaks rise up, and the rocky precipices are sheer on all sides. A monastery (saṃghārāma) is built between the cliffs and the valley, where the Buddha image within occasionally radiates light. In the past, the Tathāgata came to this place to briefly explain the essential Dharma for the various devas and humans, and he prophesied that a kingdom would be established here that would revere and honor the remaining Dharma and follow the practice of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). In the rocky cliffs of Mount Cow Horn, there is a large stone chamber where an arhat resides, having entered the samadhi of extinction to await the Buddha Maitreya; for several hundred years, offerings to him have never ceased. Recently, the cliff collapsed and blocked the entrance path. The king mobilized troops to clear away the fallen stones, but immediately a swarm of black wasps flew out and stung the people, and for this reason, the stone gate has not been opened to this day.

t2087_text: 王城西南十餘里，有地迦婆縛那伽藍。中有夾紵立佛像，本從屈支國而來至止。昔此國中有臣被譴，寓居屈支，恒禮此像。後蒙還國，傾心遙敬，夜分之後，像忽自至，其人捨宅，建此伽藍。
translation: More than ten *li* to the southwest of the royal city, there is the Dīrghabhāvana Monastery (地迦婆縛那伽藍). Inside is a standing Buddha image made of hollow lacquer, which originally came here from the country of Kuci (屈支國). Formerly, a minister of this country was banished and lived in Kuci, where he constantly worshipped this image. Later, after he was allowed to return to his country, he continued to venerate it from afar with all his heart. After midnight, the image suddenly arrived of its own accord, and the man gave up his residence to build this monastery.

t2087_text: 王城西行三百餘里，至勃伽夷城。中有佛坐像，高七尺餘，相好允備，威肅嶷然，首戴寶冠，光明時照。聞諸土俗曰：本在迦濕彌羅國，請移至此。昔有羅漢，其沙彌弟子臨命終時，求酢米餅。羅漢以天眼觀，見瞿薩旦那國有此味焉，運神通力，至此求獲。沙彌噉已，願生其國，果遂宿心，得為王子。既嗣位已，威攝遐邇，遂踰雪山，伐迦濕彌羅國。迦濕彌羅國王整集戎馬，欲禦邊寇。時阿羅漢諫王：「勿鬪兵也，我能退之。」尋為瞿薩旦那王說諸法要。王初未信，尚欲興兵。羅漢遂取此王先身沙彌時衣，而以示之。王既見衣，得宿命智，與迦濕彌羅王謝咎交歡，釋兵而返，奉迎沙彌時所供養佛像，隨軍禮請。像至此地，不可轉移，環建伽藍，或招僧侶，捨寶冠置像頂，今所冠者，即先王所施也。
translation: Traveling three hundred-odd *li* west from the royal city, one arrives at the city of Bhagai (勃伽夷城). Within it is a seated image of the Buddha, over seven feet high. Its physical marks are perfectly complete, and its majestic, solemn appearance is awe-inspiring. It wears a precious crown on its head, which emits light from time to time. According to local tradition, it was originally in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) and was invited to be moved here. Long ago, there was an arhat whose *śrāmaṇera* (novice) disciple, when approaching the end of his life, asked for some sour rice cakes. The arhat used his heavenly eye to observe and saw that this delicacy existed in the country of Gostāna (瞿薩旦那國); he employed his supernatural powers to travel there and obtain it. After the *śrāmaṇera* had eaten it, he wished to be reborn in that country. His past aspiration was fulfilled, and he became the prince. Once he had succeeded to the throne, his might intimidated both near and far; he then crossed the Snow Mountains (Himālaya) to invade the country of Kaśmīra. The King of Kaśmīra mobilized his troops and horses, intending to resist the border invaders. At that time, the arhat admonished the king, saying, "Do not engage in battle; I can cause them to retreat." He then explained the essential teachings of the Dharma to the King of Gostāna. The king did not believe him at first and still wished to raise his army. The arhat then took the robe that this king had worn in his previous life as a *śrāmaṇera* and showed it to him. Once the king saw the robe, he attained the knowledge of past lives; he apologized to the King of Kaśmīra, reconciled with him, and released his troops to return home. He respectfully invited the Buddha image that he had worshipped when he was a *śrāmaṇera* to follow his army. When the image reached this place, it could not be moved further, so they built a monastery around it and invited monks to reside there. The king offered his precious crown and placed it upon the head of the image; the crown it wears today is the very one bestowed by the former king.

t2087_text: 王城西百五六十里，大沙磧正路中，有堆阜，並鼠壤墳也。聞之土俗曰：此沙磧中，鼠大如蝟，其毛則金銀異色，為其群之酋長，每出穴遊止，則群鼠為從。昔者，匈奴率數十萬眾，寇掠邊城，至鼠墳側屯軍，時瞿薩旦那王率數萬兵，恐力不敵，素知磧中鼠奇，而未神也。洎乎寇至，無所求救，君臣震恐，莫知圖計。苟復設祭，焚香請鼠，冀其有靈，少加軍力。其夜瞿薩旦那王夢見大鼠。曰：「敬欲相助。願早治兵，旦日合戰，必當克勝。」瞿薩旦那王知有靈祐，遂整戎馬，申令將士，未明而行，長驅掩襲。匈奴之聞也，莫不懼焉。方欲駕乘被鎧，而諸馬鞍、人服、弓弦、甲縺，凡厥帶系，鼠皆齧斷。兵寇既臨，面縛受戮。於是殺其將，虜其兵，匈奴震懾，以為神靈所祐也。瞿薩旦那王感鼠厚恩，建祠設祭，奕世遵敬，特深珍異。故上自君王，下至黎庶，咸修祀祭，以求福祐。行次其穴，下乘而趨，拜以致敬，祭以祈福。或衣服、弓、矢，或香花、肴膳，亦既輸誠，多蒙福利。若無享祭，則逢災變。
translation: One hundred and fifty or sixty li to the west of the royal city, in the middle of the main road through the great desert, there are mounds which are all rat-earth hillocks (鼠壤墳). According to local tradition, in this desert there are rats as large as hedgehogs, whose fur is of various colors of gold and silver. They are the leaders of their groups, and whenever they emerge from their burrows to roam or rest, the other rats follow them.  In the past, the Xiongnu led several hundred thousand troops to invade and plunder the frontier cities, stationing their army beside these rat mounds. At that time, the King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那王) led several tens of thousands of soldiers, fearing that his strength was no match for the enemy. He had long known that the rats in the desert were remarkable, but he had not yet regarded them as divine. When the invaders arrived, there was nowhere to seek help, and the king and his ministers were terrified, not knowing what strategy to devise. In desperation, he set up offerings, burned incense, and petitioned the rats, hoping that they possessed spiritual power and would add a little to his military strength.  That night, the King of Gostana saw a giant rat in a dream. It said, "I wish to assist you. Prepare your troops early, and when you engage in battle at daybreak, you will surely be victorious." The King of Gostana, knowing he had received divine protection, immediately readied his horses and weapons and issued orders to his officers and men. Before dawn, they marched out and launched a surprise attack. When the Xiongnu heard of this, they were all struck with fear. Just as they were about to mount their horses and put on their armor, the rats gnawed through all their saddles, clothing, bowstrings, armor straps, and every kind of belt and fastening. When the enemy troops arrived, the Xiongnu stood with their hands bound behind their backs, waiting to be executed. Thereupon, the king killed their generals and captured their soldiers. The Xiongnu were terrified, believing that the king was protected by divine spirits. The King of Kustana (瞿薩旦那), moved by the great kindness of the rats, built a shrine and established sacrifices, a tradition of reverence followed for generations with profound and special esteem. Therefore, from the monarch above to the common people below, all perform sacrifices to seek blessings and protection. When passing by their burrows, people alight from their mounts and hurry forward, bowing to pay their respects and offering sacrifices to pray for good fortune. Whether offering clothing, bows, and arrows, or fragrant flowers and fine foods, once they have shown their sincerity, they mostly receive benefits and blessings. If they fail to offer sacrifices, they encounter disasters and calamities.

t2087_text: 王城西五六里，有娑摩若僧伽藍。中有窣堵波，高百餘尺，甚多靈瑞，時燭神光。昔有羅漢，自遠方來，止此林中，以神通力，放大光明。時王夜在重閣，遙見林中光明照曜，於是歷問，僉曰：「有一沙門，自遠而至，宴坐林中，示現神通。」王遂命駕，躬往觀察。既覩明賢，乃心祗敬，欽風不已，請至中宮。沙門曰：「物有所宜，志其所在。幽林藪澤，情之所賞；高堂邃宇，非我攸聞。」王益敬仰，深加宗重，為建伽藍，起窣堵波。沙門受請，遂止其中。頃之，王感獲舍利數百粒，甚慶悅，竊自念曰：「舍利來應，何其晚歟？早得置之窣堵波下，豈非勝迹？」尋詣伽藍，具白沙門。羅漢曰：「王無憂也，今為置之。宜以金、銀、銅、鐵大石函等，以次周盛。」王命匠人，不日功畢，載諸寶輿，送至伽藍。是時也，王宮導從、庶僚凡百，觀送舍利者，動以萬計。羅漢乃以右手舉窣堵波，置諸掌中，謂王曰：「可以藏下也。」遂坎地安函，其功斯畢，於是下窣堵波，無所傾損。觀覩之徒，歎未曾有，信佛之心彌篤，敬法之志斯堅。王謂群官曰：「我嘗聞佛力難思，神通難究。或分身百億，或應迹人天；舉世界於掌內，眾生無動靜之想，演法性於常音，眾生有隨類之悟。斯則神力不共，智慧絕言。其靈已隱，其教猶傳。飡和飲澤，味道欽風，尚獲斯靈，深賴其福。勉哉，凡百！宜深崇敬，佛法幽深，於是明矣。」
translation: Five or six li to the west of the royal city is the Samājña Monastery (娑摩若僧伽藍). Within it is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which possesses many miraculous signs and often illuminates with divine light. Formerly, there was an arhat who came from a distant land and stayed in this forest, manifesting great light through his supernatural powers. At that time, the king was in his multi-storied pavilion at night and saw from afar the light shining in the forest. He inquired about it, and everyone said, "There is a śramaṇa who has arrived from afar, sitting in meditation in the forest and manifesting supernatural powers." The king then ordered his carriage and went in person to observe. Having seen the wise and virtuous one, he felt deep respect and admiration for his character, and invited him to the royal palace. The śramaṇa said, "Things have their proper places, and one’s aspirations lie where they belong. Secluded forests and marshes are what my heart delights in; high halls and deep chambers are not what I am accustomed to." The king respected and revered him all the more, and for his sake built a monastery and erected a stūpa. The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and subsequently resided there. Shortly after, the king miraculously obtained several hundred grains of relics. He was extremely joyful and thought to himself, "Why did the relics come to respond so late? If I had obtained them earlier to place them under the stūpa, would that not have been a magnificent monument?" He immediately went to the monastery and told the śramaṇa in detail. The arhat said, "O King, do not worry; I shall place them for you now. You should use caskets of gold, silver, copper, iron, and large stone, one inside the other, to contain them." The king ordered the craftsmen, and in a few days the work was completed. He loaded them onto a precious carriage and sent them to the monastery. At that time, the king’s royal retinue and the various officials, numbering in the tens of thousands, came to witness the sending of the relics. The arhat then lifted the stūpa with his right hand, placed it in his palm, and said to the king, "You may now bury them beneath it." Thereupon, a pit was dug in the ground and the caskets were installed. When the task was finished, the stūpa was lowered back down without any tilting or damage. Those who witnessed it marveled that such a thing had never happened before; their faith in the Buddha became even more sincere, and their resolve to revere the Dharma grew more steadfast.  The king said to his officials, "I have heard that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable and his supernatural faculties are unfathomable. Sometimes he manifests billions of bodies, and sometimes he leaves traces of his presence among humans and devas. He can lift the entire world into the palm of his hand without the sentient beings within it having any sense of movement or stillness; he expounds the nature of the Dharma in a constant sound, and sentient beings attain understanding according to their own kind. This is the uncommon power of his supernatural faculties and wisdom that transcends words. Though his spiritual presence has vanished, his teachings are still transmitted. By consuming his harmony and drinking his grace, by savoring the Way and admiring his influence, we still obtain such spiritual efficacy and rely deeply upon his blessings. Exert yourselves, all of you! You should offer deep veneration; that the Buddha-dharma is abstruse and profound is evident from this."

t2087_text: 王城東南五六里，有麻射僧伽藍，此國先王妃所立也。昔者，此國未知桑蠶，聞東國有也，命使以求。時東國君祕而不賜，嚴勅關防，無令桑蠶種出也。瞿薩旦那王乃卑辭下禮，求婚東國；國君有懷遠之志，遂允其請。瞿薩旦那王命使迎婦，而誡曰：「爾致辭東國君女，我國素無絲綿桑蠶之種，可以持來，自為裳服。」女聞其言，密求其種，以桑蠶之子置帽絮中，既至關防，主者遍索，唯王女帽不敢以驗。遂入瞿薩旦那國，止麻射伽藍故地，方備儀禮，奉迎入宮，以桑蠶種留於此地。陽春告始，乃植其桑，蠶月既臨，復事採養。初至也，尚以雜葉𩚅之，自時厥後，桑樹連陰。王妃乃刻石為制，不令傷殺；蠶蛾飛盡，乃得治繭。敢有犯違，明神不祐。遂為先蠶建此伽藍。數株枯桑，云是本種之樹也。故今此國有蠶不殺，竊有取絲者，來年輒不宜蠶。
translation: Five or six li southeast of the royal city is the Ma-ża (麻射) Monastery, which was established by a former queen of this country. In ancient times, this country did not know of mulberry trees or silkworms. Hearing that they existed in the eastern country, the king sent an envoy to request them. At that time, the ruler of the eastern country kept them secret and would not bestow them, strictly ordering the frontier guards not to allow the seeds of mulberry or silkworms to pass out. The King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) then used humble words and low courtesies to request a marriage alliance with the eastern country. The ruler of that country, having a desire to extend his influence to distant lands, granted the request. The King of Gostana ordered an envoy to receive the bride and instructed him, saying: "Convey this message to the daughter of the eastern ruler: our country has never had silk, floss, or the seeds of mulberry and silkworms; she may bring them with her so that she may make her own garments." Upon hearing these words, the princess secretly sought the seeds and placed the silkworm eggs inside the padding of her hat. When she reached the frontier, the officials searched everywhere, but they did not dare to inspect the princess's hat. She then entered the country of Gostana and stopped at the former site of the Ma-ża Monastery. Only after the proper rites and ceremonies were prepared was she escorted into the palace, and the mulberry and silkworm seeds were left at this location. When the warmth of spring began, she planted the mulberry trees, and when the silkworm month arrived, she proceeded to gather and raise them. When they first arrived, she still fed them with various leaves, but from that time on, the mulberry trees grew in continuous shade. The queen then had a decree carved into stone, forbidding their injury or killing; only after the silkworm moths had flown away could the cocoons be processed. Anyone who dared to violate this would not be protected by the bright spirits. She then built this monastery for the first silkworms. Several withered mulberry trees are said to be the trees of the original stock. Therefore, in this country today, silkworms are not killed; if anyone stealthily takes their silk, the sericulture will surely be unsuccessful the following year.

t2087_text: 城東南百餘里有大河，西北流，國人利之，以用溉田。其後斷流，王深怪異。於是命駕問羅漢僧曰：「大河之水，國人取給，今忽斷流，其咎安在？為政有不平，德有不洽乎？不然，垂譴何重也？」羅漢曰：「大王治國，政化清和。河水斷流，龍所為耳。宜速祠求，當復昔利。」王因迴駕，祠祭河龍。忽有一女凌波而至，曰：「我夫早喪，主命無從；所以河水絕流，農人失利。王於國內選一貴臣，配我為夫，水流如昔。」王曰：「敬聞，任所欲耳。」龍遂目悅國之大臣。王既迴駕，謂群下曰：「大臣者，國之重鎮；農務者，人之命食。國失鎮則危，人絕食則死。危、死之事，何所宜行？」大臣越席，跪而對曰：「久已虛薄，謬當重任。常思報國，未遇其時，今而預選，敢塞深責。苟利萬姓，何吝一臣？臣者，國之佐；人者，國之本，願大王不再思也。幸為修福，建僧伽藍。」王允所求，功成不日。其臣又請早入龍宮，於是舉國僚庶，鼓樂飲餞。其臣乃衣素服，乘白馬，與王辭訣，敬謝國人。驅馬入河，履水不溺，濟乎中流，麾鞭畫水，水為中開，自茲沒矣。頃之，白馬浮出，負一栴檀大鼓，封一函書。其書大略曰：「大王不遺細微，謬參神選，願多營福，益國滋臣。以此大鼓，懸城東南，若有寇至，鼓先聲震。」河水遂流，至今利用。歲月浸遠，龍鼓久無。舊懸之處，今仍有鼓。
translation: More than a hundred li to the southeast of the city is a large river flowing northwest; the people of the country benefit from it, using it to irrigate their fields. Later, the flow ceased, and the king was deeply puzzled and alarmed. He then ordered his carriage and went to ask an Arhat (阿羅漢) monk, saying: "The water of the great river is what the people rely on for their needs; now that it has suddenly stopped flowing, where does the fault lie? Is my governance unjust, or is my virtue not in harmony? If not, why is this reprimand so severe?" The Arhat said: "Great King, your governance of the country is clear and harmonious. The river's flow has ceased because of the dragon. You should quickly offer sacrifices and pray, and the former benefits will return." The king then returned and offered sacrifices to the river dragon. Suddenly, a woman arrived, walking upon the waves, and said: "My husband died early, and I have no one to follow; this is why the river's flow has ceased and the farmers have lost their livelihood. If the King selects a noble minister from within the country to be my husband, the water will flow as before." The king said: "I respectfully hear your request; it is for you to choose whom you desire." The dragon then cast her eyes upon a high minister of the country. The king, having returned, said to his subordinates: "A high minister is the heavy pillar of the state; agricultural work is the life-sustaining food of the people. If the state loses its pillar, it is in danger; if the people are cut off from food, they die. Regarding these matters of danger and death, what is appropriate to do?" A minister stepped across his mat, knelt, and replied: "I have long been hollow and meager, yet I have mistakenly occupied a heavy responsibility. I have always thought of repaying the state, but have not yet encountered the time to do so. Now that I have been selected, how would I dare to refuse this profound duty? If it benefits the myriad people, why should I begrudge one minister?" "Ministers are the assistants of the state; the people are the foundation of the state. I hope the Great King will not hesitate further. I pray you cultivate merit and build a saṃghārāma." The King granted his request, and the work was completed in a few days. The minister then requested to enter the dragon palace early. Thereupon, the officials and commoners of the entire country played music and held a farewell feast. The minister donned plain white garments, mounted a white horse, bade farewell to the King, and respectfully thanked the people of the country. He urged his horse into the river, treading upon the water without sinking. Upon reaching midstream, he brandished his whip and traced a line on the water; the water parted in the middle, and he vanished from there. After a short while, the white horse floated to the surface, carrying a large sandalwood drum and a sealed letter. The letter said in brief: "Your Majesty did not overlook my humble status and allowed me to be mistakenly chosen by the divine; I hope you will perform many meritorious deeds to benefit the state and nourish your subjects. Take this large drum and hang it to the southeast of the city; if invaders approach, the drum will sound a warning first." The river water then flowed on, and it remains useful to this day. As the years and months have passed, the dragon drum has long been gone, but at the place where it was formerly hung, there is still a drum today.

t2087_text: 王城東三百餘里大荒澤中，數十頃地，絕無櫱草，其土赤黑。聞諸耆舊曰：敗軍之地也。昔者，東國軍師百萬西伐，此時瞿薩旦那王亦整齊戎馬數十萬眾，東禦強敵，至於此地，兩軍相遇，因即合戰。西兵失利，乘勝殘殺，虜其王，殺其將，誅戮士卒，無復孑遺。流血染地，其迹斯在。
translation: More than three hundred *li* to the east of the royal city, in the midst of a vast marsh, there is an area of several tens of *qing* where no vegetation grows and the soil is reddish-black. According to the elders, this is the place of a defeated army. In the past, an eastern country raised a million troops to invade the west. At that time, the King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) also prepared hundreds of thousands of soldiers to resist the powerful enemy from the east. When the two armies met at this place, they immediately engaged in battle. The western army suffered defeat, and the victors, taking advantage of their success, slaughtered them cruelly, capturing their king, killing their generals, and massacring the soldiers until not a single one remained. The blood shed stained the ground, and the traces are still visible there.

t2087_text: 戰地東行三十餘里，至嫓摩城。有彫檀立佛像，高二丈餘。甚多靈應，時燭光明。凡有疾病，隨其痛處，金薄帖像，即時痊復，虛心請願，多亦遂求。聞之土俗曰：此像，昔佛在世憍賞彌國鄔陀衍那王所作也。佛去世後，自彼凌空至此國北曷勞落迦城中。初到此，城人安樂富饒，深著邪見，而不珍敬，傳其自來，神而不貴。後有羅漢禮拜此像，國人驚駭，異其容服，馳以白王。王乃下令，宜以沙土坌此異人。時阿羅漢身蒙沙土，餬口絕糧。時有一人，心甚不忍，昔常恭敬尊禮此像，及見羅漢，密以饌之。羅漢將去，謂其人曰：「却後七日，當雨沙土，填滿此城，略無遺類。爾宜知之，早圖出計。猶其坌我，獲斯殃耳。」語已便去，忽然不見。其人入城，具告親故，或有聞者，莫不嗤笑。至第二日，大風忽發，吹去穢壤，雨雜寶滿衢路，人更罵所告者。此人心知必然，竊開孔道，出城外而穴之。第七日夜，宵分之後，雨沙土滿城中。其人從孔道出，東趣此國，止嫓摩城。其人纔至，其像亦來，即此供養，不敢遷移。聞諸先記曰：釋迦法盡，像入龍宮。今曷勞落迦城為大堆阜，諸國君王、異方豪右，多欲發掘，取其寶物。適至其側，猛風暴發，煙雲四合，道路迷失。
translation: Traveling more than thirty *li* east from the battlefield, one arrives at the city of Pimo (媲摩城). There is a standing sandalwood Buddha image over two *zhang* in height. It possesses many miraculous powers and at times emits a brilliant light. Whenever people have illnesses, they apply gold leaf to the part of the image corresponding to their own area of pain, and they are immediately cured. Those who make requests with a sincere heart often have their wishes fulfilled. I heard the local people say: "This image was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) of the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) when the Buddha was still in the world. After the Buddha passed away, it traveled through the air from there to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country." When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to erroneous views and did not treasure or respect it; although they heard it had come of its own accord, they considered it divine but did not value it. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the city were shocked, finding his appearance and clothing strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat was covered in sand and earth, his mouth blocked and his food supply cut off. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had long held this image in reverent worship, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man: "Seven days from now, it will rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they have brought this calamity upon themselves." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and soil, and it rained various treasures that filled the streets; the people then berated their informant even more. This man, knowing in his heart that it was inevitable, secretly opened a tunnel, exited the city, and took shelter outside. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also arrived; he immediately worshipped it there and dared not move it. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the dragon palace. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures, but as soon as they reach its vicinity, fierce winds suddenly arise, smoke and clouds gather from all sides, and the roads become lost.

t2087_text: 嫓摩川東入沙磧，行二百餘里，至尼攘城，周三四里，在大澤中。澤地熱濕，難以履涉；蘆草荒茂，無復途徑，唯趣城路，僅得通行。故往來者莫不由此城焉。而瞿薩旦那以為東境之關防也。
translation: Going east from the Bhīmā River (嫓摩川) into the sandy desert, one travels more than two hundred li and reaches the city of Niyang (尼攘城), which is three or four li in circuit and situated in the midst of a vast marsh. The marshy ground is hot and damp, making it difficult to walk or wade; the reeds and grasses are overgrown, and there are no longer any paths, so that only the road leading to the city is passable. Therefore, all those who come and go must pass through this city. The kingdom of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) considers it a strategic frontier post for its eastern border.

t2087_text: 從此東行入大流沙，沙則流漫，聚散隨風，人行無迹，遂多迷路。四遠茫茫，莫知所指，是以往來聚遺骸以記之。乏水草，多熱風；風起則人畜惛迷，因以成病。時聞歌嘯，或聞號哭。視聽之間，恍然不知所至，由此屢有喪亡，蓋鬼魅之所致也。行四百餘里，至都邏故國。國久空曠，城皆荒蕪。
translation: From here, traveling east, one enters the Great Quicksand (Taklamakan Desert), where the sands shift and flow, gathering and scattering with the wind. As human footsteps leave no trace, many people lose their way. The vast expanse stretches out in all directions with no landmarks to point the way, so travelers collect the bleached bones of the dead to serve as markers. There is a lack of water and vegetation, and there are many hot winds; when the wind rises, both people and animals become dazed and confused, thereby falling ill. At times, one hears singing and whistling, or hears wailing and crying. Amidst these sights and sounds, one becomes utterly bewildered and loses all sense of direction; this has led to frequent deaths, for it is surely the work of demons and malevolent spirits. Traveling more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Tu-huo-lo (都邏故國; *Tukhāra*). The country has long been empty and vast, and its cities are all desolate and overgrown.

t2087_text: 復此東北行千餘里，至納縛波故國，即樓蘭地也。推表山川，考採境壤，詳國俗之剛柔，繫水土之風氣，動靜無常，取捨不同，事難窮驗，非可仰說。隨所遊至，略書梗概，舉其聞見，記諸慕化。斯故日入已來，咸沐惠澤，風行所及，皆仰至德。混同天下，一之宇內，豈徒單車出使，通驛萬里者哉。
translation: Traveling northeast from here for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Navapa (納縛波故國), which is the land of Loulan (樓蘭). Regarding the mapping of mountains and rivers, the investigation of territories and soils, the detailing of the hard or soft nature of national customs, and the connection to the local climates and airs—since movement and stillness are impermanent and choices differ, these matters are difficult to verify exhaustively and cannot be explained merely by looking upward. Following where I have traveled, I have briefly written down the general outlines, citing what I have heard and seen, and recording those who admire the civilizing influence. Therefore, from the place where the sun sets, all are bathed in the grace and benevolence; wherever the wind of his influence reaches, all look up to his supreme virtue. He has unified the world and brought oneness to all within the universe; how could this be merely the act of a solitary envoy in a single carriage traveling ten thousand *li* through postal stations?

t2087_text: 東主乘勝，撫集亡國，遷都中地，方建城郭。憂其無土，恐難成功，宣告遠近，誰識地理。時有塗灰外道，負大瓠，盛滿水，而自進曰：「我知地理。」遂以其水屈曲遺流，周而復始，因即疾驅，忽而不見。依彼水迹，峙其基堵，遂得興功，即斯國治，今王所都於此城也。城非崇峻，攻擊難剋，自古已來，未能有勝。
translation: The Eastern Lord, taking advantage of his victory, comforted and gathered the people of the defeated state, moved the capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. He worried about the lack of soil and feared that the project might not succeed, so he made a proclamation far and near, asking who understood the geography of the land. At that time, there was an ash-smearing ascetic (pāśupata) carrying a large gourd filled with water who stepped forward and said, "I understand the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, circling back to the beginning, after which he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully undertaken; this became the seat of government, and the current king has established his capital in this city. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome in an attack; since ancient times, no one has ever been able to conquer it.
